This study addresses the high-dimensional parameter estimation challenge concerning eigenvalues and eigenfunctions within the Schrödinger equation, utilizing both convolutional neural networks (CNNs) and transformers. Through extensive cross-entropy loss minimization experiments conducted via the Adam optimizer, we analyzed the learned parameters using our previously developed ParamNetExam tool. These findings reveal that transformers rely heavily on first-layer parameters to resolve this estimation problem, whereas CNNs do not, a fact evidenced by the significant reduction in prediction error when transformer first-layer nets are removed. Additionally, we examined whether this dependence stems from insufficient training or a prior capability, employing the time-steps method to estimate the number of training iterations required. Finally, we evaluated the robustness of this first-layer reliance by introducing Gaussian noise to the input data and assessing performance on unseen data. The results indicate that first-layer parameters are essential for solving this estimation issue, even with unseen data, though they are less critical when Gaussian noise is present in the input data. Our analysis of this dependence relies on examining prediction errors, the distribution of input data, and the model's prior capabilities. The primary contribution of this research is the demonstration that prediction errors can serve as an effective metric for analyzing neural network behavior. Furthermore, our work underscores the necessity of conducting such analyses to deepen our understanding of how neural networks function, thereby guiding the design of more efficient architectures. The accompanying code is available at: https://github.com/ChenchenLi1997/DeepLearning.

The constraint on the entropy difference between equilibrium and non-equilibrium states in a constrained state system is examined. It is demonstrated that, at temperature $T$, the entropy $S$ of a non-equilibrium steady state constrained by $m$ operators does not exceed that of the equilibrium state by more than $mT$; that is, $S \leqslant S+mT$. The concept of a vertex woodland is introduced, and an algorithm is provided for calculating the area of such a woodland within a half-plane under a constraint of the form $f(x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_n)\leqslant 0$. Utilizing this algorithm, the stationary vertex woodland is shown to be localized within a half-plane under the same constraint condition. Furthermore, an estimate is derived for the difference in entropy between a quantum field and a free quantum field under an interaction Lagrangian local to a half-plane, where $S$ denotes the difference in Hamiltonians localized in the same region. Specifically, $S \leqslant mT$, with $m$ representing the difference in the numbers of fields and $T$ the temperature. Consequently, the difference in entropy between interacting and free quantum fields is bounded by $mT$, where $m$ is the count of interacting fields. Finally, the paper addresses the regional constraint on the stationary vertex woodland. This study examines a migration-transmission process where a source migrates to a sink via a series of intermediate steps, with each transition governed by a specific rate. The core objective is to derive an expression for the effective transmission rate. We begin by analyzing a three-step process to demonstrate how a simple approximation method fails to accurately represent the transmission dynamics. Subsequently, we derive an exact expression for the effective transmission rate for this basic scenario and demonstrate its applicability to more complex processes involving multiple migration pathways. Furthermore, we establish conditions under which the previously mentioned approximate expression yields an accurate transmission rate. Finally, we illustrate how the exact transmission rate formula can be adapted to model various biological systems, including gene flow between populations, neuronal migration, and cellular movement. These findings are pertinent to diverse fields such as genetics, neuronal biology, cellular biology, epidemiology, and social science modeling. A detailed tutorial on utilizing the package is available at https://neerajkumar2000.github.io/MigrationTransmissionProcesses/. We anticipate that these results and tools will facilitate the modeling of migration and transmission processes in various disciplines. This study verifies a sequence of resonances identified in the Kepler-128 system, originally proposed by Li et al. (2018) to explain the observed period ratios of its planets. While the previously favored model suggested a 3:2 resonant chain, we demonstrate that this interpretation is incorrect. Instead, the data are best explained by a 5:3 resonant chain, which more accurately accounts for the period ratios. We also confirm that the 3:2 resonances previously attributed to the system actually describe the resonances of K2-138 b and c. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the circular model used by Li et al. (2018) is inferior to an eccentric model for explaining the period ratios of K2-128. Finally, we highlight that the superior eccentric model reveals a complex web of resonances within the system, including a 2:1 resonant pair (c and d) and a 3:1 resonant chain (b, c, and d). These findings are derived from a new fit to the data that utilizes Li et al. (2018)'s period ratios and eccentricities to constrain their migration model. We conclude that the migration model favored by Li et al. (2018) is inferior to an alternative model that assumes planets migrate adiabatically and conserve their resonances. This alternative model, which is also preferred by Li et al. (2018), predicts that planets c and d will eventually merge, while planet b will escape the system. We discuss the implications of these predictions for the system's future evolution. Additionally, we examine the implications of these findings for the circular migration model, which Li et al. (2018) also considered. We find that the circular model fails to explain the observed period ratios of K2-128 and is therefore inferior to the eccentric migration model. We conclude that the circular migration model is unlikely to be the correct explanation for the formation and evolution of the K2-128 system. This paper investigates the tensor structure of the authentic Whittaker functor and the reciprocity between cellular Schur–Weyl duality and affine quantum group action within the category of weight modules with restricted weights. The affine quantum group considered here is a reduced quotient of the Drinfeld double of the Drinfeld–Jimbo type for the quantum affine algebra of type $A_{1,1}$. By analyzing the cellular modules over the affine Hecke algebra of type $A$ and their tensor products, we derive the matrix elements of the affine quantum group acting on these modules. This approach offers a distinct alternative to the methodology presented in [L. Li, J. Zhang, Affine Schur–Weyl duality and affine quantum group actions, arXiv:2009.07770]. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the cellular central characters associated with simple cellular modules correspond to Drinfeld polynomials of type $A$, which are polynomials with roots in $\mathbb{N}$. This correspondence provides a concrete means to identify tilting modules. Additionally, we establish that the quantum affine group action on type $A$ weight modules with restricted weights is integrable. Our methodology also enables the extension of our results to the general type $A_n$ setting. Finally, we outline a strategy to address several open questions by adapting our approach to other Lie types. In this context, we compute the matrix elements of the quantum group acting on cellular modules over affine Hecke algebras of general type $A$. These elements are expressed as rational functions involving Drinfeld polynomials of general type $A$, along with shifted affine Dynkin diagram automorphisms. The structure of these rational functions relies on the affine Weyl group action on the affine root system of type $A$. The SiD detector design features a sampling electromagnetic calorimeter built from silicon-wrapped lead glass bricks arranged in a honeycomb layout. This configuration enables fine granularity and precise position measurements, allowing each brick to function as a standalone readout unit. The SiD calorimeter design was selected for the International Linear Collider (ILC) due to its compatibility with the ILC's slow-growing background rate and the ability to measure dE/dx. To demonstrate the adaptability of this concept, the design was modified to create two distinct silicon calorimeters: the SiIC and the SiSC. The SiIC configuration employs a Si3N4-wrapped ceramic calorimeter paired with Si3N4 sensors, whereas the SiSC design utilizes a Si3N4 wrapped calorimeter alongside Si sensors. The SiSC configuration is specifically tailored for the Super Proton Proton Collider (SPPC), which serves as the secondary collider option for the Chinese Future Circular Collider. Both SiIC and SiSC designs maintain the core SiD philosophy of fine granularity and individual brick measurement capabilities. The paper outlines the design philosophies behind these Si-calorimeter options, detailing the specific modifications applied to the SiIC and SiSC configurations. Additionally, the performance of both designs was evaluated through simulations, with the SiSC layout achieving the superior energy resolution. The study also addresses the detector materials inventory and production timelines for these Si-calorimeter concepts. Ultimately, the SiIC design is deemed suitable for the Future Circular Collider (FCC-eh), while the SiSC design is recommended for the Chinese Circular Collider (CCPPC). Furthermore, the SiSC configuration is identified as a viable alternative for the LHeC, a high-luminosity polarized deep-inelastic scattering facility integrated into the Large Hadron Collider. The SiSC's ability to achieve superior energy resolution stems from its lower material budget, which results in fewer interactions between the signal and the detector material. This advantage is achieved through the use of Si sensors and Si3N4 dielectric structures, which offer higher active sensor fill factors and reduced material inventory compared to traditional Si designs. The Si3N4 dielectric's high radiation tolerance and robustness against particle showers are key enablers for these innovative Si-calorimeter concepts. Ultimately, the SiIC and SiSC designs offer a cost-effective and material-efficient solution for next-generation collider calorimeters. We introduce a method for detecting crystalline-ice regions within non-crystalline (amorphous) ices by utilizing the recently developed pair distribution function (PDF) analysis technique. This approach is demonstrated using amorphous water ice generated in cometary nuclei and on spacecraft surfaces. Our findings indicate that the presence of crystalline-ice areas in these amorphous ices is influenced by the energy levels and types of impacts that formed them. Furthermore, the study successfully identifies low-temperature amorphous water ice (LTA) and high-temperature amorphous water ice (HTA) in ultrahigh vacuum-generated amorphous water ice samples. These results demonstrate that the proposed method is effective for detecting crystalline-ice regions in non-crystalline ices, offering the advantage of requiring no prior knowledge of the sample's formation history. Consequently, this technique is applicable to analyzing amorphous ices produced through various formation processes, including thermal treatments. These discoveries are anticipated to enhance our understanding of the amorphous-crystalline phase transitions of water ice on comets and on spacecraft surfaces. Additionally, the same methodology can be extended to investigate crystalline regions in amorphous regions of other volatiles and ices on comets and spacecraft surfaces. This paper is part of a series; the companion paper (Kajitani et al., 2019b) will discuss the implications of these results for amorphous and crystalline water ice on comets and spacecraft surfaces. Keywords: comets: nuclei; comets: nuclei; spacecraft; spacecraft; spacecraft; spacecraft.

This study presents atomically resolved images of the surface structures for bulk silicon, gold, and graphite, alongside analysis of the square root of the tunneling current ($I^{1/2}$) to evaluate the local density of states (LDOS) at the Fermi level ($E_F$). The experiments were conducted at 4.2 K using a new Scanning Tunneling Microscope (STM) featuring a novel tip fabrication method. The research utilized both constant voltage and constant current spectroscopy modes. For silicon, topographic scans revealed atomic corrugations, while $I^{1/2}$ measurements indicated a constant LDOS. Gold surfaces displayed atomic corrugations with a lattice constant of 0.24 nm; the $I^{1/2}$ data showed a constant LDOS, confirming that the Fermi level lies within the d-band. Graphite's topographic scan revealed hexagonal atomic corrugations with a lattice constant of 0.26 nm, and $I^{1/2}$ analysis demonstrated a constant LDOS, consistent with the material's metallic nature. The paper concludes by summarizing the experimental findings. The interaction between the solar wind and Earth's magnetic field generates ultra-low frequency (ULF) waves within the magnetosphere. These waves induce fluctuations in Earth's magnetic field, which can be detected by ground-based magnetometers. This phenomenon creates a unique scenario where the solar wind is "heard" through its magnetic interactions. However, because magnetometer data consist merely of time-series recordings, the solar wind's spectrum lacks visual context, making it impossible to identify structures or orient the signal in space. Consequently, this study aims to develop methods for rendering ULF spectra visually and audibly in three dimensions to facilitate navigation. We demonstrate various strategies for navigating ULF spectra using both synthetic and actual magnetometer data, with a specific focus on methods applicable to ground-to-ground cross-spectral analysis. This research is driven by the need to detect and interpret magnetospheric substorms and to assess ground-based power grid resilience against geomagnetic storms. Our findings indicate that visual and auditory representations of magnetometer data offer valuable insights into the ULF spectrum's characteristics and provide intuitive navigation of magnetic fluctuations in 3D space. Furthermore, we show that this approach is particularly effective for rapidly identifying ULF wave sources and their driving mechanisms. We conclude that this methodology is essential for enhancing the monitoring of the Sun-Earth system and for improving the early warning capabilities of power grids against geomagnetic storms. Natural Language Queries form a natural and recall-driven approach for representing textual data, yet they have not been fully explored. This paper introduces a framework for text information representation that leverages NLQs. Our method prioritizes human-centric features, including TLXQs (Natural Language Queries with missing information), examples, and semantics. We illustrate the application of this framework through a text-based Question Answering system. Our findings indicate that TLXQs and TLExs serve as effective means for text representation, while TLQs and semantics provide valuable context for retrieval and ranking, respectively. Additionally, the framework is applied within the context of knowledge graphs. Graph patterns, which are minor-subgraph queries for labeled graphs, have become increasingly significant due to their widespread use in knowledge representation and integration. The GP 2 format stands out as a highly expressive and widely adopted graph pattern format. However, the existing theoretical analysis of GP 2 is limited to a major-step logic, as the interaction between graph patterns and automata in GP 2 introduces a level of complexity that major-step semantics struggle to capture. To address this, we propose a minor-step operational semantics for GP 2. We demonstrate that this new semantics is equivalent to the existing major-step semantics and that the resulting graph pattern evaluation machine operates in polynomial time. Furthermore, we prove that the polynomial-time decidability for query equivalence between two GP 2 queries established by Huang et al. (PODS 2018) remains valid under our proposed semantics. Finally, we confirm the consistency of our work by integrating it into KGon, a graph pattern matching system. Keywords: graph pattern, operational semantics, query equivalence, consistency.

Our results indicate that the spectral index and thermal flux of the disk align with the MHD disk breeze model, while the derived temperature is consistent with the model's predictions. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the NGVTO is capable of resolving the TW Hydrae disk with an angular clarity of approximately 10 arcseconds, yielding a spectral resolution of roughly 1 MHz. This level of detail will enable the investigation of the disk's spatial structure and dynamics. We conclude that the NGVTO is ideally suited to test the MHD disk breeze model for TW Hydrae and to explore the potential for detecting similar emission from other young stars. This study aims to guide NGVTO observations of TW Hydrae and other young stellar objects. Additionally, we provide a comprehensive overview of the photoevaporation model, which offers an alternative explanation for the radio emission from TW Hydrae. Finally, we discuss the future scientific potential of the NGVTO. Our analysis confirms that the NGVTO is essential for advancing our understanding of the origins of planetary systems. Multicast communication is essential for delivering services to multiple users, particularly in ultra-dense millimeter-wave (mmWave) networks. However, traditional hybrid automatic repeat request (ARQ) mechanisms in wireless systems often result in retransmitting the same data multiple times, leading to significant throughput degradation. To address this, we propose a multi-group multi-user broadcasting framework that employs hybrid error correction coding (ECC) combined with multi-user scheduling. This approach first applies hybrid ECC to each group of users, followed by a joint optimization process that simultaneously selects a multi-user scheduling scheme and a retransmission group selection scheme. The objective is to maximize the overall network throughput while adhering to specific constraints. Simulation results demonstrate that the proposed method achieves substantial throughput improvements compared to conventional multi-user scheduling approaches. Furthermore, the hybrid ECC strategy outperforms traditional ARQ-based hybrid ECC methods in terms of throughput. Additionally, the computational complexity of the proposed scheme remains low, making it highly suitable for mmWave broadcasting services. Finally, we illustrate how to optimize multicast services for mobile video streaming in mmWave networks using the proposed method. To achieve this, we suggest a video quality adaptation scheme that adjusts the encoding parameters of hybrid ECC based on real-time channel conditions. This ensures that users receive video streams at appropriate qualities, thereby maximizing network throughput. Simulation outcomes confirm that this optimization scheme effectively delivers high-quality video services to mobile users. Ultimately, the proposed solution offers a viable multicast service framework for mmWave networks, capable of enhancing throughput by leveraging hybrid ECC and multi-user scheduling. Consequently, it holds promise for mobile video broadcasting and other similar applications. To our knowledge, this is the first study to investigate multi-group multi-user broadcasting in mmWave networks through the lens of hybrid ECC and multi-user scheduling. Our findings provide a novel perspective on optimizing wireless multi-casting services. Additionally, the proposed method is well-suited for future 5G mobile video broadcasting, which will increasingly utilize mmWave frequencies. We also introduce a new concept for mmWave mobile video broadcasting, which has not been explored in existing literature. The corresponding author is Dr. Wei Chen. Keywords: mmWave networks, multi-group multi-user scheduling, hybrid error correction coding, mobile video broadcasting.

This paper demonstrates that for any natural number $n$, there exists a group $G_n$ with $n$-exponential residual finiteness expansion that is also residually finite $p$-groups for a prime $p$ distinct from that of $G_n$. Additionally, for each $n$, we construct a group $H_n$ possessing exponential residual finiteness expansion, where $H_n$ is both residually finite and metabelian. Finally, we establish that if a group $G$ has exponential growth and its sequence of subgroup indices grows faster than linearly, then $G$ necessarily exhibits exponential residual finiteness expansion. Furthermore, if the subgroup indices grow faster than $n!$ for some $n$, then $G$ possesses $n$-exponential residual finiteness expansion. We also provide a partial classification of groups with superlinear subgroup index growth. Finally, we prove that no group $G$ with exponential growth can have subgroups of index $f(n)$ growing faster than $(n+1)!$ for any $n \geq 2$, nor can it exhibit $n$-exponential residual finiteness expansion. Finally, we show that for each $n$, there exists a metabelian group $M_n$ with a subgroup of index $n!$ that cannot be a small-cancellation group. This study investigates the stability of a damped extended Euler-Bernoulli beam defined on a star-shaped graph. The system couples two identical beams with rotational inertia at their joined center via an elastic torsional damper. Boundary conditions are configured such that the beams' ends are fixed at the origin, and theendom of each beam points along the y-axis. By employing extended state variables, the beam is modeled by a coupled system of damped wave equations featuring rotational inertia terms and memory terms within the boundary conditions. This framework results in an infinite-dimensional dynamical system governed by a non-self-adjoint operator, generating a $C_0$-semigroup on a suitable Hilbert space. Although the spectrum of this operator is discrete, its accumulation point is located on the imaginary axis. The primary contribution of this work is demonstrating the asymptotic stability of the semigroup and establishing an algebraic rate of decay for the energy within a neighborhood of the origin. These results rely on a detailed analysis of the eigenvalues and eigenfunctions of the generator, specifically their asymptotic expansions and the separation of large eigenvalues from the imaginary axis. Furthermore, logarithmic convexity of the energy is proven only locally around the origin, as global validity fails due to the non-self-adjoint nature of the operator. Finally, the paper confirms exponential stability within the same local region, while the asymptotic stability exhibits a polynomial rate of decay in energy. Numerical computations were utilized to identify a specific boundary resonance and to verify the validity of the derived asymptotic formulas. The methodology employed is broadly applicable to systems of coupled damped hyperbolic partial differential equations with memory terms and rotational inertia. Additionally, the techniques used to estimate the eigenvalues and eigenfunctions can be adapted to other coupled hyperbolic systems, including those involving Timoshenko and Kirchhoff beam models. The approach is also pertinent to the study of boundary layer phenomena in the eigenfunctions of such systems. The extension to graphs with more than five vertices requires only minor adjustments. The paper concludes with an outline of potential future research directions. This model was originally proposed by the authors in their 2019 work. This current version incorporates significant refinements, particularly regarding the asymptotic behavior of eigenvalues and eigenfunctions, alongside a substantially expanded set of numerical computations. The initial draft was prepared in 2019, and the final publication is scheduled for release in 2023. The abundance ratios of heavy elements in the universe are influenced by the weights assigned to nuclear properties, which vary depending on the specific astrophysical context. However, the vastness of potential astrophysical scenarios necessitates weights that are both precise and reliable. We introduce a neural network model designed to rapidly calculate nuclear weights. By training the model on Monte Carlo simulations of the nuclear statistical equilibrium (SSE) across a diverse range of astrophysical conditions, we achieve high precision. Our study utilizes a dataset of 1,000 nuclear properties derived from 1,000 SSE scenarios, employing various electron fractions and nuclear masses to train the network. We demonstrate that the model's forecasted weights align with those from traditional SSE calculations, with relative errors remaining below 0.1% for most elements. Furthermore, we apply these weights to analyze the production of $r$-process elements, revealing that their abundance patterns are governed by nuclear properties spanning a broad spectrum. This underscores the necessity of comprehensive nuclear data, which can be efficiently obtained using the neural network model. Additionally, the model is publicly accessible via an online interface, offering an efficient platform for nuclear astrophysics research. We have engineered a microwave vacuum probe station featuring a 50 $\mu$m diameter coaxial transmission line, capable of measuring dielectric dissipation factors with 100 ppb resolution. Utilizing this station, we conducted dielectric loss assessments on high-purity synthetic sapphire specimens at cryogenic temperatures. The experimental results demonstrate an accuracy superior to that of the nominal dielectric loss tangent specifications provided by the manufacturer. Furthermore, our measurements identified an excess loss mechanism attributable to the transmission line, which exhibits temperature-dependent conductivity consistent with high-purity copper. This line demonstrates a quality factor (Q-factor) of 1.5 parts per billion, representing the highest values recorded to date for copper transmission lines at low temperatures. Consequently, the microwave vacuum probe station is ideally suited for evaluating ultra-high-purity dielectrics, such as those required for quantum applications. Additionally, we analyzed the impact of sapphire surface treatments on dielectric loss, revealing that polishing the surface reduces losses by up to 50%. These findings underscore the critical necessity of achieving high surface quality to minimize dielectric losses in quantum technologies. Ultimately, our research establishes a new sensitivity benchmark for microwave dielectric dissipation measurements. By combining this sensitivity with a broad temperature measurement range, our work holds significant promise for advancing the development of high-performance quantum devices. Future studies will focus on characterizing additional dielectric materials to further support quantum technology advancement. We introduce an uncommon phenomenon termed "Optical Pull," wherein a dielectric particle is drawn toward an optical field despite experiencing a net repulsive force. This effect manifests in two distinct regimes: (i) a particle situated outside a dielectric medium can be pulled by a standing wave field if its polarizability is predominantly dielectric, whereas a metal sphere within the same medium can be repuled; and (ii) a standing wave field can pull a metal sphere located within a dielectric medium. We provide an analytical formulation to elucidate the mechanisms behind this phenomenon and present numerical simulations to validate our findings. Furthermore, we explore potential applications of "Optical Pull" in manipulating particles within dielectric media and in reducing the pull-pinch instability encountered in optical trapping of dielectric objects immersed in liquids. Our proposed method offers a novel approach to controlling the transport of particles using light. Additionally, we examine the critical role of the refractive index contrast between the particle and the surrounding medium in enabling "Optical Pull." This capability to attract particles expands the scope of particle manipulation and paves the way for new applications in optical trapping and transport. Specifically, "Optical Pull" may facilitate particle manipulation in biological media, particle transport within optical waveguides, and the fabrication of photonic crystals. Finally, we anticipate that "Optical Pull" will find extensive utilization across various fields of physics.

This study addresses a two-stage stochastic programming model incorporating binary decision variables to enhance system resilience against disruptions. In the initial stage, fixed and variable investments are chosen to fortify the network against potential attacks. The network operator assumes a defensive role by inferring partial information about the adversary's strategy from observable consequences, utilizing this knowledge to make operational decisions that minimize losses in the second stage. The resulting min-max optimization problem is computationally difficult due to its nested structure and the non-convexity introduced by variable adversarial and operational actions. We introduce a dual-based heuristic that leverages dual cuts to approximate the dual of a linearization of this nested problem. Computational results on real-world power network cases demonstrate that the proposed approach effectively balances the trade-off between security and cost, while also highlighting the value of defensive investments and intelligence gained from monitoring. Furthermore, numerical experiments reveal that the dual-based heuristic achieves near-optimality within a reasonable computational timeframe. Finally, a case study on the Spanish power grid illustrates the benefits of the methodology for both defensive and adversarial perspectives. The availability of high-quality, relevant, and reliable data is fundamental to the success of data-driven tasks. However, real-world data is frequently heterogeneous, multi-modal, multi-dimensional, and fragmented across various sources. This paper introduces H4M, a large-scale dataset designed for socioeconomic analysis in Beijing. The H4M Multi-Modal Multi-View Multi-Distributional Data Generation System (H4M MMVDMG) is a novel framework that transforms heterogeneous, multi-modal, and multi-view data into diverse, multi-distributional datasets. By employing a multi-modal graph attention network, H4M MMVDMG identifies the optimal fusion strategy for input modalities, thereby enhancing the accuracy of the generated data. Experimental results demonstrate the model's ability to improve the quality and diversity of the data it produces. The H4M dataset is freely accessible at https://github.com/Chenchenchenchen/H4M-Dataset. We anticipate this resource will significantly advance research in the fields of data generation and socioeconomic analysis. Furthermore, we aim to foster a collaborative community dedicated to multi-modal data generation, multi-view data fusion, and their applications within socioeconomic analysis. This study underscores the critical role of high-quality data in data-driven endeavors and provides a new perspective on multi-modal data generation. Additionally, it offers a fresh approach to addressing challenges in socio-economic analysis, particularly concerning data quality and availability. Template-driven methods are valuable for exploring and analyzing vast datasets, yet humans often struggle to comprehend them because they lack visual elements. To address this limitation, this paper introduces the concept of "visual template-driven investigation," which leverages the extensive experience humans possess with template-based data exploration to maintain both interpretability and scalability. The study outlines the rationale behind this approach and presents two proposed techniques: template space navigation and multi-level visual template reasoning. Finally, the paper examines the advantages of visual template-driven investigation through the lens of human cognitive processes. Additionally, two demo applications are provided to illustrate how visual templates can enhance investigation outcomes. Finally, potential applications and future research directions are discussed. Keywords: Visual Analytics, Exploration, Investigation, Templates, Reasoning.

Graph Neural Architectures (GNNs) have become a standard approach for creating intelligent software systems capable of handling complex, networked data. While these models are highly effective, they are also resource-intensive, often requiring substantial computational power and time for training. Consequently, researchers are increasingly exploring transfer learning to apply knowledge gained from graph tasks to new domains. This study investigates the characteristics of GNNs that facilitate knowledge transfer, examining how architectural design choices influence the ability to reuse information across different datasets. The research analyzes the impact of network depth, graph structures, and node features on transfer learning outcomes, with a specific focus on graph classification tasks within the software engineering domain. By employing systematic ablation studies, the study quantifies and compares the effects of these factors, ultimately offering practical guidelines for designing GNNs that optimize performance in such scenarios. The findings aim to assist practitioners in optimizing GNN designs for efficient transfer learning applications. The source code is accessible at: https://github.com/DeepSecLab/GraphTransEval.

Recommendation systems are a critical component of information retrieval services on the web. This paper introduces a suggestion system that utilizes a dual-featured distribution model, incorporating both user behavior and item attributes. We evaluated our system against two baseline approaches, and the results indicate that both the efficiency and effectiveness of our proposed method surpass those of the comparators. The findings demonstrate that integrating more comprehensive information through the dual-feature distribution model yields superior performance. The implementation details can be accessed at: https://github.

We introduce a novel and streamlined proof for a set disjointness problem, addressing queries of the form: "Do these two sets share any common elements?" This problem is significant in computer science, particularly within data stream algorithms. Given two sets, $A$ and $B$, an algorithm receives a data stream over a universe of size $u$ where each element appears at most once; after processing $n$ such elements, the algorithm must determine if disjointness holds. In our model, the algorithm is constrained by a memory limit of $n^\epsilon u^{1-\epsilon}$ bits, where $\epsilon > 0$ is a constant. We demonstrate that if $\epsilon > 1/3$, the problem remains trivial to solve. This finding yields a new result: a data stream algorithm capable of identifying duplicates in a data stream of size $n$ over a universe of size $u$ using only $n^{1/3}u^{2/3}$ bits of memory. Our proof is conceptually simpler than the previously best-known algorithm for this task. Furthermore, our approach extends the applicability of the previously best-known duplicate detection algorithm, which was limited to prime universes, to arbitrary universes. Our primary application lies in data stream algorithms; specifically, we establish that if $\epsilon > 1/3$, the dense disjointness problem becomes easy, thereby enabling the identification of duplicates in data streams with superior memory efficiency. Our current best application achieves this using $n^{1/3}u^{2/3}$ bits of memory. Additionally, our method offers advantages in both computational time and memory usage compared to the prior best application. This study investigates the momentum dependence of the static spin-momentum susceptibility within the paramagnetic phase of the classical 3D Heisenberg magnet. It demonstrates that this dependence is non-analytic at the zero-momentum limit, a property that is essential for determining the momentum scaling function and the associated critical exponents in the critical region. The findings are derived using the high-temperature (H-T) series expansion method. Specifically, the non-analytic nature of the susceptibility at zero momentum is quantified by the relation $\chi_{S}(k)\sim T^{-\gamma_{S}}f_{S}(k^{2}t)^{0.60\pm0.01}$, where the error margins represent the 1$\sigma$ uncertainties in the calculated coefficients. Furthermore, the critical exponents $\gamma_{S}$ and $\nu$ are identified as 1.22$\pm$0.02 and 0.70$\pm$0.01, respectively. These results align with the high-precision estimates provided by the recently developed Wilmott-Feeney-Burnell (WFB) series expansion method. The paper also examines the momentum dependence of the magnetic field amplitude $B$ and the correlation length $\xi$, yielding the critical exponents $\gamma_{B}$, $\gamma_{\xi}$, and $R$ with values of 1.22$\pm$0.02, 1.22$\pm$0.02, and 0.69$\pm$0.01, respectively. Additionally, the critical amplitude $C$ is defined by the relation $R=(2\gamma_{B}+2-\gamma_{\xi})/\gamma_{\xi}$, resulting in a value of 0.99$\pm$0.02. These outcomes are consistent with recent WFB calculations and other reliable estimates found in the literature. Finally, the study confirms that the momentum scaling function $f_{B}(x)$ for the magnetic field amplitude $B$ possesses a non-monotonic structure. Collectively, the derived critical exponents and the non-analytic momentum dependence of the static spin-momentum susceptibility at the zero-momentum limit are essential for constructing the Hamiltonian of the classical 3D Heisenberg magnet. We introduce a multi-diffraction architecture intended for on-chip atomic physics applications. In this setup, an input laser beam is diffracted into multiple beams, each resonantly exciting a trapped single atom to generate an array of atomic wave packets. The optical lattice diffracting the atomic probability distribution is engineered to facilitate coherent manipulation and interference of the atomic states. One specific excitation beam is optimized for the capture of a cold atom, while the multi-atom system is designed to support a full quantum non-demolition measurement cycle. This multi-diffraction design is applicable to various quantum information processing tasks and can be readily implemented using a compact chip. This study investigates the impact of interactions on both linear and nonlinear Hall conductivities within a two-dimensional topological system characterized by broken time-reversal symmetry and spatial inversion. The nonlinear Hall conductivity arises from the anomalous velocity of electrons in real space, driven by a gradient in their dynamical effective mass. Both linear and nonlinear Hall conductivities exhibit diffusive behavior as interactions increase, with their interaction-dependent components scaling linearly with the interaction strength. Furthermore, the relationship between chaos and the nonlinear Hall conductivity is explored through Lyapunov exponents and Krylov-Bogoliubov vectors. Based on these findings, we conclude that interaction-induced contributions to the nonlinear Hall conductivity can be interpreted as a quantum analog to the classical anomalous current resulting from anomalous velocity. Finally, we propose a feasible experimental scheme to detect the nonlinear Hall conductivity in the quantum regime, where this quantum contribution remains significant despite the presence of interactions. Our results demonstrate that interacting effects on nonlinear Hall conductivity are substantial and potentially observable experimentally. Additionally, we show that nonlinear Hall conductivity can be modulated by inducing chaos, offering a viable method to experimentally observe this phenomenon. These contributions to nonlinear Hall conductivity are expected to be experimentally accessible in topological materials where time-reversal symmetry is broken. Specifically, we suggest that high-mobility topological insulators, such as HgTe quantum wells, could be utilized to detect these effects. The proposed proposal is compatible with existing experimental techniques, including nonlinear magneto-transport measurements and gate voltage tuning. We anticipate that these results will stimulate further research into interacting effects within Hall conductivity. Specifically, we propose that nonlinear Hall conductivity measurements can serve as a viable alternative to anomalous Hall effect measurements for detecting many-body localization in quantum systems, thereby expanding the scope of localization research beyond conventional methods. This approach is expected to facilitate the study of many-body localization in high-mobility topological materials, such as HgTe quantum wells. Our findings may also inspire novel proposals for observing interacting effects in Hall conductivity across a broader range of physical systems. For instance, we suggest that these effects could be investigated in both two-dimensional and three-dimensional topological materials, as well as in various quantum simulation platforms, including cold atom systems and superconducting qubit circuits. This could lead to the discovery of interacting effects in various quantum systems where semiclassical effects are expected. Overall, our results are expected to expand the field of Hall conductivity research and deepen our understanding of interacting electron systems. The COVID-19 pandemic has exposed the critical role of language enhancement in disseminating vital, accurate information to the public. This process begins with the immediate transcription of spoken content into text, which then undergoes further enhancement. This article details our experience producing an immediate transcription for a case study involving two respiratory doctors discussing patient breathing mechanics during the pandemic. The resulting transcript was subsequently enhanced to improve readability and searchability, thereby facilitating better public understanding of the science behind the virus. We believe this workflow represents a significant contribution to the community, and we hope our efforts inspire others to engage in similar activities. The paper is structured into two sections: the first provides a technical overview of the methods used, while the second outlines the enhancement pipeline and presents the transcript. We believe the findings in this report will be a valuable resource for the community. The paper is available at: https://arxiv.org/pdf/2007.01009.pdf. The code can be found at: https://github.com/rajkumar1997/immediate-transcription-for-dynamic-enhancement. The pre-enhanced transcript is available at: https://github.com/rajkumar1997/immediate-transcription-for-dual-patient-breathing-during-the-covid-19-outbreak. The post-enhanced transcript is accessible at: https://github.com/rajkumar1997/immediate-transcription-for-dual-patient-breathing-during-the-covid-19-outbreak/tree/main/data/enhanced_transcript.json. Our work demonstrates how spoken content can be efficiently converted into a highly enhanced state, significantly improving the content's value. We believe this approach will greatly benefit the community. The paper's title is: Immediate Transcription for Dynamic Enhancement: A Guide with a Case Study on Dual-Patient Breathing During the COVID-19 Outbreak.

Let $P_{\lambda}(z)=z^4-\lambda$ define a quadratic bicritical family, and let $f_n$ represent the $n$-th iterate of the map $f$. The set of escape times $E_{n,\lambda}$ for $f_n$ under a specific parameter $\lambda$ forms a quasi-circular set. We investigate the groups of quasi-conformal homeomorphisms that map $E_{n,\lambda}$ to itself; these are termed the platform groups for $f_n$. This study aims to classify the platform groups associated with quadratic bicritical dynamical systems. Furthermore, we establish an upper bound for the platform groups of $f_n$ and characterize the parameters $\lambda$ for which this upper bound is achieved. The methods employed in this work are also applicable to other bicritical rational functions. Our findings were presented at the 2021 Dynamical Systems Conference in Buenos Aires. Additionally, we offer a novel perspective on platform groups through the lens of circle maps. This article serves as a foundation for future research into platform groups, particularly within the context of quadratic bicritical rational functions. Our work provides an explicit, albeit large, generating set for these groups. Finally, we demonstrate that, in general, platform groups cannot be fully characterized by their elements outside the escape time sets. The techniques utilized here are also relevant to understanding spinners. We conclude by formulating an open problem regarding platform groups and their relationship to Julia sets. Our results extend to any bicritical rational function $R$, where the post-critical set $P(R)$ consists of critical points and their forward orbits. For such functions, the platform groups are defined as the subgroups of $\text{Homeo}^+(S^1)$ generated by all degree-$d$ circle maps that map $P(R)$ to itself. The paper includes illustrative examples and illustrations of these groups. Our approach extends to studying spinners, which are constructed from finite collections of disjoint quasi-circles. We also examine the platform groups of the Mandelbar set and present an open problem concerning this topic. The concepts herein can be generalized to broader contexts, such as multi-critical polynomials and polynomials with connected Julia sets. This work serves as a basis for future research into platform groups. The term "platform groups" was suggested by Dr. Juan L. H\'{a}nse. We extend our gratitude to Dr. H\'{a}nse for his insightful discussions and valuable suggestions.

The nanoscale properties of transition metal dichalcogenides (TMDs) are governed by interlayer coupling, which induces unique two-dimensional characteristics. This study employs density functional theory (DFT) and the GW approximation to analyze the electronic structures of MoX₂ and WX₂ (where X = S, Se, Te) as bulk materials and as free-standing monolayers, bilayers, and few-layer configurations. The findings indicate that the ionization potential varies with the number of layers, showing reduced distance dependence in Te-based compounds. Conversely, work function and electron affinity exhibit strong dependence on layer count in monolayer-to-trilayer systems but become nearly constant for structures containing four or more layers. These results are attributed to the reduction of interlayer coupling in electron-rich TMDs, which occurs as the layer count increases. These observations provide a basis for understanding charge transfer mechanisms in TMDs and offer insights into their potential applications in nanoelectronics. Additionally, the study confirms that GW calculations yield more accurate electronic structures for TMDs than the Perdew-Burke-Koch (PBK) functional. Universal supervised learning can be modeled as the transfer of modifications via $\delta$-lenses, alongside other mechanisms such as bidirectional data portability between formats and the use of external resources like knowledge bases. As artificial intelligence evolves, its components increasingly exhibit a modular structure, where $\delta$-lenses serve to model the interfaces between these modules. This paper proposes a unified formalism that simultaneously models both the supervisory learning processes and the modular architecture of learning systems. The framework is grounded in established formalisms for modification transmission and modularity, specifically $\delta$-categories and $\delta$-graphs. We demonstrate that the universal supervised learning framework itself constitutes a $\delta$-category. Furthermore, we introduce a new $\delta$-graph that captures the modularity of artificial intelligence, incorporating examples of various $\delta$-lenses that define its interfaces. This research represents the initial step toward a more comprehensive study of modularity within supervised learning systems. Additionally, the framework offers broader applications, including a unified model for the modularity of knowledge-based systems and a method for describing data interoperability. Finally, we outline potential future directions for applying this approach to the modularity of artificial intelligence. The paper includes several new examples of $\delta$-lenses that define the interfaces of an AI system, modeled within this framework. These include $\delta$-lenses for the modularity of reinforcement learning, a recurrent neural network, transfer learning, and data interoperability involving knowledge bases. The proposed methodology can also be extended to model other learning types, such as unsupervised learning. Ultimately, this work establishes a foundation for a unified theory of modularity in learning systems, which could facilitate the development of new learning architectures and learning operating systems. This represents a significant step toward achieving learning operating systems, an objective that has been a primary focus of our research. We demonstrate that the uniform constant phase approximation holds for any smooth propagation function $f(x)$ satisfying a phase constraint, even if $x$-differentiability is absent or limited. While previously proven only for four times differentiable functions, our general approach yields significant practical advantages. Specifically, this uniform method reliably predicts experimental results for propagation scenarios up to roughly one wavelength, a range where typical differentiability assumptions fail. Furthermore, we establish a lower bound for required differentiability in phase-constrained propagation problems and examine the impact of different phase constraints on the constant phase approximation. Although this method is primarily applied to phase objects, it is equally applicable to the Schwinger-Keldysh constant phase problem. Additionally, the technique can be extended to address other issues in wave physics and applied mathematics. The proof is implemented in the Python package `uniformCPA`. This study examines the potential for rapid discovery of steady-state solutions in rarefied gas flows involving multiple scales. The investigated flows include the three-sphere reentry scenario, the two-sphere reentry, the two-sphere pull-apart configuration, and the three-sphere reentry involving solid spheres coated with light gas. These scenarios feature both small and large Knudsen numbers, where the latter signifies the presence of distinct gaseous and vacuum regions. The analysis is conducted using the ES-GKCA (ESGKCA) method, a recently developed collision operator that merges the Cartesian-Euler-Spherical (CES) approach with the Gaussian half-range (GR) technique. This hybrid operator aims to enhance computational efficiency by combining the advantages of both methods. Results indicate that the ESGKCA collision operator enables the swift determination of steady-state solutions within just dozens of time iterations. Furthermore, the ESGKCA scheme demonstrates superior stability and convergence characteristics compared to conventional BGK-type collision operators. Finally, the study confirms that steady-state solutions can be accurately obtained using the ESGKCA collision operator. To achieve this, the study employs the discrete unified gas kinetic (DUGK) finite-volume (DUGK-FV) scheme, which is known for its accuracy and stability. The DUGK-FV scheme is applied to a time-dependent framework, where the collision operator is updated at every time step. The ESGKCA collision operator is derived by extending the principles of the light gas extension (LGE) method, which was originally formulated for Cartesian-Euler-Spherical (CES) operators. This paper provides a comprehensive review of the theory behind the ESGKCA collision operator. The ESGKCA method is validated by comparing its results with the discrete unified gas kinetic (DUGK) finite-volume (DUGK-FV) scheme. The DUGK-FV scheme is a highly accurate and stable method that has been extensively validated for various flows. The ESGKCA collision operator is validated by comparing its results with those obtained using the DUGK-FV scheme. The results show that the ESGKCA collision operator is able to rapidly converge to the steady-state solution within dozens of time iterations. Furthermore, the ESGKCA collision operator is shown to be more stable and convergent than the BGK-type collision operator. Finally, the ESGKCA collision operator is able to accurately obtain the steady-state solution, as confirmed by the comparison with the DUGK-FV scheme. The non-linear evolution of strongly turbulent plasmas, driven by a non-thermal distribution of charged particles, is hypothesized to generate a cascade of electromagnetically grouped, multi-modal plasma events. This model is evaluated against data from the Horizon-10T experiment, which utilized a satellite equipped with a 10 Teraelectronovolt (10 TeV) electron beam to induce electromagnetic (EM) wave bursts. The 10T satellite was launched into a highly elliptical orbit featuring an apogee of 42,000 km and a perigee of 300 km. Upon reaching its orbit, the satellite's 10T beam generated high-energy EM waves, creating a non-linear plasma environment characterized by high electron density and energy. The experiment detected multiple EM events ranging from 10 MHz to 100 GHz, with amplitudes reaching up to 100 V/m. These observed events align with the predicted grouped EM events resulting from non-linear EM evolution. Furthermore, the EM wave signatures linked to multi-modal plasma events may facilitate the detection of axion quark particles. Consequently, the 10T experiment offers a promising avenue for investigating novel quantum fields and phenomena. This study provides the first analysis of the Horizon-10T dataset, demonstrating that the 10T beam can generate complex, multi-modal plasma events. The analysis also explores the potential for detecting axion quark particles (AQP) within the 10T experiment's EM signatures. Specifically, the work examines the statistical properties of the EM events, including their temporal and spectral characteristics, to identify signatures indicative of AQP existence. The results indicate that the 10T experiment is capable of generating a diverse range of EM events, some of which may serve as signatures for AQP. Additionally, the study proposes a method for detecting AQP based on the multi-modal nature of these events. Overall, this analysis marks a significant advancement in understanding the complex physical processes occurring in strongly turbulent plasmas and paves the way for future research into AQP. The findings suggest that the 10T experiment can provide valuable insights into the non-linear evolution of strongly turbulent plasmas and contribute to the broader field of quantum field research. The study also underscores the potential for the 10T experiment to advance our understanding of quantum field theory and the search for new particles. The Stiff Fibrations project offers a sequence of precisely calculated two-dimensional models designed to explore the mechanical properties of complex materials. This note examines the accuracy of these models and demonstrates how specific functional forms for the elastic modulus can yield materials with notable characteristics, such as high Poisson's ratios exceeding 0.4. Furthermore, we introduce two analytical theorems that refine the modeling process by reducing reliance on numerical computations. Specifically, these theorems enable the analytical determination of the Poisson's ratio for stiff fibrations and the effective Young's modulus for cross-fibrations. Collectively, these theoretical and computational advancements facilitate the design of stiff fibrations with target elastic moduli and Poisson's ratios. Additionally, we extend the definition of stiff fibrations to include loose fibrations and compute their effective moduli. Finally, we derive closed-form expressions for the effective moduli of circular stiff fibrations and apply these formulas to calculate the moduli of stiff and loose fibrations. This work is based on the first author's PhD thesis [1]. We offer a statistical physical analysis of 2D Pauli structures, which model various 2D topological order phases. Our primary finding is the demonstration that 2D Pauli structures are in one-to-one correspondence with 1D spin structures. This connection provides an alternative method for constructing 2D Pauli structures and a structural framework for analyzing their properties. Specifically, we examine the representation categories of both 2D Pauli structures and 1D spin structures, as these categories characterize the topological properties of the physical systems they represent. We define and examine two key properties of 1D spin structures: factorization and 1D topological order. As a consequence, we establish that the representation categories of 2D Pauli structures are either factorization categories or factorization with 1D topological orders, and we offer a characterization of 1D spin structures based on their representation categories. Furthermore, we investigate the symmetry properties of 1D spin structures, demonstrating that they generalize 1D permutation structures. We prove that 1D spin structures can be formulated using groupoids, leading to the development of 1D spin homology, a generalization of standard spin homology. Finally, we illustrate that 1D spin homology effectively captures the properties of 1D spin structures, such as their factorization and detection of 1D topological order, by serving as a useful tool for this purpose. Notably, we demonstrate that 1D spin homology can also factorize, thereby providing an algebraic method for achieving the factorization of 1D spin structures. In summary, this paper introduces a novel and effective framework for 2D Pauli structures, with significant applications in the study of classical statistical systems. For instance, we successfully apply 1D spin homology to analyze 2D classical spin systems, revealing a new and useful connection between 2D spin systems and 1D spin structures. Additionally, we show that 1D spin homology can characterize the symmetry protected topological phases of 2D classical spin systems. Our work paves the way for a comprehensive study of the topological properties of 2D classical spin systems. In conclusion, this research represents a significant step toward understanding the relationship between statistical systems and topology. Specifically, our findings suggest that the relationship between 2D spin systems and 1D spin structures is more fundamental than previously recognized, potentially leading to a more profound understanding of the connection between statistical systems and topology. This study introduces an on-off center-surround sensory field designed for image classification within deep neural networks (DNNs). The mechanism functions by comparing an input patch against a randomly selected reference image; it produces an "on" response if the similarity exceeds a set threshold and an "off" response if it falls below. DNNs incorporating these center-surround fields demonstrate superior performance compared to models using solely random fields. Furthermore, the proposed approach yields sparser activation maps and significantly enhances robustness against adversarial attacks. Notably, these benefits are realized without necessitating modifications to the residual blocks through which the sensory fields are integrated. Extensive experiments were conducted using the CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 datasets. Additional findings indicate that the method maintains high performance even when sensory fields are substituted with other types of random fields. The efficacy of the proposed approach is further validated by its successful application to the Object Recognition in Space (ORS) dataset. The corresponding source code is available at https://github.com/zhongtao-liu/CS-SF. The paper can be accessed at https://arxiv.org/abs/2101.01002. X-ray optical components are essential for enabling broad-field astronomical instruments, including current and future missions like Chandra, XMM-Newton, and the upcoming Athena X-IFU. This review examines the recent advancements in the design, materials, and testing of these components, specifically focusing on both curved and flat Wolter telescopes and how these innovations have improved the performance of astronomical X-ray instruments. The discussion also covers the development of broad-angle x-ray cameras, such as the Soft X-ray Integral Field Instrument (SXIFU) for the European Space Agency's Athena mission, which utilizes microcalorimeters to provide spectral imaging across the 0.2–12 keV range. Additionally, the paper explores the development of on-orbit x-ray optics, detailing the proposed techniques and results from the X-ray Optics Testbed (XOT) mission, which is a technology demonstration included in the second phase of the NASA Small Explorer program. Finally, it briefly addresses the emerging field of adaptive optics for X-ray optics. The objective is to provide an overview of the current state of the art in this area and to identify future research directions. Keywords: X-ray optics, Wolter optics, microcalorimeter, SXIFU, XOT, adaptive optics.

The magnetic Bloch theorem, which governs electron dynamics in periodic systems under a uniform magnetic field, is extended to twisted bilayer graphene (TBG) under $2\pi$ flux. This generalized theorem introduces a novel invariant known as the magnetic winding number, a concept essential for defining magnetic Chern numbers and characterizing topological states within magnetic fields. A specific field configuration, termed a "magnetic Brillouin zone," is identified, yielding reentrant flat bands at zero field. This discovery is attributed to a nontrivial magnetic winding number associated with Landau levels, alongside a magnetic analog of the Berry curvature defined over a real-space plane perpendicular to the field. These findings provide a foundation for investigating correlated physics, including magnetism and superconductivity, in twisted bilayer graphene. Furthermore, these results offer a framework for reentrant flat bands in twisted bilayer materials through the concept of "magnetic band folding." Finally, the study examines the implications of these results for quantum Hall physics, offering a unified description of quantum Hall states in both electronic and bosonic systems under $2\pi$ flux. This phenomenon is termed "reentrant quantum Hall physics," with the bosonic case specifically occurring at $4\pi$ flux. Additionally, the analysis elucidates the unitary transformation linking the original twisted bilayer graphene Hamiltonian to the effective Hamiltonian for bosons or electrons with internal degrees of freedom. Ultimately, the study demonstrates the emergence of reentrant quantum Hall physics, revealing a reentrant quantum Hall effect at zero field alongside reentrant flat bands. This phenomenon is driven by the same mechanism responsible for bosonic reentrant quantum Hall physics at $4\pi$ flux, alongside the $2\pi$ flux scenario. Consequently, these results establish a pathway to reentrant quantum Hall physics in twisted bilayer materials. Finally, the study confirms the existence of reentrant quantum Hall physics in twisted bilayer graphene, thereby completing the unified description of quantum Hall phenomena across all regimes. This achievement stems from the interplay between the $2\pi$ flux case and the $4\pi$ flux case for bosons. Ultimately, these findings provide a comprehensive understanding of the quantum Hall effect in twisted bilayer graphene, offering a unified framework for future research and applications. Steganography involves concealing the presence of secret data within a cover message. This paper examines creating steganographic files using Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks. Although prior research has primarily focused on image-based steganography, we demonstrate that LSTM-based approaches are also effective for textual steganography. Our methodology involves training an LSTM model on a specific domain to produce a generator capable of creating natural-appearing text. By substituting segments of target text with the model's outputs, we achieve stealthiness that surpasses earlier techniques. Furthermore, we utilize a sequence-to-sequence model to enhance capacity and facilitate the analysis of our generated results against existing methods. Additionally, we introduce a novel steganographic system designed for PDF files; this system employs a line insertion strategy to embed secret data while preserving the visual integrity of the document. Finally, we assess the robustness of our algorithms through various attacks, including denoising, quantization, formatting alterations, redactions, and reformatting. Our capacity achieves new state-of-the-art performance for PDF steganography and reaches approximately 10% for textual steganography. Additionally, the security of our approach is superior to that of previous methods. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/ahmedfouad/Text-Stega-LSTM. Unit commitment (UC) is a critical challenge in power system operations that seeks the optimal scheduling of power plants to meet demand at the lowest cost. However, the high computational complexity of UC makes it difficult to solve quickly, particularly for large-scale systems. To address this, this paper introduces a new machine learning-based approach to enhance UC efficiency. Expense models, which characterize UC expenses as functions of plant outputs, are widely used in commercial software to significantly reduce solution times. This study introduces a novel method for generating expense models. Unlike existing techniques, our approach utilizes neural networks to learn these models directly from the UC solution space, thereby eliminating the need for time-consuming pre-processing steps. Numerical experiments demonstrate that the proposed method achieves high accuracy while maintaining low computational costs. This study examines the stress-induced dimerization and the suppression of antiferromagnetism in the Kitaev material $\alpha$-Li$_2$IrO$_3$ through a combination of experimental techniques and first-principles calculations. Mechanical stress transforms the long-range antiferromagnetic order into a paramagnetic state by reducing the superexchange interaction between adjacent Ir atoms. This stress also diminishes the Kitaev coupling constant, shifts the magnetic ground state from ferromagnetic to antiferromagnetic, and triggers a first-order structural phase transition from monoclinic to rhombohedral symmetry. Furthermore, the magnetic properties of $\alpha$-Li$_2$IrO$_3$ exhibit temperature-dependent behavior, with the ferromagnetic state becoming unstable above approximately 100 K. Finally, these findings are compared with the effects of hydrostatic pressure observed in this and other Kitaev compounds. Overall, the research underscores the critical role of structural distortions in shaping the magnetic characteristics of Kitaev systems. Finally, we explore the potential for tuning Kitaev physics in this material via mechanical stress. This paper introduces a theory for synthetic controls, control variates, and projection. We demonstrate that the difference in the synthetic control from the control group represents the difference between the synthetic control and the control variate, which is a linear combination of the synthetic control coefficients. Furthermore, we prove that the difference between the synthetic control and the control variate is orthogonal to any observable. Consequently, we conclude that within a local observable framework, the synthetic control difference can be interpreted as the difference between the control variate and the residual. Additionally, we show that if the synthetic control coefficients are positive, the control group serves as a lower bound for the synthetic control. Finally, we extend this reasoning to propose a projection model. In this model, we propose a new estimator, the projection difference, and provide an asymptotic normality result. We also recommend an optimal bandwidth selection method for this new estimator. Through both theoretical and simulation analyses, we find that the projection difference offers a more robust alternative to the traditional synthetic control difference. Furthermore, we illustrate the application of our projection difference to the 2003 Iraq War data. Our results indicate that the projection difference offers a more stable and reliable inference compared to the synthetic control difference. Overall, our projection difference offers a more robust and reliable alternative to the traditional synthetic control difference. This work aims to enhance the robustness and reliability of causal inference using the synthetic control method. Additionally, our projection difference serves as a valuable alternative to the difference-in-weights method proposed by Abadie et al. (2021). Finally, our projection difference is expected to significantly improve and advance synthetic control-based causal inference. This paper introduces a novel, privacy-preserving method for calculating the Gromov-Wasserstein divergence (GW-divergence) between structural graphs. Our approach enables learning from distributed data without the need to share raw samples, instead utilizing aggregated gradients derived from a specific learning rule. This technique is particularly effective for distributed structural graphs, which are prevalent in IoT and mobile edge computing environments. We demonstrate that our method achieves a divergence of at most $\mathcal{O}(\frac{1}{\sqrt{T}})$, where $T$ represents the total number of iterations. Furthermore, we prove that the method converges with a privacy loss of at most $\varepsilon$ per iteration under Differential Privacy (DP) guarantees. Finally, experimental results on both synthetic and real-world datasets validate the method's efficacy, showing performance comparable to centralized learning while successfully protecting sensitive data. Additionally, the proposed method is proven to be robust against gradient descent attacks. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/ChenYi2019/GW-DPL. Double beta decay serves as a valuable mechanism for investigating nuclear structure, refining mass models, and setting constraints on neutrino properties. This study presents a re-evaluation of double beta decay limits for the systems $^{194}$Pt and $^{198}$Hg, alongside $^{204}$Hg and $^{206}$Pb, utilizing a novel analysis framework. The calculated half-lives are $(1.2\pm0.2)\times10^{21}$ yr for $^{194}$Pt, $(1.0\pm0.1)\times10^{21}$ yr for $^{198}$Hg, $(1.1\pm0.1)\times10^{21}$ yr for $^{204}$Hg, and $(1.0\pm0.1)\times10^{21}$ yr for $^{206}$Pb. These results align with prior experimental findings and theoretical predictions. Additionally, we explore implications for neutrinoless double beta decay, a process that could reveal neutrino nature and provide insights into nuclear models. Furthermore, we examine constraints on neutrinoless double charge-current reactions, which offer a complementary method for studying nuclear structure and detecting dark matter. Our analysis indicates that $^{194}$Pt and $^{204}$Hg are particularly promising candidates for future investigations into double beta decay and dark matter-induced nuclear transitions. The comprehensive data and analytical tools presented here are available to support future research endeavors. Finally, we conclude with recommendations for advancing the field. Utilizing a novel renormalization scheme for the flavor-singlet axial-vector current within dimensionally regulated QCD, we demonstrate that the axial-vector anomaly necessitates a renormalization group-dependent counterterm, thereby altering the evolution of the renormalized current. Consequently, we establish a relationship between the renormalization group-invariant charge and the renormalized charge, both in the absence and presence of a gluon background field. Furthermore, we derive the charge evolution equation under these specific background field conditions. Finally, employing the minimal-subtraction scheme, we re-examine the evolution of the axial-vector current to four-loop order. While colorization is essential for both video restoration and video enhancement, existing methods often struggle with color inconsistencies and failures when applied to video material that differs significantly in content or appearance. To overcome these limitations, this paper introduces COCA, a cross-camera and content-agnostic approach designed to color diverse videos. COCA integrates two key components: the Multi-Camera Appearance Model (MCAM) and the Spatio-Temporal Appearance Model (STM). STM is engineered to learn color patterns from various colorized videos, while MCAM utilizes multiple cameras to model appearance variations across different contents. Together, these components enable the model to effectively handle appearance differences in cross-camera and cross-content scenarios. Extensive experiments demonstrate that COCA successfully colors a wide range of diverse videos and surpasses state-of-the-art methods in most metrics. The code and models will be made available online. Our video demonstrations can be viewed here. Additionally, we have released a new dataset comprising diverse videos and their ground-truth colored versions for research purposes. This dataset is available at our website. The Ermakov framework extends the classical second-order Ermakov equation into an $n$-dimensional generalized form defined by a vector potential. This generalization encompasses several existing conservative and non-conservative $n$-dimensional frameworks as special cases, including those by Anderson, Dafermos, and Mura. The study establishes connections between the conservation laws of associated Lagrangians and the time-reversal symmetry of the corresponding Euler-Lagrange equations. Additionally, it is demonstrated that a specific gauge transformation preserves both the Euler-Lagrange equations and the conservation theorems. We demonstrate that a massless Nambu-Goldstone boson necessarily arises from an infinitesimal, non-reversible symmetry breaking in any continuous stochastic dynamics, specifically including diffusion processes and heat baths. A non-reversible symmetry is defined as one under which the stochastic drift, or generator, of the dynamics transforms into a different, albeit equivalent, dynamics. While this result is well-established for unitary (reversible) symmetries—where the drift remains invariant—we show that the phenomenon persists for the broader class of non-reversible cases. The core of our proof relies on verifying a specific identity concerning the Hessian of the free energy. This same identity is instrumental in establishing spectral gap stability for non-reversible Markov chains, notably within the framework developed by Chatterjee, Groenevelt, and Guionnet. We explicitly link these two applications of the identity. Furthermore, we examine an example of non-reversible symmetry breaking within a diffusion process. Our methodology is applicable to both finite-dimensional and functional frameworks, including measures on infinite-dimensional spaces. We conclude by outlining several promising directions for future research. This work extends findings from C. Landim, A. Pimentel, and C. Presutti, *Commun. Math. Phys.* **330**, 1033 (2014), and related literature. Additional context can be found in our prior publication, *J. Stat. Phys.* **178**, 1077 (2020). A locally acyclic split graph is defined as a split graph where the maximum independent sets form a locally acyclic directed hypergraph. The term "semi-transitivity" is derived from this property. This study examines various characteristics linked to semi-transitivity, including its relationship with chordal graphs, maximum clique and independent set sizes, and the graph's dominator and independence numbers. Additionally, the document presents a constructive approach for creating such graphs. Finally, the concept of locally bipartite split graphs is introduced, along with an analysis of their associated traits. Specifically, maximum independent sets in locally bipartite split graphs possess a distinct property that enables the semi-linear determination of their size. Furthermore, an algorithm is presented that achieves linear complexity for finding these maximum independent sets within this specific class of graphs. This method also supports the semi-linear calculation of the graph's dominator number. The paper includes examples of locally bipartite split graphs and their maximum independent sets. These examples illustrate that the dominator number of a locally bipartite split graph can be arbitrarily far from both its maximum clique size and its maximum independent set size. Consequently, the maximum clique size cannot be semi-linearly derived from the size of a maximum independent set in this context. Finally, the section concludes with an outline of the paper's structure. This overview details the background information and definitions utilized throughout the work, as well as the theorems and lemmas employed to establish the results presented in the subsequent chapters. The conclusion also references related findings from the literature. Specifically, it mentions that the directionality of maximum independent sets in chordal graphs exhibits certain properties, including semi-transitivity. It also notes that several subclasses of chordal graphs exhibit locally acyclic or locally bipartite directionality for their maximum independent sets. The section highlights that the minimum number of maximum independent sets required to create a cycle in the directionality graph of a chordal graph is 4. Finally, it states that the minimum number of maximum independent sets needed to create a bipartition in the directionality graph of a chordal graph is 6. These findings are used to derive the results presented in this paper. Additionally, the locally acyclic split graph was introduced in [1], and the bipartite nature of maximum independent sets in bipartite graphs was established in [2]. The characterization of locally bipartite split graphs was developed in [3].
