The identification of tau leptons and the accurate measurement of their decay modes are critical components of many physics analyses at the LHC. This study introduces a novel convolutional neural network (CNN) architecture designed for hadronic tau lepton recognition and decay mode categorization. The model was trained and validated using simulated data from proton-proton collisions at a center-of-mass energy of 13 TeV, processed with the CMS experiment's simulated detector response framework. We demonstrate that our proposed CNN model achieves performance comparable to current state-of-the-art methods while utilizing a significantly smaller quantity of training data. Furthermore, we establish that a unified CNN model can effectively address both tasks simultaneously without compromising individual performance levels. These findings indicate that deep neural networks offer a highly efficient solution for hadronic tau lepton reconstruction and decay mode identification at the LHC. The CNN implementation is provided as public software. This work is based on the doctoral thesis of Dr. Martin Kretzer. I contend that the proliferation of big data resources, such as the Virtual Observatory, has transformed the landscape of data analysis. Although many existing analyses were conducted decades ago, their methodologies were often suboptimal for contemporary data volumes. Conversely, the current generation of Bayesian Neural Networks (BNNs) is uniquely equipped to handle modern data while providing a straightforward assessment of parameter uncertainties. This study demonstrates the efficacy of BNNs by applying them to two tasks using the 2MASS star catalog: distinguishing stars from galaxies and classifying stars into O, B, and A types. The analysis involves processing 200,000 stars, utilizing two distinct datasets, and evaluating six different configurations. These findings illustrate the viability of BNNs as a category analysis tool in this context. Ultimately, I argue that the combination of advanced algorithms like BNNs and access to vast data like 2MASS marks the beginning of a new era in data analysis. This approach is particularly relevant to the current trend of constructing massive telescopes, such as the Vera Rubin Observatory, which will generate unprecedented datasets. I conclude that this analysis serves as a demonstration of how Bayesian methods can be applied to such data, thereby facilitating more effective scientific discoveries. This work is derived from my doctoral thesis, which is available in Portuguese at the following link: https://repositorio.ufsc.br/bitstream/handle/123456789/195054/1/471704.pdf. The thesis includes detailed methodological explanations for the analysis presented here. Additionally, the complete source code is available at: https://github.com/brunofgsc/bayes-2maSS. The code is written in Python and utilizes the Scikit-learn and PyMC3 libraries. I extend my gratitude to all collaborators who contributed to this project. Finally, I hope this demonstration inspires other scientists to employ Bayesian methods in their own research. Thank you.

We present a theoretical framework for intermodal forward Brillouin scattering (IBSB) within solid-core photonic crystal threads (PCTs). This model incorporates the modal overlap between optical modes and the spatial distribution of the mechanical diffusion mode. By applying the framework to circularly symmetric PCTs, we derive a prediction for the IB SB bandwidth that aligns with available experimental data. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the IB SB bandwidth remains relatively stable across variations in frequency, size, and background refractive index, while also exhibiting an inverse relationship with wavelength. These results indicate the potential for IBSB to serve as a method for sensitive optical frequency detection in PCT devices. Additionally, we observe that the coupling coefficient between a propagating mode and the diffusion mode scales with the square of the former's overlap with the latter, a finding that may be applicable to other photonic systems. Finally, we outline how this theoretical model can be extended to more complex PCT geometries. This model is published under an Open Access license and is intended for reuse. Specifically, for any given foundation $T$, we explicitly characterize the Weyl group orbit containing $-1$ within the associated reflection group. This study addresses two optimization challenges: the Set-Union Rucksack Issue (SUR) and the Budgeted Maximum Coverage Challenge (BMC). The SUR involves selecting a subset of items such that their union encompasses all elements in a universal set, maximizing the total value of chosen items. Conversely, BMC aims to identify $k$ facilities within a fixed budget to maximize the coverage of the greatest number of requests. Both problems are NP-hard. We introduce a hybrid local search algorithm that integrates three strategies: the reduced cost-based (RCB) method, the restricted search-based (RSB) method, and the alternating search-based (ASB) method. The RCB method is proven to converge to a local optimum, while the RSB method ensures convergence to the global optimum. The paper provides a detailed analysis of the computational complexity for the proposed algorithm. Furthermore, we present experimental results comparing our approach against existing literature methods. The conducted experiments demonstrate that the proposed algorithm is highly effective and efficient, yielding superior results compared to other approaches in the literature. Additionally, the algorithm exhibits strong performance across both small and large-scale instances. Finally, we explore applications of SUR and BMC in the analysis of microblogging data. The computational results indicate that the proposed algorithm performs well in this context. Surprisingly, the algorithm also shows promising performance in a real-world application: the Budgeted Maximum Influence Spread Challenge. The computational results confirm that the proposed algorithm outperforms other approaches from the literature. The source code is accessible at: https://github.com/Reza-Aghaei/ESLSS. Keywords: Set-Union Rucksack Issue, Budgeted Maximum Coverage Challenge, NP-hard, Exact Algorithm, Local Search Algorithm.

Attrition forecasting is a critical challenge for businesses, particularly in the rapidly expanding online gaming sector. Online game operators utilize these models to analyze historical player data and predict future cancellations. However, most existing approaches rely on machine learning techniques that demand extensive feature engineering and complex implementation. In contrast, this paper introduces a straightforward yet effective rule-based model designed to estimate attrition. We present the results of applying this model to forecast churn within an online gaming environment. The study demonstrates that our rule-based approach is both easy to implement and performant, offering predictive power comparable to machine learning methods while requiring significantly less effort for feature extraction. Furthermore, we outline how these predictions can be utilized to proactively retain at-risk players. Given the growing interest in player retention, we make our source code available to facilitate replication of our findings. Our implementation can be accessed at: https://github.com/SebastianKlapp/AttritionModeling. Additionally, all code has been deposited in a GitHub repository to ensure reproducibility. We hope this resource will prove valuable to researchers interested in online player attrition, enabling them to replicate our results and explore novel applications of our rule-based solution. The paper concludes with a discussion on potential use cases and directions for future research. Online gamers are integral to the success of game operators, as their engagement drives revenue through microtransactions and in-game purchases. Consequently, retaining these players is paramount for the industry. The two-dimensional Ising field theory under an external magnetic field corresponds to a deformed $SO(4)$ invariant model. This deformation transforms the massless excitation spectrum into that of the deconcini-Fateev-Zamolodchikov (dfZ) theory, which describes a system with two distinct mass gaps. We demonstrate that the dfZ theory can be decomposed into two independent $c=1/2$ $SO(4)$ invariant theories. In this framework, the Nambu-Goldstone fermion associated with the deforming operator becomes confined, resulting in the restoration of the central charge to $c=1/2$. Furthermore, we establish that this model constitutes the field-theoretical foundation for the Yang-Lee critical point. The dfZ theory possesses a unique scaling dimension, $\Delta_{\phi}$, associated with the deforming operator, which governs the system's properties in the infinite volume limit. We computed $\Delta_{\phi}$ to high precision using both Monte Carlo simulations and perturbative field theory methods, determining it to be approximately $1.00325000(1)$. Finally, we derived the complete set of one-particle and two-particle amplitudes for the large volume limit, enabling a detailed comparison with Yang-Lee singularity data. This comparison yields the dfZ scaling dimension and all dfZ masses with substantial accuracy, with uncertainties at the $10^{-4}$ level. Additionally, we calculated the residues of the Yang-Lee poles, achieving a $10^{-3}$ precision. We also present preliminary findings regarding Yang-Lee residues in finite volumes. In this regime, the dfZ spectrum does not fully describe the theory; instead, a second set of poles, termed dfZ' masses, emerges. We demonstrate that these dfZ' masses are not isolated but form a dense tower, the nature of which remains an open question. Finally, we discuss the implications of these results for the conformal field theory of the Yang-Lee model. Specifically, we show that the dfZ scaling dimension aligns with the Kac table formula when $\Delta_{\phi} = \Delta_{r(1,1)}$, and we provide a detailed comparison with the two-particle amplitudes of the Yang-Lee model. This comparison reveals a significant discrepancy between the two-particle amplitudes in the dfZ theory and the Yang-Lee model, suggesting that the dfZ theory may not accurately represent the Yang-Lee model.

Our analysis demonstrates that various helicity and orbital angular momentum (OAM) distributions correspond to specific coefficients of these effective actions. Furthermore, we establish that all gluon distribution functions are formulated using gauge links oriented along the light-cone, thereby ensuring a uniform definition. Our approach employs light-cone gauge, leveraging the fact that light-cone gauge links reduce to the identity matrix when the gluon OAM equals zero. We illustrate that the gluon distribution function associated with the Sivers effect exhibits a sign flip between the nucleon and $\Delta$ baryons, a phenomenon naturally accounted for by the distinct orientations of the effective actions in this framework. Our findings indicate that distribution functions derived from HET can be directly connected to the gluon wave function on the light-front, which is constructed from the HET effective action. We anticipate that our methodology will offer a novel and potent perspective on gluon distribution and momentum distributions, potentially aiding in the resolution of longstanding puzzles regarding OAM. Additionally, our results provide a fresh perspective on the color glass condensate (CGC) and its connection to gluon PDFs. We illustrate that our formalism allows for the systematic resummation of gluon ladders, which can be directly linked to gluon distribution functions. Finally, we demonstrate that our approach naturally incorporates saturation effects, which are not present in the traditional PDF formalism. Ultra-relativistic heavy-ion collisions serve as a potent source of virtual photons, a characteristic particularly valuable for ultra-peripheral collisions (UPCs) where no direct particle interaction occurs. These events generate abundant photon pairs, including low transverse momentum ($p_T$) photons that are difficult to produce through other mechanisms. Furthermore, electron-positron pairs arising from such photon-photon interactions can also achieve low $p_T$ values. This study simulates these processes involving low $p_T$ photons and $e^\pm$ pairs during UPCs of dense nuclei, such as lead, utilizing the ELCEP code. Results indicate that approximately 10% of simulated low $p_T$ photons and 20% of low $p_T$ $e^\pm$ pairs engage within the dense nuclear environment. This interaction may manifest as photon-nucleus or pair-nucleus interactions, potentially leading to hadron production, or through interactions with the nuclear electromagnetic field, resulting in photon or pair deflection. Consequently, these phenomena may be observable in upcoming experiments, such as those at the Large Hadron Collider's future Electron-Ion Collider. The paper presents the simulation results for low $p_T$ photons and $e^\pm$ pairs, along with their interaction rates in the dense nuclear field. Additionally, the influence of nuclear form factors on these processes is discussed. The study also examines the impact of virtual photon polarization and flux, as well as the effects of nuclear size and the number of participating nucleons. Finally, the potential for detecting low $p_T$ photons and $e^\pm$ pairs following their interaction with dense nuclei is explored. This could be achieved by analyzing the final state of photons or pairs, including changes in momentum, polarization, and position, or by investigating produced hadrons, such as their momentum spectra and azimuthal anisotropy. The paper concludes with a discussion of the significance of these findings. Overall, the research demonstrates that electromagnetic interactions between low $p_T$ photons and dense nuclei are significant, which must be accounted for when searching for low $p_T$ photons or $e^\pm$ pairs in UPCs of heavy ions. The findings may have implications for various observables, such as the production of low $p_T$ photons, electron-positron pairs, or hadrons, in the context of photon-photon interactions with dense nuclei. Cyclists are increasingly vulnerable to traffic accidents, with up to 30% of traffic-related fatalities involving cyclists. To enhance safety, it is crucial to understand the factors contributing to these accidents. This study introduces a novel risk identifier that integrates contextual and historical data to detect risk levels in real-time during cycling. The system is context-sensitive and utilizes video-driven inputs, including cyclist behavior, environmental conditions, and cyclist characteristics. By combining behavioral and environmental cues, the identifier effectively captures contextual risk, while incorporating cyclist-specific traits allows for a more comprehensive risk assessment. Experimental findings indicate that the proposed risk identifier outperforms existing solutions in detecting risk contexts. Additionally, the results demonstrate that accounting for contextual and historical information significantly improves detection accuracy. To the best of the authors' knowledge, this represents the first effort to develop a context-sensitive and video-driven risk identifier for cycling safety. Furthermore, the study confirms that considering contextual and historical factors substantially boosts risk detection accuracy. The resilient security of modern robotics is a critical concern, particularly for autonomous vehicles and robotic agents operating in unstructured environments where they must navigate unpredictable, time-varying obstacles while maintaining safety. This paper introduces a motion planning framework designed to ensure safe navigation for dynamic robotics systems, even during cyber-attacks. The approach utilizes control barrier functions (CBF) and integrates them with model predictive control (MPC) to generate motion plans that guarantee collision-free trajectories. Furthermore, CBF constraints are enforced within an MPC controller to ensure resilient operation against cyber threats. The proposed method is validated through numerical simulations, which demonstrate the algorithm's ability to produce collision-free paths in the presence of time-varying obstacles and while accounting for system uncertainties caused by cyber attacks. Additionally, simulation results confirm that MPC-based motion plans remain robust and effective, even when the system is subjected to cyber attacks. Finally, the study provides experimental results supporting the proposed approach, and the code is made available online. For each pair of positive integers (m, n), we define the concept of an (m, n)-encompassing ring and investigate several of its properties. Let R denote an infinite commutative ring with identity where the ideal generated by any two elements either contains or is contained within the other. We establish that if both the spectrum and the lattice of ideals of R are chains, then R is an (m, n)-encompassing ring for every pair of positive integers (m, n). Furthermore, if R is local with a maximal ideal M such that M^n = M^{n+1} for some integer n greater than 1, then R is an (m, n)-encompassing ring for all positive integers m greater than 1. Additionally, we demonstrate that an infinite commutative ring with identity, in which the ideal generated by any two elements is either equal or contains the other, possesses both a chain spectrum and a chain lattice of ideals if and only if it is isomorphic to either a local ring or a local ring modulo an ideal. We also provide a sufficient condition under which such a ring is an (m, n)-encompassing ring and construct a specific infinite commutative ring with identity that has a chain spectrum and chain lattice yet fails to be an (m, n)-encompassing ring for any pair (m, n) where m and n exceed 1. Finally, we present several examples and open problems related to these (m, n)-encompassing rings. Specifically, we offer a commutative ring with identity that is not multiplicative but is an (m, n)-encompassing ring for all positive integers m and n; furthermore, this example is not an integral domain, though its spectrum and lattice of ideals are both chains. This work investigates the interaction between model training and the behavior of adversarial examples. Specifically, we explore whether the hostile inputs that attack a model can be transformed into beneficial adversarial examples that aid in the model's training and enhance its security. To achieve this, we introduce a novel category of models termed the Adversarial Generative Model (AGM), which is capable of generating these beneficial examples. Currently, AGMs are trained in an agnostic setting where the data distribution remains unknown to the model. Our approach leverages the inherent ability of deep generative models to learn complex data distributions, while the features extracted by the discriminator serve to refine the generator's output. Consequently, our proposed AGMs can produce high-quality, diverse adversarial examples. Furthermore, we demonstrate that these generated examples improve the classifier's performance and robustness against test-time attacks. Finally, our results indicate that the AGM can successfully learn representations from adversarial data without requiring cleaning. Experimental results confirm the model's effectiveness in learning from corrupted datasets such as MNIST-SVHN and CIFAR-10-POISONED. Additionally, the AGM outperforms state-of-the-art methods on the challenging CIFAR-10-SVHN benchmark. Our code is publicly available on GitHub. Nonlocal congestion partial differential equations represent a widely used class of transport models designed to describe phenomena ranging from traffic flow to the propagation of viral infections. These equations rely on the first-order term $F(\rho)$ alongside a nonlocal congestion factor $(1-\phi(\rho))$, where $\phi$ is a congestion kernel dependent on density $\rho$ and $\phi(\rho) \to 1$ as $\rho \to \infty$. When $\phi$ is a local density, this framework reduces to the well-known vanishing viscosity MUR entropy admissibility criterion. However, when $\phi$ is a smooth function of density derived from the convolution of a kernel with the density, the MUR criterion no longer applies. This paper investigates the singular limit of such equations as viscosity vanishes, deriving entropy admissibility criteria that extend the MUR condition to a broader class of models. Furthermore, we demonstrate the convergence of viscous solutions to entropy solutions in the zero-viscosity limit and analyze the convergence rate, finding that it is significantly slower than the convergence speed for standard first-order conservation laws. Finally, numerical experiments are conducted to validate these theoretical findings. To the best of our knowledge, the significantly slower convergence speed constitutes a novel result. Our methodology is applicable to models featuring various types of nonlocal interactions. Additionally, we establish entropy admissibility criteria that generalize the MUR condition to various forms of nonlocal congestion effects. These criteria may also hold value in the context of machine learning, where congestion kernels serve as essential components in generative adversarial networks (GANs). This value extends to machine learning contexts involving continuity equations. Furthermore, our results generalize previous findings by demonstrating that certain functions are inadmissible even within the narrower context of local congestion equations. Finally, the proof techniques employed may be useful for analyzing models incorporating both nonlocal interactions and interactions of higher order than the first order. Horizon saddle links, originally discovered by Thurston as examples of incompressible tori within the convex core of specific hyperbolic 3-manifolds, have recently been generalized to dilation surfaces. This paper presents a novel characterization of horizon saddle links utilizing Thurston's dilation patterns. Specifically, for any generic dilation surface featuring a single singularity, we demonstrate that the horizon saddle link is uniquely characterized as the unique closed geodesic within the singular orbit that cannot be expressed as a product of Dehn twists. Additionally, we offer a new construction of horizon saddle links and investigate their properties on dilation surfaces with multiple singularities. Furthermore, we establish that for any closed geodesic represented by a dilation pattern, its mapping class is an elementary mapping class formed by a sequence of Dehn twists. Finally, we examine the mapping class group associated with horizon saddle links. In the singular orbit case, we prove that the mapping class group is infinitely generated and infinite-rank, comprising only mapping classes with finite orders that are not mapping class group generators, thereby providing a negative answer to a related question posed by J. Park and A. Raibaut. In the multi-singular case, we demonstrate that the mapping class group is infinitely generated and infinite-rank, with all its generators possessing negative Euler characteristics. These findings extend several recent results concerning dilated geodesics and their mapping class groups, which were previously established in the context of affine surfaces. Our methodology relies on a newly developed family of braid groups, a key component of our primary contribution. Specifically, we define braid groups for horizon saddle links and calculate their ranks, revealing that these groups are generally not finitely generated. Leveraging the specific structure of these groups, we derive various novel results regarding horizon saddle links and their associated properties. Finally, we outline several open problems within this framework. This research was conducted under the supervision of the second author, A. Raibaut. Additionally, the first author, J. This study proposes a method for analyzing complex networks that incorporates both the magnitude and angle of pairwise correlations. We apply this approach to a functional network model of the human mind, constructed using the "Complete Correlation" technique to ensure the network's robustness. By assigning a probability to each brain region for the thought of any specific word, we establish a functional network with complete correlation. To analyze its structure, we developed a new metric termed the "Probability Density Network" (PDN). This method involves calculating the probability density between any two regions by aggregating the probabilities across all nodes within a network's connected component. We demonstrate that the PDN exhibits a power-law distribution, characterized by a scaling exponent of 2. This outcome is highly significant, as it indicates that the method can identify the power-law property of the original network even when it is fragmented into disconnected pieces. Furthermore, we show that the method's sensitivity to network structure remains stable across various graph topologies, including ring, line, and star configurations. These findings suggest that the proposed approach is suitable for analyzing human cognitive processes, where the "mind" is metaphorically described as a network of interconnected regions. We anticipate that this research will advance the field of cognitive science. The Python code required to replicate our results is available at: https://github.com/ChenYi2020/Complete-correlation. Classical Segal-Bargmann theory extends into Clifford algebra frameworks, where functions are represented as spinor-valued entities. While classical theory links the Fourier transform and analytic continuation via the Segal-Bargmann (SB) transform—an linear mapping from $L^2(\mathbb{R}^n)$ to holomorphic functions on a complex space of matching dimension—Clifford extensions of this transform have yet to establish this connection. This paper introduces a unified approach to Segal-Bargmann transforms across various Clifford algebra settings and demonstrates that these extensions retain the core properties of the original theory. Specifically, we show that the SB transform serves as the isomorphism between a Fourier transform and a Taylor series expansion, with variables shifted to the center of the transform. This result relies on a new Taylor isomorphism theorem for Clifford-valued functions. Additionally, we derive an inverse SB transform formula tailored for functions exhibiting exponential growth. Finally, we generalize these findings to include signature-dependent SB transforms and explore their implications for quantum mechanics within Clifford algebra-valued spinor frameworks. The study begins with a review of the SB transform in the Euclidean $\mathbb{R}^n$ setting. Subsequently, we develop an isomorphism theorem for Clifford-valued functions based on a novel Taylor expansion formula. Using this, we prove that the SB transform acts as an isomorphism mapping Fourier transforms to shifted Taylor transforms for Clifford-valued functions exhibiting exponential growth. We further extend these findings to signature-dependent SB transforms and their corresponding exponential growth conditions. Within this generalized signature context, we derive specific inverse SB transform formulas for functions with exponential growth. Finally, these findings are applied to analyze the SB transform and inverse SB transform for Clifford algebra-valued functions in quantum spinor theory. The paper concludes with an outline of several open research questions regarding quantum spinor theory under the influence of electromagnetic fields. These questions address functional spaces, transformation existence and invertibility, and the analysis of inhomogeneous SB transforms. The final section also presents initial research findings on solving the Schrödinger equation using Clifford algebra-valued wave functions within an inhomogeneous SB transform framework. The primary conclusion is the successful development of a comprehensive quantum spinor theory utilizing Clifford algebra-valued functions and the signature-generalized SB transform. This achievement marks a significant advancement in quantum spinor theory, which has previously been limited by the lack of suitable functional spaces and appropriate SB transforms for general signatures. This work investigates the conditioning Gaussian process resulting from imposing a conditioning event $A$ on a Gaussian process defined over a set $T$. Specifically, when $A$ mandates that the process path remains within a subset $K$ for the entire domain, we demonstrate that the resulting process characterizes a Gaussian (semi-)diffusion with a specific boundary speed. In contrast, if $A$ is defined by a finite set of constraints, the resulting process is a Gaussian process that repels itself from a specified subset of $T$. We detail applications of this phenomenon to Gaussian (semi-)diffusions and Gaussian fields. Notably, our methodology extends beyond Brownian motion and the Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process to include general Gaussian fields. For instance, we establish that Gaussian white noise, conditioned to remain within the positive orthant, constitutes a Gaussian process exhibiting infinite total variation on any interval of length greater than zero. Furthermore, we demonstrate that this process functions as a boundary local time for the process within the closure of the positive orthant. We also analyze the case where the conditioning event involves boundary conditions, revealing that the resulting process is the time-reversal of the process derived from a different conditioning formulation. Additionally, for Gaussian (semi-)diffusions, we provide a characterization of the probability of the event that the process stays within $K$ over a given time interval. Finally, we examine the scenario where the conditioning event involves the process remaining in $K$ only over a subset of the time interval, finding that the resulting process is no longer a diffusion but rather a Gaussian process with finite variation on every interval. These findings are supported by simulations. Many of these results were previously conjectured regarding Brownian motion and the Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process; consequently, we address these cases separately to leverage existing literature and provide proofs that may differ from those required for more general Gaussian processes. To facilitate this, we have structured the paper into two distinct sections. The first section presents conjectures and their proofs for Gaussian (semi-)diffusions, while the second section offers an analysis of boundary conditioning for general Gaussian processes, including examples, conjectures, and simulations. This paper aims to extend the existing literature by offering an analysis of boundary conditioning for general Gaussian processes. Additionally, the initial section is designed to be accessible to a broader audience, as it does not rely on concepts beyond those typically encountered in the field. This paper introduces a ground-based sensor network designed to monitor the ionosphere by wireless connecting each ground sensor with a corresponding sky sensor. The ionosphere's dynamics are monitored through two complementary perspectives: ground and sky. Each sky sensor consists of an antenna suspended within the ionosphere, alongside sensors mounted on the ground directly below them. This architecture enables ionospheric monitoring at a specific altitude, facilitating measurements of ion drift velocity, electron density, and related parameters. The system utilizes a wireless module featuring a compact, lightweight design with extended battery life, robust communication capabilities, and a user-friendly interface. A prototype of this wireless linkage has been developed and tested in a controlled environment. The paper details the design and testing of this prototype. Additionally, the proposed system is being tested in a controlled ionosphere simulation chamber, with the current status of these tests presented in this paper. Future developments will address design enhancements and ionospheric monitoring applications. The paper concludes by outlining potential ionospheric applications for the proposed system.

The Deep Underground Neutrino Experiment (DUNE) is a comprehensive neutrino research initiative currently under construction. As a global scientific venture, it involves over 3,000 scientists from 130 institutions across 28 nations. DUNE aims to investigate the fundamental properties of neutrinos and their role in the universe through a multi-pronged strategy. This paper outlines the project's objectives, technical specifications, and scientific potential. Upon completion, DUNE will serve as a precision instrument for neutrino science, offering multiple methods to measure fundamental parameters and test the Standard Model. It will also function as a sensitive detector for rare events, such as supernovae, dark matter, and neutron star mergers, while enabling studies of nuclear physics, astrophysics, and cosmology. Ultimately, DUNE will provide a unique window into the dynamics of extreme environments, including supernovae, neutron star mergers, and cosmic-ray interactions within the Earth's atmosphere. These capabilities will facilitate a multifaceted analysis of the neutrino sector, with the ultimate goal of determining the neutrino mass hierarchy. Furthermore, DUNE will explore a wide range of physics topics, including the CP violation phase, low-energy hyper-weak interactions, nuclear physics, and the nature of dark matter. This review examines the specific scientific goals of the experiment and the technological advancements required to achieve them. Finally, we analyze the anticipated scientific outcomes and the significant impact DUNE is expected to have on future research. We conclude by highlighting the experiment's potential to usher in a new era of high-precision neutrino science. Additional details can be found at http://arxiv.org/abs/1901.01519. Shapley values originate from cooperative game theory and have recently been suggested as a viable technique for interpreting machine learning models. This study presents an investigation into the utilization of Shapley values for explaining and interpreting a contemporary experimental analysis focused on enhancing the identification of jet-like standard model objects known as "top quarks." The primary objective of the experimental top tagger examined here is to maximize the tagger's efficiency. We demonstrate that interpreting the classification results through the lens of Shapley values provides both quantitative and qualitative insights into the characteristics of these jets. Furthermore, we explore the potential application of Shapley values to other physics analyses, highlighting their capacity to elucidate the behavior of the experimental models employed in such investigations. Additionally, the provided code is open-source, offering a showcase of its functionality and extensibility. This work represents an application of machine learning interpretation techniques to the standard Higgs boson analysis, representing one of the most widely utilized searches in the field. The inclusion of our analysis in this investigation underscores the potential for developing general methods to interpret results from machine learning searches involving the Higgs boson. Both the superbosonization equation and the generalized Hubbard-Stratonovich transformation effectively address global supersymmetry within quantum field theories. This study concentrates on the massless QM $\phi^4$ theory, comparing how each method handles the $\beta$-function. The analysis demonstrates that both approaches yield identical results for the $\beta$-function. Furthermore, it is noted that applying superbosonization to theories involving fermion matrices—such as matrix QM $\phi^4$—necessitates careful attention to the noncommutativity of matrix-valued fields $\hat{\phi}$. Finally, calculations for the matrix model confirm that, contrary to expectations, both superbosonization and generalized Hubbard-Stratonovich transformations successfully manage the noncommutativity of $\hat{\phi}$. Consequently, both methods produce accurate results for the $\beta$-function in this context. Additionally, it is observed that superbosonization fails to correctly compute the $\beta$-function for a theory featuring chiral symmetry. In contrast, the generalized Hubbard-Stratonovich transformation yields the correct $\beta$-function for both the chiral symmetric and chiral symmetric broken phase models. These findings suggest that superbosonization is ineffective for theories with chiral symmetry, whereas the generalized Hubbard-Stratonovich transformation remains applicable. Finally, the issue of operator ordering in matrix models is examined, revealing that it does not influence the computation of the $\beta$-function. However, this problem persists in theories with chiral symmetry, where it complicates the determination of the $\beta$-function. These conclusions are supported by explicit calculations. Finally, the final section of the paper offers a discussion of these findings. We investigate neutrinoless double-beta decay occurring within colliders, focusing on the specific scenario where initial and final state nuclei are Majorana states. In this context, the standard beta decay amplitude is substituted with a term involving the product of two beta decay amplitudes, linked by an additional factor known as the Majorana overlap. This overlap represents a product of beta decay kinematic functions and encodes information about the vacuum expectation value of the Higgs field within the nuclear wave function. We examine the sensitivity of experimental searches for collider-based neutrinoless double-beta decay, incorporating constraints derived from laboratory studies of conventional beta decay. Our findings indicate that while this specific decay mode could be detected in the near future if the neutrino mass is non-zero, it will likely not constitute the primary method for achieving astrophysical limits on the effective Majorana neutrino mass. Furthermore, although the proposed decays could potentially contribute to event identification in collider experiments, their impact on achieving the necessary precision for neutrino mass measurements will be minimal. Consequently, the main utility of these decays lies in determining whether neutrino masses are predominantly Dirac or Majorana in nature. Finally, we have implemented a Fortran code capable of calculating both the beta decay amplitude and the Majorana overlap, which is made available to the community. This tool is designed to be easily adaptable to any beta decay formalism. Additionally, we have prepared a version of the code that includes constraints from beta decay experiments, allowing users to easily assess the detectability of collider neutrinoless double-beta decay. This functionality will be accessible via an online interface. Our findings will be published in Phys. Rev. D. [arXiv:2109.07700]. When two astronomical images are merged, their point spread functions (PSFs) do not simply add together. We introduce a method to model the combined image as a convolution with a new, effective PSF, accounting for variables like image scale, orientation, and the profiles of the individual PSFs. This approach is particularly valuable for photometry, as it enables the calculation of how stellar magnitude estimates are biased when stacked with other images. We have developed an open-source Python package, psf_combination, which implements this model and is available at https://github.com/brunob/psf_combination. Our method is broadly applicable, though it is optimized for cases where the individual PSFs follow a power-law or a Gaussian function. We provide illustrative examples using both synthetic and real data to demonstrate the model's effectiveness. Additionally, we show that the method's accuracy is highly sensitive to noise levels in the input images. Finally, we discuss the implications of image combination for detecting exoplanets via direct imaging.

Traditional methods for independently verifying quantum computation suffer from an exponential duration gap relative to modern algorithms. We present a solution to this by establishing validation with linear time complexity against the standard gate model. Our approach employs a quantum algorithm designed to verify classical computations, utilizing novel tools such as the analysis of non-interactive quantum proof systems and the specific duration characteristics of quantum circuits. We demonstrate that a single quantum query is sufficient to validate the traditional output of any quantum algorithm solving a specific problem class. Furthermore, we extend this guarantee to the simultaneous verification of multiple problems, provided their durations are scaled in proportion to their count. These findings are supported by applications, including the efficient verification of linear time quantum computation for graph problems like independent set and matching. Additionally, our construction reveals a novel, exponentially concise classical representation for any language recognizable by polynomial time quantum machines. Finally, we explore applications within the realm of classical verification. Specifically, we show that traditional independent validation of quantum computations is achievable in linear time only if the exponential sum-of-squares hierarchy collapses at its second level. More broadly, we generalize our main result to classical computation, establishing that traditional validation with duration $O(T(n))$ implies the existence of an $O(T(n)/\log(T(n)))$ time classical validation method. Consequently, the possibility of achieving linear time traditional validation for any exponential complexity problem class remains an open question. This work is the foundation for the research presented in arXiv:2101.01001v2. Furthermore, we extend our findings to the scenario where the traditional computation is permitted to produce an approximate answer. In this context, we demonstrate the traditional validation of any exponential complexity problem class using linear time, traditional accuracy, and minimal quantum resources. We also examine the trade-off between approximation quality and resource usage, thereby establishing the first traditional verification scheme for any exponential complexity problem class with linear time, high traditional accuracy, and low quantum resource usage. This completes the spectrum of traditional verification schemes for exponential complexity problem classes. This work is based on the research presented in arXiv:2101.01001v2 and arXiv:2103.05355v1. Additionally, we explore the challenge of traditional validation for quantum computation with sub-linear duration. We show that the quantum complexity class DTIME$(2^{o(n)})$ possesses an input-dependent input-size exponential lower bound on the time required for traditional validation. Blockchain technology is increasingly being adopted in the Internet of Things (IoT) to enhance transparency and trust. This paper introduces a framework for a transparent supply chain that leverages the primary advantages of blockchain, including decentralization, transparency, and immutability. Specifically, we present a practical deployment of a blockchain-based solution for food supply networks. Our approach utilizes cryptographic hash functions to create a transparent ledger for tracking food products, while smart contracts facilitate transparent transactions. Oracles are integrated to enable the IoT blockchains to interact with the external environment. We provide a detailed description of this framework and validate its effectiveness through a case study of a food supply network. The study demonstrates that our solution enables stakeholders to transparently monitor food items at every stage of the supply chain and establishes a secure, trustworthy environment for all participants. Additionally, we address the scalability of blockchain applications by analyzing the performance of our solution, with a focus on the data structure of the underlying distributed ledger. Finally, we outline the security challenges associated with such architectures and propose potential security enhancements. We conclude that blockchain offers a promising avenue for creating transparent supply chains. Furthermore, our proposed solution can be adapted for use in other sectors, such as the automotive industry. Given the current lack of research on the scalability of blockchain applications within the IoT domain, we believe this work holds significant scientific value. The source code for this solution is publicly available at https://github.com/akosk/Blockchain-Framework-for-Transparent-Supply-Chain. Document accessibility is crucial for individuals with disabilities, such as blindness, who face challenges in consuming standard print formats. This paper aims to identify the documents that are most accessible to non-traditional readers and to explore methods for accessibility enhancement. We introduce the concept of accessibility scores to facilitate the comparison of accessibility across different document types. Additionally, we present a case study examining the needs of students with reading difficulties and their approaches to accessing various documents. The insights gained from this study inform our selection of document formats yielding the highest accessibility scores. Our ultimate goal is to create a universal translator capable of converting any document format into the most accessible equivalent. We have developed a basic version of this translator and demonstrated its effectiveness through a series of experiments. The results indicate that converting documents to PDF/UA formats produces the highest accessibility scores. The paper concludes by outlining directions for future research. We anticipate that the document translators proposed in this work will assist in developing universal translators that can automatically adapt document formats to the specific needs of accessibility, readability, and security. Furthermore, the document scoring system introduced here is designed to be extensible for accommodating diverse user requirements. We also propose that accessibility scoring should become a standard metric for evaluating documents, similar to how security scoring is standard for assessing software. Finally, we intend to extend this scoring system to other user groups, such as students struggling with reading, to ensure that document formats optimize access for a broader range of individuals. Additionally, we plan to investigate the security implications of these document transformations, as well as the challenges and opportunities for authors and organizations in creating accessible documents. We introduce XLNet, a pretraining approach designed to address the inherent autoregressive nature of language modeling. Unlike BERT, which utilizes both directions of context simultaneously, our method employs an autoregressive training objective that leverages the positional information within the training sequence to predict unseen tokens. This autoregressive pretraining technique is applicable to any masked language modeling (MLM) model, enhancing BERT's performance on downstream tasks by up to 20%. Furthermore, when applied to the GLUE benchmark, XLNet surpasses BERT by an average margin of 7.8 points across 20 tasks, demonstrating its superiority on both standalone MLM tasks and downstream tasks. High-resolution stellar spectra can serve as a means to correct low-resolution observations of exoplanet transits, which are otherwise compromised by stellar activity. However, the degree to which this mitigation technique is effective remains uncertain. To address this, we developed a framework that integrates a realistic stellar activity model with a high-resolution exoplanet transit observation model. Our analysis indicates that, when employing a high-resolution instrument, a purely statistical approach to accounting for stellar activity is insufficient. Instead, we demonstrate that a high-resolution spectrum of the host star enables the characterization of both the temporal and spectral distribution of activity, thereby facilitating the derivation of a robust noise model for exoplanet transits. This noise model is expected to be critical for the future analysis of high-resolution transit data. We illustrate the application of this model using the HD 189733b system. Additionally, we have made our code, named HARO, accessible to the community. [abridged]

We investigate the development of constant curvature metrics on non-compact, $\frac 1 2$-isolated singular Riemann surfaces $M$ featuring prescribed cone angles $\beta_i \in (-1,0]$ at singular points $p_i$ and end behaviors $\beta_\infty \le 0$ at ends $z=\infty$. Our methodology involves solving a system of singular nonlinear elliptic equations on $M$ to identify conformal factors that transform a fixed conformal structure into a constant curvature metric characterized by these specific cone angles and end behaviors. This framework allows us to establish a existence theorem for hyperbolic metrics on $M$ (Theorem 1.1), addressing a question originally raised by J. Jost. Furthermore, we apply our findings to analyze the stability of constant curvature metrics near singularities, demonstrating that stability holds for metrics with negative curvature but fails in the case of zero curvature (Theorem 1.2). Additionally, we offer a novel proof of the Thurston Uniformization Theorem for annuli, which relies on the main existence result (Theorem 1.1). Finally, Theorem 1.3 presents a generalization of the Andreev theorem regarding discrete groups acting on $\mathbb{H}^2$. The initial section of the paper presents a general existence theorem for conformal factors that transform a given metric into a constant curvature metric, while the second section provides a uniqueness result under specific constraints. These two papers collectively present an alternative proof of the Andreev theorem. Furthermore, we introduce a new proof of the Thurmston Uniformization Theorem, which utilizes solutions to a system of singular nonlinear elliptic equations, thereby extending the application of this method to singular surfaces. The blocked discs method successfully generates two-dimensional masses channeled into a specific region through the obstruction of flat discs. By coordinating the placement and removal of these barrier discs, the system can produce two connected blocks, thereby simulating the blocking and unblocking processes characteristic of cellular automata. This approach offers a flexible framework for constructing one-dimensional cellular automata using two-dimensional blocked discs, enabling the creation of cellular computers and the automation of tasks. This paper outlines various designs for directed and undirected committed sequences, which serve as the foundational components of committed cellular automata. Furthermore, the discussion explores concepts such as the minimal blocking time, the optimal sequence of barrier disc operations, and the implementation of committed logic circuits. Finally, the potential applications of these committed logic circuits within cellular computers are considered. The proposed design for the directed committed counter machine, utilizing both low and high counters, achieves an optimal block size of $4\times 20$. Additionally, the design for the undirected committed counter machine with a single counter, based on the optimal blocked disc counter machine, results in a block size of $6\times 10$. The design for a counter machine with two counters relies on a non-optimal blocked disc counter machine, yielding a block size of $8\times 16$. The methodology for the two-dimensional blocked disc committed counter machine can be adapted to design the corresponding high-level committed counter machine with both low and high counters, potentially reducing the block size from $8\times 16$ to $4\times 16$. Keywords: blocked disc, blocked disc counter machine, blocked disc committed counter machine, committed sequence, committed logic circuit, cellular computer.

Non-affine deformation, a phenomenon often observed in jammed systems, refers to the asymmetric nature of local deformations, which are typically modeled using the non-affine parameter $\xi^2$. This study presents a straightforward method to measure $\xi^2$ via small-angle light scattering in two-dimensional systems. We apply this technique to both quasicrystals and the amorphous solid transition, analyzing how $\xi^2$ varies with density and stress. Furthermore, we demonstrate that $\xi^2$ can be derived from the structure factor by examining a Gaussian approximation of the displacement field. This approach proves advantageous for jammed systems where nonaffinity arises from both entropic and energetic factors. Finally, we show that $\xi^2$ can be linked to the compressibility modulus through a simple linearized analysis of the scattering function. This finding is validated by comparing our results against data from both numerical simulations and experimental studies. Our findings indicate that near the amorphous solid-liquid transition, $\xi^2$ exhibits a linear dependence on density, whereas in jammed packings, it scales linearly with excess stress. These results provide strong support for the criticality hypothesis regarding the glass transition. Additionally, our findings corroborate the stress-induced melting model for jammed packings, which posits that the system melts when excess stress surpasses the characteristic stress of thermal fluctuations. This paper offers a comprehensive analysis of the weakening, cut, and embedding rules within substructural logics of inorder and order properties, specifically within the hypersequent framework. We introduce a variant of the cut rule designed for formulas embedded in sequents. Our primary findings include the decidability of satisfiability and the $\coNP$-completeness of the associated decision problem for these logics. Furthermore, we present a hypersequent embedding for BGIP (the logic corresponding to the Gödel implication pseudocommutativity property) that retains the cut rule; this rule applies to embedded sequents and enables a more straightforward demonstration of satisfiability decidability. Finally, we extend this embedding to various combinations of substructural logics involving involution and dualizing properties, demonstrating that satisfiability remains $\coNP$-complete for the resulting logics. These findings offer a substantial framework for understanding the characteristics of substructural logics through various hypersequent embeddings. Notably, our results surpass previous complexity bounds for similar embedding problems in modal logics and substructural systems. Additionally, we establish the PSPACE-completeness of the corresponding decision problem for these logics when formulated within the single-structured (sequent) setting. *This research was conducted during the first author's visit to the University of Oxford as an Oxford University Visiting Fellow.* Keywords: substructural logics, hypersequents, cut rules, embedding rules, complexity.

This paper introduces a robustness formulation for cyber-physical systems, which integrate computational control software with physical components. Specifically, the task involves finding a control input to ensure a software-controlled physical system remains within a specified safe region defined by a temporal logic formula, even under input disturbances. Temporal logic allows for the precise specification of complex trajectories within this safe region. The proposed approach is grounded in Signal Temporal Logic (STL), a formalism designed to describe time-dependent behaviors and evaluate them against specific trajectories. To address the robustness of the generated trajectories, the study introduces a robustness metric that quantifies the "margin" by which a trajectory deviates from the boundaries of the logic formula. This metric indicates how much perturbation a trajectory can withstand while remaining valid. Furthermore, the paper demonstrates how to efficiently compute both the degree of robustness and the robustness gradient for STL formulas representing time intervals. Finally, the method is validated through numerical experiments. The results indicate that incorporating the robustness constraint into the trajectory generation process yields a more robust solution for the task, and numerical comparisons confirm the effectiveness of this approach. Additionally, the paper explores the relationship between STL-derived robustness and Input-to-State Safety (ISS), a fundamental control theory concept used for analyzing system robustness. It highlights that STL-derived robustness can be viewed as a trajectory-based extension of ISS, offering a more expressive and task-specific means to assess robustness in cyber-physical systems. Finally, the authors outline potential applications of this robustness notion in various control tasks, such as learning control policies for robotic systems and planning missions for autonomous vehicles. This work investigates the distributional solutions of a specific nonlinear diffusion equation (1.1) across a wide class of non-compact manifolds $M$ that possess non-negative Ricci curvature. The objective is to establish key properties of these solutions, including their non-negativity, integrability, and the validity of the gradient structure $(1.3)$ in the sense of measures. To achieve this, we introduce and utilize gradient approximations for both the source term $f$ and the diffusion operator $\Delta_p$. The analysis encompasses scenarios where $M$ is sigma-compact or possesses finite volume. Our findings rely on specific functional analytic characteristics of the Steklov-Poincaré operator linked to the Laplacian on $M$. Furthermore, the proof methodology is adaptable to other $p$-diffusion equations of the form $\Delta_p u + \nabla V \cdot \nabla u^p + v u = f$. As an application, the theory is employed to derive solutions to the Yamabe equation on manifolds with non-negative Ricci curvature. The developed gradient approximation framework is expected to be a valuable instrument for researchers working on nonlinear elliptic equations on manifolds. Additionally, we establish new regularity results for weak solutions, enhancing the findings of Cabré and Kowalczyk (2018) regarding the Yamabe equation. Our approach to proving the uniqueness of weak solutions also yields new insights into the positive uniqueness radius for the Yamabe problem. Finally, we demonstrate that the distributional solutions identified here possess sufficient regularity to satisfy the differential equation pointwise. This study investigates the angular dimensions and source counts of compact, faint radio sources using a stacking analysis of the 1.4 GHz LOFAR Two-metre Sky Survey (LoTSS) and the First Hubble Deep Field (F8502). The research examines sources with a flux density of $S_{1.4GHz} \geq 0.5$ mJy across various redshifts, utilizing photometric redshift estimates derived from deep optical imaging of the F8502 field. Results indicate that the average full width at half maximum (FWHM) angular size for these compact sources is approximately 1.5 arcsec, though there is significant dispersion around this mean. The source counts for compact, faint objects are found to be roughly 1.5 times higher than those of extended sources, and the fraction of compact sources rises as flux density decreases. Furthermore, the study explores the potential link between the angular dimensions of compact radio sources and their star formation rates, noting that radio morphology may serve as an indicator of star formation activity. Finally, the paper examines the relationship between these sources and starbursts, as well as their association with galaxies exhibiting low star formation rates. These findings are essential for understanding the source population within this faint regime. The derived average angular size and source counts for compact, faint radio sources can be utilized to estimate the number of such sources in other fields lacking deep optical imaging. Additionally, the source counts for compact, faint galaxies are compared with predictions from galaxy evolution models. Ultimately, the study demonstrates that stacking analysis is a highly effective method for characterizing compact, faint radio sources. These results have significant implications for the proposed Square Kilometre Array (SKA) and its anticipated discovery of numerous compact, faint sources. We introduce a new category of data flow models termed "concealed Markov models" (COMMs). This class extends hidden Markov models (HMMs) by permitting data to be emitted in arbitrary quantities from any state, rather than limiting emissions to single items. To provide a cohesive mathematical framework for handling "quantity-based" data flow, we utilize the concept of "abstract monads." This approach offers a unified language for describing the behavior of data sources, the analysis of data by sensors, and the coupling between these two entitiesaguall.

Computationally, COMMs serve as a general framework for modeling data flow behavior, extending applicability beyond traditional sequential models to systems where data is processed in batches. Furthermore, they enable the calculation of the likelihood that a specific data sequence originates from a particular data source.

To achieve this, we first establish the monadic framework for quantity-based data flow. Subsequently, we demonstrate how COMMs can be constructed from HMMs and how they can be viewed as collections of associated probability distributions. Finally, we illustrate the utility of COMMs by abstracting the behavior of various real-world data sources, such as keyboard inputs and network traffic.

The theoretical foundation for this work is drawn from category theory, where monads function as an abstract representation of data flow behavior. This allows for the definition of "computation with uncertainty" in a manner that is independent of any specific computational model.

This study introduces the concept of statistical nonlocality, which arises from the interplay between spatial and temporal scales in the evolution of complex systems. The framework is grounded in the principle of statistical non-invasiveness, which asserts that a system's internal complexity is preserved when its components interact only through locally measured fields. We demonstrate that structures evolving under the rules of locally interacting cellular automata exhibit significant deviations from this principle. To address this mismatch, we propose a class of models based on dynamically consistent structures, which integrate both spatial and temporal non-locality. These models serve as a valuable tool for investigating the formation of large-scale self-organized structures within cellular automata. Furthermore, we examine the dynamics of such structures and identify a unique mechanism for large-scale pattern formation driven by their behavior. Our findings suggest that analogous mechanisms are inherent to the evolution of complex systems in both physical and biological domains. This study examines a blackbody thermodynamic system subject to the Casimir effect, where the energy spectrum is altered by imposing periodic boundary conditions on the standing electromagnetic waves within the cavity. Although the shift in the zero-point energy density caused by this effect is known to be significant, standard thermodynamic analysis reveals that contributions from excited states are negligible. In contrast, we demonstrate through explicit calculation that, when the system is subject to the ultraviolet divergence of blackbody radiation, the changes in thermodynamic potentials resulting from the shifts in zero-point and excited-state energy densities are of comparable magnitude. Furthermore, our explicit calculations indicate that these shifts do not vanish in the limit of large cavities. These findings suggest that the common argument regarding the negligibility of excited-state contributions is flawed. Finally, we offer a resolution to this paradox. Notably, this analysis is independent of the specific form of the mode energy density. Additionally, it is worth mentioning that the implications of these results extend beyond the context of Casimir's phenomenon. Specifically, if one were to accept the standard thermodynamic results, the only way to explain the finite change in energy density would be to assume that the space surrounding the blackbody is not empty but filled with a finite number of excited photons. This would imply that the universe is surrounded by a cloud of real photons, a concept that contradicts the conventional understanding of blackbody radiation. Consequently, the issue of ultraviolet divergence in blackbody radiation is not merely a technical problem of renormalization but also a fundamental one. It appears that the only viable solution is to acknowledge that the change in zero-point energy density is indeed significant, as the calculations clearly show. This conclusion is consistent with the results of our previous work. Finally, we suggest that further research is needed to explore the implications of these findings in greater detail. For instance, it would be valuable to investigate whether these results have any implications for the concept of quantum vacuum energy. If so, this could have profound implications for our understanding of quantum gravity and cosmology. In this regard, we believe that our findings could provide a new perspective on the problem of quantum vacuum energy, which has been a subject of intense debate for many years. In summary, our findings suggest that the change in zero-point energy density is indeed significant, and that the standard thermodynamic analysis needs to be revised to take this into account. This has important implications for our understanding of quantum vacuum energy and its role in the universe. This paper introduces a new privacy metric called "privacy under conditional expectations." Unlike prior measures that rely on probability thresholds, this metric evaluates the average reduction in uncertainty regarding a location's privacy, calculated based on the conditional expectation of the entropy difference before and after revealing the location. We assess this metric across various location tracking systems. Our findings indicate that for most tracked locations, the source of the signal is the primary entity exposing the location, rather than the tracking system itself. Additionally, we propose several improvements to existing tracking systems to further enhance location privacy under conditional expectations. We acknowledge that no system can guarantee absolute privacy for every location; however, we argue that the goal should be to minimize the number of locations with the highest risk of being exposed. To address this, we present four novel privacy-preserving protocols designed to identify and protect highly sensitive locations. These protocols leverage the concept of "privacy under conditional expectations" to safeguard user sensitivity without compromising the tracking system's objectives. We demonstrate the effectiveness of these protocols through a simulation based on real-world data. Ultimately, our approach aims to strike a balance between privacy and utility by utilizing an optimization framework that maximizes the count of protected locations under a specific utility constraint. This constraint is defined by the expected number of locations where the tracking system can achieve its utility goals, such as reducing user uncertainty about their whereabouts. We provide a detailed analysis of our proposed method and conclude that it successfully identifies and protects the majority of highly sensitive locations. Furthermore, we show that the protection of these sensitive locations does not significantly hinder the tracking system's utility. In summary, our method effectively strikes the optimal trade-off between privacy and utility for location tracking systems. To the best of our knowledge, this represents the first method to address the privacy-utility dilemma in location tracking. We believe this work holds significant potential for driving future advancements in the field. Additionally, our method is general-purpose and can be adapted to other domains where protecting sensitive user data is essential, such as mobile health applications. We anticipate that our work will inspire further research into privacy preservation for mobile health, which remains an underexplored area. This paper introduces NDT-Transformer, a new network designed for training large-scale Normal Distribution Transform (NDT) models using 3D point clouds. NDT is a state-of-the-art alignment technique that estimates a probabilistic model for an unknown environment based on point cloud data, determining a best alignment pose for incoming data. However, NDT is a non-convex optimization method prone to converging to local minima, which is particularly problematic in ambiguous scenes like open oceans. Transformer-based networks have recently shown superior performance in computer vision by capturing long-range dependencies and global relationships. We adapt these transformers to localize poses under the NDT framework, enhancing both performance and efficiency. NDT-Transformer is trained on extensive public datasets, including the 6.2 million images from KITTI and 1.2 million images from Mapillary Vistas. Our method achieves a 10x reduction in Root Mean Square Error (RMSE) compared to nets2vec and 5x compared to NDT-Net. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/Chenchenchenchen/NDT-Transformer. Furthermore, we will release additional public datasets and pre-trained models to support reproducibility and facilitate further research. Resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging (rs-fMRI) connectivity is essential for both understanding brain organization and investigating brain-related disorders. However, the reliability of connectivity metrics derived from finite, noisy rs-fMRI data remains a critical yet underexplored issue. This study introduces a statistical framework to evaluate prediction precision and signal-to-noise ratio within connectivity networks. We developed a high-dimensional connectivity model that accounts for noise correlations within local brain regions, utilizing a sparse precision matrix to identify critical connections. Furthermore, we created a prediction metric that quantifies the precision of connectivity estimation. By applying this framework to public fMRI datasets, we assessed the reproducibility of connectivity patterns across multiple sites. Our results indicate that while signal strength varies by site, prediction precision remains consistent across all sites. Additionally, we observed that prediction precision diminishes as the number of connections increases, suggesting that extensive connectivity cannot be reliably inferred from short-duration rs-fMRI scans. These findings offer valuable guidance for designing connectivity experiments and interpreting reproducibility in multi-site rs-fMRI studies. We examine a beeping network consisting of $n$ nodes, where each node operates in one of two modes: sleeping or awake (capable of listening and transmitting). Communication occurs through "beeping," defined as a scenario where a sleeping node and an awake node simultaneously access a shared wireless channel. The network's objective is to enable any pair of nodes to exchange messages within a specific time frame while minimizing total sleep-mode power consumption. We establish both upper and lower bounds on the total sleep-mode power consumption required to facilitate message delivery between nodes in both worst-case and best-case scenarios. Furthermore, we propose a distributed algorithm that achieves an optimal worst-case bound on sleep-mode power consumption. Additionally, we explore how these results apply to distributed computing environments where nodes are subject to a locality constraint. Specifically, we demonstrate that when the locality constraint is set to $O(\log n)$, the bounds previously derived for worst-case and best-case sleep-mode power consumption remain virtually unchanged. Finally, we illustrate how to adapt our message delivery protocol to satisfy the locality constraint by introducing a novel distributed data structure known as "beeping network registers." This structure enables distributed nodes to read and write data with sub-logarithmic locality. Leveraging this beeping network register, we successfully adapt our message delivery protocol to meet the locality constraint while preserving optimality regarding sleep-mode power consumption. Our findings are supported by both theoretical analysis and experimental validation. To the best of our knowledge, this represents the first investigation into sleep-mode power-efficient communication protocols for beeping networks within the context of distributed computing. Furthermore, our work presents the first theoretical bounds on sleep-mode power consumption for such networks under locality constraints and introduces the beeping network register, the inaugural distributed data structure designed for power-efficient communication in beeping networks. This structure holds significant potential for future research aimed at developing power-efficient distributed computing systems. This study employs first-principles calculations to analyze the superconducting transition temperature of sulfur within the H$_3$S environment, focusing on isotopic effects and pressure variations. Our findings indicate that the phonon-deformation potential (DP) is not uniform across all electronic states. Specifically, the DP is significantly smaller for electronic states near the Fermi level compared to those around the van Hove singularity (VS). Consequently, the DP exhibits notable variability depending on the chemical environment. Furthermore, the VS shifts with changing environmental conditions, thereby altering the vibrational characteristics of the system. These results underscore the importance of considering DP's dependence on electronic states when investigating superconducting materials. Additionally, the sulfur atom's contribution to the DP is significantly lower than that of hydrogen atoms, suggesting that hydrogen atoms play a more critical role in the superconducting properties of H$_3$S. This study provides a theoretical basis for exploring the superconducting mechanisms of other high-temperature superconductors. Finally, the variable nature of the DP offers a new perspective for explaining the isotope effect in H$_3$S. The accompanying code is publicly accessible at https://github.com/zhijunwang1986/Phonon-superconductivity. Furthermore, the methodology employed in this research is applicable to investigating the DP in other materials. This paper introduces a new approach for generating spatial restrictions to support motion planning and control of agents within dynamic environments. Our primary objective is to identify feasible, connected regions of the configuration space that agents can occupy, ensuring these regions are robust against environmental uncertainties and D-class complete. We propose two methods for spatial restriction creation: the Spatial Restriction Creation (SRC) method and its extension, the Generalized Spatial Restriction Creation (G-SRC) method. The G-SRC method is designed to handle scenarios where agents must remain within the reach of a specific tool, such as a robotic arm's end-effector. Both approaches utilize a set of uncertainty-bounded regions derived from the environment and the agent's own uncertainty to define spatial constraints. Furthermore, we provide theoretical proofs demonstrating the computational complexity of these methods and their ability to produce motion plans that remain feasible despite uncertainties. Finally, we validate the effectiveness of our approach through various simulation-based experiments. The results indicate that planning with an appropriate set of uncertainty regions enables agents to avoid dynamic obstacles and obstacles with holes. Additionally, our method successfully generates motion plans for both a simulated agent and a tool-restricted agent (a simulated robot arm with a gripper) in dynamic settings. Our findings show that this method is effective for agents of any size and can produce plans in a higher dimensionality configuration space than traditional motion planning algorithms. Furthermore, the method is applicable to a broader range of agents than tool motion planning, as it does not rely on a tool. Finally, the proposed methods are computationally efficient, as they reduce the dimensionality of the configuration space and the number of obstacles during the planning phase. To the best of our knowledge, this method is the first to address the joint problem of spatial restriction creation and tool motion planning in dynamic settings. The method is implemented in Python and will be made available as open-source software. This work was supported by the National Science Foundation under Grant No. 1909067. This paper introduces a new visual relocalization approach that integrates learned descriptors with surface normal vectors to achieve robust 3D relocalization. Unlike traditional methods relying on manual design, our technique learns image features to efficiently exploit the geometric context of 3D scenes. To fully leverage 3D geometry, we incorporate surface normals, represented as surfels, into these features. Furthermore, we apply a learned transformation to standard visual features, enhancing their ability to withstand significant viewpoint changes. Experimental results demonstrate that our method surpasses state-of-the-art techniques. In the KITTI benchmark, we secured first place in the 3D relocalization challenge, achieving an average precision of 75.0% and a recall of 71.5%. Additionally, we attained first place in the semantic visual relocalization task within the same challenge, reaching an accuracy of 75.6% and a recall of 70.0%. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/alex-pfurgell/surfel_map.
