The Monte Carlo Quasi-Maximum Likelihood (MCQML) estimator is a computationally efficient alternative to the standard maximum likelihood estimator (MLE). This paper examines the asymptotic behavior of the MCQML estimator within a class of nonlinear time series models that include threshold autoregressive models as a subset. Our analysis demonstrates that the MCQML estimator consistently converges to the quasi-MLE derived from the Q-procedure introduced by Chen and Linton (2002, J. Econometrics). Furthermore, we establish that the resulting QMLE based on the Q-procedure is both $n$-consistent and $\sqrt{n}$-asymptotically normal. This finding is significant because it confirms the validity of applying standard likelihood-based inference to the more computationally efficient MCQML estimator. Additionally, our results extend and enhance the convergence proofs provided by Chen and Linton (2002) for specific models, offering a more general framework for convergence proofs applicable to a broader range of nonlinear time series models. Finally, a simulation study indicates that the finite sample performance of QML computed via the Q-procedure is comparable to that of the traditional MLE. This article explores the relationship between the Vassiliev characteristic of order three and the Frankl distance within the power set of a finite set. It demonstrates that the characteristic can be expressed as a linear combination of distances between powers, where the weights correspond to the weights of the Dynkin diagram associated with the pure braid group. The interplay between antiferromagnetism and nematicity in iron-based superconductors is a subject of significant interest. While BaFe$_2$As$_2$ exhibits both ordered states below its structural transition temperature $T_{\rm s}$, the coexistence of these phases in LiFeAs remains unclear. This study investigates the nematic order in LiFeAs using a spin-fluctuation theory. Our findings indicate that, despite LiFeAs undergoing a first-order structural transition at $T_{\rm s}$, nematic order does not emerge. Based on our results, we propose that the structural transition in LiFeAs is driven by spin fluctuations. This study introduces a set of neuroevolutionary algorithms designed to train particle systems for self-assembly. These methods aim to generate materials with targeted structural and mechanical properties by optimizing the interaction potentials of individual particles. Additionally, neuroevolution is employed to accelerate the formation of the desired target structures. The algorithms rely on particle-swapping procedures inspired by artificial neural networks, where interaction potentials are represented as weighted connections between particle states. Their versatility is demonstrated across three self-assembly scenarios: forming crystalline materials from spherical particles, creating jammed structures from non-spherical particles, and assembling functional devices from particle systems with multiple degrees of freedom. Furthermore, advanced mechanical properties, such as those found in shape memory materials, can be engineered through these methods. Ultimately, this work offers a comprehensive toolkit for material design, capable of producing a wide range of synthetic materials with specific characteristics. By integrating design and simulation, these approaches facilitate a data-driven methodology for materials science. Furthermore, they provide a means to explore the complex phase diagrams of soft materials, thereby advancing materials science through high-throughput computational design. Finally, the tools are applied to address open challenges in shape-memory materials, including the development of materials with memory capacity and those capable of learning new shapes. Consequently, we deduce local ill-posedness for these equations when initial data lie in $B_{p, 1}^{-1+\frac{3}{p}}$ for $1 \leq p < \infty$. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the steady Navier-Stokes equations are ill-posed in the critical homogeneous Besov space $B_{p, p}^{-1+\frac{3}{p}}$ for $1 < p \leq \infty$. These findings extend the results of S. Kato (2006) regarding critical well-posedness. Additionally, the techniques employed herein enable an alternative proof of local ill-posedness for the Navier-Stokes equations in the critical homogeneous Lebesgue space $L^{\infty}$. Finally, we provide a proof of the nonexistence of boundary layer solutions in $B_{p, p}^{-1+\frac{3}{p}}$ for $1 < p \leq \infty$ as $t$ approaches $0$ from above. This work investigates the equation of state for magnon-based equation-of-state gases, a framework defined by thermal pressure, thermal compression, and spectral displacement. Within this model, thermal pressure arises from both Pauli blocking and the statistics of bosonic magnons. These phenomena characterize magnon gases near their saturation point and are essential for understanding magnon condensation. Specifically, thermal pressure drives thermal compression, a process that stabilizes magnon gases by mitigating magnon condensation. Furthermore, Pauli blocking induces spectral displacement, which alters the magnon spectrum. These mechanisms are pivotal for magnonics, governing the generation, propagation, and interaction of magnons. Specifically, thermal compression regulates the density of magnon waves, while spectral displacement enables the excitation, detection, and manipulation of magnon condensates. These concepts are demonstrated using antiferromagnetic dielectrics. Notably, thermal compression exhibits a non-monotonic dependence on temperature, a feature that can be detected through terahertz spectroscopy of magnon spectral density. Ultimately, the equation-of-state magnon gas provides a comprehensive framework for modeling magnon generation, propagation, and interactions. This model is particularly significant in contexts involving magnon condensates, magnon Bose-Einstein condensation, and magnon superfluidity. Loidreau's code-based cryptography relies on the hardness of decoding general linear codes to construct public key systems, including public key encryption and digital signatures. This paper introduces a public key encryption scheme utilizing constant weight codes, which achieves a reduced key size compared to Loidreau's original proposal. The theoretical framework for this scheme is established, and a digital signature scheme is also suggested. The proposed public key encryption system was simulated, revealing that the decryption process is significantly faster than in the original system, with only a slight increase in encryption speed. Additionally, the public and secret key sizes are substantially smaller, and both the modulus and error code dimensions are noted to be reduced. Furthermore, the computational complexity for solving the decoding problem is assessed, demonstrating that it remains essentially unchanged. Finally, a public key encryption scheme was proposed where the public key consists of a matrix with a rank no greater than 2, resulting in a dramatically diminished key size. Regarding the latter proposal, the simulation outcomes indicate a very slight decrease in encryption speed compared to Loidreau's original system, while decryption speed is substantially faster. Similarly, the sizes of the public and secret keys are reduced, and the generalized dimension of the error code is smaller. The complexity of public key decryption is also evaluated, showing no significant change. Ultimately, this paper introduces two novel public key encryption schemes; numerical simulations confirm that their performance is comparable to Loidreau's original system. Future work will explore the application of the second proposed public key system to the construction of digital signature schemes.

This study derives the volume and range of the minimal spanning complex and the corresponding linear embedding for a random simplex complex within a random Poisson point process in Euclidean space, as the embedding dimension approaches infinity. Additionally, we establish a general formula applicable to various geometric random complexes. These findings demonstrate that, as the embedding dimension increases, the relative range of the minimal spanning complex converges to zero. Furthermore, we derive estimates for the characteristics of continuity diagrams associated with multivariate data sets. Specifically, we prove that the number of minimal spanning acycles, which represent data gaps, exponentially approaches zero as the embedding dimension grows toward infinity. Consequently, we conclude that topological data analysis methods based on minimal spanning acycles are viable for such analyses. Finally, we examine the application of this technique to the "noisy sphere" problem. Our results indicate that both the number of components and the number of 1-holes of the minimal spanning complex for a noisy sphere converge to the expected number of components and 1-holes of a sphere, respectively, as the embedding dimension tends to infinity. This demonstrates that the method successfully recovers the fundamental topological invariants of the underlying shape. These conclusions are supported by numerical experiments. The paper also includes a discussion of the novel approach employed to derive these results. Notably, the formula for the expected volume of the limits of minimal spanning acycles holds significant potential for applications in multivariate data analysis. Specifically, it can be utilized to identify the optimal embedding dimension for constructing topological models of data sets. The formula's effectiveness is illustrated through numerical experiments involving data sets generated from the 2-sphere, 2-torus, and the real projective plane. In these experiments, the distance from the data set to the Fubini-Study metric was used as an indicator of the quality of the topological model. The analysis reveals that the distance to the Fubini-Study metric decreases as the embedding dimension increases, with a marked decrease occurring at embedding dimensions of 7 or greater. This suggests that embedding dimensions of 7 or higher are optimal for constructing topological models of data sets derived from the 2-sphere, 2-torus, and real projective plane. These results align with the theoretical analysis of the optimal embedding dimension for topological data analysis. The optimal embedding dimension is calculated by determining the minimal embedding dimension required to reduce the volume of the limit of the minimal spanning complex to no more than 1% of the volume of the data set. Vertical Federated Learning (VFL) represents a privacy-preserving framework where multiple parties possessing distinct data from different perspectives collaborate to train joint machine learning models. However, when parties utilize heterogeneous models, the specific functional roles of each participant within the collective remain ambiguous. This paper leverages such role information to design a novel multi-party learning framework termed Vertical Federated Education (VFE). By conceptualizing the learning process as an interaction between an "educator" and a "student," VFE enables the educator to regulate the student's acquisition of a target model through two distinct strategies: soft and hard assaults. The soft assault aims to prevent the student from reaching a specific accuracy threshold, whereas the hard assault ensures the student can successfully decode a steganographic message. We propose a naive implementation for both methods and validate them using the MNIST and FashionMNIST datasets. Experimental results demonstrate that VFE can effectively manage the student's learning trajectory, successfully obscuring the specific capabilities of the model the student obtains. Furthermore, we reveal that VFE introduces a trade-off between privacy and efficiency, showing that the time required for the student to learn a model is inversely proportional to the assault strength. Finally, we explore the application of VFE in a new context known as Model-as-a-Service (Maas), where we illustrate how the educator-student dynamic can regulate the cost of accessing a model. Our findings indicate that VFE can significantly reduce the expenses for users seeking to access models. Consequently, we propose VFE as a promising practical application for future research. Intelligent Urban Defense (IUD) represents a growing field within artificial intelligence, encompassing diverse applications such as air defense, autonomous ground vehicles, and resource management under socio-cyber-physical attacks. This paper introduces the Intelligent Urban Defense Game (IUDG), a board game designed to foster research and development in the realm of tactical resource administration amidst multi-domain urban assaults. The IUDG features two players: one controlling a city and its various subsystems, and the other acting as an adversary with resources across multiple cyber domains. Through a series of discrete time steps, both players expend their respective assets to damage the other's systems. The scenario is multi-criteria, as the defender must balance defending against diverse threats while managing economic and social criteria. We detail the game's rules and provide a novel task specification for tasking systems, which involves learning tactical tasking policies to execute actions at each time step. Furthermore, we establish performance metrics to evaluate these policies and demonstrate their training and evaluation using deep reinforcement learning. The IUDG serves as an effective tool for developing intelligent systems capable of tactical tasking and resource management in complex, multi-domain urban environments. We examine Hawking–Page phase transitions for black stars confined within a cavity, determining the specific thermodynamic conditions under which these events occur. These results are highly relevant for modeling small remnants of black holes that may result from the high-energy Big Bang. Our analysis reveals that for Schwarzschild geometry, small black holes behave similarly to standard large black holes, whereas de Sitter and anti-de Sitter small black holes exhibit distinct thermal properties. Specifically, remnant black holes possessing small black hole entropy and internal structure demonstrate unique characteristics, including the potential for internal structure to trigger thermal instability. Furthermore, remnant black holes are found to be thermally stable within a narrow temperature range, a phenomenon that may manifest as a peak in their entropy. Additionally, we observe that remnant black holes can undergo Hawking–Page transitions, leading to the formation of larger black holes. This phase transition may offer an explanation for why black holes in our universe appear to possess a minimum size. Finally, we explore the possibility of a complete black hole remnant evaporation cycle, which would prevent the loss of information into the cosmic void. This outcome aligns with the principle that information must be conserved. We also address the related issue of whether a final remnant can exist, concluding that it is possible provided the remnant retains a finite-size horizon. In this scenario, the remnant functions as a black hole with a temperature near the Planck scale, ensuring it does not evaporate completely. Consequently, the information originally contained within the black hole remains preserved within the remnant. These findings suggest that the Big Bang successfully resolved the black hole information paradox. To further support this conclusion, we examine the issue of whether a final remnant can exist, examining the properties of theories that could facilitate its formation. Label scarcity is a prevalent challenge in graph classification tasks. To address this, we introduce a novel pseudo-labeling framework designed to enable graph neural networks to generate high-quality pseudo-labels under limited annotated data conditions. This approach is straightforward and efficient, comprising two core components: the Pseudo-Tagging Module (PTM) and the Pseudo-Label Refinement Module (PRM). The entire process is orchestrated by a dynamically updated knowledge base. Experimental evaluations across multiple datasets demonstrate that our method outperforms state-of-the-art approaches. The AWAKE experiment at CERN's Large Hadron Collider aims to demonstrate the viability of Self-Modulation and Plasma Wakefield Acceleration (SWFA) as a method for particle acceleration. To validate this technique, proton beams are utilized to generate a plasma, while electron beams are accelerated within this plasma to demonstrate enhanced energy gain. This study presents a detailed analysis of betatron radiation emitted by electrons during SWFA, incorporating magnetic focusing effects from the proton beam. The research compares radiation predictions from various models against available experimental data, covering both AWAKE Run 2 trials and potential future experiments. The results indicate that SWFA could produce detectable betatron radiation using existing detectors. Furthermore, detecting this radiation would offer a valuable tool for characterizing plasma formation and beam dynamics. Ultimately, this approach may facilitate real-time feedback control of wakefield acceleration, thereby advancing the development of plasma accelerators.

This work introduces a framework for distributed decision tree learning under differential privacy (DPDTL), integrating a general distributed decision tree learning algorithm with differentially private local histogram estimation. The integration relies on two critical properties: first, the base algorithm must admit a specific histogram estimation mechanism as a special case; second, it must adhere to the composition property of differential privacy. We demonstrate that integrating the proposed DP histogram estimation mechanism preserves privacy within these base algorithms. Furthermore, we extend two established distributed decision tree learning methods—Randomized Node Split (RNS) and Parameterized Histogram (PH)—to function effectively in local differential privacy settings. We establish precise privacy bounds for the proposed mechanisms and empirically validate their performance on this paper and the DPDTL algorithm through extensive experiments. Our results show that, with minimal accuracy loss, the proposed mechanisms can substantially scale up the number of samples permitted in practical distributed decision tree learning scenarios. This paper introduces a variational approach based on regularized minimization of the $k$-th order Rényi divergence, designed to enforce a log-concave probability density structure for image probability measures. This divergence effectively quantifies distribution differences, with its limiting case recovering the well-known Kullback-Leibler divergence. The study provides a complete analysis of the minimization problem and its solution properties, demonstrating that the regularization stabilizes the otherwise ill-posed task of adjusting a density to minimize Rényi divergence against a data fidelity term. Numerical experiments illustrate the method's application in image denoising and labeling, highlighting its performance as a kernel-based alternative to Gaussian Markov Random Field-based regularization. Furthermore, the paper develops a Bregman proximal gradient algorithm utilizing the specific geometry of Rényi divergence and proves the asymptotic convergence of this iterative scheme. Finally, numerical experiments confirm the efficiency of the proposed algorithm. The code is accessible at https://github.com/andreaferrari1983/regularized_renyi_divergence. This research was partially conducted while the first author was a postdoctoral researcher at the University of Paderborn. A portion of this work appeared in the 2021 IEEE International Conference on Image Processing (ICIP), held in Orlando, Florida, USA, from August 12–15, 2021. This version incorporates several enhancements, including more comprehensive proofs and numerical experiments, and implements a new kernel-based approach to Rényi divergence that achieves the KL divergence limit as $k \to 1$. Although the focus remains on 2D images, the methods are applicable to any dimension. Furthermore, Rényi divergence offers additional flexibility compared to KL divergence, allowing control over the balance between fidelity and regularization, a feature explored in the numerical results. Key innovations include: (i) a novel kernel-based approximation of Rényi divergence for discrete measures; (ii) a new kernel-based approximation of the entropy term; and (iii) a new kernel-based approximation of the KL divergence within the Reynolds limit, all of which offer improved numerical stability. These advancements are detailed in Sections 3, 5, and 6, respectively. Additionally, Section 6 presents an analysis of the method's performance. Chain event analysis (CEA) is a structured interview method designed to gather data on how decision-makers evaluate options. These decisions are influenced by multiple factors, including stated preferences, perceived risks, and performance metrics. By constraining respondents to allocate a limited number of points or to make consistent choices across different tasks, chain event networks (CENs) ensure that the data collected is internally consistent. Bayesian methods are increasingly utilized to analyze CEA data due to their ability to handle small sample sizes and their capacity to integrate prior knowledge. Although a prior study established consistency within a specific class of CENs, the broader space of general CENs remains largely unexplored. This work addresses that gap by proposing a framework for model selection based on Bayesian model comparison, which is essential for Bayesian analysis. We demonstrate the application of this framework for selecting the most appropriate CE N model using a dataset focusing on the criteria considered by consumers when purchasing a new mobile phone. The results indicate that CE N models featuring between two and four arcs per node provide the best balance between model fit and complexity. Furthermore, we conclude with recommendations for future research regarding the application of this framework in other contexts. Additionally, the accompanying R package, ceno, offers functions to facilitate the implementation of this framework. The package is available at https://github.com/QuantitativeDecisionAnalysis/ceno. We introduce a robust asymptotic framework for analyzing a dynamic approach rooted in gradient descent, designed to minimize the Tikhonov regularization functional. This method ensures convergence to the minimum norm solution for linear ill-posed problems affected by noisy data. Our analysis demonstrates that the gradient descent algorithm's convergence speed can be substantially enhanced by employing Bregman iteration, which effectively mitigates the typically slow convergence associated with minimizing Tikhonov regularization functionals. Furthermore, we examine a family of dynamical systems that weakly converge toward the minimum norm solution. These systems are mechanically interpretable through a generalized heavy ball method incorporating Tikhonov regularization and damping. Specifically, we identify a particular undamped system exhibiting strong convergence to this solution. Additionally, we provide a comprehensive review of various literature approaches for regularized numerical solutions to ill-posed problems and situate our research within this broader context. Finally, we validate our theoretical findings with numerical experiments on synthetic data. Notably, we observe that the undamped system can experience a substantial acceleration in convergence toward the minimum norm solution when compared to other existing methods. Finally, we explore the relationship between our research and the broader field of Bregman iterative methods. In this regard, we demonstrate that the application of Bregman iteration within a mechanical framework yields a conservative system converging to the minimum norm solution, a phenomenon that contrasts with the behavior observed in standard gradient descent. This finding aligns with recent findings by Bauschke et al. [10]. However, we also note a significant discrepancy between our results and those of Bauschke et al. [10], as our approach employs a more general class of Bregman iterates. We further investigate the link with the Bregman Kaczmarz method, which generalizes the classical Kaczmarz algorithm for solving linear systems. In this context, we show that applying Bregman iteration to our mechanical approach results in a conservative system that converges to the minimum norm solution, thereby confirming our findings. This confirms that our mechanical interpretation offers a novel perspective on Bregman iterative methods and their applications. Our results also highlight the link with the generalized proximal point method, which is closely related to Bregman iterative methods. In this context, we show that the application of Bregman iteration to our mechanical approach leads to a non-smooth convergent system that converges to the minimum norm solution. This confirms the link with the generalized proximal point method, which is closely related to Bregman iterative methods.

This study investigates the unpredictable behavior of self-similar barrier-adhering robots. The model comprises a particle moving along the real line, governed by a parameter $\beta$ that represents the adhesion strength of the monomial map $x \mapsto \beta x^p$ with the ground. The particle is subject to a noise term and a repulsive drift that diminishes as it moves away from the origin. The dynamics are analyzed by examining the critical values of $\beta$ where the Lyapunov exponent changes sign. It is demonstrated that the set of critical $\beta$ values exhibits complex, unpredictable characteristics, potentially containing a dense subset of positive real numbers. These findings are illustrated through various examples, including those with homogeneous noise, specific inhomogeneous noise distributions, and constant adhesion forces. The methodology employed connects to the theory of Lyapunov exponents, random graphs, and the dynamics of self-similar groups. Additionally, numerical computations were utilized to support the conjecture regarding the complex nature of critical $\beta$ values. The paper concludes with several open questions for future research. This work is based on the authors' respective theses. The source code for the manuscript titled "Doping and energy reliant microwave conductivity of kinetic energy driven superconductors with extended contaminants" is provided. In kinetic energy driven superconductors, low-frequency electromagnetic responses are governed by the collective motion of Cooper pairs. This study investigates the microwave conductivity of such materials containing extended contaminants, specifically examining the impact of a single impurity plane on microwave permeability. Our findings indicate that beyond the superconducting transition temperature, the system's response is independent of the plane's position; however, below this temperature, the response varies with the plane's location. The microwave conductivity rises as the plane approaches the Fermi surface, a phenomenon attributed to the suppression of the superfluid density. Furthermore, at zero temperature, the superfluid density is significantly reduced when the plane is situated near the Fermi surface. At finite temperatures, the conductivity exhibits a non-monotonic dependence on the plane's position, peaking when the plane aligns with the Fermi surface. This behavior arises from the temperature-dependent overlap between the Fermi surface and the plane. Additionally, the microwave conductivity is sensitive to the plane's orientation, though this effect is notably weaker than its dependence on position. The study also explores the implications of these results for the cuprate superconductor Bi$_2$Sr$_2$CuO$_6$$_{x}$Cl$_2$$_{2-x}$CuO$_8$. Finally, we outline potential applications of our methodology in analyzing the microwave conductivity of cuprates. A key insight is that the non-monotonic variation of microwave conductivity with the position of an extended contaminant serves as a distinct signature of the superconducting state in cuprates. Consequently, the absence of such variations in the microwave conductivity of cuprates suggests that their low-energy response is not driven by collective modes. These conclusions are supported by the distinct qualitative differences between the microwave conductivity of cuprates and Bi$_2$Sr$_2$CuO$_6$$_{x}$Cl$_2$$_{2-x}$CuO$_8$. We examine a generalized mean curvature flow of graphs defined by the evolution equation $u_t = c(u) \frac{u u_{xx} - u_x^2}{1 + u_x^2}$, where $c(u)$ represents a crystalline-like anisotropic surface tension function. A key characteristic of this generalized model is the emergence of standing shockwaves, which distinguish it from standard curvature-based motions. Following our previous findings, we analyze the asymptotic behavior of this model, highlighting the unique role played by contact angle conditions at the boundary. Furthermore, we investigate how specific properties of the function $c(u)$ influence standing shock formation, boundary regularity, and long-time behavior, offering insights into potential phase transitions. We also present a comprehensive phase diagram for solutions featuring standing shocks, covering various possible shockwave scenarios. Additionally, we explore solutions that exhibit power-law growth as $t \to \infty$, demonstrating that anisotropy significantly impacts the long-time dynamics of this model. Finally, we outline several open questions regarding the model's behavior. This work serves as an expanded and refined version of our 2019 ICM contribution, now enriched with more detailed proofs, numerical examples, and an extended discussion on open problems. These developments address several inquiries raised in the original ICM paper. Given the extensive nature of this topic, we have incorporated various supplementary results and references that were not included in the original conference contribution. We hope these additions provide valuable insights for future research into related problems. Our approach to modeling and analyzing this model is also expected to inform novel research directions in curvature-driven motions with anisotropic surface tension, characterized by sliding standing shocks and stationary contact lines. Plants are vital to human survival, yet their natural growth patterns often clash with practical needs. While previous research has focused on modeling how environmental factors influence plant development, this study shifts the focus to discovering external mechanisms for manipulating plant forms. We introduce GrowSpace, an external growth medium that allows plants to expand into diverse shapes. By investigating how various materials affect growth, we found that firm GrowSpace enables plants to sculpt into configurations impossible with other media. To automate this shaping process and make the system accessible to non-experts, we developed a method to simulate plant growth on 3D surfaces and created an AI agent utilizing these simulations to learn strategies for achieving target shapes. Our approach successfully learned how to deform plants into specific configurations using GrowSpace and can physically realize these designs with minimal human input. The system demonstrates a wide range of possible shapes and requires only a few examples to match desired outcomes. We believe GrowSpace offers a novel capability for manipulating physical objects and may inspire new research into how to control other biological systems. We establish a conformal gluing theorem for semi-infinite directed interval ensembles and apply it to construct the SLE cycle through the gluing of quantum disks. Specifically, by gluing the directed interval ensemble generated by the product of two independent half-plane imaginary bosonizations with a semi-infinite directed interval ensemble, we derive the first non-trivial characterization of the SLE cycle. This cycle is defined as the coset of the Virasoro algebra generated by the conformal descendants of the minimal degenerate field ${\chi}_{1,2}$. The image indicator (II) serves as a critical metric for evaluating the quality of seismic imaging projects. Recently, various methods for calculating images using different indicators have emerged; however, these images often suffer from discrepancies in scale and contrast, hindering their comparison. To resolve this, we introduce a new standardization framework designed to harmonize image quality assessments across different imaging procedures. This paper outlines the development of this initiative, which comprises three primary components: (i) a set of reference images selected to span the full range of image quality, (ii) objective image quality indicators used to normalize the scale of images generated by various methods, and (iii) a protocol for choosing images and defining the evaluation metrics. We provide a step-by-step illustration of how to apply this initiative in practice. Furthermore, we have established a public repository containing the image collection, objective indicators, and example workflows to facilitate adoption by the research community. We anticipate that this developed initiative will become a standard for evaluating imaging quality in future studies. The image collection and related code are accessible at https://github.com/SeismicImagingStandardizationInitiative. The repository also includes a tutorial and a collection of reference images for testing new image quality indicators. New indicators are encouraged to be submitted to the repository for inclusion. Additionally, we invite researchers to collaborate with us to further expand the collection of reference images and image indicator collections. We evaluated the MORPH-II dataset, which comprises 32,969 face images featuring variations in pose, illumination, and expression. To evaluate the efficacy of the OpenCV toolkit for automatic face detection, landmark localization, and face alignment, we applied the toolkit to the entire dataset. Furthermore, we implemented a comprehensive image pre-treatment pipeline utilizing OpenCV, encompassing face alignment, image cropping, face image resizing, histogram equalization, and color space conversion. Our analysis demonstrates that these pre-treatment steps significantly enhance the quality of input images for biometric recognition systems. Finally, we present experimental findings regarding the impact of color space conversion and histogram equalization on face recognition performance. Our results indicate that converting to the grayscale color space yields the most substantial improvement in recognition accuracy. Additionally, histogram equalization consistently outperforms the grayscale conversion across various recognition experiments. Finally, we examined the effects of face image resizing on recognition accuracy, revealing that a 48x48 pixel size produces the most significant improvement. Given that the morphological operations within the OpenCV toolkit are computationally efficient, they are highly suitable for large-scale face recognition applications. Furthermore, the simplicity of the toolkit facilitates the development of user-friendly applications for automated face detection and alignment. Finally, our results suggest that the effectiveness of image pre-treatment is contingent upon the specific characteristics of the input images. Consequently, we propose that researchers conducting large-scale face recognition experiments should conduct thorough experiments to assess the benefits of image pre-treatment within their specific contexts. Finally, we have made the processed face images available to the research community to facilitate comparative studies on image pre-treatment in large-scale face recognition. A primordial black hole formed in the early universe could have survived to the present day if its mass exceeds 10^50 (10^46 M_sun). We demonstrate that such an ancient black hole can arise as a byproduct of operating curvaton inflation, which explains both the cosmic microwave background anisotropies and the large-scale structure of the universe. This scenario predicts an inflationary model with a flat potential, a very heavy curvaton field, and a stochastic gravitational wave background. Furthermore, the event would have heated the surrounding space to temperatures reaching 10^10 K. Consequently, this primordial black hole would be detectable through its gravitational lensing effects, its influence on the cosmic microwave background, and the gravitational waves it emits. Additionally, the intense radiation from the black hole would trigger further evaporation, potentially leaving no remnant. We also explore a related possibility involving an evaporating stellar-mass black hole. In both scenarios, the cosmic microwave background would exhibit a distinct signature. Finally, we discuss the implications of discovering such an ancient black hole. This study introduces a novel vehicle platoon assembly regulation framework utilizing differential contests. Initially, a differential contest model is developed to manage the speed regulation of a leading vehicle. Subsequently, a linked differential contest game is established to address the speed control of remaining vehicles within the formation. As an alternative, a linked vehicle platoon formation planning system based on differential equations is also proposed to enable comparison. The objective functions for both leading vehicle differential contests and the linked differential contests feature logarithmic terms, ensuring that trailing vehicles maintain a non-zero spacing from their predecessors during acceleration and deceleration. For the linked differential contest game, we analyze the existence and uniqueness of Nash equilibrium (NE) solutions and the convergence of iterative learning toward this equilibrium. Additionally, stability is guaranteed for the iterative learning process. Performance evaluations through simulations and hardware-in-the-loop experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of the linked differential contests method compared to the differential equations approach. Furthermore, the proposed method exhibits robustness in handling unexpected events. Results indicate that the proposed methods outperform the differential equations-based approach in terms of formation time, average inter-vehicle spacing, and energy consumption. Finally, the validity of these methods is confirmed by applying them to real-world driving scenarios involving emergency braking and acceleration. This work offers a new perspective for the research on intelligent vehicle platoons. Consequently, the linked differential contests method can be effectively employed to regulate speed, optimize space, and conserve energy within vehicle formations. Headlines serve as concise summaries of news articles that are easily digestible for readers. While various studies have explored generating these headlines from different source materials, a specific focus on detecting already published articles remains underdeveloped. This paper introduces a fine-tuned transformer model designed to automatically identify news articles and generate corresponding headlines. Experimental results demonstrate that the model achieves a precision of 0.815, recall of 0.811, and an F1 score of 0.813 on the Datasets4News dataset. Additionally, the study examines the model's performance across different article lengths to evaluate how text duration influences headline generation. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/ahmed-ayoub/recognizing-headlines. Future research will aim to enhance headline quality by incorporating external knowledge through models that utilize both the news article and associated domain-specific knowledge. We introduce a novel class of chiral spin liquids in the spin-1/2 Kagome Heisenberg antiferromagnet, achievable through the application of a single crystallographic magnetic field. This magnetic field induces significant spin polarization within the unit cell, resulting in a system with local chiralities at each triangle. We demonstrate that a unique spin fluid phase, characterized by low entanglement entropy and topological degeneracy, resides within the ground state phase diagram of both honeycomb and polycrystalline Kagome lattices. Furthermore, we outline experimental signatures that could confirm the existence of this spin fluid phase. These phases emerge in regimes where the system behaves as an effective Heisenberg model with a perturbation that breaks inversion symmetry on the Kagome lattice, thereby generating nonzero local chiralities in the ground state. Consequently, we propose a general framework for constructing spin fluid phases in a broad range of materials. Notably, this work identifies a unique spin fluid phase in the semiquantum phase diagram of the amorphous magnet CuPy, offering distinct neutron scattering signatures to detect this phase. Additionally, we present neutron scattering data from CuPy collected across various magnetic fields, which aligns with our theoretical predictions for phases in polycrystalline CuPy. Our findings suggest that the spin liquid phase observed in CuPy is a semiquantum spin liquid rather than a quantum spin liquid. Finally, we discuss the implications of our results for establishing spin fluid phases in materials with weak symmetry-breaking perturbations, such as the recently discovered iridates and ruthenates exhibiting Kagome lattice structures. This study significantly expands the known phase diagram of Kagome Heisenberg models and offers new insights into the electronic and magnetic properties of Kagome materials. Our findings indicate that spin fluid phases are accessible in materials possessing spin-rotation symmetry, even when the Hamiltonian lacks inversion symmetry, provided that local chiralities are not enforced by the Hamiltonian. This work paves the way for constructing spin fluid phases in systems with spin-rotation symmetry, including Kitaev materials and other candidates for exotic states of matter. Specifically, we show that spin fluid phases can be accessed in Kitaev materials by applying a magnetic field to break the point group symmetry of the Kagome lattice, thereby inducing local chiralities. This research significantly advances the understanding of Kitaev materials and offers a pathway to achieving spin fluid phases in these systems. Calibration techniques utilizing matrix multiplication to correct antenna gain and phase errors are a cornerstone of radio interferometry, yet they are typically restricted to small baselines due to computational constraints. This study introduces the development of efficient strategies for large-scale projects, demonstrating that when stations are arranged on a regular grid, the complexity of these techniques can be reduced to $\mathcal{O}(N\log{N})$ per visibility. The proposed method relies on the observation that stations on the same baseline exhibit highly correlated gains, enabling the use of banded matrix multiplication. Furthermore, for grid-based arrays, these correlations are not confined to adjacent stations but extend across the entire array, resulting in the proposed linear scaling. We illustrate this approach through examples of gain and phase correction for baselines derived from stations on the same row and column. Additionally, we show that gain correlations exist between stations on diagonals, allowing for the implementation of a diagonal correction technique with the same scaling behavior. Finally, we outline a viable strategy for future extensions of these methods to achieve global scalability. Our findings suggest that these techniques are broadly applicable to large-scale projects, particularly regular-grid arrays, and may also benefit irregular arrays if computational resources are limited. This study introduces a new method for asset allocation diversification, utilizing an autoencoding conditional Generative Adversarial Network (GAN) to model the correlation structures of historical asset returns. By inputting market conditions, such as the S&P500 index, the framework automatically generates correlated scenarios and employs an optimization process to determine the optimal diversified investment allocation. We empirically validate this approach across various settings, demonstrating its effectiveness in producing superior allocations through comprehensive numerical experiments. Furthermore, ablation studies are conducted to highlight the significance of the autoencoding GAN component and the utilization of multi-dimensional market conditions. Finally, given the dynamic nature of the financial market, numerical experiments are performed to assess the robustness of the framework under different scenarios. Social media has become essential for many individuals to connect with loved ones, maintain friendships, and engage with global events. However, for people with disabilities, participating in these platforms often presents significant hurdles. While research has extensively examined how users consume social media content, there is a notable lack of studies on the barriers and facilitators affecting content creation. This paper aims to advance accessibility within social media creation by shifting the focus from end-users to design professionals. It achieves this by presenting the outcomes of a participatory design workshop that explored the specific obstacles and enablers in this area. The discussion centers on two primary findings: first, a proposed framework outlining key design considerations for creating social media content; and second, the obstacles and opportunities facing such efforts, which are analyzed through the lenses of social design, social influence, and human factors. Ultimately, this study advocates for involving people with disabilities early in the design process to ensure social media environments are more inclusive for content creation. Additionally, we offer a framework for designers to apply when designing for social media consumption. The study's outcomes are grounded in a dataset comprising 22 interviews and 10 observations conducted with people who have various disabilities, including hearing, visual, and cognitive impairments. These findings are available at https://bit.ly/PD21-workshop. Our hope is that this research will inspire further initiatives to broaden the range of groups engaging in social media content creation. Furthermore, the proposed framework for designing accessible social media environments can assist other researchers and practitioners in developing tools and applications to facilitate content creation for diverse disability types. Finally, the underlying data is accessible at https://bit.ly/2Z51Q2p to support replication of the study and enable other research on social media accessibility. This study investigates natural cubic splines for modeling Alzheimer's disease trajectories, utilizing clinical data from the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI) as a preliminary example. We introduce a statistical model for longitudinal continuous outcomes that incorporates random effects, smoothing splines, and natural cubic splines. The primary motivation for employing natural cubic splines lies in their capacity to effectively model continuous covariates while addressing the frequent discontinuities in the effect of categorical covariates. We develop a model that accommodates non-normality in the longitudinal response and demonstrate how to apply the partial likelihood principle for inference. Furthermore, we establish identification conditions for the model parameters and propose a computationally efficient estimation method. Our simulation results indicate that the proposed approach performs well in finite samples. Additionally, we illustrate the method's utility in analyzing Alzheimer's disease data, with a specific focus on the distinct impacts of categorical covariates and the influence of amyloid-$\beta$ accumulation on Alzheimer's progression. The computational code is accessible at https://github.com/ChenchenLi1990/PCL. Keywords: Alzheimer's disease; discontinuous effects; non-normal response; smoothing cubic splines; spline coefficients.

We present an enhanced formulation of the action principle that facilitates the identification of systems', or regions'1 prevailing transition routes (PTRs). This approach builds upon the widely accepted concept of Pseudo-trajectories (PTs)2, which are constructed by assigning a PT action functional to every pseudo-trajectory of a transition process. The core innovation of our enhanced PT action is the uniform global enhancement of the original action functional, ensuring that all PTRs are globally uniformly minimized. This optimization eliminates the need for any a priori knowledge regarding the number, types, or specific locations of PTRs, thereby streamlining the discovery process. We demonstrate that this globally enhanced action principle is equivalent to minimizing the total transition energy across all PTRs. Our proposed method is illustrated through several examples, including the derivation of the well-known index theory for the Morse index of a critical point of the action functional, which characterizes the prevailing index of all PTRs. Furthermore, we show that PTs forming a specific type of bifurcating PTR structure are globally uniformly minimized by the enhanced action principle. Finally, we demonstrate the applicability of this principle in identifying prevailing transition routes for systems exhibiting complex PTR structures, such as those with multiple co-existing PTRs or nested PTR structures. These findings suggest that the globally enhanced action principle serves as a general and effective framework for investigating the prevailing transition routes of various types. Additionally, we have developed numerical methods based on this principle to identify PTRs, which are currently being applied to various physical systems. This work introduces subclasses of $n$-regular functions by utilizing indexed multi-type lambda calculi equipped with recursion operators. A two-way correspondence exists between these calculi and the regular subfunctions of $\mathbb{N}^k\rightarrow \mathbb{N}$. The presented calculus encompasses both extensional and intensional versions, which correspond to $n$-regular and $(n+1)$-regular functions, respectively. Leveraging the intensional calculus, we establish a hierarchy of subfunctions based on their inductive and coinductive degrees. Furthermore, we demonstrate that any $n$-regular function can be represented within a specific multi-type lambda calculus variant lacking recursion operators. This insight enables a regular domain-theoretic model for the multi-type lambda calculus, a result derived from the properties of a novel class of $n$-regular functions termed "n-convex." We also provide a sub-regular counterpart, the "k-sub-convex" functions, alongside their associated class sub-regular subfunctions of $\mathbb{N}^k\rightarrow \mathbb{N}$. The paper concludes with a regular lambda calculus that is expressive enough to encode any $n$-regular function of arity $k\leq n$. This is achieved by extending a previously defined extensional, sub-regular function—the finite sets of natural numbers—with a generalization of the power set operation. The resulting calculus successfully encodes the Stern-Brocot function, the Ackermann function, and any $n$-sub-convex function with arity $n$. Additionally, we illustrate how to represent $n$-regular functions using an inductive-coinductive multi-type lambda calculus, a system that incorporates n-convex functions alongside coinductive types. The construction relies on a sub-regular function mapping $\mathbb{N}^n\rightarrow 2^{\mathbb{N}^n}$ that enumerates all $n$-regular functions of arity $n$. Finally, we depict a regular domain-theoretic model for the multi-type lambda calculus utilizing this latter function. The paper ends by outlining several open problems. This research investigates structures within stochastic differential equations (SDEs) that possess functional dependencies. It introduces structure-specific criteria for converting standard Ito integrals into those involving functional integrands. The study examines characteristics of flows defined by conditional distributions and their associated SDEs, demonstrating that the distinction between Ito and Stratonovich integrals in these equations arises from specific structural terms within the SDEs themselves. Consequently, this paper proposes a novel perspective on the relationship between Ito and Stratonovich integrals. Furthermore, the authors present a new criterion for the existence and uniqueness of SDE solutions with functional integrands by leveraging the properties of conditional distribution flows. This criterion relies on the conditional moments of the SDE's functional Ito integrals and provides sufficient conditions for continuity and Lipschitz continuity. As an application, existence and uniqueness are established for a conditional distribution flow SDE featuring a conditional Laplace-type kernel, utilizing only a priori estimates of its functionals' conditional moments. The paper also incorporates existence and uniqueness criteria based on the conditional SDE's functional Ito integrals, utilizing conditional estimates for its functionals' Laplace transforms. These findings are applied to SDEs with a conditional Ornstein-Uhlenbeck kernel, where existence and uniqueness are confirmed under a Lipschitz condition applied to the Laplace transform of the functionals' conditional densities. Additionally, a conditional variant of the Burkholder-Davis-Gundy inequality is derived, which relies on a conditional estimate for the Laplace transform of a conditional moment of the SDE's functional Ito integrals. This yields a conditional existence and uniqueness criterion that relies on a conditional Lipschitz condition concerning the Laplace transform of the functionals' conditional densities. This paper introduces a concept of quasi-characters extended to all groups and investigates their properties, culminating in the definition of the standard structure space. For locally compact abelian groups, this new concept aligns with the classical theory of characters and the well-known structure space. In the case of locally compact groups, the framework applies to Bochner characters; for finite groups, it generates a new structure space where sub-representations correspond to maximal ideals. Additionally, for finite groups, the study explores the relationship between positive sub-representations and the standard structure space alongside the group algebra, yielding a result analogous to the Wiener-Letvin theorem. The paper concludes with several examples of finite groups. Key concepts include quasi-characters, sub-representations, and the standard structure space. This work is dedicated to the memory of Professor Miroslav R. Rakić.

Cross-domain text-to-SQL remains a challenging area that requires a deep grasp of both natural language and SQL. Although current methods have made significant strides, they often depend on intermediate representations like abstract syntax trees (ASTs) or semantic parse graphs, which demand high-quality alignment data and increase inference costs. Additionally, many approaches lack meaning-awareness, frequently generating incorrect or redundant outputs. To address these issues, this paper introduces a novel cross-domain text-to-SQL framework enhanced by a supportive task. This framework enables end-to-end mapping between text and SQL without relying on intermediate ASTs or parse graphs. Furthermore, the supportive task leverages supportive reading to refine meaning representations and boost overall performance. Empirical results demonstrate that our method achieves state-of-the-art performance on the Spider and Semantic Textual Recognition benchmarks. The Andromeda Galaxy (M31) is a spiral galaxy notable for its extensive halo of dwarf satellites. This study presents the discovery of Andromeda XXV (And XXV), a new dwarf satellite within this halo. With an apparent magnitude of approximately 17.5, And XXV ranks as the third faintest known dwarf galaxy orbiting M31. Its position in the color-magnitude diagram aligns it with ultra-faint dwarfs associated with the Milky Way. The object's color and magnitude suggest a stellar population dominated by old stars, with an age exceeding 10 billion years. Furthermore, And XXV exhibits a low metallicity of roughly 0.001 solar metallicity. By analyzing its proper motion, we determined that And XXV is gravitationally bound to the Andromeda Galaxy. Additionally, we estimated the mass of M31's central dark matter distribution to be less than 1.5 billion solar masses. These findings indicate that And XXV is a unique miniature galaxy characterized by a low dark matter density at its core. Grant-free massive non-orthogonal pattern (NOP) design aims to enable efficient access for a vast number of devices with low complexity and high energy efficiency. This paper introduces a dual-stage genetic procedure to generate high-quality NOPs. The first stage focuses on constructing robust patterns that minimize confusion between pairs of devices, while the second stage refines the patterns to reduce confusion between triples of devices. We demonstrate that the solutions produced by this proposed dual-stage genetic approach significantly outperform those derived from standard optimization techniques. Specifically, they achieve a 30% to 40% reduction in confusion probability and a 20% to 30% decrease in the minimum required signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) for successful communication. Additionally, numerical results indicate that the methods can support up to 100 times more simultaneous devices than the maximum supportable by conventional optimization-based patterns. Furthermore, the dual-stage genetic procedure exhibits superior performance compared to existing state-of-the-art algorithms, achieving a 20% to 30% lower confusion probability and a 10% to 20% reduction in the minimum required SNR. Finally, we outline the implementation complexity of the proposed dual-stage genetic algorithm and compare it against other NOP design methods. We conclude that the approach strikes an optimal balance between computational complexity and performance, making it well-suited for practical implementation. Finally, we demonstrate that the algorithm can be easily adapted to design correlated patterns, which are commonly used in real-world applications. The resulting correlated NOPs achieve a 20% to 30% reduction in confusion probability compared to uncorrelated NOPs. Moreover, the algorithm exhibits a quadratic computational complexity with respect to the pattern length, rendering it computationally efficient. Consequently, the proposed method is highly promising for practical implementation. Notably, the superior performance of the uncorrelated NOPs underscores the potential of the dual-stage genetic algorithm for future NOP design. Finally, we illustrate the algorithm's versatility by applying it to create binary, quaternary, and hexagonal patterns, which reduce the confusion probability of binary, quaternary, and hexagonal patterns by 20% to 30%, respectively. These findings highlight the algorithm's potential to significantly enhance the performance of grant-free massive connectivity systems. Additionally, the algorithm's ability to generate patterns with various alphabets demonstrates its flexibility and applicability across a wide range of grant-free massive connectivity scenarios. This study examines various variants of the widely used psychrometric approximation for modeling humid air. Although these approximations offer simplicity and efficiency, they fail to meet the thermodynamic exactness required by modern simulation tools. We evaluate the appraisal framework for approximate thermodynamic property models, specifically the Mixture-based Thermodynamic Approximation (MiTA) and the Thermodynamic Approximation with Corrections (TAC), when applied to these propagation scenarios. Our findings indicate that the appraisers are highly effective in identifying and addressing inconsistencies across diverse humid air models. Furthermore, we introduce a novel hybrid model that integrates the speed of the TAC formulation with the accuracy of MiTA, successfully resolving the inconsistencies detected by our appraisal method. This result underscores the utility of the MiTA and TAC Corr appraisers as general evaluators for thermodynamic property models. Additionally, we provide a concise overview of the recently developed MiTA Corr, which offers even greater accuracy for multidimensional systems. All property models and appraisers utilized in this work are publicly accessible via the MiTA repository. The comprehensive appraiser for MiTA and TAC Corr, along with a specific appraiser for the more advanced MiTA Corr model, can be found at https://github.com/ThermoMLGroup/MiTA/tree/master/thermo_ml/property_models/humid_air. We demonstrate that these appraisers effectively identify numerous inconsistencies in humid air property models and facilitate the creation of new, more accurate models, such as MiTA Corr. Furthermore, the appraisers are designed to be adaptable for evaluating other thermodynamic property models. Finally, we illustrate that MiTA Corr, being the most accurate model assessed, can be efficiently propagated using a simple linearization technique. This outcome validates the effectiveness of the thermodynamic appraisers in enhancing both the accuracy and efficiency of thermodynamic property models. The entire appraisers package is available as a separate repository at https://github.com/ThermoMLGroup/MiTA/tree/master/thermo_ml/property_models/humid_air_appraisers. The concept of the "sum" of matroids on a shared ground set, introduced by Edelman and Reiner, is generalized through a more outer-covariant operation termed the "product" of matroids. This new operation exhibits desirable distributive and dual properties and is closely linked to the deletion of matroids. Specifically, a series of examples demonstrates that the closure of the "sum" of matroids can be derived from their "product" combined with deletions. Consequently, this approach yields a streamlined proof for the distributivity of matroid closures, as established by Edelman and Reiner. For further details, please consult arXiv:2001.07108. The dynamic nature of conversation makes it difficult to fully capture spoken utterances using Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR). Consequently, ASR confidence modeling is essential for building robust Dialogue State Tracking (DSL) systems. This paper introduces a new word-level confidence model based on Word Confusion Networks (WCN), which explicitly represents the uncertainty surrounding individual word recognition. We trained and evaluated this WCN model alongside a Word Embedding based Confidence Network (WECN) and a Wordless Confidence Network (WCN). Experimental results on the Cambridge Dialogue (CamDialog) dataset demonstrate that our WCN model surpasses both WECN and WCN approaches, achieving state-of-the-art performance in DSL. Furthermore, our WCN model shows a greater ability to detect homophone errors compared to the alternative confidence models. We offer an explicit description of the moduli spaces $\mathbb{M}_{\mathcal{C}}(v)$, which consist of $\mathcal{C}$-stable sheaves on a smooth curve $\mathcal{C}$ defined on a quasi-projective scheme, subject to a fixed rank and determinant. Leveraging this modular construction, we demonstrate that the virtual counts of these spaces on smooth complete curves yield values that are polynomials in the $l$-torsion points of the Jacobian, dependent on the rank and determinant. Consequently, the number of $\mathcal{C}$-stable sheaves on such curves on a complete intersection can be expressed as an alternating sum of products of Betti numbers and counts for $\mathcal{C}$-stable vector bundles with a fixed rank. Furthermore, we extend these findings to v-cycles and provide concrete examples. Specifically, for K3 surfaces, we confirm that the virtual number of $\mathcal{C}$-stable sheaves on lines within the v-curve equals the count of $\mathcal{C}$-stable vector bundles with a fixed rank and determinant, differing by at most a sign. Additionally, on the v-Kudla-Ruan surface $X_{K,R}$, we demonstrate that the virtual number of $\mathcal{C}$-stable sheaves on v-lines is the virtual number of $\mathcal{C}$-stable vector bundles with rank at most $l$ and a fixed determinant, also varying by at most a sign. Finally, we establish that the numbers of $\mathcal{C}$-stable sheaves on lines in the v-K3 component of the moduli space of stable objects on K3s are polynomials in the even indices of the intersection form on the second homology of the K3 surface. These findings suggest a potential generalization of the Yau-Tian-Donaldson conjecture to $\mathcal{C}$-stable sheaves. This study investigates the minimum intricacy of universal entry frameworks, introducing a novel concept known as the "intricacy" of such frameworks. We demonstrate that the minimum intricacy for universal $k$-entry frameworks is exactly $k$. Furthermore, we establish an upper bound for the minimum intricacy of universal $k$-entry frameworks as $O(k\log(k))$, and provide universal entry frameworks with $\omega(1)$ entry points that cannot be represented using any equivalent framework with fewer than six entry points. Additionally, we examine the minimum intricacy of universal frameworks regarding their domains and provide an upper bound for the minimum intricacy of universal $k$-dimensional frameworks as $k^{O(k)}$. Finally, we outline several open problems concerning universal entry frameworks and their minimum intricacy. We introduce a general framework for inferring the entanglement of arbitrary multimode optical quantum systems. This approach relies on determining the classical entanglement within the phase-space representation of the underlying quantum state. Specifically, we optimize the classical entanglement measure using the optimal linear positive map (LP map). By employing the discrete Wigner function, our formalism achieves full entanglement characterization for general multimode optical quantum states while substantially reducing the data required. We demonstrate that the entanglement of Gaussian states is optimally revealed through our method, effectively distinguishing it from separable states. Furthermore, we extend these findings to multimode continuous variables. Finally, we analyze the sensitivity of different entanglement measures to experimental noise. The proposed method is fully automated and can be readily applied to experimental settings. Additionally, we have developed a corresponding open-source software tool. This technique is particularly valuable for practical applications where specific, tailored entanglement measures are necessary. Finally, we illustrate how our formalism facilitates the fine-tuning of quantum resources in continuous-variable optical systems. These advancements hold significant promise for the development of practical quantum technologies. (Software available at: https://github.com/QuantumOpticsGroup/LOPIT). The JET tokamak has experienced a persistent issue involving intermittent, regular bursts of energy loss and particle expulsion, a phenomenon known as "Palm Tree Disruptions" due to the visual resemblance of the plasma's outer edge to a fan. This study offers the first quantitative analysis of the plasma modes responsible for these Palm Tree Disruptions during JET deuterium discharges. Utilizing both nonlinear and linear methods, we demonstrate that these disruptions are driven by a single neoclassical Tearing Mode (NTM) with a rational surface at q=2. This finding confirms the origin of Palm Tree Disruptions and elucidates their nature as NTMs. Furthermore, we illustrate how NTMs generate such regular plasma structures by analyzing the eigenmodes of the JET plasma. Additionally, we examine the impact of the q=3 NTM on the formation of Palm Trees and explain why the symmetric Palm Tree Disruption observed in D-discharges is invariably accompanied by an m=2 mode. Finally, we explore how the symmetry of the Palm Tree Disruption can be altered by the presence of an m=3 mode. These findings are supported by JET disruption data and a simplified tokamak model. The acquisition of new knowledge by pretrained models often suffers from catastrophic forgetting, a problem typically addressed by training on all past experiences, a strategy that is often impractical. While various methods have been proposed to mitigate this forgetting during ongoing learning, their relative effectiveness remains unclear. This study introduces the Basic benchmark for evaluating such methods, designed to replicate real-world scenarios where data is highly imbalanced and contains noise. The analysis reveals that the order in which classes are introduced significantly impacts learning performance. Furthermore, experiments on the Basic benchmark demonstrate that the Alpha and S2SNP approaches outperform several other methods. A subsequent code-based implementation of Alpha yielded results comparable to the original, indicating that the core mechanism of Alpha is straightforward. Finally, theoretical analysis suggests that the success of Alpha may stem from its ability to identify and discard irrelevant data. These findings offer valuable insights for the development of more effective methods capable of learning from new experiences without forgetting the past. This study seeks to identify instances of hate speech across three social media platforms by integrating textual and visual data. While prior research indicates that models utilizing text-only inputs from these sites achieve accuracy between 80% and 95%, our approach yields a significant performance boost, surpassing human-level accuracy by 1.5%. To enhance interpretability, we employ multiple understandability techniques, including Shapley values, to reveal which image features contribute most to model predictions. Furthermore, we introduce a new multi-level multi-modal dataset specifically for hate crime identification. We also provide a comprehensive overview of various image text classification datasets to facilitate the selection of pre-training models for this domain. Finally, we present a series of experiments designed to improve the performance of existing models in this context. Finally, we examine the challenges associated with multi-modal classification tasks and offer recommendations for future research in this area. Our work offers a detailed understanding of the task and establishes a foundation for subsequent studies. This study examines how the variability in dendritic arborization affects the dynamics of self-organized synchronization within a large-scale network of randomly connected, electrically excitable neurons. Specifically, we analyze a model where neurons are grouped into clusters based on shared dendritic origins, with intra- and inter-cluster connections derived from anatomical data. Our results indicate that increased heterogeneity in neuron arborization can trigger the emergence of large-scale synchronous activity. Furthermore, this effect is amplified when considering axonal projections, which are typically characterized by a greater degree of heterogeneity compared to dendritic structures. These findings underscore the critical role of both dendritic and axonal architectural characteristics in the functional dynamics of neural networks. Finally, our methodology is applicable to various biological systems, facilitating the investigation of the functional implications of anatomical structures across diverse biological scales. Additionally, the approach allows for the exploration of how structural variations influence collective behaviors in artificial neural networks. To facilitate this analysis, we have made our code publicly available at https://github.com/afgarcia1982/NeuronModels. Supplementary material is accessible at https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0304397521005001/suppl-material. Keywords: computational neuroscience, mathematical biology, computational neuroscience, mathematical biology.

Creating antagonistic tests for existing tests to trigger failures on code that previously compiled successfully is a challenging task. This paper investigates the application of antagonistic test generation to automatic program fixing. We outline the mechanism behind antagonistic test generation and demonstrate how it can be integrated with program fixing workflows. Additionally, we present an experimental evaluation utilizing the Eclips eFix tool to assess our approach. Our results indicate that generating antagonistic bugs within Eclips eFix targets produces a more difficult-to-fix subset of bugs that aligns with human perceptions. Furthermore, when compared to targeted random bug generation, antagonistic bug generation produces programs with fewer spurious failures and higher code change similarity to fix suggestions. Finally, we demonstrate that incorporating antagonistic test generation into the fixing process enhances the overall effectiveness of automatic program fixing. To support this work, we have open-sourced our tool, which includes an improved antagonistic test generator, alongside our benchmark dataset of failed Eclips eFix targets. The capability region (CR) serves as a potent tool for analyzing cooperative communication systems, offering a holistic perspective on performance. Defined as the union of achievable rate tuples across all cooperative strategies, it uniquely captures the total performance of any cooperative system. This paper investigates the CR of a general interference-generating cooperative network featuring co-interference management (GIFC). Since the complete CR of GIFC is difficult to characterize, we focus on its "data spectrum," which organizes the region by ranking inequalities based on their summation length. We first examine the data spectrum of a simplified scenario where receivers possess no side information, revealing that it comprises exactly three inequalities. Next, we characterize the data spectrum segments where two of these inequalities hold. Finally, we derive a sufficient condition to ensure the validity of the third inequality. We demonstrate that existing GIFC schemes, including interference alignment, fall short in tightening this critical segment. To address this, we propose a new scheme termed "interference randomization," which achieves a tighter characterization for this region. Furthermore, we introduce a novel method for combining rate splitting with random interference alignment, yielding a further improvement. Our findings indicate that this randomization technique is generally applicable to various GIFC scenarios. Numerical results confirm that the proposed approach effectively tightens the most significant data spectrum segment, thereby more accurately reflecting the overall performance of GIFC networks. This study offers a new analytical perspective for evaluating GIFC networks and establishes a foundation for future research in this area. The collision dynamics of nuclear matter, particularly under asymmetric neutron-proton conditions, are central to understanding various cosmic phenomena, including the internal structure of neutron stars and the rapid neutronization process. This study introduces a new tool for analyzing experimental data from heavy-ion collisions, designed to investigate collision dynamics and determine the equation of state. The novel 3-dimensional flow examination method is demonstrated using ARIS Monte Carlo event generator data, which incorporates the equation of state from the Relativistic Quantum-Hydrodynamic (RQH) framework. Results indicate that 3-dimensional flow plots offer a more effective means of discerning collision dynamics than traditional flow plots. Furthermore, the correlation between the slope of the 3-dimensional flow parameter ($\alpha$) and the compression modulus ($K_0$) of the EoS is examined. This relationship is shown to be independent of incident energy, initial asymmetry, and the specific collision system, suggesting a universal characteristic. Additionally, the correlation between the 3-dimensional angular flow parameter ($\beta$) and the symmetry energy is highlighted. Finally, the observed correlation between the 3-dimensional asymmetry parameter ($\gamma$) and the in-medium symmetry potential is also reported. These findings are expected to facilitate the development of new theoretical models for the Equation-of-State. The 3-dimensional flow examination is anticipated to become a valuable instrument for the upcoming FAIR, NICA, and ICARUS facilities, which are expected to generate data ideal for examining both the in-medium symmetry potential and the compression modulus. The experimental datasets utilized in this work can be accessed at https://github.com/ARIS-Group/ARIS. Detecting COVID-19 early is crucial for mitigating its severe health impacts. While deep learning models utilizing chest X-rays offer a promising avenue for diagnosis, they face challenges when trained on limited data and are prone to privacy attacks. This study introduces a novel framework for early COVID-19 detection that employs adversarial training to enhance model robustness. Our results demonstrate that this approach not only boosts predictive performance but also fosters diverse model behaviors, thereby strengthening defense against privacy breaches. Furthermore, we highlight the role of chest X-ray findings in revealing the effects of adversarial training. Additionally, we propose a new evaluation metric for quantifying model behavior diversity, which we believe will serve as a valuable tool for developing trustworthy machine learning models in future medical applications. To support this domain, we have made our code, data, and models publicly available. This work was conducted in collaboration with the University of Oxford.
