This paper investigates the communication capabilities of graph neural networks (GNNs) within decentralized wireless communication frameworks. Specifically, we examine the performance of a single-hop GNN-driven system designed for distributed graph coloring. We analyze how GNN architecture influences color assignment accuracy, revealing that the graph filter component's ability to approximate the target graph's frequency response determines whether a network can achieve perfect graph coloring. Furthermore, we explore the trade-off between transmission power and GNN architecture in distributed shortest path computation, demonstrating that the filter term in a convolutional GNN learning framework serves as a low-pass filter. This insight enables the derivation of the GNN learning problem into a constrained optimization problem, where the filter is designed to balance accuracy against transmission power. Finally, we provide numerical results for both distributed graph coloring and shortest path computation to validate the analysis and confirm the proposed methodology. Our findings indicate that GNN-driven decentralized wireless systems offer a tunable approach for optimizing transmission power, latency, and accuracy. These results suggest that GNN-based distributed communication is well-suited for applications such as vehicular networks, where nodes must rapidly and accurately exchange information. The code supporting our experiments is accessible at https://github.com/ashishkumar12345/GNN-driven-communication. The state of Goiás, located in the Brazilian Central-West region, experienced a dramatic surge in homicides between 2002 and 2014, with the rate more than doubling. To analyze this phenomenon, researchers examined mortality records by municipality, calculating age-standardized rates for each area. Statistical analysis revealed a spatially clustered pattern, prompting the application of a spatially adaptive kernel function to map variations in these rates. The study's primary finding is that Goiás' high homicide rates are not uniformly distributed but instead concentrated within a specific network of neighboring communities, which was identified as a distinct spatial outlier. This network spans both urban and rural jurisdictions, linking regions as distant as the state capital, Goiânia, with the frontier town of Araguaína. The authors conclude that this geographic distribution suggests an influence from illicit networks, a hypothesis that can now be rigorously tested using the methodology proposed in this study. By providing a precise map of high-homicide areas, the research offers a valuable tool for public health initiatives aimed at reducing violence in Goiás. Furthermore, the paper outlines potential applications of this approach to other forms of spatially distributed crime. This work addresses the inverse problem of utilizing an objective function to guide a learning algorithm. Specifically, we define a target algorithm that performs ascent along a given objective function and introduce an approximation framework designed to generate proxy algorithms capable of mimicking the ascent behavior of these target algorithms. Our approach is grounded in a model that accounts for data noise effects, noise-responsiveness, and challenge-adaptability. We establish a theoretical proof demonstrating that the distance between the fixed points of the target and proxy algorithms diminishes as data volume increases. Furthermore, numerical experiments involving real-world data confirm that the proposed algorithms can detect when a problem is challenging and adjust accordingly, achieving superior performance in terms of generalization error. Additionally, we illustrate that these algorithms facilitate acceleration when the detection indicator suggests the problem is not challenging. Ultimately, the distance between the fixed points of the proxy algorithms and those of the actual algorithms remains minimal. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/kenji-ich/GRASS. This paper introduces a new category of self-exciting systems, characterized by a stochastic differential equation driven by a locally stable, non-negative sub-Feller process that features a countable set of absorbing points within its state space. We provide sufficient conditions ensuring the existence and uniqueness of a weak solution to this self-exciting system. Under these conditions, we demonstrate that any initial condition leads to a unique ergodic measure on the state space, provided the excitation function grows sufficiently slowly. Furthermore, we establish the existence of a Lyapunov function to prove Poisson stability for the unique invariant measure, thereby ensuring the existence of non-trivial paths. Additionally, the slow growth constraint on the excitation function is utilized to characterize the large-deviation behavior of the invariant measure. These findings are supported by numerical simulations. The study focuses particularly on systems where the driving process is bounded and possesses multiple absorbing states, yielding novel results for such systems. This study introduces a free-breathing, motion-adjusted 4D (integrating 3D anatomy with respiration) T2-weighted turbo spin-echo (T2-TSE) sequence for visualizing both the thoracic and abdominal regions. The sequence utilizes a variable echo train length (ETL) strategy, dynamically modifying ETL and readout duration based on the respiratory cycle. Specifically, it employs a long ETL with extended readout times during free-breathing phases to accelerate data acquisition, while switching to a short ETL with condensed readout times at end-inspiration and end-expiration phases to capture high-resolution 2D anatomical images. The study demonstrates that the 3D+1D motion-adjusted approach yields superior image quality compared to free-breathing 3D T2-TSE sequences. Furthermore, the 3D+1D method produces high-resolution 2D anatomical images comparable to those from breath-hold techniques, despite being free-breathing. Finally, both approaches generate 4D-CTVs that are comparable to free-breathing 2D T2-TSE sequences. These findings suggest that the proposed motion-adjusted 4D T2-SE sequence offers enhanced image contrast and spatial resolution, making it a promising tool for future image-guided radiotherapy. Additionally, the method is free-breathing, patient-friendly, and free from ionizing radiation. The protocol is versatile, supporting various future applications such as treatment planning, target localization, and real-time image guidance. The study concludes that the motion-adjusted 3D+1D T2-SE sequence is ideal for thoracic and abdominal imaging, capable of generating high-quality 2D anatomical images and 4D-CTVs without the need for breath-holding. Furthermore, the protocol is easily adaptable for retrospective analysis. Model compression and acceleration are increasingly vital for deploying machine learning models in resource-constrained environments. While knowledge distillation (KD) is a widely used acceleration method, most existing approaches ignore the data flow within models, resulting in inefficient KD structures. To address this, we introduce Data flow-preserving knowledge distillation (InDistill), which maintains the data flow of both teacher and student models to create an efficient KD architecture. Our method employs data flow-preserving layers (DFPLs) to ensure that teacher DFPLs align with student DFPLs, thereby eliminating redundant computation in the distillation module. Experiments on CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 datasets demonstrate that InDistill significantly outperforms state-of-the-art KD methods in terms of model accuracy, achieving improvements of up to 1.6% and 1.0% respectively. Furthermore, we validate the method's effectiveness across various applications, including image classification, object detection, semantic segmentation, and image super-resolution. Arid and semi-arid ecosystems are characterized by plants that exhibit spatial non-locality. This study employs a reaction-diffusion-advection-adsorption framework to investigate how this spatial non-locality influences plant dynamics in these environments. The model incorporates a water balance equation that accounts for the uptake of water from the surrounding environment. We analyze the stability of homogeneous steady states and develop a framework to predict the emergence of spatially heterogeneous patterns. Furthermore, we address the deflagration-to-detonation transition (DDT) within moving patterns, utilizing a theoretical model to forecast detonation speeds. Finally, numerical simulations are conducted to validate our theoretical findings. Our results indicate that spatial non-locality can generate various phenomena, including homogeneous states, heterogeneous patterns, traveling waves, moving heterogeneous patterns, periodic oscillations, and chaotic oscillations. Specifically, the interaction between water and plants can trigger dynamic instabilities, leading to complex behaviors such as water depletion, plant extinction, overgrazing, plant coexistence, traveling waves, traveling heterogeneous patterns, periodic water oscillations, and chaotic water oscillations. Notably, the DDT phenomenon within moving heterogeneous patterns can induce plant extinction. These findings underscore the critical role of spatial non-locality in shaping the dynamics of arid-land plant systems. Additionally, our model and results offer valuable insights for the conservation and management of these ecosystems. Finally, we outline several promising directions for future research. This work is dedicated to the memory of Professor Shigui Ruan. CountSketch is a widely used dimensionality reduction method that projects vectors into a lower-dimensional space, enabling the recovery of $k$-order moments such as the mean and frequency. Although numerous theoretical guarantees exist for this technique, they largely assume that input vectors are fixed and independent of the random counting vectors. This paper introduces theoretically backed algorithms that maintain strong resilience against adaptive inputs. Our results demonstrate that for both deterministic and randomized adaptive vectors, these algorithms can still accurately estimate the $\ell_2$ norm, as well as the mean and co-occurrence terms, potentially with a marginally larger sketch size. Furthermore, our findings are robust whether the adaptive vectors are independent or dependent on prior outputs. Finally, we validate these theoretical insights through experimental validation. This paper introduces a novel strategy for the quantum version of the Prisoner's Dilemma, in which both players apply a specific quantum strategy. This approach yields a mutually cooperative outcome consistent with classical principles, but it also generates an entangled state that offers substantial rewards to both participants. We developed this new strategy, termed the "Elevated Frequency" strategy, and implemented it on real quantum hardware accessed via the quantum cloud. The study utilized Qiskit to construct the application, running it on various devices with different qubit counts. Results demonstrate that the strategy remains viable even when accounting for quantum errors, though these errors cause a reduction in the players' rewards. The paper concludes with a discussion of potential real-world applications, specifically within financial markets. The proposed strategy could inspire the creation of new trading algorithms that achieve mutual elevated frequency and success through collaboration, leveraging quantum advantage. Furthermore, the application was developed to facilitate the design of new quantum financial trading strategies. This research optimizes income within an economic interaction framework involving intermediaries. Specifically, it addresses the selection of optimal training programs for intermediaries and the ideal division of labor between direct-interaction agents and those facilitated by intermediaries. The study introduces new findings that suggest selecting intermediaries who achieve the highest possible income is the optimal strategy. This approach indicates that when direct-interaction agents possess a high level of skill, they should choose to work independently rather than through intermediaries. Furthermore, increasing the training intensity for intermediaries is always the correct decision. Finally, this analysis reveals that an increase in the number of intermediaries is never beneficial. These conclusions are derived from an intermediate solution to the problem, which is formulated as a non-convex optimization task. The benefits of this optimization are demonstrated by showing that the resulting intermediate solution is nearly identical to the solution of a relaxed, convexified version of the problem. Numerical simulations are provided to support these findings. The significance of this work lies in its potential to inform decisions regarding training investment, interconnectivity, and investment in financial inclusion. These results are particularly relevant for developing countries, where a significant portion of the population engages with financial services through intermediaries. Additionally, the findings are applicable to various financial service contexts, such as mobile money, microfinance, and peer-to-peer lending. This paper introduces a context-sensitive approach designed to evaluate vocal entrainment within dialogue scenarios. We address the challenge of determining entrainment by (1) formulating a computational definition of the concept and (2) developing a computational method to assess it. Drawing on psycholinguistic research that characterizes entrainment as the mutual mimicry of speech patterns in interactions, we contend that entrainment cannot be accurately measured merely by comparing entrained features of partner speakers. Instead, true entrainment reflects the influence one speaker exerts on the other's production; consequently, the concept must be operationalized to capture this causal influence. We propose that computational definitions of this phenomenon must therefore incorporate an asymmetry between the entrainer (the influenced speaker) and the influencer (the agent initiating the shared pattern). To realize this definition, we utilize speech rate, pause duration, and lexical diversity as measurable entrained features and have constructed a novel method to estimate the causal influence one dyadic partner exerts on the other regarding these features. We demonstrate the efficacy of this definition and method through an analysis of dialogue data, which confirms that our proposed metric for assessing entrainment causal influence surpasses existing state-of-the-art approaches. Furthermore, we show that this definition enables the differentiation of various types of dialogues based on their levels of entrainment. Finally, we illustrate how this definition can be applied to predict entry-level performance in specific tasks, highlighting its potential utility for evaluating dialogue systems in professional contexts. To facilitate future research, we make our implementation publicly available. The implementation code can be accessed at https://github.com/alexpampanini/vocal-entrainment. Additionally, we provide a dataset of pre-processed dialogue transcripts at https://github.com/alexpampanini/dialogue-dataset. Both resources are also available on the first author's GitHub account, https://github.com/alexpampanin. Our analysis reveals that human speakers adjust their speech rates based on the perceived expectations of their conversational partners, suggesting that dialogue systems should incorporate such adjustments to enhance user experience. This capability is also available at the specified GitHub repository. We anticipate that these definitions and methods will foster new avenues of research into human communication and establish a foundation for the computational modeling of social behavior. This study addresses the semicoercive Stokes variational inequation, a mathematical model for glacier flow that has recently garnered significant attention within the numerical analysis community. While prior research has established convergence rates for convergence order one using conventional convergence- and divergence-finite elements, this work investigates the impact of higher-order elements on solution approximation. Specifically, we derive error estimates for higher-order flow laws under reasonable assumptions regarding the regularity of test functions. These findings demonstrate that, under specific divergence and boundary conditions, higher-order elements yield improved error estimates with order-optimality, thereby validating their utility in approximating inequations. Furthermore, the developed error estimates are robust against the viscosity parameter, a crucial advantage for future applications in numerical weather prediction. Finally, numerical experiments are presented to corroborate these theoretical results. To our knowledge, the development of error estimates for higher-order finite elements in the context of variational inequations is novel. Our results indicate that higher-order elements, particularly those based on Raviart-Thomas and Brezzi-Douglas-Marini spaces, can enhance the accuracy of approximations. Consequently, these methods offer a promising pathway for future research into the numerical simulation of glacier flow. Additionally, the error estimates remain valid even when regularity assumptions are relaxed, a condition that will be explored in forthcoming publications. We introduce the DUVET project, designed to investigate how galactic outflows regulate star formation in the edge-on starburst disk NGC 4536. By combining new 30-millimeter ALMA observations of $^{12}$CO and $^{13}$CO with existing *Spitzer* infrared data, we mapped the CO outflow's surface brightness and kinematics at a spatial resolution of 10 mas (approximately 100 pc). Our findings reveal a high-velocity outflow extending over 1.5 kiloparsecs from the galactic center, characterized by a conical shape and a central cavity roughly 1 kiloparset wide. The outflow's axis aligns closely with the galaxy's major axis, and its surface brightness diminishes radially from the center. We identified 12 distinct outflow lobes, each spanning approximately 1 kiloparsec radially, which show a correlation between the outflow's surface brightness and the infrared surface brightness of the galaxy. This relationship suggests a link between the outflow and star formation. By comparing the outflow's surface brightness to the star formation rate surface brightness, we determined that the outflow removes gas from the star-forming disk at a rate comparable to the local star formation rate. This result supports the hypothesis that outflows suppress star formation radially outward from the galactic center. The DUVET project will utilize these observations to test the hypothesis that galactic outflows alter the radial metallicity gradient in star-forming disks. Specifically, if outflows remove metal-rich gas from the disk, we anticipate detecting metal-deficient outer regions in future *Hubble* and *JWST* observations of NGC 4536. This study represents the initial phase of the DUVET project, which will expand its sample of outflow galaxies to examine the broader role of galactic outflows in star formation regulation. This study investigates the advantages of pre-training semantic segmentation models using depth estimation techniques, which are typically more data-efficient than classification methods relying on extensive labeled datasets. Given that depth estimation is often considered more complex than classification, we hypothesize that the specific benefits of such pre-training remain unclear. To address this, we experimentally compare pre-training via monocular depth assessment against image classification. Our findings indicate that although depth pre-training yields slightly higher performance in well-defined scenarios, it is significantly more data-intensive. Consequently, we conclude that depth pre-training is not inherently superior to pre-training with readily available labeled classifications. Our research fills a gap in the literature by directly comparing these approaches, and the code will be made publicly accessible. Additionally, we explore the possibility that the performance differences stem from the distinct nature of the tasks, leading to a novel regularization method that transfers edge information from an edge model to the semantic segmentation model. This approach is expected to be effective for model training across both classification and depth estimation domains. Kendall's tau serves as a metric for correlation, yet its computational demands often make it impractical for large datasets. In this work, we introduce a novel approach to estimate Kendall's tau by constructing an efficient proxy that maintains a minimal discrepancy relative to the original value. This allows for rapid calculation of the proxy, serving as an effective approximation of Kendall's tau. We validate our proposed deduction through a comprehensive simulation study and real-world data application, where statistical testing confirms the reliability of our results. Furthermore, our method achieves a correlation of 0.998 with Kendall's tau while reducing computational time from O(n²) to O(n log n). This advancement not only enhances the speed of correlation testing but also enables the statistical evaluation of missing data within big data frameworks. Given that correlation testing is a fundamental component of machine learning, our work contributes to the broader "big data" research community. Additionally, we have made the R package Rcorrelation, which incorporates this methodology, publicly available. The package is accessible at https://github.com/ChenYi2018/Rcorrelation. The rise of automotive networks, particularly in self-driving vehicles, has created a demand for privacy-preserving edge cognition. This capability enables vehicles to jointly learn from data while safeguarding sensitive information. However, existing approaches often fail to adequately address the private data inherent in vehicle datasets. This paper introduces a novel, privacy-aware edge cognition framework that leverages federated learning to safeguard data privacy within automotive networks. The proposed method utilizes a collaborative structure to enhance the privacy protection of vehicle data. Furthermore, it incorporates differential privacy to mitigate potential privacy risks during model training. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed framework effectively preserves vehicle privacy. Additionally, the application of federated learning through this collaborative structure significantly outperforms traditional centralized learning methods. These findings indicate that edge cognition offers a promising solution for privacy preservation in automotive networks. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/zhongyuanwang1992/Privacy-aware-Edge-Cognition. This paper expands upon our work presented at the IEEE International Conference on Vehicular Electronics and Science 2021, where it was awarded the Best Paper Award. Keywords: Automotive Networks, Edge Cognition, Privacy-Preserving, Federated Learning, Differential Privacy.

This study investigates how non-top standard model processes impact the shape of the reconstructed top quark mass distribution in $t\bar{t}+j$ events. To address this, we developed an analytical model capable of describing these contributions across various kinematic and event selection parameters. Our results indicate that off-shell effects are negligible for the primary observables used in current ATLAS and CMS top quark mass measurements. Furthermore, we demonstrate that these influences can be readily accounted for within standard likelihood frameworks employed by experimental collaborations. Although this work primarily addresses off-shell contributions in $t\bar{t}+j$ events, the proposed modeling approach is also applicable to other relevant standard model processes. Finally, we outline a strategy for incorporating these effects into future mass extraction efforts utilizing full $t\bar{t}$ data. These findings will assist future analyses in determining the optimal reconstruction and reconstruction-weighting techniques for extracting the top quark mass. Evolutionary methods have been extensively applied to optimization challenges, particularly those involving multiple, often conflicting objectives. While evolutionary algorithms rely on iterative generations of solution refinement, their computational cost becomes prohibitive for large-scale problems. Consequently, recent research has focused on parallelizing these algorithms to leverage distributed computing. However, parallelization strategies must align with evolutionary mechanisms and specific problem characteristics. This study introduces a frequency-centered parent selection approach for asynchronous parallel evolutionary methods, designed to mitigate evaluation-time bias during solution comparison. The proposed method employs a parallel non-dominated sorting genetic algorithm, utilizing frequency information from the archive of non-dominated solutions to guide optimization. A planetary candidate designated as OGLE-2017-BLG-1434Lb was recently identified through finite-source microlensing caustic crossings recorded by the OGLE and ADONIS surveys. This system is characterized by a host star (OGLE-2017-BLG-1434L) with a mass of 0.11 solar masses, located at a distance of 1.8 kiloparsecs. The planet, weighing 7.1 Earth masses, orbits at a distance of 2.0 astronomical units. With an equilibrium temperature estimated between 150 and 200 Kelvin, OGLE-2017-BLG-1434Lb is among the coldest super-Earths confirmed to date. To further constrain the lens mass and distance ratio, we conducted Adaptive Optics Near-Infrared photometry using Keck Adaptive Lenses. Our findings indicate that the microlensing distance ratio $R$ is less than 0.018 at a 95% confidence level, which significantly narrows the allowable parameter space for the host star mass ($M_L$) and distance ratio ($q$). Consequently, we have successfully constrained these parameters to the point where OGLE-2017-BLG-1434Lb is now considered a validated exoplanet. Additionally, we demonstrate that the lens mass can be determined with a precision of 10% using a single ALP observation, a capability that may facilitate future direct measurements of cold exoplanets via microlensing. Furthermore, we show that the mass of the host star can be accurately derived from a combination of adaptive optics near-infrared photometry and prior parallax data. This marks the first instance of utilizing adaptive optics near-infrared photometry to constrain host star masses in microlensing events. Our results suggest that integrating adaptive optics near-infrared photometry into future analyses could substantially enhance the precision of microlensing exoplanet host star mass estimates. Finally, we propose that the host star's mass could be directly measured using a single ALP observation. The presence of OGLE-2017-BLG-1434Lb expands the known population of cold super-Earths and sub-Neptunes, offering valuable insights into the frequency of such planetary systems. This work investigates the high-rate behavior of time-regular evolution equations, a category encompassing many physically relevant dynamics. We establish that the high-rate limit of these systems can be derived from a time-irregular evolution equation, for which we propose an exact solution method based on series expansions with rigorous error bounds. The paper includes a reread of existing literature to analyze the implications of these findings and discusses their potential applications within quantum information theory. A key advantage of this approach is that the high-rate limit yields a simplified evolution equation, free from integral terms, which is easier to solve and allows for a clearer understanding of the dynamics. Furthermore, the computational cost of the expansion solution is comparable to that of numerical methods. In the limit, the quantum differential equation is replaced by a linear algebraic equation, which is expected to be highly beneficial for quantum information applications. Finally, the paper demonstrates the utility of these results by calculating the high-rate limit and its associated error bounds for the average fidelity of time-regular evolution equations. These calculations provide valuable insights into optimizing the average fidelity of quantum gates, a critical task in quantum information theory. Additionally, this methodology offers a viable alternative to the parameter optimization approach, which is often computationally demanding and prone to local optima. This alternative is also expected to be more robust against experimental errors. We anticipate that these results will serve as a valuable tool for researchers in quantum information theory. Deep neural networks are increasingly deployed across various industries, prompting the need to evaluate their robustness and generalization capabilities. This study addresses data scarcity by investigating domain adaptation techniques for image classification. Specifically, we compare pre-training, transfer learning, and meta-learning approaches for dataset scaling. We evaluate these methods across four distinct scenarios: adapting from ImageNet to CIFAR-10, from combined ImageNet and CIFAR-10 to CIFAR-100, adapting the larger COCO dataset to CIFAR-100, and finally adapting both ImageNet and COCO to the smaller Tiny-ImageNet dataset. Our findings indicate that these domain adaptation strategies can enhance both the accuracy and stability of certain architectures, though their efficacy varies by context. Furthermore, we demonstrate that a specific ensemble of these methods yields superior performance across all tested scenarios. Finally, we highlight that our proposed ensembles deliver an accuracy boost of up to 10% across the evaluated architectures and scenarios. The code for this study can be accessed at https://github.com/DeepMind/assessating-domain-adaptation.

Furthermore, we apply these counting methods to specific curves, such as those parameterized by rational functions and conics, to establish novel results on the existence of arcs. Additionally, we offer a concise proof of the classical bound $m \le 2$ for complete arcs situated on hyperbolas. For arcs that are either incomplete or complete, we derive lower bounds for the span of rational curves; these findings generalize and unify various results previously found in the literature. Finally, our work extends to arcs in $\mathbb F_q^d$ by incorporating the concept of "complete" arcs, thereby enabling the application of our techniques to the study of designs and coding theory. In this context, we revisit and generalize several results from existing studies. Specifically, we demonstrate that any arc in $\mathbb F_q^3$ possessing a span of 3 must contain at least $q+1$ points, and we establish a lower bound for 4-spans in $\mathbb F_q^4$ as an extension of a result by Ray-Chaudhuri and Shrikhande. Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have gained significant traction for analyzing graph data, yet the intricate inner workings of the GNN parameterization function remain underexplored. This study investigates the representability of that function within the framework of compressed sensing theory. We demonstrate that under specific conditions, the GNN parameterization function can be represented as the solution to an $\ell_1$-minimization problem. Leveraging this representation, we establish recovery guarantees and provide insights into the generalization error of GNNs. Furthermore, we develop an interpretable GNN model based on this parameterization, where the network's intermediate layers correspond to selected features, and the output layer reflects the final prediction. We validate the interpretability of our approach and the effectiveness of the resulting interpretable model through a classification task on a real-world dataset. Additionally, we obtain promising results for a real-world application involving a railway track fault detection system. Finally, we explore potential future research directions and applications for our work. This paper aims to enhance our understanding of GNNs and their parameters, while also advancing the broader field of interpretable machine learning. A recent study (Burger et al., 2022) introduced the parallel training of a single Legendre Memory Module (LMM) across a cluster of GPUs, leveraging a parameter-parallel strategy. This work extends that research by implementing Distributed Legendre Memory Efficient Transformers (DiLeMET), a parameter-parallel framework capable of training multiple LMMs simultaneously on GPU clusters. We demonstrate that DiLeMET enables the training of models like BLOOM (Hurst et al., 2022) on large-scale clusters with minimal communication overhead. Furthermore, we evaluate memory efficiency and training performance using various LMM configurations on state-of-the-art GPU clusters, including those featuring NVIDIA A100 and V100 architectures. Our results indicate that DiLeMET achieves up to a 4.5x improvement in memory efficiency compared to standard Distributed Data Parallel (DDP) training on BLOOM. Additionally, we show that DiLeMET maintains training times within 1% to 2% of those achieved by DDP. Finally, we successfully trained an 184 LMMs on 1,024 GPUs, completing the process in just 10.5 hours. This work is released under an Apache 2.0 license. We present a model featuring migrating agents engaged in a signaling game focused on the assignment of linguistic tags. Each agent functions as a noisy best response to their expectations regarding others' strategies, while dynamically updating these expectations through the migration of players who act greedily. Our results demonstrate that, despite individual noise and migration dynamics, the system converges to a discrete Bayesian Nash equilibrium. This equilibrium corresponds to a labeling game where all agents accurately predict opponent strategies and select an optimal response. Furthermore, numerical simulations reveal the system's dynamical behavior upon approaching this discrete Bayesian Nash equilibrium. Additionally, we observe that agents can efficiently acquire the ability to assign linguistic tags to new words through repeated interactions, even when the population size is small. Finally, we illustrate an application of this system to the labeling behavior of online users. Specifically, online forums are modeled as systems with migrating participants, and our findings indicate that the system successfully reproduces the labeling dynamics observed on such platforms. Consequently, this model may contribute to a deeper understanding of linguistic consistency. Physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) have become a widely adopted method for addressing problems in physics-informed machine learning. However, during training, PINNs frequently suffer from spectral bias, where low-frequency components of the target function are learned significantly faster than high-frequency ones. This learning speed disparity causes PINNs to become trapped in suboptimal regions, often converging prematurely to poor local minima. This study demonstrates that incorporating a momentum term into the PINN training framework can substantially diminish this spectral bias. Specifically, we apply momentum to the residual function rather than the parameters, alongside a tailored training protocol. We validate the efficacy of this proposed momentum framework on two benchmark tasks that PINNs struggle to solve, as well as on two additional benchmark problems where the momentum approach achieves superior accuracy compared to standard training methods. Furthermore, we illustrate the potential of this framework by addressing a challenging inverse problem where the momentum-based approach yields results of higher accuracy than those obtained from the conventional PINN method. Finally, we provide comprehensive experiments on a large-scale dataset to examine the robustness of the momentum framework. Our code is publicly accessible at https://github.com/ChenchenWang1997/MomentumPINN.

These findings rely on a novel technique for handling coupled problems, which we expect to be applicable in future research. In safety-critical domains, the risk of reinforcement learning (RL) agents making erroneous decisions necessitates the ability to explain agent behavior. This study introduces a hierarchical RL framework utilizing Explanable Inductive Logic Programming (ExoILP) to foster trust and support decision-making. By decomposing tasks into coarse and fine levels of granularity, the approach accelerates training, reduces the amount of data required, and enhances the interpretability of actions. Asymmetry is a fundamental characteristic that enables many natural phenomena, such as directional propagation, chirality, and gauge fields. Although significant progress has been made in creating synthetic dimensions, achieving physical symmetry breaking within these synthetic spaces remains a critical challenge. In this study, we introduce quantum compression as a viable method to break optical symmetry in a two-dimensional lattice. By integrating quantum compressors into specific sites of the 2D model, we induce symmetry breaking, which substantially enhances nonreciprocal transmission. Furthermore, we observe a marked increase in nonreciprocity within the non-Hermitian skin effect, a substantial expansion of the topological phase, and a shift in the Majorana zero mode's position within a non-Hermitian system. These findings offer a novel approach for breaking symmetry in synthetic dimensions and provide new avenues for advancing quantum simulation and device applications. Additionally, our proposed schemes are compatible with current experimental setups. Our model was analyzed using the density-matrix formalism, with results verified through numerical simulations. This research was conducted without the collection or use of personal identifiable information. To our knowledge, no conflicts of interest exist. This study required no funding. This paper addresses minimax (Fenton-type) issues concerning the Lp-norms of the sum of translates for bandlimited functions of a single variable. Specifically, we examine the optimal joint spectrum set D for functions u in the space BLw2, where u is defined as the translate of a polynomial multiplied by a Gaussian. Our approach involves solving a specific finite-dimensional linear programming problem to determine the optimal joint spectrum set D. Furthermore, we explore the relationship between this linear programming problem and a multivariate generalization of the famous Riesz product. Finally, we demonstrate that this finite-dimensional problem represents a multivariate extension of a well-known result by Dalibard regarding the joint spectrum of a function and its derivative. Additionally, we investigate multivariate extensions of Fenton-type minimax problems within the framework of shift-invariant spaces. The study is motivated by a multivariate filtering problem formulated in [10]. We provide a detailed analysis of the one-dimensional case and subsequently present findings for the multi-dimensional scenario. Notably, we demonstrate that the multi-dimensional problem admits an explicit solution when polynomials are involved. However, we also highlight that the multi-dimensional problem is significantly more complex than its one-dimensional counterpart. To address this, we develop an iterative method to compute the Fenton-type spectrum set up to a specified precision. We introduce a novel method to investigate spin-dependent (SD) interactions within the $^6$Li nucleus, specifically targeting those involving color-octet operators. This approach leverages the nuclear wave function derived from the no-core shell model (NCSM) and the Green's function shell model (GFSM) to calculate the spin-dependent form factor for $^6$Li using the ab initio method. Our findings indicate that the NCSM form factor is approximately 10% larger than the one obtained from a simple effective field theory (EFT) framework. Furthermore, the computed form factors for $^6$Li are compared against the widely accepted results from lattice Monte Carlo simulations. Finally, the resulting form factors are utilized to establish limits on SD interactions mediated by an $S$-wave operator, based on the spin-dependent WIMP-nucleon scattering cross section derived from XENON1T data. The derived constraints are $|\lambda_a| \lesssim 1.0 \times 10^{-39} \, \mathrm{cm}^4$ and $|\lambda_b| \lesssim 1.0 \times 10^{-39} \, \mathrm{cm}^4$, which are approximately 1.5 and 1.3 times tighter, respectively, than the constraints obtained using the EFT form factor. These results highlight the significant potential of the NCSM and GFSM methods for exploring nuclear effects in SD interactions. Additionally, the calculated form factors are made publicly available to facilitate future research. Blind image restoration (BUR) aims to recover high-quality images from low-quality versions without prior knowledge of the degradation processes. This study introduces a novel approach to address a specific parameter estimation challenge in BUR by utilizing a sophisticated degradation model. This model is built upon a non-negative kernel mixture framework, which effectively represents a broad spectrum of degradation operators for BUR tasks. By integrating advanced techniques in model design, optimization, and analysis, we successfully estimate degradation parameters, thereby significantly enhancing performance across key BUR applications including denoising, blur, blur-noise, and super-resolution. Extensive experiments on diverse synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate that our method outperforms state-of-the-art solutions in most scenarios. Nonuniform associative algebras constitute a noncommutative generalization of pseudofree algebras, offering a framework for the construction of integrable lattice models. This work introduces the concept of nonuniform associative Yang-Baxter equations (ASYB), which are satisfied by noncommutative R-matrices associated with these algebras. We demonstrate the existence of solutions to the nonuniform ASYB within specific cases, including cases where the noncommutativity is governed by an abelian solution to the standard Yang-Baxter equation. These R-matrices hold significant utility in integrable lattice models, enabling the derivation of both dynamical and generalized quantum inverse scattering methods. Furthermore, we establish a relationship between nonuniform ASYB and q-associative Yang-Baxter equations. Specifically, we prove that if a noncommutative matrix A satisfies the nonuniform ASYB, then the matrix B, defined as $B = (\exp(q\sigma_2 \Lambda))^{-1}A(\exp(q\sigma_2 \Lambda))$, satisfies the q-associative Yang-Baxter equation. As an application, we derive solutions to the nonuniform ASYB from several solutions of the quantum Yang-Baxter equation. Additionally, we derive solutions to the dynamical noncommutative quantum Yang-Baxter equation by appropriately modifying the noncommutative R-matrices. Finally, we derive solutions to the quantum dynamical Yang-Baxter equation by applying a linear transformation to the noncommutative R-matrices. These findings provide a systematic approach for generating integrable lattice models. Notably, our results extend and complement recent findings by various authors. Specifically, the models derived in this paper include the quantum XXZ model, the quantum principal chiral model, and the quantum affine Toda model. Furthermore, the quantum integrable models obtained herein are novel and have not been previously reported in the literature. This achievement is facilitated by the recent development of the quantum inverse scattering method utilizing the quantum R-matrix. Consequently, our findings offer a new approach to the construction of integrable lattice models. To illustrate this, we present a solution to the quantum affine Toda model based on a solution of the quantum Yang-Baxter equation. Our results thus provide a nonuniform generalization of this solution. This work was partially supported by the National Natural Science Foundation of China (Grant No. 11471161). The first author is currently a Visiting Scholar at the Department of Mathematics, University of California, Los Angeles.

This paper presents a formal framework for validating the logical properties of statements that combine the natural language description of programs with Hoare triples. To accomplish this, we propose utilizing Abstract Syntax Trees (ASTs) to represent natural language sentences. This approach enables the value of program variables to be extracted from those sentences. Furthermore, we demonstrate how to employ ASTs to capture the ASTs defining the associated Hoare triples, thereby facilitating formal validation. Our formalism is grounded in the syntax of the Mizar proof assistant, which allows for the formal verification of statements linking program behavior to the described natural language. We provide examples of valid and invalid assertions, illustrating them with the corresponding ASTs and Hoare triples. These examples serve to motivate the framework and pave the way for natural language description and formal validation in subsequent research. The proposed method supports the value extraction needed to verify assertions, such as confirming that "for all integers x, y, and z, if x is assigned the value of x plus y, then y equals z" is valid given the corresponding Hoare triple. Ultimately, this work lays the foundation for natural language descriptions and formal validation in future endeavors. Additionally, we show that the framework can validate assertions involving probabilistic programs, such as determining whether a program outputs heads or tails with a 50% probability. Consequently, this approach enables formal validation of both deterministic and probabilistic programs. The paper includes illustrative examples with their respective ASTs and Hoare triples to demonstrate how to validate assertions derived from them. Ultimately, the system supports the value extraction required to verify these assertions. In summary, the framework facilitates formal validation of programs based on logical forms of natural language descriptions. Although significant research has been conducted on Byzantine fault-tolerant (BFT) replicated state machines (RSMs), most existing solutions are either unsuitable for cloud environments due to their heavy reliance on specialized hardware, or they depend on stringent and often unrealistic assumptions regarding the behavior of cloud services. This paper introduces RCanopus, an efficient BFT RSM designed to withstand both hardware and software failures within public cloud settings. Unlike many of its predecessors, RCanopus operates with minimal dependencies on external configuration services. RCanopus is built upon a novel cloud model that captures the realistic failure patterns of cloud storage and compute services. We developed an optimized failure detector for this model and integrated it with an adaptive, failure-driven replication strategy. This approach enables the system to maintain high availability by utilizing a reduced quorum for progress, provided that a sufficient number of correct, non-failing services are available. Furthermore, by dynamically adjusting its replication factor, RCanopus ensures low-latency operation as long as a quorum of non-failing services exists. Extensive experiments involving various failure scenarios demonstrate that RCanopus achieves superior availability and performance compared to other BFT RSMs. Additionally, we evaluated an external benchmark using multiple failure models, which confirmed the robustness of RCanopus against diverse failure scenarios. To our knowledge, this represents the first study to address failures in both object and block storage services within public clouds. Finally, we have deployed 20 million requests per second using 40 instances, validating the system's scalability. The implementation, written in Java, is available on GitHub. Our source code and benchmarking code can be found at \url{https://github.com/ist/ricanopus}, and the paper is accessible at \url{https://arxiv.org/abs/2001.00100}. The modulus of lipid membrane bending is a critical property governing processes like budding and fusion. This study employs molecular dynamics simulations to investigate how cholesterol affects the bending modulus of both pure and mixed lipid bilayers. Our results indicate that replacing DPPC lipids with cholesterol enhances membrane flexibility up to a 25-30% concentration, after which the bending modulus increases. We attribute this initial rise to cholesterol's ability to reduce the area per headgroup, an effect that diminishes at higher concentrations. Furthermore, we observe that the bending modulus for DPPC/cholesterol bilayers aligns with experimental data, whereas the behavior in POPC/cholesterol systems contradicts both simulations and experiments, suggesting the presence of additional factors in the latter. The POPC/cholesterol system fails to match experimental trends because the reduction in area per headgroup is insufficient to account for the experimentally observed decrease in bending modulus. Finally, we demonstrate that a simple continuum model accurately reproduces the bending modulus of DPPC/cholesterol bilayers. This model incorporates the bending modulus and viscosity of water, the friction coefficient between monolayers, and the area per headgroup, which is influenced by cholesterol. We propose that the area per headgroup serves as an effective descriptor for the degree of cholesterol ordering within the bilayer. These findings offer a quantitative framework for understanding the impact of cholesterol on membrane flexibility and the associated underlying mechanisms. This could facilitate the design of novel cholesterol-modifying agents for potential biomedical applications. Additionally, our results provide a baseline for developing and evaluating new forcefields and models for simulating lipid membranes. **Keywords:** lipid membrane, cholesterol, molecular dynamics, bending modulus. **Abbreviations:** POPC = 1-palmitoyl-2-oleoyl-sn-glycero-3-phosphocholine; DPPC = 1,2-dipalmitoyl-phosphatidylcholine. **Acknowledgments:** This work was funded by the Spanish Ministry of Economy and Competitiveness (grants CTQ2015-67300-P and FIS2016-77284-P), the Autonomous Community of Madrid (grant S2018/TPM-4335), and the European Regional Development Fund. We examine the constraints arising from the vaning of the Hamiltonian constraint, which models a single particle within a homogeneous, isotropic, one-bubble universe under quantum loop constraints. This model is derived from the ADM Hamiltonian for a single-bubble one-dimensional anisotropic cosmological space, incorporating both inverse volume and flux modifications. By applying the Demkov model to solve the resulting differential equation, we analyze the modifications to the spectrum and wave functions. Our findings indicate a redshift of the spectrum alongside modifications to the wave functions. Furthermore, we observe that quantum effects diminish as the density increases, a conclusion supported by the behavior of the wave functions. These results demonstrate that modifications to the ADM Hamiltonian offer a viable method for incorporating quantum gravitational effects into field theory. Additionally, the inclusion of the Demkov model enables the determination of the resonance condition, revealing features such as zero transmission and unit reflection, alongside the previously noted spectral modifications. Finally, the presence of momentum in our model results in the formation of an effective potential, a phenomenon absent in the standard ADM formulation. We also explore the implications of the Demkov potential regarding its relationship with the Coulomb potential. Ultimately, these findings suggest that modifications to the ADM Hamiltonian provide a framework for investigating gravitational effects in cosmology. Specifically, the analysis of spectral behavior in a homogeneous, isotropic, one-bubble universe indicates that loop corrections may influence the behavior of cosmic microwave background radiation. Consequently, the application of quantum gravitational modifications to the ADM Hamiltonian holds significant potential for advancing our understanding of cosmology. In this context, we examine the implications of these findings, particularly the existence of a zero-energy state, and discuss its relevance to the dark energy problem. Finally, we outline several promising future research directions. Notably, we investigate the possibility of using loop corrections to explain dark energy, alongside the potential for constraining quantum gravitational effects through observations of the cosmic microwave background. These outcomes underscore the broader significance of the work, demonstrating that quantum gravitational effects may be detectable in cosmology. We conclude by suggesting future research avenues, including the development of observational tests to constrain loop quantum gravity effects in cosmology. Specifically, we explore the possibility of detecting these effects through the analysis of the cosmic microwave background spectrum and suggest that future observations of the large-scale structure of the universe may provide constraints on the magnitude of quantum gravitational effects. Deep object detectors are widely used across numerous computer vision tasks, yet their predictions lack uncertainty assessment, which is crucial for practical applications. To address this, we introduce BayesOD, the first Bayesian approach designed to estimate uncertainty in object detection. By employing Bayesian neural networks, BayesOD generates both deterministic outputs and uncertainty metrics. Our primary contributions include: (1) the development of a Bayesian backbone that is lightweight and efficient; (2) the proposal of a Bayesian Feature Pyramid Network to enhance performance; and (3) the implementation of Bayesian spatial attention to refine uncertainty estimates. We evaluate our method's uncertainty estimation capabilities using the standard PRA metric on the COCO dataset. This study investigates short-term traffic prediction using urban traffic data from New York City. We introduce a novel dataset comprising 10,000 samples of two-minute traffic flow segments. For each sample, we compile comprehensive statistical features describing the traffic state and its evolution over the previous two minutes. Experimental results demonstrate that both prediction accuracy and model interpretability surpass those achieved by recent long-term traffic prediction models. Additionally, we develop a simple yet effective baseline model that outperforms other approaches. Finally, we explore the application of this methodology for next-link traffic prediction. We conclude that our proposed method utilizing short fragments represents a valuable alternative for long-term prediction tasks. Furthermore, the features extracted for prediction inherently characterize the traffic state, offering a means to interpret model behavior and enhance transparency. This paper introduces the notion of a coherence category with implementations and demonstrates that this concept is equivalent to that of a reifying category. Furthermore, we establish that any reifying category possesses a universal reversion category, which serves as an equivalent to the construction of coherence limits. A representative example of a reifying category is the category of Reynolds categories and functors preserving colimits of essentially small families of essentially compact objects. Additionally, we provide an example where an reifying category arises as the change of base functor of an adjunction linking to a category of Reynolds categories. These examples suggest a generalized construction for obtaining reifying categories from categories of Reynolds categories via implementations. Finally, we outline an inductive procedure for constructing reversion categories based on specific properties of the initial category. This paper serves as a foundational step toward developing a methodology for constructing Reynolds categories with implementations, thereby enhancing the expressiveness of the category of Reynolds categories. Such an advancement would facilitate the modeling of various programming paradigms, including those involving mutable state. This library includes implementations of relevant 2-Functors, 2-Natural transformations, and 2-Limits, along with several instances and potential counter-examples. This study introduces a deep learning approach for segmenting the hippocampus in MRI scans of patients suffering from Alzheimer's disease or epilepsy. Traditional segmentation techniques rely on either data-driven deep learning models or hybrid methods that integrate prior knowledge with deep learning, both of which have limitations. The former often fails to generalize effectively to unseen data due to overfitting, while the latter is constrained by the need for extensive manual effort in defining organ boundaries. To address these challenges, we developed hippocampus partitioning models utilizing numerous convolutional neural networks. Our results demonstrate that the proposed deep learning models outperform existing hippocampus segmentation techniques. Specifically, the average Dice Similarity Coefficient (DSC) for Alzheimers' patients improved by 1.5%, and for epilepsy patients by 2.5%. Additionally, the overall DSC for the entire dataset, encompassing both patient groups, increased by 1.6%. This indicates that the suggested deep learning models surpass current state-of-the-art hippocampus segmentation methods. We examine the Pigeonhole phenomenon within the context of quantum communication. This phenomenon, originally described by Bužek and Bergholt as a conflict between the unitarity of quantum evolution and the locality of projective measurements, represents the most fundamental explanation of the no-cloning theorem. Its mathematical formulation involves equating a unitary matrix with a sum of projection matrices. In this study, we demonstrate that an infinite solution set exists for a specific scenario characterized by the coincidence of pigeonhole phenomena, where the unknown state resides in a two-dimensional subspace spanned by two transversal modes. This situation is analogous to measuring a qubit using only horizontal and vertical polarizations. The existence of these solution states underscores the nonlocal nature of quantum mechanics. Consequently, our findings suggest that a cloning machine could be constructed by preparing an input state at a singular point within this family of solutions. Furthermore, we explore the relationship between pigeonhole phenomena and isotropic states. Finally, we outline a solution to the old quantum riddle concerning the distinction between cloning and deforming qubits. These conclusions are supported by experimental demonstrations. Additionally, we examine a variant of the phenomenon that does not rely on matrix coincidences but instead on the orthogonality of evolved states, illustrating its application in quantum key distribution. This alternative formulation highlights a potential advantage of cloning machines over other quantum resources. Overall, this work provides a new perspective on quantum cloning and establishes a foundation for developing quantum cloning machines. Specifically, we have designed and demonstrated a quantum cloning machine that utilizes transversal modes. This device holds significant potential for applications in quantum error correction and quantum key distribution. Finally, we outline two new directions for quantum resource theory. One direction addresses the characterization of optimal universal cloning machines for d-dimensional qudits, while the other investigates optimal symmetric qudit cloning machines. The most critical component of space weather is the galactic cosmic ray (CR) and its associated secondary radiation, which is evaluated using space-weather models. This paper outlines the development of a Monte Carlo (MC) model designed to simulate the transport of CR protons within the Earth's magnetic field. Specifically, the model calculates the time-dependent particle flux intensity and differential energy spectrum in Low Earth Orbit (LEO) based on geocentric magnetic latitude, solar modulation parameters, and the geostationary geomagnetic cutoff rigidity. The MC approach is benchmarked against McPSL (McElroy-Parker-Spencer-Lee) transport theory results, and an analytical model for protons in LEO is also presented and compared. The findings demonstrate that the proposed MC model can accurately reproduce protons in LEO when compared to McElroy-Parker-Spencer-Lee theory, McPSL, and the CRAND model. Furthermore, the MC model successfully replicates the characteristics of the CRAND model, including the relationship between CR energy spectrum and geocentric magnetic latitude, as well as the temporal evolution of CR intensity in LEO. Consequently, the MC model can effectively simulate and predict proton radiation in LEO, offering a valuable tool for space radiation protection. Additionally, the model is applied to assess the radiation environment aboard the Tiangong space station. The results indicate that protons in LEO constitute the primary space radiation threat to the Tiangong station. Proton flux rates in LEO range from 10⁻⁵ to 10⁻⁴ Sv/day, with a maximum dose of 10⁻³ Sv/day. Proton dose rates for individual organs are approximately 10⁻⁵ to 10⁻⁴ Sv/day, with a peak of 10⁻³ Sv/day. The dose contribution from protons in LEO is approximately 10⁻⁴ Sv/day, or about 10% of the annual effective dose. Proton radiation in LEO is the dominant source of stochastic cancer risk for astronauts on the Tiangong station. However, the probability of deterministic effects is negligible. This study provides a reference for the radiation protection of astronauts on the Tiangong space station. Ultimately, the MC model is also applicable for predicting the space radiation environment of the Tiangong space station. Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have become essential tools for analyzing graph data across various fields. Building upon the Universal Pyramid-like Shrinkage Skeleton (UPSS) of traditional graph theory, we introduce a new GNN framework that UPSS-driven models can reduce to. This process involves connecting local structures in a twisted manner, transforming a graph into a shrunk model. We demonstrate that the significant information loss in conventional UPSS-based approaches during graph shrinking can be largely recovered through the local link rewiring introduced by our framework. The shrinkage of local structures acts as a dimensionality reduction mechanism for GNNs, enabling model compression and accelerating inference. Furthermore, our framework design is versatile, allowing for the creation of multiple GNN architectures. Experimental results confirm that the proposed framework outperforms several state-of-the-art GNNs, achieving both higher accuracy and greater efficiency. Additionally, extensive model compression experiments illustrate how our framework facilitates the compression of GNN models. Finally, extensive ablation studies investigate how local link rewiring influences the sensitivity of graph shrinking and the resulting GNN performance. These comprehensive experiments highlight that local link rewiring is a general and effective strategy for graph shrinking. The proposed framework is expected to inspire future research on GNN architecture design. The source code is available at: https://github.com/Chenchen2020/pyg-shrinkage. Recent years have seen growing interest in private low-rank matrix completion, a method designed to protect the structural patterns within numerical datasets. This paper presents the Huber framework, a generic and flexible low-rank matrix completion framework built on differentially private optimization. By utilizing an optimization-based approach, the framework supports various tasks beyond simple matrix completion, such as private singular value thresholding and matrix approximation. We provide theoretical guarantees for the Huber framework when applied to singular value thresholding and matrix approximation, covering both convex and non-convex scenarios. Furthermore, we introduce the DPLRF family, a collection of low-rank fulfillment methods that integrate into the Huber framework for performing private matrix approximation. Finally, through extensive experiments on both synthetic and real-world data, we demonstrate that our proposed framework achieves competitive utility in terms of reconstruction error while offering stronger privacy protections. We report the discovery of a protoplanetary disk around CIDA 1, a massive planetary-mass brown dwarf situated approximately 140 parsecs away. This disk exhibits a sharp inner edge at 0.13 AU and a pronounced outer edge near 0.5 AU, both of which align closely with the gravitational stability radius predicted for a massive planet at 1.5 AU. The disk's total mass is estimated to be 0.002 solar masses, with a gas mass of 0.001 solar masses. Additionally, we identify a candidate companion star, CIDA 1B, orbiting roughly 1000 AU from the primary. The compact size of this disk represents a significant constraint for planet formation models in low-mass stellar environments. We propose that the planet responsible for the inner edge may have recently migrated inward, while the outer edge reflects the extent of disk truncation by the massive planet. Furthermore, the presence of a binary system in a planetary-mass brown dwarf challenges current understanding of how such systems form. Finally, CIDA 1 serves as a valuable target for studying the conditions necessary for giant planet formation around brown dwarfs and for investigating planet formation in low-metallicity environments. This paper introduces a new image segmentation framework that integrates a variant of the variational partitioning model with two image recovery techniques: deblurring and denoising. The proposed system couples an area-based active contours model with two data fidelity terms to handle blurred and noisy images. The initial model variant utilizes two regularizers: an edge-drivers total variation (TV) regularizer to preserve significant features like edges and a first-order BVTV regularizer to minimize the boundary length, which stabilizes the minimization process. Subsequently, two coupling strategies are developed to apply image recovery to the segmented results. The first strategy applies denoising to both the original and segmented images, whereas the second strategy employs both deblurring and denoising on the input image before segmentation. Extensive experiments across various noisy and blurred images demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed models, with the segmentation and boundary evolution of recovered images showing significant improvement. Additionally, the numerical results confirm the algorithm's efficiency regarding computational time. Abstract interpretation operates within a feedback loop comprising an information gathering phase and a refinement phase. Historically, these stages have been tightly interdependent, where the extent of gathering is governed by the degree of refinement. This paper introduces a fully algorithmic framework for decoupling these phases within the framework of Abstract Interpretation. We demonstrate the utility of this approach through fully computable instances grounded in control-flow analysis. Our primary contribution lies in establishing fully computable criteria that dictate the volume of information collected and the level of refinement. These criteria are grounded in a novel concept of calibration, which we show is both necessary and sufficient. Furthermore, we apply this calibration-based methodology to several practical scenarios, including a precise control-flow analysis for the R5 semantic framework, a robust control-flow analysis for the more expressive CFA1 framework, and a straightforward control-flow analysis for the widely used CFL grammar. In each case, our algorithms achieve termination without relying on ad-hoc widening techniques. We validate the efficacy of these algorithms by implementing them in a prototype system. Additionally, we provide a complexity analysis for the proposed algorithms, showing that their behavior is no more intricate than that of standard abstract fixation procedures. Finally, we illustrate the practical performance of these methods by comparing them against existing control-flow analysis tools. Our results indicate that the proposed algorithms are competitive with existing techniques. To our knowledge, this marks the first instance where the rising and falling phases of an abstract interpretation can be decoupled in this manner. We anticipate that this approach will facilitate the design of new, potentially more effective and efficient iterative procedures in program analysis. To support these findings, we have made our prototype system publicly available. We demonstrate its use via a fully public instance, which we show is both practical and effective. This instance is a precise control-flow analysis for R5, which is more expressive than CFL. Our prototype achieves this through a novel application of the calibration concept. We introduce a straightforward, first-principles-based method for identifying materials with geometric phonons, a phenomenon where asymmetric atomic displacements generate large, optically active low-frequency modes. This is crucial for applications involving infrared and terahertz photonics and sensing. We forecast that approximately 10% of all oxides, including numerous perovskites, possess distinct geometric-phonon modes. In typical perovskites, the softness of these acoustic modes is primarily determined by the geometry of the B–O bonds. By employing a simple, analytically solvable model, we illustrate how geometric phonons can drive anomalous thermal conductivity in specific materials. Furthermore, we show that the frequencies of geometric phonons are highly sensitive to the energy of incident light, offering a means to tune acoustic properties in oxides. This tunability is driven by photoinduced symmetry breaking, a mechanism that operates at room temperature and is broadly applicable to perovskites.

Detecting anomalies in high-dimensional data is difficult because the inherent complexity of anomaly-free points often renders the anomalous features negligible. Although many anomaly detection methods have been proposed, they frequently suffer from either a high false positive rate or a high computational cost. This paper introduces the Closeness Graph Anomaly Identifier (CGIA), which constructs a closeness graph to capture the relationships among all data points. CGIA is the first approach to leverage the topological characteristics of the closeness graph for identifying anomalies. By applying the PageRank algorithm, CGIA efficiently ranks points based on their anomaly likelihood. Experimental results demonstrate that CGIA not only surpasses numerous state-of-the-art methods in accuracy but also achieves significantly faster computation times. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/ChenchenLi2018/CGIA. Furthermore, the implementation includes interpretable explanations of the anomalies, offering valuable insights into the identified outliers. The user-friendly interface can be accessed at https://chenchenli2018.github.io/CGIA/. This work is partially supported by the National Natural Science Foundation of China (No. 61976047). We introduce an equitable community detection algorithm that identifies communities based on their intrinsic structural properties. This method is derived from the generalized fractional Laplacian of a graph, which is subsequently approximated using the Localized Modularity Matrix. The resulting approach maintains computational efficiency while achieving higher accuracy than current state-of-the-art techniques. Furthermore, we demonstrate that our method successfully recovers communities across a diverse range of real-world networks. Additionally, we show that the relationship between our technique and the traditional modularity optimization approach is not as straightforward as previously assumed, and we offer insights into the characteristics of communities discovered via our algorithm. Finally, we highlight the limitations of the modularity maximization approach and illustrate how our method can effectively identify communities that this technique fails to detect. This study examines kinetic models governing reversible enzyme reactions, specifically distinguishing between mechanisms with and without hysteresis. It establishes the well-posedness of the associated initial-boundary value problem and demonstrates that solutions remain bounded globally in time within a positive cone. The analysis further explores long-time behavior, proving global asymptotic stability for positive steady states across all parameter regimes. Additionally, an estimate for the decay rate of solutions toward these steady states is provided. Finally, three iterative estimative methods for approximating positive steady states are introduced, accompanied by numerical simulations. For each method, the convergence of iterative sequences to a positive steady state is guaranteed, and the positivity of these solutions is analyzed. Finally, the article discusses the estimation of steady-state solutions. This study examines the stochastic dynamics of "swells," defined as significant yet temporary upswings in financial time series. These upswings are characterized by a stochastic drift that alternates between a high-reward, low-risk phase and a low-reward, high-risk phase, persisting for a random duration determined by independent geometric random variables with distinct mean-reverting parameters for each phase. The probability distribution of these swells is derived from a generalized Cox-Ingersoll-Ross (CIR) stochastic differential equation featuring a time-dependent drift. This distribution is expressed using confluent hypergeometric functions, which are subsequently approximated via a series expansion to facilitate calibration against time-series data. This calibration process yields the parameters defining the swell's dynamics, which are then compared against time-series-derived metrics such as kurtosis, skewness, and swing duration. Finally, a simulation-based methodology is introduced to replicate the observed swell distribution from these dynamics, thereby enabling the validation of the proposed stochastic model. Finally, the theoretical findings are applied to two real-world datasets: the S&P 500 index and the currency exchange rate between the US Dollar and the Euro. The analysis reveals that both the dollar-euro exchange rate and the S&P 500 exhibit multiple swells driven by independent geometric duration phases, each governed by distinct CIR-like dynamics. Furthermore, it is determined that while swell skewness and kurtosis fluctuate over time, their average values remain relatively stable, a characteristic that aligns with the properties of the underlying swell distribution. These results suggest that the models can effectively capture the dynamics of financial swells and may serve as a foundation for further research into the stochastic termination durations of such events. Ultimately, this research contributes to a deeper understanding of the temporary yet significant deviations from financial market equilibrium. Future applications could leverage the proposed models to enhance financial risk assessment, asset allocation strategies, and the development of new financial instruments. Additionally, the methodology offers a framework for investigating the broader dynamics of financial time series. To achieve this, future work could extend the current model by incorporating additional factors, such as market volatility and investor sentiment, to create a more comprehensive framework for analyzing financial market behavior. This could pave the way for more accurate and robust predictive models, ultimately leading to more informed decision-making for investors and financial institutions. Furthermore, the proposed models could be utilized to develop new financial products, such as structured products or exchange-traded funds (ETFs), that allow investors to capitalize on financial swells while managing associated risks. We introduce a path integral method to calculate the time evolution of a quantum harmonic oscillator under constant translation. To validate our findings, we compare them with direct time evolution and existing literature. Our results indicate that computational errors remain below 10⁻⁵ for a path integral segment count (N) of 50 or greater. The required resources include approximately 1 second for Python code execution on a single core, 100 MB of memory, and roughly 10 seconds for MATLAB code on a 12-core system. The provided MATLAB and Python codes are straightforward to implement and execute. Furthermore, we explore how this technique can be applied to other driven quantum systems, suggesting that our approach offers both a new analytical framework and an efficient numerical tool for investigating quantum-driven phenomena. Our work demonstrates that path integrals, when paired with standard Monte Carlo methods, offer viable numerical solutions to quantum problems. Additionally, we outline how machine learning techniques, such as neural networks, could be integrated to enhance computational speed. These advancements are expected to deepen our understanding of quantum systems and pave the way for novel quantum technologies. Our technique is also applicable to higher-dimensional systems, including those under external magnetic fields. To illustrate this extension, we present numerical results for a driven two-dimensional oscillator and discuss potential applications in quantum computing. We anticipate that these methods will find use in quantum mechanics, quantum field theory, and quantum technology. However, existing methods often fail to effectively leverage user reviews and the emotional tone expressed within them. To overcome this limitation, we introduce the Sentiment-sensitive Interactive Fusion Network (SIFN), which explicitly models the interaction between recommended items and user sentiment. This architecture comprises two core components: a bidirectional Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) block that captures temporal dynamics in user behavior, and a self-attention block that computes item-user interactions by integrating user sentiment information. Extensive experiments conducted on two real-world datasets demonstrate that our proposed model significantly outperforms state-of-the-art approaches.
