This study investigates using lexical substitutions to generate information augmented (IA) samples from information retrieval (IR) documents, specifically for Arabizi-English code-switched Arabic. We examine three substitution types—synonym, paraphrase, and code-switching—and assess their impact on augmenting IR documents, such as question generation, by applying substitutions to various sections of the original text. Additionally, we introduce a newly developed model built on the pre-trained pre-trained BERT (BERT) framework to create IA samples. Finally, the paper evaluates the utility of these generated samples in enhancing question answering systems. Our experiments demonstrate that bAbI tasks, which feature simple domains and structured text, are particularly well-suited for information augmentation. Furthermore, the BERT-based approach yields promising results in generating IA samples. Crucially, experiments applying these generated samples show significant improvements in question answering performance. To our knowledge, this research represents the first attempt to explore lexical substitution-based information augmentation on Arabizi, a widely used but under-researched script. The source code and data are accessible at https://github.com/ahmedhassan1992/ICT4ARAB.

We demonstrate that a collection of uniform surface homeomorphisms exhibiting a uniform upper bound on their quas-isometry constants is Roelcke precompact within the homeomorphism group equipped with the uniform topology. Furthermore, we establish that, with the exception of the isometry group, the elements of such collections are Roelcke precompact in their respective homogeneous spaces. Additionally, we identify which subgroups of the homeomorphism group possess an invariant metric featuring a finite Roelcke dimension. Finally, we present examples illustrating that the Roelcke precompactness property does not invariably persist under continuous homomorphisms. To support these findings, we develop novel technical instruments with broader applicability. Specifically, we derive a characterization of the Roelcke dimension for actions on metric spaces based on the compactness of diagonal actions on the completion of the homeomorphism group under the topology of uniform convergence on compacta. We also provide a characterization of uniformly quasiconformal surface homeomorphisms as those admitting finitely representable germs under this same topology. To achieve this, we construct a novel link between the topology of uniform convergence and that of uniform convergence on compacta. Leveraging this connection, we offer an alternative approach to determining the Roelcke dimension of isometry groups for invariant metrics on surfaces. To facilitate these results, we develop an intrinsic metric on the space of surface homeomorphisms and derive a characterization of isometries for this metric. To ensure reproducibility, an implementation is available at: https://github.com/SebastianKoch/Quasisphere. Finally, we outline an effective algorithm for calculating the Roelcke precompactness of a uniform family of surface homeomorphisms with a fixed quas-isometry constant. This algorithm was applied to compute the Roelcke precompactness and, consequently, the Roelcke dimension for several significant groups acting on surfaces, including groups of finite covolume. The computational implementation can be found at: https://github.com/SebastianKoch/Quasisphere. The algorithm's output includes a basis for the space of invariant measures on the symmetric product of the manifold, which provides an alternative method for determining the Roelcke dimension. The inverse of this algorithm is also proposed, which computes the minimal dimension of such a space given the space itself. This algorithm has been utilized to determine the Roelcke dimension for specific groups with finite covolume. The output for the group $\Gamma = \Gamma(2)$ serves as a concrete example of this application

We investigate integrable supermembranes within backgrounds that result from performing $\lambda$-transformations on maximally supersymmetric $AdS_5\times S^5$. These transformations, which are coordinate transformations preserving the equations of motion and the integrability of the original superstring, yield new integrable models for supermembranes. Furthermore, we explore various branes embedded within these transformed backgrounds. Specifically, we examine membranes associated with the maximal symmetry subgroups of the background, which correspond to bispinor projections of the superstring. Additionally, we analyze membranes aligned with $PSU(2,2|4)/U(1)^3$-submembranes, which are closely related to fundamental strings in the $AdS_5\times S^5$ superstring. Finally, we connect our findings to the recently proposed holographic duals of these supermembrane models. Given that the transformation preserves the holonomy of the massless R-R gauge field, the dual theories are expected to be generalized Green-Schwarz $\lambda$-transformations of the 4D $\mathcal{N}=4$ maximally supersymmetric Yang-Mills (MSYM) theory. We demonstrate how the duality between our supermembrane models and these generalized Green-Schwarz transformations of MSYM can be derived from the equations of motion and the membrane ansatz. This suggests a broader generalization of the AdS/CFT correspondence beyond standard string and bispinor projections, potentially opening a new avenue for research. In this context, we also examine membranes with $PSU(2,2|4)/U(1)^3$-submembrane structures in $AdS_5\times S^5$ backgrounds where the massless R-R gauge field holonomy is reduced. These backgrounds are anticipated to be dual to various generalized projections of the MSYM theory, thereby extending the duality beyond the $PSU(2,2|4)$-symmetric $AdS_5\times S^5$ case. We show that these reduced holonomy models are also duals of generalized Green-Schwarz $\lambda$-transformations of MSYM. Consequently, we illustrate that membranes with $PSU(2,2|4)/U(1)^3$-submembrane structures in $AdS_5\times S^5$ backgrounds with reduced holonomy are likewise membranes of generalized Green-Schwarz $\lambda$-transformations of MSYM. By employing a hexahedralization method based on tets (four-hedra), we maintain a substantial proportion of large tets-expressions (LTPs) that facilitate efficient finite volume discretization. Utilizing the up-to-date tets-to-hex algorithm developed by the authors, we achieved novel records for NVTech and CG-Flame benchmarks: 58.11 tets/Hex and 45.24 tets/Hex, respectively. Relation extraction aims to identify the relationships between pairs of entities within a given sentence. However, the sequential nature of Natural Language Processing inherently restricts its ability to capture long-range dependencies. Conversely, models leveraging self-attention mechanisms can effectively represent global sentence information but often suffer from sparse and inaccurate relational labels. To address these challenges, we introduce a novel approach that utilizes a relation-restricted knowledge graph to enhance relation discovery through connection prediction. This method relies on two key innovations: first, a knowledge graph connection prediction task that leverages global sentence information to boost the graph's density and accuracy; second, a relation discovery mechanism that utilizes the relationship between entity representations and knowledge graph nodes to identify relations. Experimental results demonstrate that our model surpasses the state-of-the-art single-modal model by 1.1 F1 points on the ACME benchmark and outperforms leading multi-modal models on the RKW benchmark. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/ChenYan1995/KGEC. Additionally, we have released a new, larger knowledge-enhanced relation extraction dataset named WebECg, which can be found at https://github.com/ChenYan1995/WebECg. The details regarding RKW and WebECg are available in our companion papers. Furthermore, our implementation supports a knowledge graph density adapter, enabling users to adjust the density to their requirements. Interested parties are invited to explore the repository. This study introduces a novel analytical method for simulating power converter delays via switching time and duty cycle characteristics. A mathematical model was developed to represent the relationship between input switching times and output pulse-width modulation (PWM) duty cycles, incorporating the effects of internal delays caused by finite switching transitions. The model demonstrates a strong fit to actual output data, with an R-squared value of 0.99. Furthermore, the findings indicate that within switching time ranges typical of power electronics, both switching time and duty cycle exhibit a linear relationship. The research concludes that an analytical approach is essential for accurately predicting output characteristics, such as duty cycle, in the presence of input switching time delays. This approach enables a more precise understanding of how internal delays influence power converter performance. The proposed methodology is particularly applicable to systems utilizing pulse-width modulation, where knowing the output duty cycle is critical. The results are expected to be valuable for power electronics researchers and engineers engaged in design, simulation, and analysis. The study's primary limitation is its focus on steady-state conditions, excluding the analysis of dynamic switching time variations. Future work will extend this research to dynamic scenarios. The paper also acknowledges that the current model is limited to a single converter and will be expanded in future studies to accommodate various power converter topologies. The authors intend to collaborate with industry partners to validate these results across different industrial applications. The resulting delay simulation, which utilizes duty cycle as a function of switching time, offers an efficient means of accounting for internal switching delays. This work addresses the challenge of identifying an optimal policy within the framework of rough graded spaces. We introduce and analyze the concept of rough-grained compactness, which extends the traditional notion of compactness by incorporating a scale-based metric perspective. Furthermore, we propose a novel policy search algorithm designed to converge to an optimal policy when the space exhibits rough-grained compactness. The effectiveness of this approach is demonstrated through an example involving policies for a mobile robot navigating a graph environment. Our primary contribution lies in extending the generalization of compactness to graded topological spaces, thereby offering a more granular perspective of compactness that serves as a foundation for future research into policy search algorithms in continuous spaces. This work is supported by the EPSRC grant EP/R003040/1. Additionally, the concept of rough-grained compactness has found applications in the study of random dynamical systems, as seen in reference [1]. Furthermore, the paper [2] has also explored policy algorithms within graded spaces.

Understanding the core principles of natural image statistics is essential for deciphering the foundation of visual processing in the human brain. While prior research has demonstrated the significance of arrangement statistics—such as the ordering of objects in scenes or the placement of limbs on a body—our study reveals a previously unrecognized critical pattern in how animacy categories are arranged across spatial frequencies. We demonstrate that an image's animacy category is predominantly determined by its high spatial frequency tail, which comprises the highest-frequency Fourier components, regardless of the frequency cutoff point. Furthermore, we show that a compact neural representation utilizing a single Gaussian bandpass filter can effectively encode these high-frequency tails, thereby successfully predicting the human brain's response to various animacy categories across different spatial frequencies. These findings suggest that distinct neural representations within the human ventral temporal cortex are specialized to extract high-frequency tails, thereby facilitating the discrimination of diverse animacy categories. Consequently, our results provide evidence for the existence of a distinct neural mechanism dedicated to processing frequency arrangement. This mechanism is vital for animacy categorization and represents a novel dimension of arrangement processing that extends beyond the traditional spatial domain. Our work identifies the essence of frequency arrangement and clarifies the functional role of frequency-domain processing in the human brain. Additionally, we introduce the concept of "frequency sorting," a new approach to image representation that relies on the arrangement of spectral energy rather than the energy spectrum itself. This demonstrates that the representation of image attributes is intrinsically linked to the sorting of arrangement information. Overall, our results offer new insights into the specialized processing of image attributes in the human brain and deepen our comprehension of the neural mechanisms underlying ventral temporal cortex function. Finally, our findings open avenues for exploring the neural mechanisms of other image attributes, such as color and texture, and their corresponding arrangement information. This could lead to a more comprehensive understanding of ventral temporal cortex processing and the neural mechanisms underlying object recognition. Ultimately, our work establishes a new framework for investigating the neural mechanisms of image processing in the human brain. By examining the functional role of frequency tails, we have identified the essence of frequency arrangement and its role in animacy categorization, thereby opening a new avenue for research into the neural mechanisms of frequency arrangement. This work also highlights the existence of frequency sorting, a new type of image representation, and underscores the functional relevance of arrangement information in the human brain. These discoveries open a new avenue for research on the neural mechanisms of arrangement information processing. Furthermore, our findings provide a foundation for exploring the neural mechanisms of other image attributes, such as color and texture

This paper introduces a new structure-preserving filter (SPF) designed for finite element simulations across multidimensional domains. The proposed method is grounded in convex optimization theory, offering a versatile framework that accommodated various optimization goals and constraints to generate diverse filtering outcomes. By employing a variational approach, the elegant structure of the novel SPF is achieved. Furthermore, detailed mathematical analyses confirm the existence and uniqueness of the optimization solution, as well as the preservation of non-negativity and mass within the SPF. Finally, extensive numerical experiments in both 2D and 3D settings demonstrate the superior performance of the SPF in maintaining simulation structures and its robustness regarding parameter selection. The results indicate that the mass of the simulation remains nearly constant throughout the process. Additionally, the 3D numerical experiments reveal that the proposed SPF surpasses existing state-of-the-art methods in preserving structure, particularly when simulations involve complex physical phenomena. The source code for the SPF is publicly accessible at https://github.com/ChenchenLi1997/Convex-Optimization-Based-Structure-Maintaining-Filter. Type-C quasi-periodic oscillations (QPOs) in black hole X-ray transients are characterized by low-frequency fluctuations (LFQPOs) that display a distinctive "trough" at the Nyquist frequency during the hard state. This study investigates LFQPOs in the black hole X-ray transient MAXI J1535-571 using the Insight-HXMT. We identified LFQPOs in the 2–10 keV band with a low-frequency component ranging from 1.8 to 2.2 Hz. Spectral analysis of the LFQPOs reveals a hardening of the photon index from 2.2 to 1.8 as the system evolves from the initial to the final outburst phase. Furthermore, the LFQPOs in the 2–10 keV band exhibit a gradual decline in hardness from 2.2 to 1.8 throughout the outburst phase. Additionally, the hard X-ray component in the 20–30 keV band shows a significant decrease in intensity from the initial to the final phase, accompanied by a softening of the photon index from 2.2 to 1.8. This evolution aligns with the corona shrinking and the accretion disk expanding. Consequently, the LFQPOs in MAXI J1535-571 demonstrate a clear decline in both intensity and hardness from the initial to the final phase, a trend that may be attributed to the evolving corona. These observations are consistent with the scenario that LFQPOs arise from the variability of the corona. Finally, we propose that the LFQPOs in MAXI J1535-571 may be linked to the accretion disk. This paper introduces a new social inherent motivation framework called TransEnable, designed for multi-robot systems. TransferEnable enables a robot to autonomously generate and execute behaviors that facilitate the knowledge transfer it previously received, thereby enabling cooperative knowledge transfer within the multi-robot system. This capability is essential for the robot to reliably re-react to the knowledge donor's actions, which are crucial for realizing the received knowledge. Furthermore, the dependability of TransEnable is ensured by verifying the robustness of the reaction behavior through formal methods. The potential of TransEnable is demonstrated across two applications: (1) the automatic self-organization of multi-robot systems to execute a task, and (2) the enablement of inter-robot communication by generating social behaviors for communication enablement. These capabilities were validated through experiments on real-world multi-robot systems, alongside case studies and additional experiments. The results demonstrate that TransEnable can reliably re-react to behavioral inputs from other robots and effectively re-reactively enable social self-organization and communication enablement in multi-robot systems. Furthermore, the computational efficiency of TransEnable was evaluated by comparing its performance against other methods. These findings indicate that TransEnable can practically realize cooperative knowledge transfer in multi-robot systems, thereby supporting the development of more capable autonomous robots. Finally, the potential of TransEnable to enable more capable autonomous robots is illustrated through a case study. To our knowledge, this represents the first formal guarantee of dependability for social inherent motivation, thereby enhancing the reliability of multi-robot systems. Additionally, TransEnable offers a more practical solution for social inherent motivation by enabling computational efficiency, which was demonstrated by comparing it with other methods. These outcomes establish the foundation for future research into social capabilities for multi-robot systems. The code for TransEnable is publicly accessible at https://github.com/taehyuklee/TransEnable. Furthermore, the knowledge and capabilities of TransEnable can be easily adapted to other applications by simply modifying the transition model of the associated Markov Decision Process. This flexibility allows TransEnable to enable social capabilities in various other domains, such as social gathering, conflict avoidance, and conflict resolution. Consequently, TransEnable can enable social capabilities for autonomous robots in diverse other applications. Finally, TransEnable can be extended to other applications for social capability enablement by following the steps outlined in Section V. These contributions demonstrate the effectiveness and efficiency of TransEnable in enabling social capabilities for multi-robot systems. This study introduces a physics-informed education-based approach to single-shot material identification, achieving success rates exceeding 90% for over 1,000 substances. The technique leverages a deep neural network that leverages a phase diagram-based data representation, utilizing fundamental single-shot X-ray diffraction data to generate a phase diagram. This visualization effectively highlights single-shot contrastive information, thereby enhancing the model's generalization capabilities. Experimental results demonstrate the method's robustness and reliability in identifying unknown substances across diverse experimental conditions, including variations in crystal orientation, lattice strain, and amorphous content. Additionally, the approach exhibits strong resilience to experimental noise. The proposed method is expected to facilitate accurate and efficient single-shot identification of unknown materials in practical applications. Furthermore, the study underscores the value of employing an education-based strategy in machine learning, where designing an optimal data representation is essential for developing generalizable artificial intelligence. We introduce a new approach for image feature matching that bypasses the traditional two-stage pipeline of local interest point detection and descriptor matching. Instead, our method establishes direct pixel-level correlations between two images using a global transformer-based matcher. To efficiently generate high-quality regional descriptors, we employ a hierarchical LoFT (Loose-coupled Fine-tune) encoder. This encoder leverages multi-scale image features to identify loosely coupled regions, which are subsequently refined through a multi-level feedback mechanism. Unlike most existing direct matchers, our approach can be independently scaled. By increasing the LoFt encoder's depth, performance improves at the cost of speed, allowing for optimization based on specific application needs. We also demonstrate that integrating a local transformer into the end-to-end framework enhances robustness. Evaluations on the standard MPII and Sintel benchmarks reveal that our method achieves a 1.5x to 2x speedup while delivering state-of-the-art matching results. Magnetograms, which capture the Sun's magnetic fields, serve as the primary data source for space weather forecasting. However, the physical quantities extracted from these images are often skewed by instrumental biases. This study examines the impact of such biases on sunspot umbras, active regions, and the quiet inter-features. The analysis utilizes HINODE's ground-based Kodaikanal Solar Telescope (KST) spectral magnetograms, which measure the Stokes parameters ($I, Q, U, V$) of solar polarized light across the Fe I 617.3 nm line. Using the Stokes inversion free (SIF) method, we determined the magnetic field orientation and strength (magnitude) for various regions on the solar disk. The findings indicate that while biases affect both field orientation and strength, their influence is most pronounced in umbral regions. Specifically, umbral magnetic fields appear more horizontal, and the bias in field strength is significantly greater than in active regions or quiet inter-features. Consequently, the umbral regions exhibit stronger signatures of instrumental bias. To mitigate this, we propose a method that corrects for such biases, which has been successfully applied to umbral regions. This approach is expected to be applicable to other magnetometric instruments. Ultimately, the research underscores the necessity of addressing instrumental biases in sunspot umbras to ensure accurate derived measurements of solar magnetic fields. Correcting these biases will significantly enhance our understanding of solar and space weather phenomena. Future work will apply this correction method to other solar disk regions. The KST's spectral magnetograms are publicly accessible at http://www.ksnso.org/kodikanal-solar-telescope-kst. The raw data were processed using the SpectroPolarimetric Data Analysis (SPDAN) software, available at https://github.com/SPDAN/SPDAN. SPDAN is an open-source tool that allows users to customize the inversion method, including the choice between the Levenberg-Marquardt and Gauss-Newton algorithms. The current analysis employed the Levenberg-Marquardt algorithm. Additionally, SPDAN is a free, open-source software that can be downloaded from https://github.com/SPDAN/SPDAN. This study introduces a novel approach to simultaneously achieve two primary goals in smart grids: optimizing overall system performance and incentivizing end-users to provide the necessary flexibility. To address the first goal, we propose a new system-wide flexibility metric that integrates the flexibility contributions of all grid participants. To satisfy the second goal, we utilize aggregative games, which offer superior performance compared to traditional mechanism design approaches when dealing with numerous end-users. Stars with metallicities $[Fe/H] < -2.5$ are scarce in the Galaxy, primarily because their faintness makes them difficult to detect. However, the recent launch of Gaia's Bright Object Spectrograph (BOS), which provides spectrophotometric data for stars with $G < 16$ mag, offers a new avenue for identifying these faint, metal-poor stars. This study introduces a method to detect metal-poor stars with $[Fe/H] < -2.5$ using Gaia's Blue Photometer and Red Photometer (BP/RP) spectra. We applied this method to 1,000,000 stars selected from the Gaia Data Release 3 (DR3) catalog, and the technique's effectiveness was validated using the APOGEE-2 metal-poor sample. Our findings reveal that this approach can successfully identify metal-poor stars with $[Fe/H] < -2.5$ at a contamination rate of approximately 10%. Additionally, we demonstrate that this method is effective for determining stellar ages. We conclude that the technique is valuable for discovering new metal-poor stars and for investigating the formation and evolution of the Milky Way. The code is publicly accessible at https://github.com/ChenchenLi2000/Metal-poor-stars. This research is based on results from the Gaia Early Data Release 3. The intricacy of a language represents a fundamental characteristic that evolves throughout historical development. Researchers have developed various indices to quantify this property; however, the underlying construct these indices represent remains largely unclear. This study seeks to elucidate the construct defined by indices of linguistic intricacy by rigorously correlating them with established, data-driven metrics of morphological complexity. We demonstrate that these two categories of intricacy measures share a common construct, which aligns robustly with well-known aspects of morphological complexity. Specifically, we find that statistically significant correlations exist between intricacy indices and the density of inflectional and derivational morphemes, as well as the size of the stem inventory. The size of the affix inventory yields a marginal correlation, whereas the proportion of productive affixes shows no significant correlation. Additionally, we show that intricacy indices are more strongly associated with inflectional and derivational morphological complexity than with affix size, indicating that the construct they define corresponds more closely to stem richness. Finally, we establish that intricacy indices derived from diachronic corpora correlate more strongly with this construct than those derived from synchronic corpora. Overall, this research confirms that the construct of linguistic intricacy is precisely defined by the wealth of a language's morphological system. Consequently, the construction of new intricacy indices should prioritize the integration of rich morphological information from synchronic and, ideally, diachronic data. Furthermore, this work underscores the value of rigorously correlating intricacy indices with independently derived, objectively defined, and empirically grounded measures of morphological complexity. By doing so, the internal structure of the intricacy construct can be better understood, and the reliability of new intricacy measures can be enhanced. Finally, our findings suggest that the concept of linguistic intricacy is best aligned with the density of inflectional and derivational morphemes, as well as stem size, rather than affix size. This conclusion is supported by the fact that the most strongly correlated intricacy indices are those derived from morphological inventories. These results reinforce the established link between morphological complexity and the density of inflectional and derivational affixes, while also providing new evidence for the relationship between linguistic intricacy and morphological density. The paper concludes with several suggestions for future research. We conducted a statistical analysis of gravitational lensing data from the Sloan Digital Sky Survey (SDSS) to investigate the core-cusp problem in dark matter halos of satellite galaxies within groups and clusters. Our findings indicate that the observed lensing data align well with a universal density profile characterized by a power-law core, which can be derived from Self-Interacting Dark Matter (SIDM) models. Furthermore, we demonstrate that SIDM halos can be characterized by a single size scale, $\eta$, alongside the halo mass. By utilizing the lensing statistics, we established a relationship between the halo size scale $\eta$ and mass $M$ for both group and cluster halos. Additionally, we compared the lensing data regarding the distribution of $\eta$ between subhalos and the main halos of host galaxies, revealing consistency with SIDM predictions. Finally, we compared our results with recent lensing studies on dwarf galaxies in the Coma cluster and found that the data remain compatible with the SIDM framework. Overall, our analysis strongly supports the viability of SIDM as a candidate dark matter theory. Future lensing observations of galaxy clusters will further constrain SIDM models and provide additional support for this hypothesis. Specifically, the Euclid mission is expected to significantly enhance the precision of subhalo mass measurements, offering a rigorous test of the SIDM scenario. This paper serves as a foundational step toward such future analyses. The findings presented here are accessible via the Astrophysical Data Center (ADC) at http://apdc.naoj.ac.jp. Large-scale mathematical models are frequently developed to address intricate real-world challenges, yet their computational demands often hinder the use of rapid simulation and optimization techniques. While existing literature typically relies on domain-specific knowledge to simplify models, this approach is not always available. This paper introduces a framework that leverages partial insights into a model's behavior to derive simplified representations. The process involves identifying and eliminating computational components that do not significantly impact behavior, followed by applying optimization techniques to achieve further simplification. The resulting model maintains behavior closely aligned with the original, supported by performance metrics. We validate this framework using two case studies drawn from the field of social media. The method demonstrates that it can effectively simplify models based on limited behavioral understanding and successfully recover known simplifications when they exist. Additionally, the framework identifies previously unknown simplifications that impact the model's behavior. These findings suggest that the approach is highly applicable to models that are difficult to analyze, particularly those found in industry. Additionally, the framework can be utilized to investigate the characteristics of models that facilitate efficient computation. Keywords: Model Simplification, Computational Complexity, Optimization, Limiting Behavior. The m-ar-K-Fast algorithm is an efficient, component-wise alternative to the widely used m-ar-KM algorithm. Both methods operate within the manifold framework, where data resides on a data-driven manifold embedded within a high-dimensional Euclidean space. The m-ar-KM algorithm partitions this space into multiple regions, assigning data points to the most appropriate region based on their proximity. Conversely, the m-ar-K-Fast algorithm allocates each point to a region determined by calculating the distance to specific feature vectors. This paper introduces the m-ar-K-Fast Component Analysis (m-ar-KFCA) algorithm, which is computationally efficient regarding training time and scales well with the number of regions. Experimental results demonstrate that m-ar-KFCA achieves accuracy comparable to m-ar-KM while offering a significant reduction in training time. Furthermore, m-ar-KFCA outperforms the self-organizing map (SOM) in most tested scenarios. The method's superiority over m-ar-KM in terms of training speed and scalability with respect to the number of regions is evident, making m-ar-KFCA a highly attractive algorithm for large-scale data classification and clustering tasks. Additionally, the method is adaptable to various kernel functions, enabling its application in nonlinear classification and clustering. The source code is publicly accessible at https://github.com/ahmedgaber/m-ar-KFCA. This study introduces a framework for identifying spatial-temporal events by leveraging social media platforms that support real-time, geotagged interactions. Within this context, event detection is defined as the task of grouping social media posts into distinct spatial-temporal event clusters. The proposed solution is grounded in a new classification of events based on their generation mechanisms, which are categorized into two types: those driven by geographical proximity and those by temporal simultaneity. This classification informs a novel event identification framework that integrates ground-truth event data with machine learning techniques, specifically embedding models and clustering models. Furthermore, the framework employs an identification model that combines the aforementioned event types with pre-defined events to facilitate both quantitative and qualitative analysis. To demonstrate its effectiveness, the framework was applied to real-time data from the Twitter platform. The results indicate that the proposed framework is both effective and efficient for identifying spatial-temporal events from ground-truth data on geotagged social platforms. Additionally, the identification process yields valuable insights into event generation mechanisms, including the relative significance of geographical proximity and temporal simultility, as well as the dominant types of events. These insights assist researchers in gaining a deeper understanding of event dynamics and characteristics, which is essential for subsequent event analysis. In display advertising, bidding strategies typically rely on historical data to forecast click-through rates (CTR) and conversion rates (CVR). However, this standard approach often fails to account for bid costs, budget constraints, and the risk of budget exhaustion. To address these shortcomings, we introduce a novel budget-aware bidding framework that dynamically adjusts bids based on the risk of budget depletion. This framework encompasses two new algorithms: Adaptive Risk-conscious Bidding (ARB), which operates without model training, and Adaptive Risk-conscious Bidding (ARB*), which utilizes online learning. The Feller process, or Feller diffusion, represents a diffusion on the non-negative half-line governed by specific generator conditions. This paper introduces a sampling algorithm for Feller processes defined on the non-negative half-line, derived from general methods applicable to any diffusions on various state spaces. These sampling procedures modify the basic linearly diffusing Feller process (Feller class 1) by incorporating non-negative killing at an intensity determined by an auxiliary function with a known integral, alongside diffusion and drift components on $\mathbb{R}^+$ governed by one-dimensional Sturm-Liouville operators. The algorithms rely on a random series expansion of the Laplace transform of the modified process's transition density. This series is constructed using eigenfunctions derived from the Laplace transform of the Feller process's transition density on $\mathbb{R}^+$, weighted by power series determined by the integral of the auxiliary function and the eigenvalues of the diffusion and drift processes. Furthermore, the representation reveals that for Feller class 2 and 3 processes, the transition densities can be expressed as convergent series expansions of the Feller class 1 transition density, weighted by powers of the eigenfunctions and the eigenvalues of the corresponding Sturm-Liouville operators. Consequently, we demonstrate that the series representation remains convergent in these scenarios. Finally, we illustrate the application of these methods with examples involving Feller processes on $\mathbb{R}^+$. Notably, the examples for Feller class 4 and 5 processes involve kernels that are not integrable and therefore fall outside the scope of the current sampling algorithm. However, we provide an alternative sampling algorithm for these cases that utilizes a dual process representation. The dual process is defined as a diffusion on $\mathbb{R}^-$ with a drift term representing the reciprocal transformation of the original process and an auxiliary killing intensity determined by an auxiliary function with a known integral. This sampling algorithm is applicable to any one-dimensional Sturm-Liouville operator defined on $\mathbb{R}^+$. Additionally, the dual process is shown to correspond to a sub-Markov diffusion, indicating that the transition density is no longer expressible as a series expansion of Feller class 1 transition densities with weights determined by the eigenvalues of the eigenvalue problem. Instead, the transition density is represented as a series expansion of the Feller class 1 transition density, where the weights are determined by the eigenvalues of the eigenvalue problem and the trace class property of the associated integral operator. We introduce a diagrammatic scattering method to derive analytical expressions for the scattering matrices of multiple photons interacting with atoms embedded in a waveguide. These formulae are valid for regimes involving strong light-matter interactions and varied polarization configurations. Although focused on a waveguide environment, the approach is broadly applicable to diverse photonic systems supporting one-dimensional propagation of light-matter excitations. We present numerical simulations for various configurations to validate the method, including scenarios with one, two, and three photons, as well as coherent states impinging on a single atom within a waveguide. Furthermore, we outline potential applications of this technique in designing novel quantum devices, such as quantum gates and switches, by analyzing the case of a two-qubit system in a waveguide featuring cross-coupling mediated by a single photon. Finally, we discuss extensions of this work to three or more interacting atoms or qubits. Reward learning seeks optimal policies by maximizing feedback received from unknown reward functions. However, defining rewards effectively remains a significant challenge, as users often struggle to articulate their intentions, leading to ill-specified signals. Consequently, there is a need for a robust reward specification method that is both efficient and resilient. This paper introduces an innovative approach that integrates human perception into reward learning by incorporating visual examples. We propose visually supported cluster ranking (ViSCR), which leverages user intuition regarding data distribution to specify rewards. ViSCR operates by clustering state-action-reward tuples and iteratively presenting the resulting groups to users for ranking. We demonstrate that cluster identification within groups facilitates a vision-driven specification strategy, enabling the method to converge to a well-specified reward function. Furthermore, we show that the learned reward functions accurately reflect user intentions, whether the goal is to enhance or improve upon perceived performance. Finally, we introduce the concept of "reward learning efficiency" and empirically show that ViSCR achieves this efficiency, making it the fastest reward learning method to date. This paper investigates the topological characteristics of the frustrated Toric code, a system that exhibits a gapless boundary when unconfined by the boundary condition. We demonstrate that specific boundary conditions yield not only gapped edges but also topological edges, the latter of which are classified by the $\mathbb{Z}_2$ Kosterlitz-Thouless phase. This classification is confirmed through boundary correlation functions, transfer matrix formalism, and numerical analysis. Furthermore, we extend our study to the generalized frustrated Toric code, showing that it supports topological edges under certain conditions, a finding corroborated by numerical evidence. These results provide a comprehensive classification of all possible edge states in the frustrated Toric code and its generalized variants. Additionally, we explore the implications of these findings for the surface code, a framework with significant applications in quantum computing. Finally, our methodology is expected to be applicable to other lattice gauge theories, offering a pathway to discover and characterize new topological phases. A companion publication will present an in-depth analysis of the transfer matrix and correlation functions. This study investigates the interaction between random band matrices and complex alternating matrices. We demonstrate that the eigenvalues located far from the origin in the spectrum of the combined operator can be estimated via the alternating sigma-model. This approach extends a previous finding by the first author and T. Shcherbina, which applied the same method to the case of Wigner matrices. Our assumptions on the individual interaction components are notably broad and significantly more general than those in standard literature. Specifically, we allow entry-wise independent entries in each factor to follow arbitrary centered distributions, provided they satisfy a uniform moment condition. Furthermore, we establish a strong form of asymptotic freeness between the two matrix types and prove that the empirical spectral distribution of their sum converges almost surely to a deterministic limiting distribution as the dimension tends to infinity. We explicitly derive the limiting distribution's expression and characterize its key properties, including support, moments, and convergence speed, for various significant particular cases. Additionally, we prove that all limiting moments are strictly positive, thereby ensuring the existence of a limiting spectral gap, and we provide a detailed analysis of these limits within the spectral gap context. Finally, the methodology employed is sufficiently general to facilitate the analysis of more complex alternating matrix structures, such as those arising from generalized Wigner matrices. This broader framework enables us to examine limiting moments corresponding to Hermitian operators of arbitrarily large rank, a scenario that may be practically relevant in specific applications. We explicitly analyze these limiting cases for alternating generalized Wigner matrices. The techniques utilized in this work also play a crucial role in our subsequent paper, where we derive the limiting empirical spectral distribution for a generalized version of the sum of random matrices considered here. In that context, we employ the same sigma-model approach in a more intricate setting to derive a semi-circular limiting distribution. This generalized scenario involves generalized Wigner matrices rather than simple alternating matrices, and we are able to derive the limiting distribution's expression under the assumption of appropriate entry-wise independence. We also demonstrate that this limiting expression remains valid even when this independence assumption is relaxed. The methodology applied in this paper serves as a foundational step toward our future objective of determining limiting expressions for band random matrix models featuring alternating entries, a problem currently under investigation. In that related study, we will apply the same sigma-model technique to analyze random band matrices, thereby extending the analysis to a setting that differs substantially from both Wigner and band matrix frameworks. This study explores a new, meaning-oriented approach to conversation understanding, which leverages natural language inference (NLI) to derive conversation- wide logical relations. Since current state-of-the-art methods rely heavily on word embeddings and fail to capture the dynamic context shifts inherent in conversational data, we introduce Conversation Tree Autoencoder (CTAE), a self-supervised language model that jointly learns word representations and context transition representations. Specifically, we propose two tasks to facilitate this learning process: 1) logical label prediction, which utilizes off-the-shelf NLI tools to predict logical labels for utterance pairs, and 2) logical representation reconstruction, which employs an autoencoder to reconstruct logical representations derived from utterance pairs. Experimental results demonstrate that CTAE effectively captures dynamic context transitions and yields state-of-the-art performance in conversation understanding. The surge in algorithmic performance has been accompanied by a growing emphasis on interpretability, which facilitates human comprehension of algorithmic decisions. This understanding is crucial for establishing trust, confidence, and faith in these systems. However, the relationship between humans and algorithms varies depending on the task; consequently, an algorithm may be interpretable to one group of people but not to another. While algorithmic interpretability has been extensively studied, its significance in the context of machine learning remains underexplored. Furthermore, a gap exists between how algorithms are defined and how humans perceive them. This paper introduces a cognitive science-driven framework for human learning, which informs a novel framework for evaluating human-centric algorithmic interpretability. We also propose a cognitive complexity metric to quantify the difficulty of interpreting specific algorithms. The proposed cognitive score framework demonstrates that human scoring of algorithmic complexity is highly accurate and that scoring performance is significantly influenced by an individual's cognitive ability. Our approach advances machine learning research by offering a precise method for humans to assess algorithmic complexity, thereby aiding in the selection of models that balance performance with interpretability. This facilitates more transparent machine learning systems and enhances human trust and faith in these algorithms. We demonstrate the utility of this framework within the Algorithm Visualizations Society (AVS) by illustrating how it can guide the design of machine learning models that optimize the trade-off between performance and interpretability. We believe this cognitive science-based framework for human learning will prove valuable in the broader field of human-centered algorithm design. Unsupervised anomaly detection is unsupervised machine learning designed to identify data points that deviate from normal patterns. Isolation Forest is a widely used anomaly detection algorithm that isolates points by randomly partitioning them into smaller subsets. However, it often struggles to distinguish anomalies in complex datasets. This paper introduces TiWS-iForest, an enhanced version of Isolation Forest that leverages a lightweight Vision Transformer to extract features from unlabeled data, enabling the isolation forest to better handle difficult anomalies. TiWS-iForest is suitable for anomaly detection in scenarios where data collection is expensive and supervision is limited. The proposed method is evaluated across various real-world datasets, including the well-known UCI benchmark, the challenging EMBC dataset, and the widely used Kaggle Splice dataset. Experimental results demonstrate that TiWS-iForest outperforms other anomaly detection algorithms, achieving a 10% improvement over the state-of-the-art method. Furthermore, the paper includes code and tutorials to assist readers in quickly understanding the method and replicating the experiments. This research introduces a new distribution parameterization for the Poisson process tailored for light-tailed distributions, designed to facilitate unconstrained Bayesian inference on the associated exponential distribution. Additionally, it develops a broad family of minimal sufficient statistics for the Poisson process that are uniquely suited for applications within extreme value theory. A wide array of distributional assumptions is examined under this framework, demonstrating that the approach naturally extends to various generalized extreme value distributions. The proposed method is validated by applying it to model the maximum annual sea surface temperatures recorded in the Southern Ocean. The resulting inference code is implemented in Python and made publicly available. Furthermore, the study explores extensions to multivariate settings, highlighting the utility of this technique for multivariate tail dependence estimation. The authors argue that this novel parameterization represents a significant advancement for both theoretical and applied statistics. This paper investigates the concept of a sub-mean ordered region, originally proposed by P. G. L. Dirac, and explores its connection to the mean cross section. We demonstrate that the Dehn twist acts as an isometry regarding the mean cross section and identify specific examples, including a fixed point of the Dehn twist and a region with a single hyperbolic component whose boundaries are geodesics. Furthermore, we establish criteria for fixed regions and Fuchsian groups and apply these findings to determine the existence and non-existence of fixed regions. Finally, we suggest methods for calculating the mean cross section of super-geodesic regions and introduce a novel formula for computing the mean cross section of a sub-region defined by a single point and a geodesic. Additionally, we calculate the mean cross sections for point-geodesic regions and point-polygon regions. As an application, we derive a formula for the mean cross section of a triangle and derive a condition for its existence and a formula for its value based on the three angles. We also compute the mean cross sections for specific polygons and provide a method for its calculation in super-geodesic regions. Finally, we calculate the mean cross section for a sub-region determined by a point and a geodesic. To our knowledge, this represents the first instance of fixed regions and their associated mean cross sections being calculated. We suggest that these findings may have applications in physics.
Keywords: mean cross section, fixed region, mean cross section of a triangle, mean cross section of a sub-region determined by a point and a geodesic.

Building a comprehensive symbolic common sense knowledge network, such as ATOMIC (Algebraic Trajectory of Mind-Inspired Common Sense Knowledge), is a highly challenging endeavor. While recent advancements in deep learning have enabled the automatic acquisition of extensive symbolic networks, these systems often struggle to generalize beyond narrow domains. Conversely, neural networks excel at learning and generalizing from large-scale datasets but lack interpretable knowledge representations. This paper introduces a hybrid architecture that seamlessly integrates symbolic and neural components, designed to leverage the strengths of both approaches. We demonstrate that our method can effectively learn a large-scale common sense knowledge network and highlight the benefits of such a system for AI applications. Furthermore, we present novel experiments on open-ended question answering, showing that our model can generate answers to questions for which no related knowledge exists in pre-trained datasets like ReClor. The experimental results indicate that our model can infer answers from neurally learned knowledge and subsequently update its symbolic knowledge base. The Hi-GAL survey, conducted by the Herschel Space Observatory, has mapped the Galactic plane across three wavelength bands (25, 70, and 160 microns) to identify and characterize dust structures within the interstellar medium. These maps serve as a foundation for studying star formation and the chemical evolution of the Galaxy. However, the raw Hi-GAL data volume is so extensive that it hinders the development of new analysis methods and tools. This work presents the data compression pipeline developed to address this challenge. By integrating the GILD data compression algorithm with modifications to the Hi-GAL survey, we achieved data compression ratios of 10, 5, and 2.5 without compromising the survey's scientific utility. The primary objective of this pipeline is to facilitate the analysis of Hi-GAL data, thereby supporting the survey's original scientific goals. Additionally, we introduce a method for quantifying and assessing the loss of information resulting from data compression. A detailed algorithmic description of the pipeline is available at https://github.com/hi-gal/hi-gal-compression. The resulting compressed data files can be downloaded from the Hi-GAL survey website at http://higal.esac.esa.int/hi-gal-data/hi-gal-compressed-data/, and a web-based data viewer is also accessible there. **Context.** Globular clusters (GCs) serve as laboratories for studying stellar astrophysics, with NGC 2808 being a notable example due to its unique main-sequence turnoff region and horizontal branch. This region is hypothesized to result from the mixing of stars with varying chemical compositions. **Aims.** This study aims to determine the masses and luminosities of the blue horizontal branch stars in NGC 2808 across four distinct metallicity scenarios. **Methods.** We conducted a multi-colour photometric analysis of the Hubble Space Telescope Wide Field Planetary Camera 2 (HST-WFPC2) images of NGC 2808, utilizing a new set of isochrones to derive masses and luminosities for these stars. **Results.** The derived isochrones align well with the observed colour-magnitude diagram. The analysis reveals that blue horizontal branch stars in NGC 2808 exhibit masses ranging from 0.8 to 0.9 solar masses and luminosities between 40 and 80 solar luminosities, with variations dependent on the assumed metallicity. **Conclusions.** These findings support the presence of a composition spread in NGC 2808, suggesting that both a horizontal branch composition spread and an initial mass spread of 0.02 solar masses are necessary to explain the data. Furthermore, the study confirms the existence of a blue loop in first-generation stars, which is absent in second-generation stars. Finally, the research demonstrates that the HST-WFPC2 can achieve a precision of 0.01 mag in isochrone fitting, enabling the detection of metallicity differences as small as 0.002. This capability is crucial for interpreting the stars' positions in the colour-magnitude diagram. Additionally, the study underscores the necessity of using isochrone fitting for accurate photometric analysis, particularly when applying to other GCs. The intense absorption of intergalactic hydrogen at Lyman-$\alpha$ (1216 \AA) renders the diffuse intergalactic medium effectively opaque at this wavelength, creating a boundary known as the Lyman-$\alpha$ forest. Consequently, high-redshift phenomena are primarily observable not through Lyman-$\alpha$ emission, but via Lyman-$\alpha$ absorption features. This paper introduces a novel instrument design intended for deployment on the upcoming Large UV/Optical Transient Survey (MAXIT) space telescope. The Lyman-$\alpha$ Screen Prototype aims to detect transient phenomena such as supernovae, gamma-ray bursts, and active galactic nuclei within the Lyman-$\alpha$ forest. The design utilizes a single layer of polymer film impregnated with europium-doped strontium aluminate ($\mathrm{SrAl_2O_4:2\%Eu^{3+}, 0.1\% Dy^{3+}}$), which stores ultraviolet photons and releases them as visible light over several days for later detection. This approach offers a new method for studying the early universe, potentially enabling the observation of phenomena currently undetectable in Lyman-$\alpha$ wavelengths. Additionally, the design is compatible with existing MAXIT optical systems, featuring a straightforward manufacturing process and a large active area. We outline the fundamental principles of the Lyman-$\alpha$ Screen Prototype and provide a theoretical analysis of its performance. This paper introduces a novel method for modeling and analyzing distributed algorithms on symmetric networks using graph devices. A network is defined as symmetric if its automorphism group acts transitively on both its edges and nodes. Within this framework, we demonstrate that distributed algorithms operating on a graph device $N$ can be represented as functions mapping $N$ into graph devices of lower dimension. Leveraging this representation, we design a method to globally detect symmetry-breaking in these networks by utilizing an algorithm that determines the minimal dimension of a graph device for any given dimension. We illustrate the efficacy of our approach through examples of modeling distributed ideal colorings and generating symmetric network functions as representations of such colorings. Furthermore, we establish that for every prime $p$, there exists a $p$-coloring protocol that succeeds on all prime $p$-colorable networks by breaking their symmetry. Finally, we prove that for any prime $p$, no oracle-free protocol can achieve a $p$-coloring for the complete graph $K_{p^2}$ within $o(p^{1.5})$ rounds.

The primary contribution of this study is the development of an efficient procedure to identify whether a symmetric network can be described by a graph device of minimal dimension $D$. This capability enables the design of breaking symmetry algorithms for symmetric networks that rely on the assumption that the underlying graph device possesses dimension greater than $D$. We anticipate that these assumptions will hold true in realistic network environments. Additionally, we present a symmetry-breaking algorithm for 2-coloring networks with $O(n)$ nodes and demonstrate that an $O(n)$-coloring algorithm can be constructed for networks with $O(n)$ nodes by assuming the graph device dimension exceeds 3. We also present an $n$-coloring algorithm for networks with $n$ nodes that operates under the assumption that the graph device dimension is at least 2. Finally, we show that no oracle-free algorithm can successfully produce an $n$-coloring for an $n$-vertex network in $o(n^{0.75})$ rounds while assuming only that the network's graph device has a dimension of 2.

We argue that the graph device dimension serves as a critical metric for characterizing network topology, a factor that has been largely overlooked in previous research. This paper presents a method for estimating graph device dimension and demonstrates its application in network topology analysis. We contend that the graph device dimension is a valuable topological invariant for symmetric networks, which have been underexplored in prior studies

Image Cataloging (IC) represents a novel information retrieval challenge where an unannotated image collection must be organized based on a single query image, which includes a specific label. Unlike traditional approaches, the system must propagate this label to all remaining unlabeled images while ensuring label consistency among visually similar items. While most existing research relies on static image datasets, numerous real-world scenarios demand dynamic catalogs that support images uploaded in real-time. This paper introduces the concept of Dynamic Image Cataloging (DynamicIC), a new task that extends beyond standard IC. We present a straightforward yet effective method for addressing DynamicIC, demonstrating that it significantly outperforms both regular IC and naive strategies. Our findings indicate that this new task holds substantial potential for real-world applications. The code is accessible at https://github.com/DeepakBhatnagar1998/DynamicIC. For reproducibility, supplementary materials are available at https://drive.google.

The keyless communication framework eliminates dependency on a shared secret key by utilizing public information to derive a shared random string capable of distinguishing messages. Originally developed for the binary erasure channel, this paradigm has seen significant advancement through the application of sketch and fingerprinting techniques. This paper investigates the keyless verification scheme for power-limited additive white Gaussian channel (AWGNC) encoding, comparing the proposed method with recent keyless AWGNC encoding protocols that utilize random strings derived from channel outputs. Our analysis demonstrates that the proposed approach outperforms existing schemes by leveraging the statistical independence of AWGNC noise. Furthermore, numerical results indicate that the keyless AWGNC encoding proposed here achieves a higher reliable rate than current keyless coding schemes for this channel. Finally, we establish that the proposed scheme attains the optimal achievable rate for keyless encoding of AWGNCs. Additionally, we examine the keyless AWGNC encoding problem under both average and worst-case error probability constraints, deriving corresponding achievable random string rates for each scenario. In both cases, we prove that the random string rate achieved by our proposed scheme is optimal. Consequently, our findings confirm that the proposed scheme is optimal regarding reliable communication rates under all considered conditions. Notably, our results further reveal that the keyless verification scheme is more efficient than traditional key-based verification for AWGNC encoding. Overall, this work advances the field of keyless communication by providing a comprehensive analysis of keyless verification for AWGNC encoding across various settings. The study not only deepens theoretical understanding but also offers practical guidance for implementing keyless communication systems. Specifically, the research contributes to the development of next-generation keyless communication technologies by establishing theoretical foundations and performance benchmarks. The paper also explores practical implementation challenges and potential solutions for keyless verification in AWGNC encoding, thereby facilitating the creation of robust and reliable keyless communication systems. Ultimately, this work holds the potential to significantly impact the future of wireless communication by enabling more secure and efficient data transmission without the need for shared secret keys. By demonstrating the superiority of keyless verification over traditional key-based approaches, the research paves the way for new applications and services in keyless communication systems. The authors believe that these contributions will advance the field and enable new opportunities for research and innovation in the coming years. Finally, the paper concludes by suggesting several directions for future research in keyless communication, including the extension of keyless verification schemes to other types of channels and the development of new security metrics and analysis techniques. This approach is applied to investigate how magnetic anisotropy and exchange interactions influence the dynamics of domain walls in thin films. The analysis reveals that a single mode determines the domain wall's properties and dynamics, validating the earlier assumption that wall shape remains static during movement. The study further explores how exchange interactions enable multiple stable dispersion-free states, with the transition between them induced by the applied magnetic field. Finally, the article outlines the conditions under which the exchange integral can be neglected, thereby simplifying the mathematical model. These findings are specifically illustrated using the magnetic properties of permalloy. Additionally, the article includes a glossary defining key terms and concepts. This paper introduces a new framework for estimating impulse responses via local projections, designed to adaptively leverage additional data from the response variables. The primary benefit of this method is its capacity to achieve substantially more precise response estimates using a significantly smaller number of cross-sections, making it ideal for applications with limited sample sizes. The framework includes an estimator utilizing principal component analysis to recover structural shocks, estimators for confidence intervals and variance-covariance matrices, and application-wide inference procedures. Notably, the construction of confidence intervals requires no assumptions regarding the number of shocks or the strong exogeneity of response variables. Extensive simulations demonstrate that the proposed estimator performs reliably across various configurations of weak and strong exogenous variables, as well as different counts of responses and cross-sectional units. A key advantage over competing methods is its ability to generate accurate structural shock estimates even when using a very limited number of response variables. Furthermore, the framework allows for the generation of confidence intervals based on either parametric or non-parametric approaches. Finally, the paper applies the proposed framework to two datasets with few time series but numerous cross-sections to derive impulse responses. The first dataset consists of 100 countries' data to analyze the impact of US monetary and fiscal policy, while the second includes 1,000 firms' data to study the effects of stock and bond market news. In both cases, the results indicate that the proposed framework yields more precise estimates compared to traditional local projection-based approaches. Additionally, the study finds that US monetary policy has generated significantly smaller responses in both output and inflation across the two datasets. These findings are robust to several model design choices, including the selection of stock versus bond news, the number of response variables, and the use of parametric versus non-parametric confidence intervals. However, the traditional approach fails to achieve these levels of precision in this application. Finally, the paper discusses potential extensions of the proposed framework. The angular momentum exhibits an algebraic relationship with the charge's time component, mirroring the classical angular momentum of a point charge in anti-de Sitter space, though with a distinct coefficient. Let $\mathcal{S}$ represent the class of all univalent functions defined on the open unit disk $\mathbb{D}$. Let $\mathcal{U}$ be the subcategory of $\mathcal{S}$ comprising univalent functions of the form:
$$f(z)=z+az^2+...$$
where $a$ is a non-zero complex constant. Given a fixed $a \in \mathbb{C}\setminus\{0\}$, the paper examines functions $f \in \mathcal{S}$ that satisfy:
$$\left|f(z)-\frac{z+az^2}{1-e^{-2i\theta}z}\right|<1 \quad \text{for all } z \in \mathbb{D}.$$
This condition defines two distinct subsets of $\mathcal{S}$, denoted as $S_a$ and $T_a$. The study analyzes functions $f \in S_a \cap T_a$ that are subordinate to $g(z)=z+az^2$. Furthermore, the paper derives sharp bounds for the second Hankel determinants of these functions and establishes sharp inequalities for the second Taylor-Maclaurin coefficients. Additionally, the work computes the extremal values for $|a_3|$ and identifies the extremal functions. Finally, the radii of starlikeness and convexity are calculated for $S_a \cap T_a$. Key subjects include univalent functions, subordination, and related concepts. Keywords: univalent functions, subordination, extremal problems, starlikeness, radii of starlikeness and convexity.

The widespread adoption of virtualization has enabled the consolidation of multiple virtual machines on a single physical host, thereby enhancing resource utilization. This study introduces Prepartition, a load distribution strategy designed to minimize response times for virtual machines within a cloud data hub. Prepartition functions as a partitioning-based load distribution mechanism that dynamically adjusts the partitioning policy based on the performance metrics of virtual machines. We evaluated this method against two baseline approaches: Static Partitioning, which maintains a fixed partitioning rule regardless of VM performance, and Dynamic Partitioning, which adapts load distribution based on real-time performance data. Experimental results indicate that for a cloud environment comprising 50 virtual machines, Prepartition reduces response time by 10% compared to Static Partitioning and by 20% compared to Dynamic Partitioning. Furthermore, we developed a closed-form analytical model to predict response times using CPU usage as the primary performance indicator. This model accurately forecasts response times for both Prepartition and Dynamic Partitioning environments with an error margin of less than 1%. Leveraging this model, we created a prediction tool capable of estimating VM response times within the cloud environment. This tool assists cloud administrators in selecting appropriate VMs for specific user requests by evaluating performance predictions. Ultimately, Prepartition serves as a partitioning-based load distribution technique that optimizes resource allocation by considering VM performance, thereby improving overall cloud efficiency. The source code for this prepartitioning tool is publicly accessible at https://github.com/Deepak-2000/Prepartition. Additionally, the performance evaluation code is available at https://github.com/Deepak-2000/Prepartition/tree/master/code_for_evaluation. We introduce an unsupervised learning framework designed to derive a latent representation of an input distribution that minimizes variance under specific constraints. Related approaches typically rely on maximum likelihood estimation, which necessitates a density estimator for the target distribution; however, this estimator is often difficult to train and may fail to converge. In contrast, our method utilizes a variational autoencoder applied to the latent distribution, eliminating the need for maximum likelihood estimation. By incorporating constraints via Lagrange multipliers, we train the autoencoder to minimize the sum of squared variances for each latent dimension. We demonstrate the application of this approach to single-cell RNA sequencing data, where it successfully identifies biologically significant features of the distribution. The methodology is implemented in Python and accessible on GitHub. Furthermore, we provide detailed guidance on parameter selection and interpretation. Overall, our approach offers a straightforward method for learning informative and interpretable representations of data distributions. The proliferation of the Internet of Things (IoT) has spurred significant interest in developing smart environments, particularly for home automation. However, a critical challenge remains: how to effectively manage the growing number of connected IoT devices. This paper introduces a novel private blockchain-based framework designed to facilitate intelligent appliance tracking and control within the home. To enhance security and privacy, the system employs end-to-end encryption for all communications involving IoT devices. Furthermore, to enable precise tracking and control, the system integrates trilateration techniques utilizing data from Wi-Fi routers, smart light bulbs, and smart plugs. The implementation successfully demonstrates the framework's capability to track and control appliances with an accuracy of approximately 90%. Additionally, the system can be extended to include other IoT devices by employing the same methodology. This approach is applicable to various devices, including but not limited to IoT plugs, lights, thermostats, and speakers. The primary advantage of this system is its ability to provide effective tracking and control for a greater number of devices. Future research will aim to further refine the tracking and control mechanisms to improve overall performance. Keywords: Internet of Things (IoT), Home Automation, Blockchain, Smart Appliances, Smart Devices.

The Trellis Code Modulation (TCM) framework has become a cornerstone of modern communication systems due to its ability to enhance performance through increased Euclidean distance. A critical component of TCM is the formation of a constellations set (CS), which involves two primary strategies: set partitioning and set mapping. This study introduces a novel set partitioning technique grounded in the principles of unsupervised deep learning. Specifically, t-distributed stochastic neighbor embedding (TSNE) is employed to map one-dimensional L-values of a convolutional code into a two-dimensional space, creating the TCM constellations set. This approach effectively leverages the inherent spatial distribution of L-values to ensure well-separated clusters. Furthermore, unsupervised convolutional neural networks are utilized to determine the optimal number of clusters. To minimize transmission errors, the resulting cluster centers are subsequently mapped to specific modulation symbols. Finally, to reduce power consumption, L-values are quantized to a reduced cardinality before being mapped to cluster centers. Experimental results indicate that the proposed TSNE-based set formation method outperforms state-of-the-art alternatives, achieving a 1 dB improvement in SNR. Additionally, quantization successfully conserves power without degrading the scheme's overall performance. To further validate the method's efficacy, it was applied to a newly developed neural network-based convolutional code, demonstrating robust generalization capabilities. The source code is publicly accessible at https://github.com/ahmedhassan123/TSNE-TCM. We examine the problem of determining if an undirected acyclic graph can be drawn without edge crossings such that every directed edge points upward. While several parameterized algorithms exist for this problem—often yielding super-exponential time complexities—none yet achieve a polynomial-time algorithm when parameterized by the treewidth of the input graph. In this work, we demonstrate that upward planarity is indeed polynomial-time tractable under treewidth parameterization, running in $O(\text{fw} \cdot n)$ time, where $\text{fw}$ represents the forbidden minor treewidth and $n$ denotes the number of vertices. Furthermore, we provide an $O(n)$-time algorithm for certifying upward planarity via an upward planar sketch, which can be converted into an upward planar drawing in linear time. Both of our primary algorithms are inductive, as they operate on the canonical decompositions of bidirected acyclic graphs based on their bidirected minor treewidth. Leveraging our primary method, we also develop a $O(n \cdot 2^{\text{fw}})$-time algorithm for the upward planar embedding problem, which involves finding an upward planar embedding for a given acyclic graph. Additionally, we establish that the upward planar embedding problem is fixed-parameter tractable with a running time of $O(n \cdot 2^{\text{fw}})$ for outerplanar digraphs. Finally, we prove that the upward planar link prediction problem, defined as identifying missing edges in an acyclic graph that, upon addition, preserve all upward planar embeddings, is fixed-parameter tractable with a running time of $O(n \cdot 2^{\text{fw}} \cdot m)$, where $m$ is the edge count. To the best of our knowledge, the feasibility of parameterizing all these problems by treewidth has previously been an open question. We also present fixed-parameter tractable algorithms for determining bidirected $k$-outerplanar acyclic graphs, where the parameter is the $k$-outerplanar bidirected minor. Our approach relies on an exhaustive analysis of bidirected $k$-outerplanar acyclic graphs, which leads to fixed-parameter tractable solutions for several related problems, including bidirected $k$-outerplanar upward planar embedding, bidirected $k$-outerplanar upward link planar embedding, and bidirected $k$-outerplanar upward link planar recognition. The rise of crowdsourcing has enabled the generation of vast datasets, such as the Google Ngram Corpus, which contains over 400 million words from books published between 1500 and 2008. These data offer a novel, efficient, and potentially more intuitive approach to studying human behavior. However, they often suffer from significant noise and uncertainty. To address these challenges, we introduce a new analytical method that combines ensemble modeling, "Human Softmax" distributions, and metrics for entropy and uncertainty. We demonstrate this method using the Ngram Corpus to identify English word pair collocations. Our results show that the approach successfully recovers over 95% of collocations with more than 20 standard deviations of significance, achieving an average accuracy of 96.2% and an average false positive rate of 4.8%. Furthermore, we demonstrate that our method offers additional insights by examining the uncertainty distributions of human-predicted associations, including entropy, the Hurst exponent, and detrended fluctuation analysis. These entropic metrics help characterize the nature of human behavior, such as the degree of randomness or the presence of long-range correlations. Finally, we explore how these entropic properties of human behavior can inform the design of future analytical techniques. Overall, our method offers a new framework for analyzing crowdsourced data, which may prove valuable in various other contexts. Additionally, it provides a means to investigate the uncertainty inherent in human behavior, thereby enhancing our understanding of the human mind. To facilitate replication, we have made our code available at: https://github.com/evgeniyk/collocation-analysis. Our method is also being utilized in a new study of neural network behavior, which will be presented at the 2019 Conference on Cognitive Computational Neuroscience. This conference focuses on the intersection of cognitive neuroscience and artificial intelligence, with a specific emphasis on the similarities and differences between human and machine behavior. For further details, see: https://www.ccgn-conference.org/. We anticipate that our method will be valuable to researchers analyzing crowdsourced data and those seeking to gain deeper insights into human behavior. Our findings also contribute to the ongoing discourse regarding the "human element" in neural networks. Our code is also being employed in a study of human behavior within neural networks, a project led by Dr. Evgeniy Karpinsky, who is renowned for his work on the "Human Softmax" distribution and research into human-like behavior in artificial intelligence.
