This paper investigates the $R_\infty$ invariant of specific nilpotent quotients of generalized Baumslag-Solitar groups, with the objective of establishing a criterion for these quotients to exhibit rational $R_\infty$-genus. Our analysis reveals that determining whether this condition holds generally requires examining infinite families of non-isomorphic groups within these quotients. Ultimately, we demonstrate that these infinite families are rational $R_\infty$-genus equivalent only under specific constraints regarding the indices of element normalizers. Furthermore, we provide a complete classification of these families based on their rational $R_\infty$-genus equivalence. Additionally, we identify a broader class of groups that are not rational $R_\infty$-genus equivalent, encompassing several other significant families within the classification of non-formal nilpotent groups. We further establish that this class is characterized by the property of its members possessing a finite first Betti number. Finally, we present a criterion for rational $R_\infty$-genus equivalence applicable to the more general class of nilpotent groups formed as nil-extensions of finite groups, and we explicitly construct representatives for this class. Notably, this construction encompasses both the previously mentioned class of non-formal nilpotent groups and the family of nil-extensions of finite cyclic groups, both of which consist exclusively of infinite groups. This work thereby advances the classification of non-formal nilpotent groups toward achieving rational $R_\infty$-genus equivalence. To facilitate this, we have developed an algorithm to compute the $R_\infty$ invariant for the relevant nilpotent quotients of generalized Baumslag-Solitar groups. Our findings indicate that this algorithm is effective for computing $R_\infty$ in a wide variety of such cases. We anticipate that the algorithms introduced in this paper will serve as a foundation for future research into the classification of non-formal nilpotent groups. To support these findings, we have also provided a comprehensive collection of examples and counterexamples illustrating the application of our results. These include instances of non-formal nilpotent groups that are rational $R_\infty$-genus equivalent to one another, as well as groups that are not rational $R_\infty$-genus equivalent. We have demonstrated that this collection is closed under the operation of taking nil-extensions with finite groups, thereby enabling the classification of these groups up to rational $R_\infty$-genus equivalence.

Time-resolved spectroscopy is a powerful method for probing dynamic processes in chemical and biological systems. However, reconstructing system evolution from experimental data is complicated by the inversion instability of Newtonian dynamics, which amplifies experimental noise. This challenge is exacerbated when using noisy data to generate time-evolving systems, as noise can trigger significant, unrealistic deviations. While recent studies have addressed these issues within the Liouville framework, those approaches often rely on assumptions that fail under conditions of high noise or large deviations. This work introduces a forward-optimization-based trajectory framework that reliably reconstructs the phase-space distribution function of a time-evolving system, even amidst high levels of noise and large deviations. The study demonstrates the model's efficacy by reconstructing the trajectories of a periodically driven, high-dose Johnson-Kendall-Zeller (J-K-Z) particle. Additionally, the approach is applied to real experimental data from time-resolved photoemission electron microscopy (time-PEEM) capturing the real-time dynamics of a photoexcited, high-dose Fermi gas. The results indicate that this technique effectively reconstructs time-evolving systems, offering a robust solution for analyzing time-resolved experiments on complex, time-evolving materials. Furthermore, the framework is versatile and can be extended to other time-resolved experiments, such as time-resolved photoemission electron microscopy (time-PEEM). The accompanying open-source code is available at https://github.com/akg2017/ForwardOpt. However, existing public datasets often lack the high-quality contextual information found in real-world driving scenarios. This paper introduces SceNDD, a novel contextual-based naturalistic driving dataset. The data was gathered using a custom-built driving recorder installed in vehicles, featuring a rear-view camera for contextual awareness alongside an in-vehicle sensor for physiological monitoring. We provide two data releases: Release 1 (R1) covers 2020 and includes 1,000 driving sessions from 20 drivers, while Release 2 (R2) covers 2021 and includes 2,000 sessions from 40 drivers. Both releases offer video clips paired with corresponding contextual metadata. Additionally, we propose three benchmark tasks to facilitate future research, with results demonstrating the potential of these resources for diverse applications. Recently, the concept of reflected entropy has been introduced to analyze entanglement structures within quantum systems in the context of quantum gravity and cosmology. This reflected entropy extends the conventional bipartite von Neumann entropy and remains applicable to entangled systems that do not satisfy the Markov property. This paper aims to derive the reflected entropy for two intervals on an entangled surface conformal field theory (ESCFT) model, representing the boundary entropy of an SCFT on a half-space. The results indicate that the reflected entropy of this model is proportional to the von Neumann entropy of an ESCFT defined on a model interface situated between two SCFTs. Furthermore, the reflected entropy for two model interfaces is calculated, demonstrating that it exhibits a dependence on the temperature gap between the two interfaces. Additionally, the reflected entropy for two model regions—where conformal boundary conditions remain constant but temperatures vary—is determined. Finally, the reflected entropy for two rectangular Model H regions is computed, revealing that it diverges when the boundaries are nearly parallel. These findings may offer valuable insights for the study of entanglement entropy within quantum gravity frameworks. **Keywords:** reflected entropy, model field theory, quantum information. **PACS:** 03.67.-a, 03.67.-a, 03.67.-a. **Acknowledgments:** This work was supported by the National Natural Science Foundation of China (Grant No. 11705018), the Fundamental Research Funds for the Central Universities (No. 20720200097), and the Beijing Municipal Education Commission (No. 201910028013). The Individual Energy Assessment Integral Fluctuation Theorem (IAIFT) establishes an invariant relationship between forward and reverse fluctuations of the individual change in Helmholtz free energy ($\Delta A_i$) during thermal fluctuations, even in systems exhibiting large non-equilibrium driving forces. This theorem is mathematically equivalent to the standard Integral Fluctuation Theorem ($\langle e^{-\Delta W_i/T} \rangle = 1$) when the boundary conditions for individual thermal fluctuations are defined by the change in Helmholtz free energy. This work outlines a non-invasive experimental strategy to validate the IAIFT, utilizing Brownian motors as a model system. By applying the principle of equivalence between work and $\Delta A_i$ for individual trajectories, we propose an approach to determine the work performed on Brownian motors without physically contacting them. This method relies on measuring the position and momentum of an undriven Brownian motor at the beginning and end of a process to calculate the work performed on it. The feasibility of this strategy is confirmed through both theoretical analysis and numerical simulations. These findings establish a foundation for the precise measurement of energy, enabling the development of energy-saving technologies. Furthermore, this research promotes the practical application of fluctuation theorems. The proposed energy assessment methodology is also applicable to other individual random processes, such as thermal fluctuations and chemical reactions. Additionally, the discussion of non-invasive work measurement is relevant to the broader field of quantum non-demolition measurement. Ultimately, this study is expected to advance both quantum and classical fluctuation theorems. This work examines the existence of deformations for $\mathrm{G}_2$-instantons defined on nearly $\mathrm{G}_2$ manifolds. We demonstrate that for a specific class of non-integrable nearly $\mathrm{G}_2$-structures, no non-trivial $\mathrm{G}_2$-instantons exist on the associated $G_2$-manifolds. Furthermore, we establish that the existence of non-trivial deformations for an instanton depends on the algebraic characteristics of these same structures. In contrast, we also investigate integrable deformations, finding that on manifolds possessing closed $G_2$-structures, every instanton admits a non-trivial integrable deformation. Finally, we present the classification of 3-forms exhibiting constant rank and analyze how their properties influence the deformation space of instantons. Additionally, we identify novel families of instantons and explore their deformation behavior. Specifically, on twisted $G_2$-manifolds, we construct a Laplacian deformation of an instanton and investigate the convergence of the associated inverse Laplacian operator. Finally, we determine which instantons are rigid by deriving sufficient conditions for their existence and calculating their deformation space based on the underlying $G_2$-structure. These findings generalize and complement prior research by explicitly constructing instances of both rigid and non-rigid instantons. Mobile applications utilizing Bluetooth have emerged as a strategy to combat the spread of COVID-19, enabling users to receive alerts when they are near or may have been near infected individuals. This study evaluates the confidentiality of such apps with a specific focus on revealing sensitive user information. We analyze the design of the Coronav\'irus-SUS application, which operates in Brazil. Our assessment includes a theoretical examination of access control mechanisms and conduct a practical attack on its anonymization protocol. We successfully reconstructed the personal data of a user within a distance of 10 meters. Consequently, we conclude that the Confidentiality property is not guaranteed by the application's design. We propose several mitigation strategies to enhance privacy, including implementing a minimum distance threshold, utilizing noise generation, and adopting a decentralized trust model. These recommendations could guide future developments to improve confidentiality and user trust. Additionally, we outline future research directions concerning security and privacy aspects. We argue that the security community must address these critical issues to foster user adoption of mobile applications as a tool for controlling the pandemic. Our analysis underscores the necessity for the software industry to collaborate with security experts to mitigate the vulnerabilities identified in Coronav\'irus-SUS. We contend that such partnerships are essential to resolve the issues highlighted in this research. Finally, we emphasize the importance of integrating security considerations into the software development lifecycle. We believe that our approach can serve as a foundation for the industry to build more secure applications. Furthermore, we note that the security community should engage with the software industry to ensure that the products they create are secure by design. We conclude that the most effective solution to the problems presented in this research lies in fostering collaboration between both communities. This study introduces a quantum-enhanced neural network architecture designed to boost the expressive capabilities of classical networks. The process begins by encoding classical data into quantum states via random encodings, followed by preparing various quantum neural network states using diverse variational circuits. Subsequently, multiple quantum measurements are performed on these states. Finally, the classical neural network is trained via supervised learning by incorporating these quantum measurement data as additional inputs. Experiments conducted on both simulated and hardware platforms using quantum neural network data demonstrate the method's effectiveness across various datasets, including MNIST, CIFAR-10, and CUB-200. The approach yields the most significant improvements on simulated systems with noise-mitigation techniques; specifically, accuracy on noisy quantum data from the 2-qubit CUB-200 dataset rises from 70.2% to 80.0%, and on the 8-qubit CIFAR-10 dataset, it increases from 85.6% to 90.0%. Additionally, the computational efficiency of the quantum-enhanced network relative to the classical one is evaluated through FLOPs analysis. Results indicate that the quantum network requires 100 times fewer floating-point operations than the classical one, representing substantial efficiency gains. The project's source code is publicly accessible at https://github.com/ChenYi-ASU/QNN-Data. Furthermore, the paper includes supplementary materials such as additional experiments, details on quantum circuit configurations, and implementation specifics. Zero-shot object localization involves estimating the positions of object instances within a target domain for which no annotated data exists. Current research in this area typically relies on fine-tuning a pre-trained detector using a large volume of training samples. However, this approach necessitates expensive data annotation and is restricted to estimating the positions of classes that were present in the source domain during the model's initial training. This paper introduces the concept of zero-shot class-level object localization. Unlike prior methods, our approach requires no fine-tuning and can estimate the positions of classes that never existed in the original training set. We evaluated the method on the COCO dataset, aiming to determine the feasibility of estimating class-level object locations in scenarios where the target domain's classes were absent from the training data. The results confirm that reliable zero-shot class-level object localization is achievable. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the performance of our method can be significantly enhanced by pre-training the model on a large number of object samples from the target domain. We anticipate that this method will prove highly beneficial in scenarios where acquiring a substantial quantity of object samples from the target domain is possible, though costly. Finally, we provide open-source code and pre-trained models to facilitate the advancement of zero-shot class-level object localization. Accurate traffic forecasting is essential for traffic management, planning, and control. While deep learning models have become a primary tool in this domain, they are typically trained on highly detailed trajectories collected by in-vehicle sensors. Consequently, these models struggle to deliver accurate predictions when applied to coarser traffic levels using only publicly available data. To address this limitation, we introduce a novel deep learning framework designed for estimating traffic flow across all urban levels using only widely accessible data. Our approach incorporates a similarity-driven attribute extraction module that identifies and isolates traffic flow patterns from publicly available data, allowing the network to learn these extracted attributes for traffic estimation. Experimental results demonstrate that this method achieves significant accuracy improvements when compared against other techniques utilizing the same input data. Furthermore, we conducted comprehensive ablation studies and sensitivity analyses to validate the effectiveness of our proposed similarity-driven attribute extraction module. Finally, we evaluated the method's performance in real-world scenarios by testing its ability to forecast traffic flow and speed across varying spatial resolutions. Graph data is prevalent across numerous domains, yet its reliability often fluctuates due to contextual changes, rendering purely observational statistics insufficient for causal inference. While graph models have been widely adopted for causal analysis, their application remains challenging when unmeasured confounding and the need for interventional or counterfactual reasoning are involved. To address these difficulties, we introduce VACA, a method utilizing variational graph autoencoders for causal inference within graph-structured data. VACA reconstructs the complex graph distribution by separating content from style; the style component captures the directed acyclic structure, while the content component holds the data distribution conditional on this structure. By employing a directed factor graph model as a prior for the style encoder and proposing a novel structure learning approach, VACA mitigates unmeasured confounding issues and supports both interventional and counterfactual queries. We validate the efficacy of VACA across various graph distributions, including synthetic and real-world data, through multiple case studies. Our results demonstrate that VACA surpasses existing state-of-the-art methods in accuracy and precision, particularly in scenarios involving confounding. The VACA code can be accessed at https://github.com/SeungWooLee1213/VACA. Supplementary materials are available at https://supplementary-materials-vaca.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com/. This resource includes case study code for 12 examples covering 6 different data types, such as social network and financial data, allowing users to replicate our findings and explore additional capabilities. This system is designed to identify real-time transients from radio astronomy sources, such as Fast Radio Bursts (FRBs) and Pulsars, and produce on-the-fly radio images. Additionally, the system has observed a large number of low-frequency Solar Flares. This presentation will detail the REALTA backend system and its initial findings. This study examines how various pre-release metrics influence a film's global box office revenue. Finally, the investigation explores how the characteristics of leading actors impact both the success and content of a movie. These findings offer valuable insights for industry stakeholders, including producers, distributors, and investors, enabling them to make more informed decisions regarding resource allocation. This study introduces and analyzes a frequency-regulation strategy for smart grids, detailing its implementation and impact on voltage stability. In contemporary smart-grid architectures, frequency regulation is typically outsourced to auxiliary devices such as battery storage systems. By engaging these tools, frequency regulation inherently influences voltage dynamics. The authors develop analytical models to characterize these behaviors under the assumption of quasi-stationary frequency regulation. These formulations are validated through a case study involving the IEEE 118-bus system, which compares open-loop and closed-loop scenarios. The results demonstrate that the proposed frequency-regulation mechanism can either stabilize or destabilize the grid, depending on specific parameter configurations. Consequently, the paper underscores the necessity of carefully selecting parameter values to ensure stable grid operation. Ultimately, the analysis provides a quantitative framework for grid operators to evaluate how the engagement of auxiliary frequency regulation devices affects the grid. The rise of intelligent systems has driven the need for new approaches to tackle intricate challenges, particularly in biological and social systems. This work introduces a unified framework to address these issues by integrating social interaction into cyberphysical networks of systems. To achieve this, we developed a theory of social intelligence, which represents a novel concept in artificial intelligence. Within this theory, social intelligence is modeled as a distinct cognitive capability that functions by applying social interactions to solve complex problems. Furthermore, we propose a general mathematical model for social intelligence networks, where social agents utilize social interactions to enhance their individual cognitive abilities and deepen their social intelligences. Finally, we demonstrate the application of this theory to a cyberphysical network of neurons, suggesting the existence of social neurons that possess social intelligence and can be identified through specific criteria. These social neurons are capable of enhancing both individual neuronal cognitive abilities and social intelligence within the network. The principles of this theory hold significant implications for social neuroscience and social robotics. Additionally, we validate the theory by training social neural networks capable of solving complex problems, such as the 8-queens problem. The network's social intelligence is further evidenced by its ability to self-heal after damage, thereby preserving its collective computational power. Our findings indicate that social neurons can self-organize into social intelligence networks capable of solving complex problems and maintaining resilience against disturbances. The social neuroscience principles derived from this research can guide future investigations into social cognition. Similarly, drawing inspiration from nature, these principles can drive the design of social cyberphysical systems with social intelligence. This study investigates whether a population of relativistic electrons at the edge of the synchrotron component, interacting with the broad-line region's soft X-ray emission, could be responsible for generating this surplus via a scissor-like modulation of the synchrotron spectrum. To address this question, we developed a modified version of the previously introduced MAPPIES code, building upon the framework established in [1]. The current implementation incorporates relativistic inverse Compton scattering (ICS) and includes the effects of soft-space-charge fields surrounding the blazar core. Our findings indicate that the combined emission from synchrotron and ICS processes can successfully reproduce the SEDs of several BL Lacertae objects, thereby supporting the existence of the UV/X-ray surplus. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the ICS process can be modeled with high precision using a simplified approximation. We present a method for extending the analytic extension of data originally defined over a flat background to a curved manifold. This approach relies on the multiplicative superposition of the spectral components of the extension kernel's impedance function, utilizing the complex Riemann zeta function. The framework is grounded in the factorization of the Gamma function and the theory of the Riemann zeta function, which connects the zeta function to the analytic extension of planar data. The technique is validated through multiple test cases, including multi-scale magnetization and gravity anomalies generated over complex terrains. These examples demonstrate that the proposed method effectively resolves scale separation issues and accurately reproduces the spectral properties of the original anomalies. This study introduces the concept of virtually detecting orthogonal pure states that possess symmetry under local operations. By employing an auxiliary system of dimension $d_{a}$, where $d_{a}$ equals the smallest nontrivial representation of symmetric groups acting on the target's Hilbert space, one can asymptotically determine whether a given state belongs to a specific set of orthogonal pure states through adaptive measurements. Furthermore, we establish the necessary and sufficient conditions for this virtually symmetric property. Consequently, this approach enables the virtual detection of: (i) all non-biorthogonal bases comprising $d+1$ or fewer states for a qudit of dimension $d$, and (ii) a specific collection of $d(d+1)/2$ multiqudits. These findings facilitate the development of new quantum state discrimination schemes and deepen the understanding of the joint limitations of distinguishability and symmetry for orthogonal multipartite pure states. Additionally, we propose a family of unconditionally optimal asymptotic schemes for multistate discrimination as a significant application of these results. Finally, we demonstrate that virtually symmetric pure states can be locally cloned with asymptotic fidelity approaching unity, a capability that eludes even optimally discriminable multipartite pure states. These contributions pave the way for the (im)possibility analysis of various tasks in multipartite quantum information processing. Notably, this work extends the feasibility of locally detecting the largest set of orthogonal qubits, which was previously thought to be unattainable. This set includes four qubits forming two non-coplanar mutually unbiased bases, which can only be locally detected using global operations. Our findings also offer a partial solution to the conjecture regarding the maximum size of an optimally discriminable set of qubits. Specifically, we propose that the limit is $6(d+1)/d$ for a $d$-dimensional system, rather than the previously conjectured $2(d+1)/d$. Finally, our work partially addresses an open question concerning the asymptotic feasibility of locally distinguishing non-multicopy entangled pure states. We show that such states can be virtually locally distinguished if and only if their Schmidt coefficients satisfy specific conditions related to their entropic properties. These findings may offer partial insights into the feasibility of asymptotically multicolorable multiqudits. This classical shape, which emerges as a solution for color-singlet baryons involving three quarks, is analyzed. The study derives the string's dynamical evolution following its splintering into two fragments of equal action. By integrating the 1+1 dimensional Hamiltonian of each string segment, the creation of baryon-antibaryon pairs is explained as the splinter desaccelerates and accelerates along the z-axis. Furthermore, the quantization of these fragments yields a mass spectrum that aligns with the required baryon-antibaryon mass spectrum. The investigation also examines the influence of non-abelian color magnetic fields on baryon-antibaryon creation. Additionally, the method for deriving the helical string from the classical equations of motion is outlined. This approach suggests that other baryon-related string profiles, such as those for mesons, can also be constructed. The proposed model addresses several puzzles regarding baryon spectroscopy and the meson-baryon mass difference. Finally, the antiproton mass puzzle is addressed by noting that the calculated QCD string splinter action along the z-axis matches the experimental proton mass. This similarity is attributed to the helical string's action along the z-axis remaining invariant under changes in transverse shape. Consequently, the model suggests that, to a first approximation, the QCD potential binding protons in the nucleus is independent of transverse string shape variations. This finding also offers a solution to the N/2 rule concerning the baryon density within a nucleus. The work concludes by suggesting that these findings may extend to other hadrons, such as mesons. Solar oscillations serve as a powerful tool for investigating the dynamics of the Sun's surface and interior. By analyzing the effects of surface features on helioseismic travel-time variations, we can gain insights into the structure of the subsurface. This study examines the impact of prominent sunspot groups on global helioseismic travel-time data collected before and after major solar cycles. Our analysis of sunspot contributions to global travel-time variations reveals that the observed differences between hemispheres are significantly smaller than previously reported. Consequently, the previously inferred north-south asymmetry in solar rotation near the surface is no longer supported. This asymmetry had earlier been hypothesized to result from the differing longitudinal tilt of active regions between hemispheres. However, we find that such a tilt alone is insufficient to explain the travel-time variations. Furthermore, we explore potential alternative explanations for these observations. Finally, we conclude by discussing the broader implications of our findings for understanding the global solar cycle. These results underscore the necessity of accurately modeling the structure of active regions to interpret global helioseismic travel-time variations and to reliably detect subtle solar phenomena, such as global hemispheric asymmetries. To achieve this, we have developed a 3D model of active regions that can be integrated into the MHD-validated radiative hydrodynamics (RHD) code Bifrost. This model is capable of generating synthetic active regions with properties consistent with those observed in the Sun. By incorporating this synthetic active region model into RHD simulations, we aim to improve the accuracy of global helioseismic travel-time measurements. This approach will enable a more precise characterization of global hemispheric asymmetries and provide deeper insights into the structure of active regions. Our work will be made available to the community through the RHD Bifrost code. Additionally, we have developed a post-processing tool to streamline the generation of synthetic active regions. This tool allows users to specify parameters such as spot size, umbral area ratio, and granulation density, facilitating the creation of realistic active regions. We anticipate that this tool will be released as an open-source project. The resulting synthetic active regions will exhibit characteristics comparable to real observations, thereby enhancing the accuracy of travel-time measurements. This advancement will ultimately contribute to a more comprehensive understanding of solar surface and interior dynamics. Our findings are available at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.8215500. Finally, we compare our findings with existing research on primordial magnetic fields and discuss the optimal pulsar timing array frequency band for detecting gravitational wave signals from both types of magnetic fields. Our analysis indicates that the most effective frequency band for these searches lies between 1 nHz and 100 nHz. Light field technology has garnered significant interest due to its capacity to capture extra spatial and angular data via spatial and spectral multiplexing. However, the high dimensionality of light field images creates substantial compression hurdles, particularly when utilizing high-resolution sensors. Addressing this, we introduce a new framework that leverages deep learning to enhance the efficacy of predictive coding. Our approach utilizes a disparity-aware model to direct the compression process, ensuring that the resulting bitstream maintains compatibility with mainstream light field rendering techniques. Furthermore, we developed an innovative strategy for the base compression component, enabling the efficient encoding of multiple views with non-uniform resolutions. This method allows for the compression of light fields featuring non-uniform pixel counts across views, achieving superior performance compared to state-of-the-art solutions. Additionally, we propose an enhanced learning model for the entropy-estimation network, which optimizes bit allocation for angular images by accounting for their strong correlation. Experimental results demonstrate that our method outperforms existing approaches in both quality and efficiency for light fields. To further improve quality, we designed a multi-stage distortion metric network capable of accurately assessing the fidelity of compressed light fields. Equipped with this tool, our method outperforms current state-of-the-art compression techniques across various benchmarks. Ultimately, our approach offers superior compression capabilities and flexibility for practical light field applications. The source code will be made publicly available at https://github.com/zhongyuan1234/LP-LFIC. The paper can be found at https://arxiv.org/abs/2101.01052. Interactive methods, including Interactive Retrieval (IIR) and Interactive Cross-Lingual Information Retrieval (ICLIR), have recently surpassed non-interactive vector-based approaches for knowledge-based search. However, these current interactive frameworks depend on standard rankers for initial result generation, thereby restricting their application within the vector-based ICLIR domain. To address this limitation, we introduce a novel framework that effectively integrates the strengths of both interactive and non-interactive paradigms. Specifically, we propose a unified framework for ICLIR, termed ICLIR++, which leverages both interactive and non-interactive techniques to maximize overall performance. Our results demonstrate that ICLIR++ surpasses existing state-of-the-art methods, achieving significant performance gains on French-English and Dutch-German test collections. Furthermore, we validate the efficacy of our approach through extensive ablation studies. To the best of our knowledge, this represents the first framework designed to fully exploit the benefits of both interactive and non-interuitive frameworks in vector-based ICLIR. This study introduces two approaches to small-area estimation (SAE) tailored for low- and middle-income countries (LMICs), with a specific focus on limited data availability. The first method, design-focused, employs a two-stage sampling strategy to mitigate data constraints. The second, model-focused, utilizes a hybrid Bayesian SAE technique combining empirical Bayesian estimation with Bayesian small-area adjustment. The proposed designs and models are demonstrated using HIV prevalence data from Mozambique, an LMIC where certain high-risk districts lack sufficient sample sizes for reliable estimation. The findings indicate that the two-stage design effectively addresses data limitations, while the Bayesian empirical Bayesian (BEB) model proves highly promising for SAE in settings with scarce data. Furthermore, the results suggest that integrating these design and model-focused strategies can enhance the accuracy of SAE in LMICs. Consequently, the study recommends adopting this integrated approach in future research within this context. Additionally, the paper offers practical guidance for implementing these methods in LMICs, including open-source software code. This work is part of a broader effort to develop practical, feasible, and replicable SAE frameworks for LMICs, with details available at https://www.researchgate.net/publication/339510583_Practical_and_feasible_approaches_to_small_area_data_estimation_in_a_low_income_country_context_Mozambique_case_study. The corresponding R code is hosted on GitHub at https://github.com/abraham12345/BEB-and-Bayesian-small-area-adjustment. Future publications will detail the application of the proposed two-stage SAE design and BEB model to other datasets. Keywords: Small-area estimation, two-stage sampling, Bayesian empirical Bayesian, low and middle-income countries, Mozambique, HIV prevalence.

Wagering strategies often depend on adjusting stake sizes based on accumulated winnings or losses, creating feedback loops where performance is typically evaluated using the Kelly criterion. This note introduces a novel approach to measuring quantum wagering performance via the von Neumann entropy of the state representing an agent's belief about state-dependent probabilities. Within this framework, stake sizes function as dispersions in the wave description of state-dependent probabilities. The strategy under examination involves applying the von Neumann entropy associated with coherent wagers as the exponent for the von Neumann dispersion of a bankroll in the waging process. This method is analyzed in the context of both discrete and continuous outcomes, yielding significant insights into the continuous case that elucidate fundamental issues in discrete scenarios. Furthermore, this technique enables the formulation of definite, non-randomized predictions regarding long-term bankroll growth rates for both waging and waging-wearing agents, alongside a straightforward algorithm for determining optimal stake sizes. For the specific case of von Neumann wagers, the von Neumann growth rate remains constant across all states of nature, implying that the optimal von Neumann wager is state-independent. Additionally, the method offers a natural definition of a randomization-free version of wealth maximization. Finally, the paper concludes with a discussion of broader implications concerning the nature of rationality and the relationship between rationality and computation. Notably, the continuous outcome analysis reveals that the von Neumann entropy of the optimal wager equals the Shannon entropy of the state-dependent probability distribution over spectral values, suggesting a continuous analog to the principle that information is the surprise of an event given its probability. This insight supports the hypothesis that information is fundamentally tied to an agent's knowledge of probability distributions. Furthermore, the relationship between spectral values and von Neumann entropy suggests that spectral values represent the boundary between the knowable and the unknowable, with only spectral values of rank 1 being knowable. The formation of stars and their associated protoplanetary disks is a critical phase in the evolution of new solar systems. This study employs the smoothed particle hydrodynamics (SPH) method to simulate the collapse of a prestellar core, where the central protostar disrupts a surrounding gas cloud. The simulation results indicate that the majority of the collapsed material settles into a disk, with a substantial fraction ejected from the system via a bipolar jet. By retaining 10% of the cloud's mass in this disk, the model offers a viable explanation for the unexpectedly high masses observed in real protoplanetary disks. Furthermore, the disk formed in this scenario contains significantly less angular momentum than the collapsing cloud, a finding that aligns with recent research. Additionally, the disk mass exceeds the total mass of all stars in the core, a condition that may trigger further star formation. The structure of this massive disk is primarily shaped by magnetic braking and the central star's rotation. Finally, the jet ejection rate is comparable to the mass accretion rate from the collapsed cloud onto the core, a result consistent with recent theoretical predictions. Overall, this paper presents a simulation that successfully explains several key characteristics of the early stages of star and planet formation. Future research will utilize this initial condition to investigate the subsequent development of the disk and the formation of planets. This study examines a scenario where multiple data providers utilize a federated learning framework to train a model on their confidential data without revealing it to the learning service. Initially, the service employs an existing method to derive a utility function based on a prior distribution over the parameters. Subsequently, a federated algorithm is developed where each data provider learns a posterior distribution for the parameters, leveraging their private information and the prior. This posterior is then aggregated by the learning service according to the utility function. The proposed algorithm is validated through a case study in radiology, involving a collaboration between the National Institutes of Health (NIH) and a private hospital. In this context, a model is trained on de-identified data from both sources, ensuring that the hospital's proprietary information remains confidential. Furthermore, justice is ensured so that no data provider is disadvantaged by the other. Finally, we demonstrate that the algorithm exhibits differential confidentiality, with a specific bound on privacy leakage. Notably, unlike many existing federated learning approaches, this method does not require data providers to disclose the quantity of data held. Additionally, it does not necessitate data providers to reveal the specific content of their data or the computational steps involved in training. We illustrate that the parameters of the model are identifiable, yet the algorithm remains confidential. The paper concludes with a discussion on the algorithm's performance. Our findings indicate that the algorithm yields utility comparable to that of a centralized approach. Finally, we explore the algorithm's relationship with differentiability privacy. While differentiability privacy is known to be NP-hard, we demonstrate that the algorithm achieves privacy under a relaxed condition. Specifically, we prove that the algorithm provides $\epsilon$-differential privacy, where $\epsilon$ is a function of the number of data providers and the dimensionality of the parameter space. This result is achieved by constructing a mechanism that samples from a distribution closely approximating the algorithm's output distribution. The number of samples required to achieve this bound is determined by the number of data providers and the dimension of the parameter space. Consequently, the number of samples needed to guarantee privacy is independent of the information contained within the data. Finally, we show that the algorithm can be implemented in a differentiable fashion, thereby enabling the application of gradient-based optimization techniques. The paper concludes with a discussion on the algorithm's performance regarding differentiability privacy. Our results suggest that the algorithm is effective in achieving privacy under differentiability privacy constraints. Assuming the gauge boson associated with $U(1)_X$ is produced at a future collider, the masses assigned to the additional charged Higgs doublets and right-handed neutrinos dictate the mass of the $Z'$ boson. Our findings indicate that, consistent with experimental limits, the heavy neutrino mixing with left-handed neutrinos remains below the threshold ($\theta_{13}$) level. Additionally, we show that the effective Majorana mass for neutrinoless double beta decay is constrained to a very small value, approximately $10^{-10}m_{45}$. Finally, we illustrate that a substantial portion of the parameter space allows for a heavy neutrino contribution to the lightest supersymmetric particle's mass, thereby facilitating coannihilation mechanisms. Consequently, this contribution can reduce the LSP mass to the GeV range, offering a solution to the muon $g-2$ anomaly. This paper introduces a new unsupervised learning framework designed to enhance the throughput of an IRS-assisted wireless energized network subject to disruption. We begin by deriving the time-averaged network throughput expression, which accounts for the stochastic nature of data generation, energy arrival, and disruption. Subsequently, we formulate a joint optimization problem aimed at maximizing this throughput by determining the optimal order of processing jobs, the order of clearing energy packets, IRS phase shifts, and the scheduling of nodes. To address the resulting high computational complexity, we propose a low-complexity solution that partitions the problem into four distinct subproblems. These subproblems are resolved sequentially and iteratively until convergence, yielding the optimal order of job processing, energy packet clearing, IRS phase shift configuration, and node scheduling. The proposed approach is proven to achieve the optimal solution for the throughput maximization problem. Furthermore, numerical results demonstrate that the achieved throughput improvements surpass those of existing schemes in the literature. Finally, we illustrate how to implement this scheme using the Python programming language. Our implementation provides an additional tool to validate the efficacy of the proposed approach. Finally, we discuss the broader applicability of this scheme to other energy harvesting-enabled communication networks. The $\beta^-$ decay of $^{186}$Hg was investigated using a high-purity germanium detector. A total of 1.5 MBq of $^{186}$Th, produced via the $^{182}$W($^{6}$Li,$^{4}$He) reaction, was utilized as the source for this study. The decay properties of the daughter nuclide $^{186}$Hg were analyzed, resulting in the measurement of its half-life, which is $3.66(5)$ ms. Additionally, eight $\beta$ decay transitions were observed and reported for the first time. The level scheme of $^{186}$Hg was constructed using these new $\beta$ transitions alongside previously documented $\gamma$ rays. A K shell X-ray was also detected, with its intensity relative to the 1123 keV $\beta$ decay transition determined to be $I_K(1123)$ = 0.004(4). Furthermore, the electron capture probability of $^{186}$Hg was established as $\sigma_{\rm{ec}}$ = 0.001(1) based on this value. The resulting data were compared with theoretical predictions derived from the QRPA method. Additionally, the $\log ft$ values for two previously reported $\beta$ decay transitions were updated. Finally, the study discusses the implications of these findings regarding the shape coexistence phenomenon in this mass region. We introduce a unified framework that interconnects the dark sector, specifically dark matter and neutrino properties, with the mechanism of leptogenesis. Within this model, the dark matter candidate is a fermionic scalar particle known as the fermion darkino, while the dark matter abundance is regulated by the decay of a supersymmetric particle, the neutralino. Simultaneously, fermion darkino production occurs through interactions with right-handed neutrinos, creating a link between dark and visible matter. This connection is further reinforced by the fact that the thermal production of dark matter and the generation of leptonic asymmetry in the early universe rely on a shared parameter, $m_N$. We investigate the interrelation between dark matter and leptogenesis within the constraints of current observational data, including dark matter density, leptonic asymmetry, neutrino oscillation parameters, and darkino decay. Our analysis indicates that a successful darkino decay, characterized by a lifetime of $\tau_{\chi}\sim 10^{26}$ s, is highly correlated with a robust generation of the required leptonic asymmetry in the early universe. Furthermore, we observe that a large neutrino mass spectrum ($m_3\gg m_2$) is strongly favored by observational data. Finally, we discuss the implications of our findings for the neutrino mass matrix and the masses of right-handed neutrinos. This study is conducted within the context of the $\mathcal{N}=1$ supergravity model of the Standard Model. Our research is part of the DarkSUSY project, which aims to unify various dark matter candidates and their detection methods into a single framework. This comprehensive approach is essential for identifying the true dark matter candidate and understanding its origin. This paper introduces a data-informed learning-to-control framework designed to achieve, adapt, and maintain robust locomotion and manipulation skills using minimal data and supplementary information. Unlike traditional approaches that rely on random exploration, our method leverages limited data to identify the underlying system dynamics and constructs surrogate models to direct policy learning. Specifically, we introduce an ensemble neural network to approximate the optimal policy, enabling the system to transition smoothly from a data-sparse to a data-abundant regime. The proposed method is evaluated on a 12-degree-of-freedom (DOF) quadruped robot across three distinct tasks: walking, swimming, and falling recovery. Experimental results indicate that, for identical computational resources, our approach achieves stable walking and cycling gaits with significantly fewer training steps compared to baseline methods. Furthermore, the method demonstrates robust performance in walking and cycling over uneven terrain and effectively recovers from falls on both dry and wet surfaces. Additionally, we show that this framework can learn and adapt stable gaits for a new quadruped design using only a few on-board trials. To extend these capabilities to higher-dimensional systems, we also implement the method for manipulation tasks on a 15-DOF robotic arm. We successfully generate stable manipulation skills from limited data and demonstrate adaptation to environmental changes, such as disturbances and variations in object mass and position. Finally, we highlight the method's ability to replicate biological behaviors, such as the gait of a real dog. The complete code is accessible at https://github.com/ChenchenWang1992/DIC-Limited-Data. This paper introduces a novel tripartite connection network designed for the relation generation task, where the goal is to infer relationship labels between entities within a knowledge base. We also present Relation GANs (RGANs), a new generative adversarial network built upon this connection framework. Specifically, RGANs are trained using a loss function that integrates both the triplet loss and the adversarial loss. We introduce a twin-field quantum key exchange (TFQKEx) protocol that operates without requiring phase synchronization between twin beams. In this approach, phase measurements on the twin beams are substituted with conventional optical intensity detection, effectively decoupling the quantum key generation rate from fiber nonlinearities. This method maintains the same maximum scaling potential as standard twin-field quantum key exchange. Furthermore, we demonstrate that our TFQKEx achieves key rates exceeding those of coherent-state quantum key exchange protocols when link lengths reach 100 km. Notably, the system exhibits robustness against phase noise, functioning without phase stabilization even under extreme conditions. Additionally, TFQKEx can be implemented using readily available, low-cost optical components. These findings establish a new paradigm for practical twin-field quantum key exchange. Furthermore, we derive partial results regarding the structure of $\mathcal T_\Lambda$, including the identification of its center, the commutant of $\{T_z^\lambda : \lambda \in \Lambda\}$, and the ideal structure. We also investigate the Toeplitz algebra on $A^2(\mathbb C^n)$ associated with homogeneous polynomials and establish that the Toeplitz algebras linked to these spaces are not isomorphic for distinct $n$. Identifying objects with open lexicons is a difficult task, as it involves detecting visual instances of items for which the system lacks predefined labels. While current state-of-the-art methods rely on supervised learning, the primary challenge remains the scarcity of data. This paper introduces a novel approach that utilizes pseudo- bounding-box annotations to facilitate open lexicon visual object identification. Specifically, we propose a self-supervised method to generate these pseudo annotations, which are subsequently leveraged by a semi-supervised model to enhance the performance of open lexicon image search systems. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of our method, with visual identification F-measures reaching 40.8% on the PASCAL-65 dataset and 50.3% on the Visual Genome dataset. Furthermore, our approach surpasses existing state-of-the-art techniques by significant margins. To the best of our knowledge, this marks the first application of pseudo- bounding-box annotations to the problem of open lexicon visual object identification. The code will be made available at https://github.com/ChenYi-chen/PBBBox.

This study evaluates a class of factor models with time-varying factor loadings for predicting mortality rates. We introduce a new factor liability model featuring time-varying loadings and develop a state-space framework to estimate these dynamics. An online forecasting approach is introduced to generate short-term mortality predictions. Through analysis of the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention data, we assess and compare the performance of our proposed model against the standard Lee-Carter model. The results indicate that the proposed method yields more accurate forecasts than the traditional approach. Furthermore, we outline a potential extension of this model designed to project long-term mortality trends. This additional section compares various parameter calibration strategies and their corresponding predictive outcomes. Ultimately, the proposed framework offers a more comprehensive characterization of mortality dynamics compared to existing literature. Notably, the model's capacity to capture shifts in factor loadings enables the integration of external information, such as the impacts of the COVID-19 pandemic. Finally, we outline promising avenues for future research. Specifically, the framework can be adapted to predict other critical demographic metrics, including fertility, migration, and morbidity rates. Additionally, extending the model to accommodate cross-sectional dynamics would allow for the prediction of dynamics across diverse demographic groups. Human Translators (HTs) are essential in the Computer-Assisted Translation (CAT) environment, serving as initial revisers for machine-translated text and acting as translators when no prior translation exists. Their quality is typically assessed using Traditional Translation Memory (TM) metrics, which measure similarity between the HT's output and reference texts. However, these conventional metrics fail to account for dependability—the probability that an HT will accept a TM proposal without revision. To address this gap, we introduce the concept of Personal Translation Memory (PTM), a customized TM built from an HT's output and corresponding source text, which allows for the evaluation of dependability. We have developed a novel algorithm to calculate translation reliability using PTM-based metrics. Our experimental results indicate that translators exhibit varying levels of dependability; some frequently revise proposals, while others often do so. These differences stem from translators' distinct psychological traits, such as their attitudes toward revision tasks. We have modeled these characteristics using a Bayesian Network to assess dependability and predict the most likely behavior of specific translators. This approach enables CAT tools to adapt to individual HT behaviors, thereby enhancing translation quality and efficiency. We validated the method's effectiveness through case studies. Ultimately, we believe this approach can improve the translation process and that its success demonstrates the value of integrating cognitive psychology into CAT systems. Furthermore, the framework is flexible and can be extended to other psychological characteristics, such as translation strategies. We present sum rules for energy absorption across a broad range of scattering and absorption mechanisms, encompassing scenarios ranging from purely elastic interactions to pure absorption. These sum principles are derived by employing a complete set of energy absorption eigenchannels, which correspond to the eigenchannels of the total scattering + absorption operator. We demonstrate that these sum rules generalize the Gerasimov-Dydak-Maximon sum rule, the Johnson sum rule, the Gerasimov-Sadovnik sum rule, and the Buras sum rule. Additionally, we derive sum rules for energy absorption at next-to-next-to-leading order in the small-angle scattering limit. This derivation relies on the sum rules for the helicity amplitudes of virtual photo- and weak-production processes, which are provided in tabular and graphical formats. We also examine the implications of these sum rules regarding the EMC effect, the Gerasimov-Dydak-Maximon sum rule, and the Buras sum rule. Finally, we outline the necessary experimental and theoretical efforts to validate the sum rules applicable to arbitrary scattering and absorption frameworks. This approach is particularly relevant for investigating time-like regions, such as $Z$-boson scattering off protons, and for analyzing the interplay between scattering and decay operators, exemplified by the interconnection between the Gerasimov-Dydak-Maximon and Gerasimov-Sadovnik sum rules. Furthermore, our formalism enables the systematic construction of model-independent sum rules for other processes, including electron-proton scattering, Compton scattering, and photo- and weak-production. Consequently, this provides a foundation for the systematic development of sum rules in the emerging field of hadronic gamma spectroscopy. In this context, sum rules serve as essential tools for disentangling the complex structure of hadronic spectral functions. In this case, we derive model-independent sum rules that extend the Johnson sum rule to the general regime of arbitrary photon polarization and energy. We also discuss the significant role of these Compton sum rules in constraining the structures of hadronic spectral functions, thereby facilitating the reconstruction of hadronic spectral functions from gamma spectroscopy data. Fully connected neural networks, including those utilizing convolutional layers, are known for their susceptibility to overfitting, which often results in a vast number of redundant weights. This study presents empirical evidence that networks can be optimized by eliminating these redundant parameters. By applying a simple and rapid trimming procedure to both 2D and 3D convolutional networks, we demonstrate that the trained convolutional "winning ticket" exhibits significantly fewer connections than its fully trained counterpart. Furthermore, these "winning tickets" display superior generalization performance, lower parameter counts, reduced computational complexity, and decreased memory usage. These findings hold true across various training scenarios, including those with limited data and limited training time. Ultimately, this work sheds light on the fundamental characteristics of neural networks and provides a straightforward method for network pruning. Additionally, we introduce a new pruning algorithm designed to further refine the winning tickets identified in this study. This proposed algorithm surpasses existing state-of-the-art deep network pruning techniques in terms of performance, computational complexity, and memory usage. We introduce a new approach to marketing and valuing lottery tickets by analyzing the decision-making process of individual players. This method relies on two key assumptions: first, that a player selects a ticket by picking a subset of numbers from the total pool; and second, that the player chooses each number independently. The value of the ticket is determined by the probability that the selected subset includes the winning subset. We demonstrate that the per-ticket anticipated value can be derived using only the number of possible outcomes and the count of available numbers. Furthermore, we compare the value of a single ticket against a fixed budget to the value provided by a forecaster who predicts winning subsets with a specified probability. The model parameters can be calibrated using either ticket sales revenue or the cost of acquisition. Our results indicate that the cost of a single ticket should ideally be no less than approximately 90% of its value, suggesting that the anticipated value of the prize is relatively low. Additionally, we show that the cost of $n$ tickets should not exceed the sum of the costs associated with buying $n$ tickets individually. Finally, we prove that the expected revenue for the lottery organization is strictly less than the cost per ticket, implying that the lottery's primary function is to generate entertainment value for participants. These findings may offer valuable insights for players, helping them make more informed decisions. The source code is publicly accessible at https://github.com/ehudk/lottery. We introduce a two-dimensional valley-phonon Hamiltonian that incorporates innovative interaction pathways involving spin and strain fields. These mechanisms are critical for precisely modeling the long-time evolution of valley coherence in two-dimensional materials. We specifically analyze graphene and graphene-like hexagonal boron nitride, comparing scenarios with remote $K$ and $K'$ valleys separated by moiré potential steps versus valleys situated in Moiré minibands. The study reveals that phonon-mediated valley dephasing is significantly slower when valleys are located within minibands. Furthermore, the valley $T_2$ times in these minibands can exceed the photon emission duration, a finding particularly relevant for graphene bilayers. In contrast, the valley $T_2$ time for $K$ and $K'$ valleys separated by moiré potential barriers is limited to the impurity scattering time, rendering them unsuitable for applications. Finally, we demonstrate that spin-valley entanglement induced by these novel electron-phonon mechanisms can be suppressed via spin resonance techniques. This capability enables the preparation of a pure valley state, which is a necessary prerequisite for high-fidelity valley qubits. Quantum emulation of fermionic systems is established as a standard and effective approach for investigating strongly correlated quantum matter. The quantum simulators built using cold atoms offer a clean, flexible platform for modeling the one-dimensional (1D) fermionic Hubbard model. However, achieving high-fidelity simulators for larger system sizes remains a significant challenge. In this work, we propose a hybrid digital-analog quantum computing method to emulate the 1D fermionic Hubbard model. Our approach involves digitally controlling the fermionic system to execute a hybrid quantum algorithm that diagonalizes the model's Hamiltonian, followed by analogically preparing the many-body eigenstate through evolution under the interaction Hamiltonian. We successfully observed a phase transition from a non-condensed to a condensed state by varying the ratio of interaction strength to Fermi energy. Furthermore, we analyzed the effects of both single- and two-qubit errors on the emulation fidelity and demonstrated that these errors can be effectively mitigated by increasing the system size. This study paves the way for developing high-fidelity quantum simulators for larger system sizes using hybrid quantum computing techniques. Additionally, our research offers a viable pathway for constructing quantum simulators for other fermionic systems. Notably, our method is applicable to a broad spectrum of quantum systems, provided one can digitally implement a quantum algorithm to diagonalize the Hamiltonian and then evolutionarily prepare the eigenstate. This represents a significant step toward achieving high-fidelity quantum emulation for larger systems. Finally, our findings offer valuable insights for advancing high-fidelity quantum computing. We establish graph-level identities for a general class of series composed of polynomials in the variable $z$, where the coefficients are determined by the expected $z$-weighted count of specific subgraphs within any graph. We interpret these identities as an analog of the Cayley-Hamilton identity, linking two graph-invariant sequences within a Hilbert space framework. We outline the construction of such identities and their graph-level functional identities, demonstrating their applicability to Polya vectors and the expected values of subgraph Poincaré polynomials. Additionally, we introduce interpretations of these identities in terms of graph morphisms and adjoint functors. Finally, we highlight the utility of these results in establishing new identities for established graph invariant sequences. Our work is grounded in the abstract theory of (co)algebras.

This paper examines how remote work impacts Scrum success, specifically within software development. While prior research indicates generally positive outcomes for remote teams, it lacks detailed insights into the nuances of distributed Scrum project success. Consequently, this study aims to deepen understanding of these dynamics by analyzing the mechanisms driving success across various team and project traits. To achieve this, the research employs a multi-approach, multi-dimension methodology, investigating the influence of team and project characteristics on success through statistical correlation analysis across three case studies. The findings reveal that certain characteristics exert opposing effects on Scrum success depending on the specific context, highlighting the complexity of remote software development teams. Furthermore, the study identifies significant correlations between the success of Scrupled projects and factors such as team size, team experience, and product complexity. These insights can assist managers in anticipating challenges and devising appropriate strategies to mitigate them. Additionally, the study confirms a significant correlation between agile maturity and Scrum success, suggesting that transitioning to agile practices is particularly beneficial for teams in distributed environments. Finally, the research confirms the critical role of communication in remote settings, noting that its impact is amplified when teams are dispersed and when utilizing video conferencing tools. The paper concludes by discussing how these results can inform decisions regarding team formation and management in remote contexts. Given that success is influenced by the interplay of numerous factors, the study emphasizes the need for a holistic approach to form effective teams and adopt management practices tailored to the remote context. Furthermore, the varying significance of these influences underscores the absence of a one-size-fits-all solution for managing remote software development teams. Instead, the study recommends that managers leverage these insights to identify and apply management practices suited to their specific team's characteristics. Ultimately, the research demonstrates the value of adopting an evidence-based perspective when managing remote software development teams. Finally, the study confirms the existence of a negative correlation between agile maturity and team formation time, indicating that teams with higher agile maturity require less time to establish themselves. This finding suggests that the agile mindset fosters self-organization, thereby reducing the time needed to build a functional team. Additionally, the study notes the critical role of team size in remote settings, where the influence of team size on success is more pronounced than in traditional contexts. This paper builds upon the concept of the Gau-Wu value, originally defined for symmetric tridiagonal matrices, and extends it to within $4$-symmetric tridiagonal matrices. We demonstrate that the ValuefW function applicable to these matrices can be expressed as a $4^{\text{th}}$-degree polynomial in terms of the value $w_4$. Furthermore, we introduce and analyze a new class of matrices known as Choose Arrowhead Matrices (CAM). By calculating the principal minors of these CAMs, we establish their definiteness and determine their Spectral Value Range (SVR). Notably, the SVR for CAMs is always a subset of the unit circle. Finally, we illustrate practical applications of these findings by calculating the SVR for the discrete Laplacian matrix ($L$) and the discrete Hilbert matrix ($H$), demonstrating that the SVR of $L$ fills the entire unit circle, whereas the SVR of $H$ occupies only the upper half of the circle. Keywords: Value of W, Choose Arrowhead Matrix, Discrete Laplacian Matrix, Discrete Hilbert Matrix.

This study investigates the influence of elliptical electron motion on beauty-hadron production within Pb-Pb collisions at a center-of-mass energy of 5.02 TeV. The analysis examines the impact of elliptic flow on the nuclear modification factor and transverse momentum spectra of electrons generated by beauty-hadron decays. Utilizing the Monte Carlo event generator PYTHIA8, elliptic motion is simulated via a magnetic field applied to the initial partonic state. The results indicate that the elliptic motion of beauty-hadrons, and consequently the electrons derived from their semi-leptonic decays, produces negligible effects under the specified collision conditions. Furthermore, the nuclear modification factors and p$_T$ spectra for these elliptic electrons align with those of non-elliptic electrons. This finding suggests that the observed enhancements in the nuclear modification factor and p$_T$ spectra of electrons from beauty-hadron decays cannot be attributed to the elliptic motion of the underlying beauty-hadrons. Additionally, the analysis confirms that the nuclear modification factors for these electrons remain insensitive to the magnitude of the applied magnetic field. These conclusions are supported by the provided data and code. Given that similar effects are expected for charm quarks, this research offers a valuable framework for analyzing such phenomena in future studies. Ultimately, the methodology employed here may prove useful for investigating other nuclear effects in Pb-Pb collisions. This work was conducted using the Pb-Pb dataset from the ALICE experiment at the LHC. The Pb-Pb data were acquired using ALICE's upgraded central barrel detector, which was fully upgraded in 2015. The data span the entire range of $\sqrt{s_{\rm NN}}$ = 5.02 TeV, covering 443,000 events with an average multiplicity of 159.5. The study focuses on the mid-central collision range of 20% < centrality < 80%, where the effects of elliptic motion are anticipated to be most pronounced. This paper presents a method for constructing colorful alpha complexes grounded in graph theory. These complexes offer an efficient method for estimating metrics, such as area and volume, for point clouds that have been given a secondary partition based on their proximity to initial seed points. The paper details the definition of colorful alpha complexes and demonstrates how to compute their persistent homology. The proposed approach holds significant potential for generating informative visualizations in scientific data analysis and for defining partitioned metric estimates for regions like the Moon's regolith or virial clusters of galaxies. A Python implementation is available at: https://github.com/brandonrappaport/ColorfulAlphaComplex. This study examines the maximum Extremal GDoF advantage of optimally scheduling transmit powers for all $K$ users in a general interference network, assuming each user has access to $\log_2(K)$ bits of interference side information regarding other users' rates. This benefit is measured against a binary power scheduling scheme, where transmitters either transmit at their maximum rate or remain silent. We derive closed-form expressions for the optimal scheduling gain for $K \geq 3$ users in both half-duplex and full-duplex scenarios. Our findings indicate that the Extremal GDoF gain achieved by optimally transmitting for all users is $\Theta(\log_2(K))$ higher than when all users simultaneously transmit at their maximum rates. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the scheduling gain in the half-duplex case exceeds that of the full-duplex scenario by a factor of $\Theta(\sqrt{K})$. For $K \geq 3$ users, we prove that the Extremal GDoF gain of an optimal schedule over a binary schedule is at least $\Theta(\sqrt{K})$. Additionally, for the specific case of $K=3$ users, we establish that this gain is precisely $\Theta(3)$. We also present an algorithm to construct an optimal schedule for any $K \geq 3$ using an inductive approach, and provide an example for $K=4$ users to illustrate the method. Finally, we propose an open research question regarding the existence of an optimal schedule for $K \geq 5$ users where every user transmits with a non-zero rate. To address this, we introduce the concept of an $m$-th degree schedule for $m \geq 0$, demonstrating that a $m$-th degree schedule is optimal for $K \leq m+2$ users. We further show that for $K \geq 5$ users, there exists an optimal schedule that can be represented as a convex combination of at most $2^{K-3}$ schedules of degree $m=2^{K-3}-1$. We conjecture that for $K \geq 5$ users, an optimal schedule exists where all users transmit with non-zero rates. This conjecture holds true for $K \leq 4$ users. This paper introduces methods to integrate existing classifier outputs with uncertainty information to create a unified, high-quality, and adaptable classification system. The proposed uncertainty data reflects the confidence levels of concepts within an formal context, which is represented as a relation between objects and attributes. This unified approach is designed to enhance the reliability of classification systems in the context of IT auditing. The study evaluates two primary algorithms for combining uncertainty: the Adams algorithm and the combination method utilizing the Dempster-Shafer theory of evidence. The proposed methodology was tested on real-world IT auditing datasets, and the results were compared against standard classification outcomes generated without uncertainty data. The analysis demonstrates that incorporating uncertainty data improves the overall effectiveness of the classification system. Furthermore, when utilizing Dempster-Shafer theory to combine uncertainty, the classification system achieves an accuracy rate of 95.5%. Finally, a comparison between the adapted algorithms reveals that the Adams algorithm is more efficient for small datasets, whereas Dempser-Shafer theory is better suited for larger datasets. IT auditing represents a specialized domain where data collection is often difficult, time-consuming, and resource-intensive. Consequently, the uncertainty inherent in the collected data must be considered during the analysis and classification processes. This uncertainty can be modeled by examining the context within which concepts are formed. The paper outlines the algorithms used to combine uncertainty and assesses their performance across various IT auditing datasets. The study concludes that Dempser-Shafer theory yields the most satisfactory results, achieving an accuracy of 95.5%. Additionally, the proposed uncertainty combination method is shown to be more effective than traditional object classification approaches. The uncertainty analysis algorithm is implemented in Java and is available as open-source software. This study introduces a novel approach to production modeling by modeling point patterns with inhomogeneous Poisson and Strauss processes, followed by " stitching" them together. We demonstrate that these produced models effectively capture the structural clustering found in real point patterns. Furthermore, we establish that they possess the necessary properties for theoretical analysis, allowing us to derive asymptotic results regarding asymptotic normality and convergence in distribution. Our simulations indicate that these theoretical findings are practical and robust. Finally, we apply these produced models to two real-world datasets: the positions of 1,476 galaxies in the Coma cluster and the locations of 1,000 individuals within a 1 km² area of San Francisco. The results confirm the superiority of these models over other commonly used production models. Additionally, we have implemented the production model based on the Strauss process in the R package `prodSaus`. The code for all simulations is available in the `ProdSaus` package.
