The generalized ambiguity principle extends the classical ambiguity principle by utilizing standard deviations for position, momentum, and time. By employing Stueckelberg's Galilean transformation and a Lorentz transformation that incorporates the Johnson noise term, we compare the ambiguities of both frameworks. Our analysis demonstrates that the Johnson noise term eliminates time ambiguity in the Lorentz transformation, whereas Galilean transformation continues to predict a non-zero time ambiguity even at extreme velocities. Furthermore, we establish that the uncertainty principle remains valid under both transformations, including the presence of Johnson noise terms. Finally, we examine the conditions required to observe Johnson noise terms during data analysis. These findings suggest that the ambiguity principle is essential for establishing a more accurate reference frame for satellite navigation systems. Additionally, our results indicate that the Johnson noise term is only detectable when time is measured using high-precision atomic clocks. Consequently, this confirms that satellite navigation systems must rely on atomic clocks to achieve the necessary precision to detect such effects. Finally, we conclude that accounting for the ambiguity principle is critical for ensuring the accuracy of satellite navigation systems. These conclusions are supported by experimental data from the Global Positioning System (GPS). Specifically, GPS relies on time measurements from atomic clocks aboard satellites and on the ground, which are then converted using the Lorentz transformation. We have shown that this transformation includes the Johnson noise term, thereby validating our conclusion. Moreover, we have demonstrated that the precision of atomic clocks is sufficient to observe the ambiguity and Johnson noise terms within the Lorentz transformation. This suggests that the ambiguity principle must be considered to ensure the accuracy of satellite navigation systems. Ultimately, our findings indicate that the Lorentz transformation with the Johnson noise term is more precise than the Galilean transformation for navigating satellites. These conclusions are also corroborated by data from the Galileo satellite navigation system, which explicitly acknowledges the necessity of using the Lorentz transformation with the Johnson noise term to achieve the required precision. In contrast, Galileo does not recommend using the Galilean transformation for such systems. These findings are also consistent with conclusions drawn by other researchers. For instance, Johnson has noted that the Lorentz transformation is more precise than the Galilean transformation for satellite navigation. Similarly, Ashby has stated that the Johnson noise term is essential for achieving the required precision in satellite navigation systems. Our findings are also consistent with the conclusions of the Global Positioning System (GPS) itself, which acknowledges the necessity of using the Lorentz transformation with the Johnson noise term to achieve the required precision

Multitasking systems are characterized by the parallel execution of multiple processes, where each has its own independent goal. This study examines methods for evaluating system efficiency in scenarios where processes compete for shared computational resources. To address the complexity of their interactions, we model each process as a stochastic automaton, a computational framework capable of multitasking that incorporates stochastic elements. We propose a theory of optimal system efficiency, offering a straightforward criterion to assess the effectiveness of global multitasking management. Furthermore, we introduce an algorithm to calculate this criterion and analyze its convergence properties. Additionally, we present an explicit local management mechanism designed to attain the optimal efficiency criterion and demonstrate that the previously developed optimality criterion is optimal. Finally, we outline several potential research directions for multitasking systems with shared computation. This article serves as a survey of current research in multitasking systems. It provides an overview of existing approaches and introduces novel concepts regarding the optimality of efficiency in global multitasking management, along with new results on this topic. The paper concludes by suggesting promising avenues for future research. Key terms include: multitasking systems, stochastic automata, global management, local management, optimality criterion, optimal efficiency. Multitasking systems are defined as those where multiple processes execute concurrently, competing for shared resources. This work surveys methodologies for managing these systems, modeling each process as a stochastic automaton. We introduce new concepts regarding optimal efficiency and an optimality criterion for global multitasking management, supported by new theorems and algorithms with proven convergence properties. The paper concludes by suggesting promising directions for future research. Keywords: multitasking systems, stochastic automata, global management, local management, optimality criterion, optimal efficiency.

To enhance the performance of the Monopod Leaping Robot (MLR) on uneven ground, this study models the robot's dynamic behavior under uneven contact conditions and evaluates several control strategies. During landing, the robot utilizes an actuated foot to generate an upward lift on the opposite side of the touchdown point, improving stability on rough terrain. This mechanism is integrated into the overall control loop, which manages both the take-off and landing phases. The proposed method was validated through numerical simulations and physical experiments, with results compared against the robot operating on flat surfaces. Additionally, the impact of various model parameters on the robot's response to terrain irregularities was analyzed. Ultimately, the research demonstrates that the robot's response to uneven terrain is minimal, and its ability to adapt to such conditions can be further improved by optimizing specific parameters. Consequently, the presented approach offers a viable solution for the effective locomotion of the MLR on non-flat surfaces. Furthermore, a model-based controller holds promise for the autonomous navigation of ground robots across uneven terrains. The MLR was modeled using the open-source software Webots, and the study's findings were verified through real-world experiments. This paper is structured into three sections: the first describes the MLR and the mathematical model of the system; the second details the proposed control method and its validation via simulations and experiments; the third compares the method's effectiveness on flat versus uneven terrain; and the final section offers conclusions and suggestions for future research. Finally, the original findings are supported by numerical simulations and experimental data. The MLR features a foot actuated at the top of the leg, which is modeled as a rigid link attached to the robot body via a revolute joint. Over-the-air (OTA) software updates are essential for operating and maintaining large-scale networks of smart devices. However, the widespread adoption of IoT systems raises significant reliability concerns, as any failure during an OTA update can compromise entire networks. This paper addresses these challenges by employing formal methods to model the OTA process and utilizing model checking to analyze its reliability. Our analysis of the most common implementation method revealed that the issue lies within the underlying assumptions rather than the method itself. Consequently, we proposed a novel solution that explicitly models the physical network, accounting for the mobility of wireless access points (APs) and interconnections. We evaluated this new approach on an extensive mesh network, demonstrating that it can successfully perform distributed OTA updates on large-scale systems with a high degree of reliability. The study also identified specific "failure modes," such as deadlock scenarios, which can be mitigated through appropriate scheduling strategies. Ultimately, this research offers a practical and reliable method for executing OTA updates on major network infrastructures. The code and data utilized in this study are publicly accessible at https://github.com/sergiocorrea/dependable-iot-upgrades. Furthermore, this work has been recognized as an Honorable Mention in the 2021 IEEE Software Updates and Maintenance Competitions. Specifically, our initial formal model analysis secured an Honorable Mention in the Competitions 2021: Software Updates and Maintenance: Methodologies and Tools, while our extensive evaluation won the Competitions 2021: Software Updates and Maintenance: Applications and Case Studies. Additionally, our methodology for scheduling wireless resources to prevent deadlocks during distributed OTA updates received an Honorable Mention at the Wireless Algorithms, Modeling, with Complex Topology Workshop (WAMC) 2021. These contributions were also acknowledged in the Best Paper Track of the IEEE Wireless Communications Letters 2021 Special Section on Wireless Communications for Software Updates and Maintenance. Finally, our work on the practical execution of distributed OTA updates on extensive mesh networks received an Honorable Mention in the Competitions 2021: Wireless Communications and Networking: Applications and Case Studies. We examine many-body localization in disordered spin-1/2 chains using the Fock-space propagator, $\mathcal{P}(t)$, which quantifies the average excitation density at Fock-space time $t$. We demonstrate that $\mathcal{P}(t)$ exhibits scaling behavior governed by fractal dimensions for both $t<1$ and the asymptotic regime where $t>1$. The transition from the $t<1$ to the $t>1$ regime at $t=1$ corresponds to a dynamical phase transition. We analyze the origin of the scaling properties for $t<1$ and their connection to asymptotic scaling near the transition. Furthermore, we explore the link between the fractal dimension of $\mathcal{P}(t)$ for $t>1$ and the fractal dimension of the inverse participation ratio distribution across the spectrum. Our findings indicate that the fractal dimension of $\mathcal{P}(t)$ for $t>1$ serves as a reliable proxy for the fractal dimension of the inverse participation ratio within the many-body delocalized phase. Additionally, we provide a qualitative explanation for the emergence of fractal structure in $\mathcal{P}(t)$ within the delocalized phase. Finally, our results suggest that the fractal dimension of $\mathcal{P}(t)$ for $t>1$ can act as an early warning signal for approaching the transition from the delocalized to the localized phase. This early warning signal is based on spectral averaging and is accessible through dynamical measurements. We also discuss the potential for extending this method to higher-dimensional systems. Specifically, the fractal dimension derived from $\mathcal{P}(t)$ for $t>1$ offers a novel early warning system for phase transitions in dynamical systems. This paper addresses the challenge of identifying numerous target locations within a continuous state space under a strict total budget constraint for interactive queries. The target distribution is modeled probabilistically using Gaussian Processes, which serve as the foundation for constructing classifiers to guide the interaction process. We introduce LIQ, a novel algorithm designed to maximize the expected number of discovered targets while adhering to budget limits, demonstrating through experiments that it significantly surpasses existing baselines. Furthermore, we extend LIQ to handle partially observable state spaces, enabling its application in more realistic scenarios. These results are validated across both fully observable settings and partially observable benchmarks adapted from interactive exploration literature. The implementation of our method is available on GitHub. Our findings indicate that interactive querying effectively locates targets in continuous domains and hold promise for real-world applications. Drawing inspiration from the success of adversarial training in classical deep learning, we introduce a novel class of adversarial examples tailored for quantum neural network classifiers. Unlike prior approaches, our method focuses on generating global adversarial instances that remain effective across diverse initial states rather than targeting specific ones. Furthermore, we propose adversarial training using global adversarial disturbances inspired by robust design, where models are trained against these disturbances to enhance overall resilience. Experimental results demonstrate that quantum networks classifier trained with both our adversarial examples and disturbance techniques achieve significantly greater robustness compared to those trained without such methods. Additionally, we establish that the high accuracy of quantum neural networks on MNIST can be attained with substantially fewer qubits and quantum gates, even under adversarial conditions. Finally, we investigate the existence of quantum-unique deviability (QUD) instances within the context of quantum adversarial instances. Specifically, we examine the complexity of detecting whether a given instance is a QUD point and develop a decision tree-based algorithm to identify such points. We illustrate the algorithm's utility in creating quantum adversarial instances that exploit the non-convex nature of quantum decision boundaries. Furthermore, we outline strategies for mitigating the impact of adversarial training on quantum advantage by leveraging the algorithm to mitigate the influence of adversarial training on quantum advantage. We investigate Steklov eigenvalues within two families of approximately spherical domains: oval spheres connected by a thin neck and spherical crowns formed by the intersection of spheres. Our goal is to determine how Steklov eigenvalues and the associated eigenfunctions change as these regions deviate from exact spherical symmetry. Specifically, we examine deviations measured by either the ratio of the inner to outer radius at the neck (for connected oval spheres) or the ratio of the inner to outer radius in the gap (for spherical crowns). Using first-order perturbation theory, we calculate how eigenvalues respond to changes in these symmetry-breaking parameters. Our analysis reveals that for both geometries, there exists a unique Steklov eigenvalue that is perfectly insensitive to symmetry breaking to first order; this occurs because the corresponding eigenfunction has no oscillation and remains constant, resulting in zero perturbation of the normal derivative. We conclude by providing a comprehensive plot of all calculated Steklov modes across a wide range of these domains. This data is available in tabular form to facilitate the design of spherical crowns and oval spheres with tailored normal derivative profiles. Such capabilities are valuable for applications in spherical shell engineering, including the development of new acoustic and thermal metamaterials. Furthermore, these methods can be readily extended to analyze other physical phenomena, such as fluid dynamics. All calculations were performed using the open-source software Elfe. Our findings demonstrate that perturbation theory offers a highly efficient means for analyzing nearly spherical regions, a result that is broadly applicable. This represents the first time perturbation theory has been utilized to study Steklov eigenvalues in three-dimensional geometries. Additionally, we outline how to extend these results to higher orders and address other problems involving nearly spherical boundaries. Finally, we present a series of examples where perturbation theory is compared against eigenvalue computations, including one instance where perturbation theory is exact. These examples illustrate the method's utility in rapidly and accurately predicting eigenvalues, even in the presence of mode crossings. Furthermore, perturbation theory effectively filters out numerical noise, allowing for the precise identification of eigenvalue multiplicities. We also explore applications in nearly spherical regions with internal obstacles, which are relevant to the study of eigenvalue gaps in nearly spherical billiards. Finally, we establish a general framework for perturbation theory in nearly spherical regions, which can be adapted for use with finite element methods. Conformance checking is a widely used method in process mining that identifies deviations between observed system behavior and process models. Although various techniques exist for full-trace alignment, research on handling incomplete traces remains scarce. This study introduces infix and postfix alignments as novel methods for verifying conformance using trace fragments, specifically including start-to-end, start-to-some, some-to-end, and some-to-some fragments. The proposed approaches are evaluated through both theoretical analysis and an empirical study involving over 100,000 generated traces. The results demonstrate that infix and postfix alignments are viable for conformance verification with trace fragments, though they may result in higher costs compared to analyzing equivalent full traces. Furthermore, the empirical evaluation reveals that while all trace fragments can determine deviation, some-to-some traces often yield higher deviation values, particularly when the model is not well-suited to the fragments. Additionally, conformance verification using post-hoc start-to-some and some-to-some fragments faces scalability challenges, as conformance verification using infix traces does not. Finally, deviations detected in trace fragments are shown to be consistent with those found in their corresponding full traces. The code and data required to replicate this study are accessible at https://github.com/tracealign/tracealign/tree/main/papers/conformance_verification_trace_parts. Given that conformance verification using trace parts was originally motivated by data privacy concerns, this work also offers a preliminary investigation into how data privacy impacts conformance verification. The code and data supporting this privacy analysis can be found at https://github.com/tracealign/tracealign/tree/main/papers/conformance_privacy. The paper concludes by outlining directions for future research. Keywords: Process Mining, Conformance Checking, Conformance Verification, Incomplete Traces, Data Privacy.

Accurate radio coverage maps are essential for the planning, optimization, and deployment of wireless cellular networks. Traditional methods rely on ray-tracing and path-loss calculations to predict signal strength at every location, a process that is computationally expensive and unsuitable for real-time applications. This paper addresses this limitation by leveraging a deep convolutional neural network (CNN) architecture, specifically YouLook4You, to generate radio coverage maps. This model learns to replicate the output of a complex, computationally intensive network (Y4Y) at nearly identical accuracy but at a fraction of the time cost. By using deep learning for radio coverage prediction, network operators can significantly accelerate key processes, including site selection, network optimization, and emergency response. The proposed model was trained on a substantial dataset of 1.5 million radio maps derived from Ansoft HFSS simulations. Extensive experiments demonstrate that the Y4Y-CNN model achieves a 100,000-fold speedup compared to HFSS simulations while maintaining high prediction accuracy. Furthermore, the model's efficacy in real-world scenarios was validated using actual measurement data collected from an indoor office environment. Additionally, the model exhibits strong generalization capabilities, performing effectively on buildings with structures and materials similar to those in the training data. To our knowledge, this represents the first successful application of deep learning to radio coverage map generation. The complete code and dataset are accessible at https://github.com/ashishgupta123/Y4Y-CNN. Our source code is also featured in the ACM Multimedia Systems Journal special issue on Deep Learning for Wireless Communications, available at https://dlmf.cs.ucdavis.edu/. We introduce a verified validation procedure for temporal planning, which examines whether provided plans are valid and executes them on a specified domain. The procedure's algorithm is proven correct through an interactive theorem prover, and this formally proven algorithm has been implemented using provably correct data structure algorithms also verified within the same environment. A key innovation is the application of a fully mechanized proof of Brafman and Shahaf (2006)'s theorem, which establishes that the validity of any plan can be confirmed in polynomial time relative to the plan's size. Furthermore, our implementation incorporates heuristics for verifying invariants and function preconditions, both supported by their own mechanized proofs. The approach was developed interactively, utilizing Coq for the proofs and OCaml for planning and data structures. We provide experimental data demonstrating the tool's applicability, including examples of plans validated in polynomial time. The implementation is available at https://github.com/brandonparker/verified-planner. The paper is accessible at https://arxiv.org/abs/2101.01308. This study examines the sensitivities of low-carbon energy system models, a critical yet often overlooked aspect when utilizing these models for policy support. We develop a large-scale, non-linear, mixed-integer linear optimization model designed to simulate the expansion of energy systems. Our sensitivity analysis explores parameter variations, functional forms, and optimization goals. The findings indicate that model results are highly sensitive to the specification of parameters, particularly within specific regions and sectors. Furthermore, the analysis underscores the necessity of conducting comprehensive sensitivity analyses to ensure a thorough evaluation of a model's performance. Finally, we provide a complete set of model parameters for Europe, which are available to facilitate future sensitivity analyses by other researchers. The model parameters, along with a sample result set, can be accessed here: https://doi.org/10.7910/DVN/222Q3A. Additionally, the source code is available at https://github.com/andreasfalkner/EnergySystemGrowthModel. Although this paper focuses on the GSGL model, the discussed principles are applicable to other energy system growth models. Given the significant impact of parameter choices on model outcomes, policymakers should be aware of this issue when interpreting results from energy system growth studies. We recommend that policymakers engage in an iterative process with modelers to refine parameters and their associated uncertainties. This approach ensures that the data informing decisions is as accurate as possible. Furthermore, policymakers should mandate that all relevant parameters be reported in model studies. This paper establishes the global-in-time well-posedness of the Vlasov-Poisson system within bounded containers featuring reflective boundaries, as well as the analogous confined Vlasov-Einstein-Maxwell system under specific conditions. The methodology is entirely based on energy estimates, incorporating novel techniques for handling boundary effects and relativistic field energies. These advancements facilitate new proofs and provide comprehensive demonstrations of existing results regarding the existence and uniqueness of solutions. Specifically, we demonstrate a global control of the $L^2$ norm of electric charge by the initial energy in non-relativistic settings, and similarly control relativistic energy by initial energy in both non-relativistic and confined relativistic contexts. Furthermore, we successfully manage boundary terms in confined relativistic scenarios through semi-classical analysis. These findings are complemented by local-in-time results derived from commutator methods and Sobolev estimates. Our findings align with and extend upon previous work. For non-relativistic systems in smooth domains, this extends the results of \cite{Balsara2018}. In contrast to the findings of \cite{Balsara2018}, our approach does not depend on the semiclassical approximation, thereby allowing for a rigorous derivation of well-posedness for the confined relativistic Einstein-Maxwell system. Additionally, our analysis avoids the need for artificial assumptions concerning the regularity of boundaries or the positivity of initial densities. Regarding the confined Einstein-Maxwell system, we introduce a novel method for the energy estimate of the wave equation that remains valid in confined regions, overcoming a significant obstacle that previously prevented such analyses. Finally, the current results are consistent with those of \cite{Balsara2018} when applied to star-shaped domains. We conclude this work with an extensive discussion of the employed techniques and their limitations. In this regard, we have adopted a conservative stance by restricting our scope to smooth domains, thereby ensuring a complete and rigorous proof. This choice leaves open the possibility of extending these results to rough domains, a task that would require substantially more intricate arguments. Such an extension would likely involve the semiclassical method used in \cite{Balsara2018}, a pseudo-differential calculus adapted for confined regions, and an in-depth analysis of the boundary layer. We intend to address these extensions in future research. Nevertheless, we are confident that the present results represent a substantial step toward achieving this objective. Over time, software systems accumulate a vast array of concepts, methods, and classes that developers must navigate. To mitigate the confusion this complexity induces, search phrases serve as a mechanism to assist users in locating specific software elements. However, crafting effective search phrases is difficult because developers often lack familiarity with the terminology used within a new codebase. Consequently, there is a need for tools that can generate and suggest appropriate search phrases to facilitate concept integration. This paper introduces STRICT, a technique that leverages data retrieval-based sentence mining to extract candidate search phrases from existing codebases. STRICT evaluates these candidates using a multi-criteria assessment approach grounded in software search principles, ultimately presenting a ranked list of options to developers aiming to identify concepts for placement. We validated STRICT across 14 diverse codebases, comprising both open-source and proprietary projects, and conducted a user study with 12 participants. The empirical results demonstrate that STRICT is both effective and efficient, successfully identifying concepts that are difficult to locate through simple queries. Furthermore, developers in our study reported that the proposed method assists them in understanding new codebases and integrating concepts more efficiently. Ultrasonic cavitation involves the creation, growth, and implosive collapse of microscopic gas bubbles within liquids. The rapid collapse of these bubbles generates shock waves and intense localized heating, driving powerful rheo-acoustic effects in soft materials. This study examines the mechanical and rheological properties of colloidal gels subjected to cavitation-induced ultrasonic oscillations. We demonstrate that ultrasonic oscillations can significantly alter the viscosity and storage modulus of various colloidal gels, including silica, polymer, and inorganic-organic hybrid gels. Our findings indicate a strong correlation between rheo-acoustic phenomena and the characteristics of the gel's equilibrium state prior to ultrasonic exposure. Specifically, we show that gels with smaller colloids and lower osmotic pressures exhibit more pronounced rheo-acoustic effects, whereas larger colloids and higher osmotic pressures diminish or eliminate these effects. These results offer critical insights into the complex interactions between cavitation and colloidal systems, advancing our understanding of ultrasonic cavitation rheology. Furthermore, this research paves the way for developing new materials with tailored mechanical and flow properties. By applying ultrasonic oscillations during gel formation, it is possible to achieve precise control over the gel's mechanical and flow characteristics. This capability holds significant potential for enhancing existing materials and creating innovative colloidal gel systems. Additionally, it may facilitate the growth of intricate 3D structures that are difficult to achieve through other manufacturing methods. These findings are particularly relevant to applications involving cavitation, including cavitation erosion, cavitation cleaning, cavitation welding, and cavitation-assisted 3D printing. Finally, this work addresses the growing need for advanced manufacturing techniques that are sustainable, precise, and capable of producing complex 3D structures. By utilizing ultrasonic cavitation and rheo-acoustic effects, this approach offers a viable solution for meeting these industry demands. This work is supported by the EPSRC grant EP/P020194/1. The objective of this note is to prove that for any positive integer $x$, the process $T(x)$—where $T(x) = x/2$ if $x$ is even and $T(x) = 3x+1$ if $x$ is odd—eventually yields a value of 1. In other words, every trajectory initiated at a positive integer ultimately reaches 1. Although this result is straightforward, the lack of an effective method to determine whether the trajectory of a specific $x$ (other than 1) always descends below its starting value has led many to consider the conjecture trivial. However, this perception is misleading; despite numerous attempts, no one has successfully proven that the initial hypothesis is correct, nor have they disproven it.

The primary challenge lies in the fact that the trajectory of certain starting values does not consistently decrease below their origin. For instance, the first 19 terms of the trajectory for $x=27$ are:
$$27, 82, 41, 124, 62, 31, 94, 47, 140, 70, 35, 106, 53, 158, 79, 238, 119, 356, 178, 89, \dots$$
This sequence initially rises before eventually falling below the initial 27.

To address this, we must analyze the growth of these rising trajectories. The key insight is that if the trajectory of $x$ exceeds the value of $x$, it must subsequently decrease below $x$ within a finite number of steps. This is because every even number is divided by 2, whereas odd numbers are transformed via $3x+1$. Consequently, any odd number that causes the trajectory to rise will be followed by an even number that reduces the trajectory's value. Therefore, if the trajectory of $x$ increases, it will inevitably decrease below $x$ within a finite interval.

Classifying scientific documents is essential for enabling intelligent document management and facilitating scientific research. However, the diverse nature of documents within scientific domains often renders categorization difficult. Specifically, automatically categorizing STEM documents faces significant hurdles due to variations in content, language, and notations. To address these issues, we introduce a novel method that leverages mathematical entities to enhance STEM document categorization. This approach capitalizes on the fact that mathematical entities serve as fundamental units for conveying concepts and concepts that recurring entities enable. By extracting mathematical entities using MathBERT and identifying semantic links between documents, we can effectively identify key concepts and detect semantic similarities. Experimental results demonstrate that our proposed method outperforms several baselines, including those relying on reprocessing content or utilizing pre-trained BERT models, and also surpassifies the performance of human annotators. Furthermore, we validate the efficacy of this approach across three distinct domains: mathematics, computer science, and physics. Matching markets are ubiquitous, ranging from school admissions and residency allocations to organ transplant systems and freelance platforms. A defining feature of these markets is the presence of strategic agents who possess knowledge of others' preferences. While existing research on strategic formative markets has explored the trade-off between efficiency and stability, this paper investigates a different critical question: a strategic agent may prefer to forgo matching rather than engage in a less preferable one. Specifically, we examine a platform like Upwork where agents receive job offers and must decide which to pursue. To address this, we introduce a novel metric called the "selective ratio," which quantifies an agent's selectivity. Our analysis demonstrates that higher selective ratios lead to more favorable outcomes for agents. Furthermore, we propose a new metric named "selective envy-freeness up to one good" (EF-1G) to evaluate how selective agents can be. We also assess various matching mechanisms based on their sensitive thresholds for this selective ratio. Finally, our empirical study, which analyzes data from a popular freelance website, reveals that agents with a higher selective ratio tend to achieve greater success. These findings offer new insights for forming markets, suggesting that restricting participation to agents with high selectivity can result in improved outcomes. Additionally, we explore alternative market design approaches aimed at attracting such selective agents. Empirical results indicate that implementing a simple selective ratio can significantly boost the average success rate of agents with high selectivity. We conclude by discussing potential directions for future research. Our work aims to inspire market designers to consider the impact of agent selectivity when designing mechanisms. We believe this perspective is essential for achieving high success rates and constructing effective formation markets. To our knowledge, this paper presents the first analysis of selectivity in matching markets. We hope these insights will inspire further research into the role of selectivity in these markets. Finally, we believe that understanding the influence of agent selectivity is crucial for market designers seeking to formulate mechanisms that maximize outcomes. We hope this paper will contribute to advancing the field of matching market design. Recent evaluations of summary quality metrics reveal that current automatic scoring methods fail to match the accuracy of human reviewers. This discrepancy stems from the fact that existing metrics rely on concise sentences to represent documents, which often overlooks critical content. Furthermore, many approaches depend on document similarity, a factor that does not always correlate with human judgments. To address these limitations, we introduce SummScore, an efficient and effective excellence-based scoring mechanism grounded in the cross-encoder architecture. This method computes scores by directly comparing pairs of human evaluations with machine-generated summaries. Extensive experiments demonstrate that SummScore surpasses current state-of-the-art excellence metrics across multiple dimensions. Additionally, assessments on summarization datasets show that SummScore effectively identifies model failures, offering valuable insights for improving summary quality. Signal restoration from noisy quadratic measurements is a fundamental challenge across numerous scientific and engineering fields. This work introduces a new approach that is provably rapid and provably convergent. The core concept involves developing a model where an initial guess, derived from a single measurement, serves as the starting point for a standard denoising model. We rigorously establish that this proposed model is equivalent to a two-step procedure: a model reduction step followed by a classical denoising step. By leveraging the efficiency of model reduction alongside the proven stability of classical denoising methods, we guarantee that our approach is both computationally fast and guaranteed to converge. Furthermore, extensive numerical experiments on real-world data confirm that the method outperforms state-of-the-art techniques. Finally, we apply this method to denoise and compress real-world images, demonstrating superior results compared to existing solutions. Fusing data from cameras and LiDARs is crucial for the development of the intelligent transportation system (ITS). However, current methods often depend on the precise alignment of camera-LiDAR perception results, which is difficult to achieve and maintain due to the distinct characteristics of each sensor. Additionally, most existing approaches lack robustness against the inevitable noise and environmental interference that ITS systems face during deployment. To address these challenges, we introduce BEVFusion, a straightforward integration technique that combines LiDAR and camera data within the bird's-eye view (BEV) plane. By projecting camera images into the BEV using the 4D convolution method, our approach directly fuses the two data sources, thereby eliminating the need for the precise camera-LiDAR alignment typically required. Furthermore, we implement a fusion strategy that enables the model to adaptively weigh the two sensors, enhancing resilience against sensor noise and interference. Extensive experiments across various benchmarks demonstrate that BEVFusion effectively improves the performance of the fusion framework. For instance, in the Waymo Open Dataset, it boosts the performance of the Camera3D model by 1.8% mAP, while in the nuScenes dataset, it achieves an average improvement of 2.1% mAP over Camera3D. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/MEGVision/BEVFusion. The project website is https://meggm.github.io/BEVFusion. The paper is available at https://arxiv.org/abs/2111.07061. Keywords: BEVFusion, LiDAR-Camera Fusion, 4D Convolution, Deep Learning, Intelligent Transportation System. In this study, we investigate the dissipation region of near-liquid turbulence and its interaction with thermal fluctuations. We demonstrate that near-liquid turbulence exhibits distinct characteristics compared to gas-range turbulence, featuring a thermal disturbance with a temperature difference of $\Delta T \sim 10^3$ K and a specific heat capacity of $C_p \sim 10^{-3}$ J/K. Furthermore, the Reynolds number in near-liquid turbulence is approximately $10^6$ times greater than that of gas-range turbulence. These findings indicate the existence of a novel dissipation-range liquid turbulence, which holds potential for applications involving intense mixing and mass transfer. Additionally, we outline the necessary conditions for generating this new type of turbulence. Finally, our results offer a quantitative explanation for the mechanism behind bubble formation during boiling. To validate the feasibility of our hypothesis, we have designed an experimental setup to measure thermal fluctuations in near-liquid turbulence. The paper includes the design specifications for this apparatus. Our ultimate goal is to measure the power spectral density of thermal fluctuations in near-liquid turbulence, thereby providing direct evidence for dissipation-range liquid turbulence and determining the value of $\Delta T$. This measurement will also help clarify the connection between near-liquid turbulence and boiling phenomena. Furthermore, we aim to explore the possibility of creating a new state of matter, termed "thermal glass," by utilizing intense mixing from dissipation-range liquid turbulence. This could potentially advance research into room-temperature superconductivity. To support these objectives, we have developed a theoretical model to describe dissipation-range liquid turbulence. The paper concludes with a summary of our proposed research directions. Ultimately, this work seeks to expand our understanding of near-liquid turbulence and its relationship with boiling, while also opening up new avenues for research into intense mixing and intense mass transfer. The proposed theoretical model serves as a foundation for future studies on dissipation-range liquid turbulence. This study presents a numerical analysis of the thermal profile generated within a liquid by a laser beam, designed to assist in interpreting complex diffraction patterns. The resulting numerical results are compared against analytical solutions and *in situ* experimental data to validate their accuracy. This methodology is applicable for thermal imaging of liquids illuminated by laser beams of arbitrary shape and power. The investigation reveals that heat conduction significantly influences the thermal profile at large radial distances from the beam center, even when convection is negligible at shorter distances. Furthermore, the liquid's thermal profile is demonstrated to be highly sensitive to the length of the illuminated zone. Finally, the thermal profile's dependence on the laser beam's power distribution is examined. These findings are broadly applicable for visualizing liquids using laser heating. The design phase of large engineering projects, particularly in software and systems engineering, often involves extensive discussions between domain experts and engineers. These discussions are frequently documented in design conversations, which can be analyzed to extract project insights. However, the conclusion stability problem hinders this analysis, as the high cost of revision forces engineers to complete design decisions in a single pass. To address this, we introduce the conclusion stability model, an abstract framework for evaluating such problems, which is applicable beyond software contexts. We demonstrate the model using design conversations from two software projects and propose an algorithm based on fixed-point theory to calculate conclusion stability. This model offers a pathway for automatically identifying and extracting key information from natural language within design conversations. Furthermore, we present an ANTLR-based tool for computing conclusion stability in design conversations. We outline initial applications of this tool in software engineering and discuss its potential for other domains. Finally, we identify open research questions and outline directions for future work. Recent advancements in data processing architectures have introduced new computing paradigms capable of handling vast volumes of data streams and semi-structured documents at massive scales. However, current processing models often lack the necessary flexibility to accommodate diverse data access and processing requirements. This paper presents H-STREAM, a novel programming model designed to process data streams in the Apache Hadoop ecosystem. Furthermore, it supports multiple output schemes, including sequential and parallel processing, as well as two-level data access mechanisms for both data streams and structured storage. The model is implemented as a Map-Reduce job within the Hadoop ecosystem. To validate the model, three use cases were developed: a data stream processing task involving data stream and record joins, a time-series data access task, and a time-series data processing task. The proposed model and its H-STREAM mapping to Map-Reduce are detailed in our recent publication, which also includes a comprehensive experimental evaluation. This evaluation demonstrates that H-STREAM is competitive with other models for specific operations, such as stream-key joins, while offering superior performance for others, including stream-time window joins. Additionally, H-STREAM enables the development of high-level data pipelines, which are also described in this paper. The H-STREAM model is available on GitHub. This paper addresses the ongoing debate regarding the reliance on various citation-dependent metrics for assessing research contributions, particularly in computer science. The discussion is often sparked by perceived inconsistencies between these metrics and subjective evaluations, alongside concerns about the gamification of citation practices. We contend that the true solution to this issue extends beyond the current "more or less" of citing citation metrics, but rather lies in substituting them with more fundamental and potentially "fairer" alternatives. By shifting the focus from quantifying individual researchers to analyzing research venues, we propose that these venues serve as superior proxies for evaluating and comparing research outputs. Our study demonstrates the viability of this approach by developing a suite of venue-level metrics that effectively correlate with author-level contributions. Furthermore, we show that these venue metrics remain stable across multiple time periods, offering a more consistent framework for assessment. Finally, we explore the broader implications of this proposed shift. The code is accessible at https://github.com/veneinsight. The data utilized in this research is sourced from Microsoft Research's Data for Good initiative, which provides open access to valuable materials to foster new discoveries and innovations. Specifically, we employed versions 4.1 and 5.0 of the DBLP Raw Data, available at https://github.com/MsrgPublic/Data-for-Good. While version 4.1 lacks abstracts, version 5.0 includes them; however, our methodology does not rely on abstracts. Version 5.0 also includes Google Scholar IDs for publications, though these were not utilized in this study. Although Google Scholar IDs are not always accurate, they can be valuable for future research. Given that venue insights are not dependent on specific citation counts, Version 4.1 is sufficient for replicating the findings. Nevertheless, to ensure the most comprehensive replication, Version 5.0 is recommended. This paper examines neural network validation techniques for regulatory purposes. Although neural networks are highly effective at solving complex problems, their "black box" nature often hinders their use in contexts requiring rigorous justification. Consequently, significant effort has been invested in developing validation methods to make these models more interpretable and trustworthy. We focus on networks employed in decision-making and risk assessment, utilizing them as a case study to demonstrate general techniques applicable to various neural network architectures. The discussion covers existing literature on neural network validation, drawing parallels to the broader field of neural network explainability, and highlights comparable trends and challenges. Furthermore, we outline directions for future research in neural network validation, emphasizing the need to establish standardized and comparable methods. Finally, we reflect on the ethical and societal implications of using neural networks and propose potential solutions. The paper concludes by summarizing the discussed topics and offering insights for future research. Overall, this work aims to serve as a comprehensive reference on neural network validation within a regulatory framework. Additionally, it provides an ethical and societal perspective, considering the consequences of validation methods and the challenges faced by practitioners. The conclusions presented are the result of a brainstorming session involving researchers from diverse backgrounds, including computer science, mathematics, and law. By integrating perspectives from these different fields, the paper seeks to foster interdisciplinary dialogue on neural network validation. We believe this collaborative approach will help shape the future of the field and promote a more holistic understanding of the challenges involved in validating neural networks for regulatory use. Furthermore, the paper encourages interdisciplinary research to ensure that neural network validation is developed in a manner that considers its broader implications for society. This work was conducted as part of the "Society and Ethics" track at the Mathematics for Policy Science 2023 conference. The track aims to explore the intersection of mathematics, policy, and ethics, with a specific focus on neural network validation in decision-making and risk assessment. By bringing together researchers from diverse backgrounds, the track seeks to foster a more comprehensive understanding of the challenges and opportunities associated with validating neural networks in society. The outcomes of this track will inform future research in neural network validation and promote a more interdisciplinary approach to ensuring the ethical and responsible use of these technologies. Streaming retrieval for large-scale images and videos is a demanding application that necessitates efficient processing of incoming data. While tensor recovery techniques have shown promise, they often suffer from excessive computational costs and memory requirements. This paper introduces a novel approach called Patch Monitoring-based Streaming Tensor Ring Restoration (PMSTR). The method initially assesses each incoming image or video using image patch similarity analysis to identify redundant data. Subsequently, a low-rank tensor ring model is applied to restore these redundant items. Experimental results demonstrate that PMSTR significantly reduces both computational and memory overheads compared to state-of-the-art tensor recovery methods, while delivering comparable or superior image quality. Furthermore, applied to streaming retrieval, PMSTR achieves high accuracy with markedly lower resource consumption. The code is accessible at https://github.com/ChenchenLi/PMSTR. Additionally, the authors' website, https://chenchenli.github.io/, showcases application demos for PMSTR. This paper presents the second installment of a series dedicated to the Nichols algebras $\mathcal{B}(V_{\alpha, \beta})$ linked to traditional Euclidean groups. We demonstrate that, with the sole exception of the previously examined type $\widetilde{C}_2$, the Nichols algebras associated with traditional Euclidean groups of rank greater than 2 possess infinite dimension. Furthermore, we provide an explicit classification for all rank 2 traditional Euro Nichols algebras. For those yielding infinite-dimensional results, we derive a structural description of the algebra $\mathcal{B}(V_{\alpha, \beta})$ by identifying its primitive elements. Additionally, we examine the case where the rank exceeds 2, revealing that the dimension of $\mathcal{B}(V_{\alpha, \beta})$ is infinite under these conditions. Finally, we analyze the structure of $\mathcal{B}(V_{\alpha, \beta})$ in the context of rank 2 to establish a comprehensive classification for this class of Euro Nichols algebras. Specifically, we characterize all $1$-parameter and $2$-parameter traditional Euclidean Nichols algebras, thereby resolving all previously open cases. Notably, this represents the first instance of a complete classification for any EO Nichols algebra. Leveraging the extensive literature on classical Nichols algebras, we are able to present a unified description encompassing all $1$-parameter traditional Euclidean Nichols algebras. This achievement marks the inaugural instance of a full classification of any EO Nichols algebra and the only $100\%$ classification of an EO Nichols algebra to date. Additionally, we explore the finite-dimensional $1$-parameter traditional Euclidean Nichols algebras, which had previously been unclassified. Our methodology relies on the identification of the simple roots of $\mathcal{B}(V_{\alpha, \beta})$. By utilizing these simple roots, we derive an explicit description of $\mathcal{B}(V_{\alpha, \beta})$ and its simple roots, thereby providing a complete classification for all $1$-parameter traditional Euclidean Nichols algebras. This work extends the findings of [10], where the classical Euclidean Nichols algebra $\mathcal{B}(V_{\alpha, \beta})$ was characterized. The techniques employed here are also applicable to the finite-dimensional $1$-parameter traditional Euclidean Nichols algebras, offering a unified approach to their analysis.

The discovery of the inverse energy cascade in three-dimensional turbulent inertial waves prompted a significant surge of interest into the Zakharov-Kolmogorov (ZK) theory, which posits that the inverse energy cascade spectrum follows an $E(k) \propto \epsilon^{-2/3}$ power law, analogous to Kolmogorov's $-5/3$ law for forward energy cascade. While numerical simulations have confirmed the validity of the ZK spectrum in both isotropic and anisotropic turbulent inertial waves, the latter often exhibits a steeper slope of $-5/4$ instead of $-5/3$. This study demonstrates the presence of the Zakharov-Kolmogorov spectrum across a broad wavenumber range in simulations of strongly anisotropic turbulence, characterized by a Rossby number $Ro \approx 0.1$ and an anisotropy ratio $r=k_2/k_1 \approx 100$. Furthermore, the turbulence's evolution is analyzed using the coarse-grained action, revealing the fundamental components of the weak turbulence theory, including the kinetic equation, the inverse energy cascade, and the inverse enstrophy cascade. These findings provide a comprehensive understanding of the Zakharov-Kolmogorov spectrum, offering a robust foundation for interpreting the energy spectra of inertial wave turbulence. Additionally, the results suggest that the $-5/4$ slope observed in simulations with lower Rossby numbers ($0.01 \leq Ro \leq 0.1$) arises from a combination of the $-5/3$ and $-3/2$ spectra. Finally, the study explores the potential for extending the ZK theory to higher-wavenumber ranges. These insights are crucial for interpreting the energy spectra of inertial wave turbulence in both laboratory and geophysical contexts. Specifically, the $-5/4$ slope is expected in simulations where the Rossby number is small, such as in Taylor-Green turbulence, while the $-5/3$ spectrum is anticipated in simulations with larger Rossby numbers, such as in geophysical stratospheric turbulence. The concept of the graph standardization problem was introduced by R. B. Leherer in 1998. Since that time, numerous studies have explored algorithmic solutions for determining standard isomorphisms, often comparing their efficiency. However, Leherer originally proposed this as a game played between a standardizer and a graph. To address this, D. A. Krotov and A. B. Leherer developed a game featuring two players: a standardizer and an automator. In this framework, the goal is to prove the existence of a winning strategy for the standardizer, alongside a corresponding strategy for the automator. Krotov and Leherer demonstrated that such winning strategies exist for any pair of graphs, with the proof relying on the concept of a maximum weight autonomous set. This paper examines graph standardization within the context of this two-player game and establishes the existence of a winning strategy for the standardizer. Furthermore, we introduce a new algorithm for constructing standard isomorphisms and apply it to prove the existence of the winning strategy. Additionally, we establish the existence of maximum weight autonomous sets, which serve as a fundamental component of these proven strategies. Finally, we outline the parameters of a modified game that includes a third player, the spoiler, and demonstrate that this spoiler can also secure a win. This proof utilizes the previously demonstrated existence of maximum weight autonomous sets as a key step. Overall, this work provides an alternative approach to resolving the graph standardization problem. Specifically, it offers an algorithm for finding standard isomorphisms that relies on constructive methods rather than non-constructive ones. This advancement enables the proof of the existence of graph standardization and the explicit determination of the required isomorphisms. In this process, maximum weight autonomous sets play a pivotal role. We anticipate that these sets will be valuable for advancing research into graph standardization. The paper is structured as follows: Section 2 reviews the definition of the standardization game and the concept of maximum weight autonomous sets; Section 3 presents the new approach to the standardization game; and Section 4 outlines the authors' future research directions regarding graph standardization.

This study reports the first low-frequency radio observations of the binary system CR Draconis, a young stellar object exhibiting numerous radio bursts. Located at a distance of approximately 140 pc, CR Draconis consists of two T Tauri stars in a 1.7-day orbit. The system is notable for its high magnetic field strength, with both stars possessing fields exceeding 1 kG. We observed 12 bursts across 10 nights over a 100-day period, utilizing the LOFAR Low-Band (LB) and Low-Low (LL) receivers. These observations identified a unique burst type characterized by extended durations of several hours, a feature never previously detected in young stellar objects. This distinct emission is attributed to electron cyclotron maser (ECM) radiation driven by the magnetic reconnection ejection from the companion star. The event is modeled as a prolonged burst, with a peak flux density of 1.5 Jy lasting roughly 4.5 hours, and is interpreted as a single reconnection episode releasing approximately $10^{24}$ J of energy. The study further examines the implications of this prolonged ECM radiation for current flare star models, specifically the magnetic breaking model. Additionally, we report a persistent radio source at 1.42 GHz with a flux density of 1.1 Jy, which may represent a new radio-emitting source in this young stellar object. Finally, we compare our findings with archival data from the Murchison Widefield Array (MWA) and the Low-Frequency Array (LOFAR) High-Band (HB) receiver. Our results align with HB observations but contradict L-band (LB) data, suggesting that LB emissions are not ECM in origin. Furthermore, the analysis indicates that the MWA detected a similar prolonged ECM burst during the same event. These observations provide critical insights into the nature of ECM radiation from young stellar objects and their associated magnetic configurations. The detection of prolonged ECM bursts in CR Draconis underscores the necessity of conducting extended observations of young stellar objects to better understand the dynamics of magnetic reconnection. Ultimately, this research advances our understanding of magnetic reconnection dynamics and the generation mechanisms of ECM radiation. The identification of a new radio-emitting source in CR Draconis may offer new clues regarding the origins of radio emissions from young stellar objects. This paper presents a method for creating virtual avatar models that are both geometrically accurate and capable of animation. Our approach begins with a 3D template featuring articulated joints, which is then refined to match a specific subject. We execute this refinement in two stages: first, we perform a coarse fit by adjusting the subject's motion capture data to align with the template, followed by fitting the captured motion to the 3D model. Second, the system is fine-tuned using 2D images of the subject. The resulting avatar can be animated using motion capture datasets from other individuals, producing geometrically accurate results that outperform state-of-the-art methods by up to 1000%. To address this, we conducted a study on the effects of various intensities of eight image modifications (contrast, brightness, blur, and colorization) across four categories: animals, faces, objects, and scenes. Finally, we observed that machines generally perform well in enhancing images for classification tasks, though they are more susceptible to the negative impacts of intensify operations compared to humans. These results offer valuable insights for both the practical application and the research and development of image improvement techniques. Our study focuses on models featuring both triangular intra-cell and square inter-cell antiferromagnetic exchanges. Our findings indicate that the coupling between cellular states is primarily mediated by a significant entropic interaction, which grows exponentially with the strength of the magnetic exchange. The advent of large language models (LLMs) has made zero-shot tasks, including education, highly popular. However, their performance in these domains remains inconsistent, and practical application requires careful consideration of prompt engineering, input design, and model selection. This study addresses the specific challenge of zero-shot education by introducing a meta-learning approach that evaluates LLM performance across two education datasets and four model architectures. To optimize assemblages of pretrained LLMs, we employ meta-training on the selected datasets. Furthermore, we mitigate overfitting by generating prompt assemblages through self-consistency and input augmentation, thereby improving generalization to unseen data. Our results demonstrate that zero-shot education is best served by an LLM assemblage, with fine-tuning on the input space proving more effective than prompt engineering. Additionally, we present a novel method for identifying the most suitable LLM assemblage for zero-shot tasks by analyzing the performance distributions of individual models. Finally, we offer a user-friendly guide to assist practitioners in implementing zero-shot tasks within the field of education. Code and examples are available at https://github.com/edunlp/LLM-Zero-shot-Education. Keywords: Large Language Models, Prompt Engineering, Input Design, Education, Meta-learning.

Our results indicate that the Sudoku sample contains 17 spurious redshifts, a figure consistent with predictions from the "noise crossing" model. This study investigates the topological and dynamical properties of spin excitations in $S=1/2$ Heisenberg antiferromagnets on a triangular lattice, specifically under conditions where 120$^\circ$ long-range order is disrupted by quantum fluctuations leading to a spin liquid state. This study examines how the intermolecular potential influences rarefied gas flows by integrating its effects into the collision frequency within the Kramers potential model. Utilizing this adjusted collision frequency, we formulate the collision operator for the linearized kinetic equation. The resulting system is then solved via the weighted residual method to derive an optimized Navier-Stokes-Fourier system. Our analysis demonstrates that accounting for the impact of the intermolecular potential allows the weighted residual system to maintain high accuracy across all rarefaction regimes, including those where the standard Navier-Stokes-Fourier equations fail. Furthermore, we show that the effects of the intermolecular potential are more pronounced in regions characterized by higher non-equilibrium. Finally, the optimized Navier-Stokes-Fourier system based on the model with the collision frequency from this work is applied to simulate gas flows around rotating spheres. The findings indicate that the effects of the intermolecular potential on such flows are more significant when non-equilibrium is elevated. Additionally, we observe that the angular velocity of the sphere exerts a greater influence than that of a translating sphere. These results are corroborated by existing experimental and numerical data. Overall, this research establishes a foundation for further exploring the effects of intermolecular potential in various rarefied gas flow scenarios. Notably, the proposed model is applicable to both polar and apolar molecules. However, it is important to recognize that while the collision frequency in the Kramers potential model can be extended to handle non-zero external forces, it remains limited to scenarios involving only weak non-equilibrium. To address stronger non-equilibrium, future work will employ the collision frequency model proposed by Liang et al. [1]. Consequently, the values of the Knudsen number reported in this paper may differ from those found in other studies. Finally, the effects of the intermolecular potential on the flow around a translating sphere have been investigated by several researchers [2-4]. Semantic grounding involves determining the mapping between natural language and symbolic representations. Recent advancements have introduced neural semantic grounding, which learns this mapping by leveraging the shared distributional properties of words within both domains. However, existing models are frequently criticized for lacking explainability, as they function essentially as opaque end-to-end predictors. To resolve this, the AmI semantic grounding benchmark was created to evaluate methods capable of learning an explicit semantic interpretation function alongside the prediction task. While current approaches to training this interpreter rely on weakly supervised techniques—such as attention mechanisms or pre-trained semantic models—these often yield sub-optimal interpreter functions. This paper presents a novel method for training semantic interpreters under minimal supervision, specifically using only a single example per concept. Our approach trains a generative text model using the few-shot interpreter as an auxiliary component. We demonstrate that this method effectively recovers the interpreter's semantic mappings even when the data distribution is misaligned, resulting in predictability that surpasses other weakly supervised strategies and remains consistent despite significant reductions in the training data volume. Additionally, we show that a small amount of additional data can be utilized to train a forward-mapping function, enabling unsupervised prediction without an explicit generative model. Finally, we provide an analysis of the discovered semantic mappings, revealing interesting insights about the learned semantic structure. Experimental results on the AmI semantic grounding benchmark confirm the efficacy of our proposed learning method. This study presents spectropolarimetric observations of HD 58260, a rapidly rotating, metal-poor star exhibiting strong magnetic fields. Utilizing the spectropolarimeter SOPHIE, we analyzed high-resolution spectra of the neutral magnesium line Mg I 5172.7 Å and the neutral iron line Fe I 5233.7 Å, which are sensitive to the radial magnetic field component. These stellar spectra were compared against laboratory spectra of HD 58260 recorded under conditions simulating the star's effective temperature and microturbulent velocity. The observed line profiles revealed a discrepancy between the two lines, indicating a variation in the radial magnetic field between the formation regions of the two lines within the stellar atmosphere. This finding supports the presence of magnetic field variations linked to the magnetic activity cycle of HD 58260. Furthermore, the paper discusses the implications of these results for future modeling of magnetized stars. Finally, we outline future observational programs aimed at characterizing the magnetic field of HD 58260. To facilitate this, we provide a complete list of the Fe I lines employed in our analysis. We create a free boson representation for the Dunkl intertwining operator within one dimension. Utilizing this representation, we derive several identities, such as the expansion of Schur polynomials in one dimension using Hermite polynomials. Additionally, we extend certain results from the standard Schur polynomial depiction to the Dunkl setting. Specifically, we establish Heisenberg relations for the Dunkl interlacing operators, which facilitate the construction of Heisenberg double representations for the affine group in one dimension. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the Heisenberg group's commutativity is equivalent to the commutativity of the corresponding self-adjoint representation of the affine symbol algebra. Our findings also encompass the case where the order of the Heisenberg group is prime. In this scenario, we prove that any irreducible representation is equivalent to either the Schur or the Dunkl representation. Finally, we examine the corresponding picture decomposition for the free boson representation of the Dunkl intertwiner. We show that the multiplicity of each Schur polynomial in this decomposition corresponds to the number of partitions of $k$ formed using powers of 2, where $k$ is an arbitrary positive integer. The case for $k=1$ is particularly significant, as it reveals that the multiplicity of the Schur polynomial associated with $k$ in the decomposition is 1. This result implies that the set of all monomials constitutes an orthogonal basis for $L^2(\mathbb{R},dx)$, a conclusion that contrasts with the situation when $k \geq 2$. The spectrum of the Schrödinger operator $-\frac{d^2}{dx^2} + \omega^2 x^2$ under the condition $k=1$ is investigated in a separate paper. In that work, we demonstrate that the spectrum consists of two parts: an embedded discrete spectrum and a continuous spectrum. The discrete spectrum is generated by the spectrum of the operator $\frac{d^2}{dp_1^2}$, while the continuous spectrum arises from the spectrum of $\frac{d^2}{dx_2^2}$. The construction of the boson representation for the Dunkl intertwiner is achieved through the introduction of a measure on Fock space. This approach relies on the commutativity of the Heisenberg group, a property that does not hold for $k \geq 2$. Consequently, an alternative method for building the boson representation is required in these cases.

We conducted ALMA observations of the H30$\alpha$ line in NGC 5253, a galaxy characterized by a metallicity of approximately 0.2 Z$_{\odot}$, to investigate the relationship between this line radiation and the star formation rate (SFR). The data reveal that the H30$\alpha$ line exhibits a spatial distribution similar to the CO(3-2) line and displays a redshifted velocity structure. By utilizing the CO(3-2) emission, we derived an SFR of 0.04 M$_{\odot}$/yr for NGC 5253. Analysis of the H30$\alpha$ emission profiles indicates that the line radiation originates from a compact region roughly 100 pc in size, which coincides with the core of the CO emission. This area is identified as a star-forming region (SFR) with an age of approximately 10 Myr. Our findings suggest that the H30$\alpha$ line is radiated by HII regions within the SFR core, driven by the photoionization of massive stars. These results demonstrate that the H30$\alpha$ line serves as a reliable tracer for studying star formation in low-metallicity galaxies. Furthermore, the H30$\alpha$ line offers a distinct advantage over other HII region line tracers by being excited by massive stars with masses between 10 and 20 M$_{\odot}$, thereby enabling the investigation of SFRs with ages ranging from 10 to 100 Myr. These conclusions are supported by a model that simulates the H30$\alpha$ line spectrum and luminosity based on the observed line properties. Finally, we conclude that the H30$\alpha$ line is highly effective for analyzing the star formation history of galaxies. This paper is the first of two companion studies; the second will explore the H30$\alpha$ line as a tool for investigating the star formation history of galaxies. This paper introduces a new class of estimators for conditional expectation functions within nonparametric regression settings. For data conforming to standard regularity conditions, estimators in this class achieve optimal minimax rates under both $L_1$ and $L_2$ norms. The approach is flexible, allowing for non-negative, kernel-based, or bandwidth-matrix weighting schemes. Notably, when applied to kernel-based methods, the proposed class encompasses most existing estimators while extending their capabilities. A primary advantage is that certain variants can eliminate the logarithmic factors typically required in the optimal $L_1$ rate. Simulations indicate that these new estimators perform competitively compared to current methods. The flexibility of this approach also facilitates the development of min-max procedures for inference. This study investigates the potential of high-peak-power Kerr-lens mode-locking (KLML) by analytically examining the stability and resonator geometry of high-power ultrafast laser systems. The analysis demonstrates that ultrafast KLML systems operating at high peak power require fundamental transverse modes with large diffraction radii. However, the stability analysis reveals a critical conflict: while high-peak-power operation demands large diffraction radii, it simultaneously necessitates low Kerr nonlinearity shifts. This contradiction represents the primary obstacle to developing ultrafast KLML lasers capable of sustaining high peak power. To address this, we propose a resonator configuration featuring an open fundamental fundamental diffraction path, which allows the fundamental mode to expand beyond the gain medium. This design effectively mitigates Kerr nonlinearity shifts even when the gain medium is small. Furthermore, the study examines the impact of gain-clipping apertures on resonator stability and the fundamental diffraction path. The proposed approach is demonstrated using a theoretical model of a ultrafast KLML system equipped with a gain-clipping aperture. Numerical simulations indicate that ultrafast KLML lasers with high peak power are feasible; however, they necessitate gain media with large cross-sections and the implementation of gain-clipping apertures. These findings are supported by peak power data from existing literature. Ultimately, this work establishes a foundation for the rational design of ultrafast KLML systems aimed at achieving high peak power. Additionally, the study explores the possibility of utilizing small inner higher-order transverse modes to further increase peak power. Numerical simulations confirm that ultrafast higher-order transverse mode (HOM) lasers can achieve even higher peak power levels. This paper introduces a new asynchronous online federated learning (AOFL) method designed to address nonlinear regression problems involving time-varying nonlinear functions. The system comprises a central server and multiple time-varying local agents, where the central server periodically broadcasts the global state and acquires updates from the agents. To enhance computational efficiency, agents optimize a local loss function constrained by time- and energy-resources. Specifically, agents leverage temporal correlations to reduce energy usage and enforce strict time limits by ensuring completion within a designated number of iterations. Numerical simulations demonstrate that the proposed AOFL approach yields superior results compared to baseline methods. Notably, the method achieves a 20% reduction in computational complexity relative to synchronous online AOFL, while maintaining comparable or better performance. Furthermore, simulations indicate that the proposed AOFL reduces the time required to reach the optimal loss value by 20% when compared to batch AOFL. Additionally, the results highlight the benefits of incorporating a bias correction term in the global loss function. Finally, an application to traffic flow prediction is presented. The authors intend this formula to offer a more accessible approach to handling complex functions than power tower series. Additionally, it serves as a valuable resource for comprehending the formation of asymptotic solutions to functional equations. The study focuses specifically on the natural numbers, though the authors believe the formula can be adapted for other sets based on the base function.

To derive the asymptotic solution, the study employs the asymptotic inversion of power series. In the conclusion, Problem 1 proposes an extension of this formula to handle multivalued functions that possess asymptotic expansions.

The term "tetration" refers to hyperoperation of degree four. This formula was formulated to address not only the asymptotic behavior of the iterated exponential function but also its inverse, the logarithm tower.

Classical expansions like the Fourier, Haar, and Zolotarev expansions originate from the concept of covering a space with a sequence of sets. This paper introduces a new class of high-dimensional expansions rooted in the idea of covering a domain with a sequence of partitions. Specifically, we develop expansions based on set partitions, where each element in the expansion corresponds to a subset of the underlying partition sequence. This approach extends the classical multilevel Hartley expansion, which is derived from the dyadic partition of the interval [0,1]. The proposed method is demonstrated through two instances: the Multilevel Hartley-Z transform and the Multilevel Walsh transform, both featuring frequency-domain representations that enable the analysis of non-stationary signals. The construction of these transforms addresses challenges posed by the non-stationary nature of the signals under consideration. Additionally, signal localization is achieved through the set partitions, mirroring the mechanism found in multilevel Hartley transforms. Signal analysis is conducted via the set-based inclusion-exclusion principle, which facilitates computation through bit-level operations. Furthermore, the inclusion-exclusion principle enables the straightforward construction of the corresponding set-based random variables. Finally, the paper establishes a link to Boolean functions, connecting the set-based random variables to specific classes of Boolean functions. The application of this novel framework to generate new transforms is also explored. The code implementing the Multilevel Walsh transform is available at: https://github.com/alexei-trofimov/Multilevel- Walsh-transform. Link prediction in dynamic networks is a critical task across numerous domains, including epidemiology, social influence, and traffic forecasting. While most current methods rely on embedding nodes into low-dimensional spaces to generate predictive features, the resulting optimization often fails to generalize well to real-world scenarios. This study introduces Sparse Sparse Node Embedding (SSNE), an efficient and general framework designed specifically for link prediction in sparse networks. By integrating temporal dynamics directly into the optimization process, SSNE produces node embeddings that enhance classification performance. Furthermore, we develop a novel deep learning model for link prediction, termed SSNE-LP, which utilizes these embeddings to improve accuracy. Empirical results demonstrate that SSNE outperforms state-of-the-art embedding techniques, and the subsequent SSNE-LPLink prediction model surpasses leading edge approaches. Additionally, we apply SSNE-LP to the link prediction challenge at the Data Mining Cup 2020, securing a top-3 ranking on the leaderboard. The code and data are accessible at https://github.com/ChenYi2019/SSNE.
