Silicon atomic vapor chambers (SAVCs) are essential components for the quantum information processing module of the single-ion quantum computer proposed in this paper. This study demonstrates that a specific nano-fabrication technique can be applied to produce deep silicon vapor chambers. Through this approach, we successfully created deep silicon chambers with thicknesses ranging from 100 to 300 µm and widths between 1.5 and 2.5 mm. These chambers were designed to house a thin layer of silicon, a material selected for its superior electrical and thermal properties, which are advantageous for integrating microelectronics into the system. The fabrication process involves direct etching of high-purity silicon wafers, followed by the deposition of an aluminum coating to serve as a silicon getter. Thermal desorption of adsorbed water from the chamber surfaces is achieved by attaching the devices to a copper plate and applying heat. Leakage rates for these fabricated SAVCs were measured at approximately 10⁻⁸ Pa·L/s. Furthermore, a micromagnetic simulation indicates that a bias magnetic field of roughly 100 mT is required to maintain a stable bias axis for the trapped ion. These experimental and simulation results confirm that the proposed nano-fabrication method is viable for producing high-quality SAVCs, thereby supporting the realization of the single-ion quantum computer. Additionally, this methodology offers a viable path for developing other sophisticated optical and electronic systems. This paper introduces a new model designed to estimate the nonlinear disruption power (NLP) affecting the digital error rate in multi-dimensional modulation schemes. The model posits that the total NLP is the sum of two components: one representing nonlinear impairment in signal amplitude and the other in signal phase. Numerical simulations were conducted to verify the model's accuracy regarding amplitude NLP, phase NLP, and total NLP. The results confirm that the proposed model aligns well with the simulated nonlinear disruption power across dual-polarization two- and four-dimensional modulation formats. Furthermore, the model's effectiveness is demonstrated by its ability to accurately predict the erasure rate for digital bit-level four-dimensional modulation formats. Ultimately, this model is expected to facilitate the efficient design of advanced transmission systems utilizing multi-dimensional modulation schemes. (Selected as a Top Pick by J-Light)

In recent years, numerous wildfires have ravaged various regions of the Earth, causing significant loss of life and property. While traditional detection methods are often labor-intensive and prone to human error, Deep Learning (DL) has emerged as a highly promising solution for monitoring and forecasting fires. However, most current DL-based fire detection models are trained exclusively on infrared imagery, a format that is difficult for humans to interpret and rarely available in open datasets. This paper introduces a novel IR-VIS integration method leveraging Deep Learning, designed to enhance human monitoring capabilities and broaden the applicability of DL models in fire prediction. Our approach utilizes Deep Convolutional Autoencoders to learn the mapping between infrared and visible-light imagery, thereby generating visible-light samples from infrared data. Extensive experiments conducted on the MSRI wildfire dataset demonstrate that this technique effectively improves fire classification performance, achieving a substantial reduction in misclassification errors. These findings suggest that our proposed method holds significant potential for future applications in weather forecasting and other relevant fields. Additionally, the dataset and all associated code will be made publicly available to support further research and development. The NIPS 2021 Datasets and Code Challenge on Deep Learning-based Weather Forecasting aims to predict the evolution of weather phenomena over the next 6 hours using infrared and visible imagery. This study serves as a foundation for the first track of that challenge, specifically focused on infrared-visible integration within Deep Learning-based fire detection. The findings indicate that our technique is highly effective for human monitoring and significantly improves DL model accuracy in fire prediction. This study presents a dataset of social media posts from individuals diagnosed with depression and their corresponding physician-validated explanations for why those posts were relevant. We demonstrate the utility of this dataset in developing methods to detect signs of depression on social media. We evaluate three baseline classifiers—Support Vector Machines, Random Forest, and Naive Bayes—using posts from 100 depression sufferers, showing that the top-performing classifier achieves 90% accuracy. Additionally, we performed word overlap analysis on the explanations associated with the top 10 classifiers to identify common terms related to depression. Finally, we discuss the potential applications of our proposed classifier. The complete dataset will be made available on GitHub to facilitate replication of our findings and experimental results. We anticipate that this approach will assist researchers in creating classifiers capable of identifying indicators of depression through social media activity.

Keywords: Depression Detection, Social Media, Sentiment Analysis, NLP.

This study introduces a random-compartmental random dynamical system (RCRS) to model the COVID-19 pandemic. The model incorporates the dynamics of susceptible, exposed, infected, and removed populations, alongside stochastic environmental noise. The primary objective is to analyze the model equation, establish the existence of a unique positive solution, examine the long-term behavior of solutions, and explore the model's dynamics. Furthermore, the research demonstrates how this framework can serve as an effective instrument for monitoring and forecasting the spread of COVID-19. Additionally, a computational approach is provided to visualize the results. This methodology holds potential for aiding in the prediction of pandemic trends and assessing the efficacy of various control strategies. Finally, the study offers insights into addressing other infectious diseases. The MATLAB code utilized in this work can be accessed at https://github.com/abdullahalshaya/COVID-19. This study presents a systematic investigation into the isoscalar monopole response of $^{24}$Mg and $^{28}$Si, utilizing the relativistic quasiparticle random-phase approximation (RQRPA) framework. By incorporating the coupling between the isoscalar monopole and quadrupole modes, we calculate the energy and strength of the isoscalar monopole giant resonance. Our findings reveal that the calculated energy for the isoscalar monopole giant resonance in $^{24}$Mg is notably lower than in $^{28}$Si, a result consistent with experimental data. Furthermore, we observe that the coupling between monopole and quadrupole modes significantly enhances the strength of the isoscalar monopole giant resonance in $^{28}$Si, whereas its effect in $^{24}$Mg is negligible. These results underscore the critical role of monopole-quadrupole coupling in enhancing isoscalar monopole strength, particularly in $^{28}$Si. Additionally, we find that the RQRPA method without this coupling fails to reproduce the energy of the isoscalar monopole giant resonance in $^{24}$Mg, whereas RQRPA with the inclusion of this coupling successfully reproduces the resonance energy in both $^{24}$Mg and $^{28}$Si. Finally, our calculated root-mean-square radii for $^{24}$Mg and $^{28}$Si align well with experimental measurements. Overall, this work demonstrates that the RQRPA model, when accounting for isoscalar monopole-quadrupole coupling, provides a robust description of the isoscalar monopole response in these nuclei. This model serves as a valuable tool for investigating nuclear structure and dynamics, particularly regarding giant resonances. Future research should extend this approach to other nuclei to further explore the impact of monopole-quadrupole coupling on the isoscalar monopole giant resonance. Additionally, the RQRPA model, with monopole-quadrupole coupling included, is expected to be highly effective for studying other nuclear responses, such as isoscalar, isovector, and isospin quadrupole modes. Experimental studies are recommended to verify these predictions and to investigate the influence of monopole-quadrupole coupling on giant resonances in other nuclei. This study examines stick-slip phenomena and trajectory convergence within feedback-controlled motion systems encountering Coulomb friction. A discontinuous friction model is utilized, yielding a stick-slip dynamic system characterized by non-Lipschitz continuous vector fields at switching points, which complicates the analysis of convergence. To address this, a stabilizing friction-compensating friction-velocity-anticipating (FV) controller is implemented, transforming the stick-slip system into a Lipschitz continuous one. By applying the comparison principle, sufficient conditions ensuring finite-time convergence to the sliding surface are derived. Furthermore, to guarantee convergence to the equilibrium point, a friction-free feedback regulator is designed, and its ability to asymptotically stabilize the sliding system is demonstrated. Finally, the effectiveness of the proposed control strategy is validated through numerical simulations. Notably, this regulator represents a novel contribution to the field, as it differs from the velocity-anticipating regulator described by Utkin et al. (1999) and is derived from the sliding system's linearization around the sliding manifold. The paper concludes with the derivation of sufficient conditions for the asymptotic stability of the sliding system. Simulation results confirm theoretical findings and illustrate the emergence of limit cycles. Additionally, the study explores extensions of the approach to systems with nonlinear friction and proposes strategies for managing chattering. This paper introduces ProBell, a model-based reinforcement learning algorithm designed for risk-sensitive decision-making. Drawing inspiration from the profound Bellman equations, ProBell utilizes a pre-trained model to simulate environmental transitions. It incorporates risk-aware information into both feature engineering and policy learning, utilizing a proposed risk-sensitive belief feature and a learned Gaussian Process (GP) value function. To manage risk, ProBell employs a GP-based risk-aware belief update mechanism. Extensive experiments across diverse simulated risk scenarios demonstrate that ProBell surpasses current state-of-the-art methods. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/Chenchen-chen/ProBell. Furthermore, the implementation for this work has been integrated into the open-source Python risk-sensitive decision-making library PySRDR, available at https://github.com/Chenchen-chen/pysdr. PySRDR includes ProBell as a state-of-the-art algorithm and features other promising risk-aware methods. Additionally, it provides various simulated risk scenarios for experimental purposes. Sequential recommender systems are designed to suggest items based on a user's historical consumption. This paper investigates the double confluent Heun equation, specifically in the context of the quantum mechanical anharmonic oscillator. By imposing specific boundary conditions at the origin, we derive a general symmetry constraint on the monodromy matrix, which significantly restricts the outset of the oscillator. This newly identified solvable model can be viewed as a symmetric version of the anharmonic oscillator, though it differs fundamentally as it lacks a potential. Instead, it features a singularity at the origin and two boundaries extending to infinity. We demonstrate that a symmetric unfolding of this singularity, when made regular, yields a potentialless, singularity-free model that satisfies the outset conditions. Furthermore, we show that this model is equivalent to the solvable oscillator, specifically the Lamé model. Finally, we discuss the relationship between our findings and the recently proposed potentialless oscillator. These results suggest that the development of potentialless quantum mechanical models, particularly within supersymmetric quantum mechanics, may be facilitated by a deeper understanding of the monodromy matrix constraints. Additionally, the methods established in this work may prove useful for advancing the broader goal of achieving a complete classification of quantum models based on their monodromy properties. These advances could ultimately contribute to the pursuit of a quantum integrable classification grounded in monodromy symmetry. The paper is structured as follows: Section 2 reviews the general solvable oscillators; Section 3 examines the symmetric case; and Section 4 concludes with final remarks. Appendix A details the specific outsets, while Appendix B outlines the monodromy matrix constraints. Appendix C presents a comparison with the recently proposed potentialless oscillator. The analysis in this work was conducted using the Mathematica package Heun. Finally, Appendix D provides the complete code for the package, heunSymmetry, which is available at the project's website. The package enables the calculation of the double confluent Heun equation's outset, symmetry, and monodromy matrix constraints. Additionally, it offers a generalization of the outset and monodromy constraints to an arbitrary number of oscillators. Appendix E is dedicated to acknowledgments. Fitting low-rank matrices to group-wise heterogeneous data serves as a foundational step in numerous statistical analyses. While various methods exist to estimate these matrices, a unified framework to compare their properties remains absent. We derive the optimal $L_2$ risk and establish its sensitivity to group-size imbalances, a critical factor for finite samples. Our findings indicate that for fixed group sizes, the optimal risk scales inversely with the number of observations within the smallest groups. We also highlight a significant bias inherent in conventional approaches, such as principal component analysis. Finally, we introduce a robust algorithm that achieves the optimal risk and demonstrate its efficacy through an application to Alzheimer's disease data. This example illustrates how bias can distort feature selection when analyzing heterogeneous data with low-rank structures. The entire procedure is available in the R package `lowrank`. Furthermore, our results offer a potential pathway to resolve the longstanding open question regarding the minimax optimal risk for general rank-$k$ matrix estimation, which, if answered, would represent a substantial advancement in statistical estimation theory. The supplementary material includes additional theoretical results, numerical studies, and an R package. Additionally, an R package is under development to facilitate a comprehensive comparison of existing methods. The study data can be accessed at https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-020-77770-1. In the absence of symmetry within physical systems, the traditional topological definition relying on Hamiltonian spectrum crossings becomes inapplicable. This work introduces the concept of an essential topological representation to address this gap. Based on the homotopy properties of the essential topological representation, we redefine the topological invariant $K$ for one-dimensional (1D) and 3D systems. By integrating this invariant with established concepts, we derive new topological classifications: previously unidentified states include multiple 1D phases and new 3D states characterized by surface and bulk contributions. Furthermore, this framework enables the identification of novel phase transitions driven by the nontrivial mapping between the Brillouin zone and configuration space. Finally, we validate these findings by revealing various topological states and phase transitions that go beyond the limitations of the conventional definition. To facilitate experimental realization, we propose corresponding models for both tight-binding and photonic systems. These results establish a novel approach for classifying topological phases in low- and high-dimensional systems that lack symmetry. Furthermore, this study expands the traditional topological classification by incorporating the essential topological representation. Finally, our methodology offers a pathway to discover new topological phases and phenomena by leveraging the unique characteristics of the essential topological representation. These advancements are expected to significantly advance the fields of topological physics and applied topological science. This study addresses the decentralized design of distributed regulation for linear multi-channel networks featuring distributed feedback and feedforward connections. The envisioned architecture is decentralized, enabling independent module design, construction, and regulation. We introduce a novel control design framework that supports distributed regulation and achieves identical convergence rates to those of centralized systems. The proposed solution is a distributed $H_{\infty}$ controller that relies solely on network topology and relative transmission delays. We demonstrate that this design is inherently robust against local delays and packet losses, provided a specific set of distributed constraints is met. These constraints are verifiable using linear matrix inequalities and can be optimized via distributed algorithms. Furthermore, we establish that distributed regulation is feasible if and only if it is achievable in a centralized context. The findings are validated through an optical transport network experiment. The implications of these results are applicable to various other systems, including power grids, robotics, and large-scale communication networks. The proposed theory is constructive and yields decentralized methods for the synthesis and testing of distributed regulation. Additionally, we present a practical algorithm for verifying distributed delays and a testing procedure that operates independently of network size. The resulting control design is robust to local delays and packet losses, assuming specific network properties. We also present a practical approach for solving the verification problem, which requires only local computations and communications. The overall algorithm is scalable to massive systems, and its computational complexity is independent of both the number of modules and connections. We demonstrate that the proposed solution achieves the same convergence rate as a centralized controller. The testbed is an optical transport network, and the application involves distributed regulation using feedback and feedforward connections. The network architecture includes distributed delay and loss compensation modules, as well as a distributed equalizer. The testbed features a 100 km link with 16 channels, where each channel is modulated at 25 Gb/s. The global COVID-19 pandemic, caused by the SARS-CoV-2 virus, has resulted in hundreds of thousands of deaths and affected billions of people. Beyond the health crisis, the pandemic has triggered an economic downturn, with many businesses facing closures and a high risk of bankruptcy. This study examines the relationship between confirmed cases and economic performance using data from the World Bank and the COVID-19 World Map. The analysis reveals that the relationship between confirmed cases and GDP per capita varies depending on the stage of the pandemic. The research is divided into two phases: the first covers the period from January 1, 2020, to April 30, 2020, while the second spans from May 1, 2020, to December 31, 2020. To investigate the distinct impacts of COVID-19 on economies at different stages, the study employs a Two-Phase BERT model. This approach demonstrates that the relationship between confirmed cases and GDP per capita is not uniform, and the model achieves an accuracy of 85%. The findings indicate that the pandemic's effect on the economy is not constant and may shift as the situation evolves. This insight is valuable for policymakers, as it suggests that containment measures should be adjusted based on the pandemic's current phase. The research concludes by recommending further investigation into the relationship between COVID-19 cases and other economic indicators. Additionally, the Two-Phase BERT model is proposed for future applications in analyzing the relationship between various indicators and the pandemic's phase. Diverse organisms, ranging from bacteria to humans, rely on cell division for growth and reproduction. Although this process is primarily driven by the elongation and synthesis of biomass, it is frequently modeled as a Poisson process governed by a constant exponential timer. However, biological systems often exhibit high phenotypic plasticity, causing the rate of molecular reactions to fluctuate in response to varying environmental conditions. These changes affect cellular durations and can trigger adaptive phenotypic shifts. Consequently, duration distributions are often non-exponential, and duration control mechanisms are complex, involving multiple overlapping events. This study examines various models for cell division times, analyzing their statistical properties and the resulting dynamics of population birth and death rates. We demonstrate that environmental changes can induce phase transitions in population birth and death rates, with critical thresholds dependent on duration distribution characteristics and the intensity of environmental fluctuations. Furthermore, we identify scenarios where these transitions are reversible and others where they are not, depending on the nature of environmental changes. Finally, we propose a new metric to quantify the complexity of cell division duration control, which can be derived from experimentally accessible data. This metric is shown to correlate with the complexity of environmental regulation and the occurrence of phase transitions. Our findings provide a framework for understanding how duration distributions influence population dynamics and how these distributions themselves may adapt to environmental changes. This offers a potential explanation for the diversity of duration distributions observed across different species and within the same species. Additionally, our metric for duration control complexity can be applied to investigate how this diversity impacts population dynamics. These results are illustrated using various models and examples, including those for bacteria and yeast. The study also incorporates data from a recent experiment involving bacteria subjected to diverse environmental changes. The paper concludes with several open questions regarding the application of these results to other biological systems. Self-supervised models (SSMs) have become a leading approach for speech representation learning, offering a cost-effective alternative to supervised models. However, their performance often degrades when trained on antagonistic data—information that contradicts their objectives. This study investigates how SSMs respond to such antagonistic data during training. We specifically examine Whisper, a prominent SSM, and its susceptibility to antagonistic content in both audio and text domains. Our findings reveal that Whisper's susceptibility to antagonistic text varies significantly based on the primary task it is trained on: models focused on speech recognition exhibit a stronger response to antagonistic text than those trained for language understanding. Additionally, we introduce a novel susceptibility metric based on representations and demonstrate that it effectively predicts the extent of model degradation caused by antagonistic inputs. Finally, we explore the impact of filtering antagonistic training data on the final performance of speech-based SSMs. These insights aim to inform future research into mitigating antagonistic effects, thereby enhancing the robustness of these models. This study examines the integration of distributed exchanges (Dexes) and decentralized trading mechanisms within cryptocurrency markets. We demonstrate that, in the absence of trust between participants, decentralized trading enables users to acquire assets without requiring trust in the asset's underlying fundamentals, the counterparty, or any third party. By leveraging blockchain technology, these systems facilitate trustless transactions through the automatic execution of smart contracts. Our analysis indicates that while Dexes enable users to bypass the risk of asset dilution and fund misappropriation, they fail to address other significant issues, such as price discrepancies and the absence of effective dispute resolution systems. Furthermore, we highlight that decentralized trading does not necessarily enhance market efficiency or liquidity. Finally, we argue that although blockchain technology allows for trustless transactions, it imposes substantial costs regarding computational resources and energy consumption. Given these limitations, we contend that decentralized trading should be utilized only when necessary. Additionally, we note that combining blockchain-based decentralized trading with effective off-chain solutions, such as decentralized oracles, may yield more comprehensive benefits. To illustrate this, we present a case study of decentralized finance (DeFi), a rapidly expanding sector within the cryptocurrency market. Specifically, we explore how off-chain order books can improve the user experience for Dexes, thereby mitigating certain challenges. In light of these findings, we offer several recommendations for the future development of decentralized trading. Finally, we suggest that further research should concentrate on hybrid exchanges, which combine the advantages of both decentralized and centralized models. This approach would address various problems associated with pure Dexes while avoiding the constraints inherent in centralized systems. Consequently, we believe that hybrid exchanges represent a promising avenue for future investigation. Overall, our research underscores the intricate complexities of decentralized trading and provides valuable insights for its continued evolution. Additionally, we emphasize the significance of decentralized trading in the cryptocurrency market and the broader digital asset ecosystem. Our findings also offer valuable perspectives on the future of decentralized finance and the potential for decentralized trading to transform traditional financial markets. Finally, we note that our research has implications for policymakers, as it highlights the need to balance regulatory concerns with the potential benefits of decentralized trading. Our study also highlights the importance of consumer protection in the context of decentralized exchanges, given the unique risks associated with these platforms. Moreover, our research has implications for investors, as it sheds light on the potential risks and rewards of decentralized trading. Finally, our research has implications for the cryptocurrency market as a whole, as it provides valuable insights into the potential impact of decentralized exchanges on market dynamics. In epidemiological research, missing data often stems from nonresponse, nonrandomization, or missing not at random (MNAR) scenarios. When data are missing completely at random (MCAR) or missing at random (MAR), established techniques such as imputation and inverse probability weighting can effectively mitigate bias. However, when data缺失 due to absence, the risk of bias escalates significantly as the likelihood of MNAR mechanisms increases. This study introduces a novel approach to quantify and account for potential bias in the presence of absent data. We assess the magnitude of missing data and the likelihood of MNAR conditions, subsequently estimating the overall impact on the analysis. This process involves augmenting the standard likelihood function with a specific sensitivity parameter that captures the degree of bias introduced by absent cases. Using this framework, we develop the E-value—a sensitivity parameter analogous to the traditional posterior probability—to evaluate whether the posterior probability of MNAR is substantial. Furthermore, we demonstrate how to incorporate the E-value into Bayesian sensitivity analysis for absent data, applying this methodology to a case study concerning the association between oral contraceptive use and myocardial infarction. The value of this method lies in its ability to measure, explain, and adjust for bias arising from absent data. By quantifying the scale of missing information, researchers can determine the extent to which missing data might have influenced their findings. Ultimately, this approach facilitates a more robust assessment of the reliability of analytical results when handling absent data. Additionally, the method is highly flexible, allowing for adaptation to various contexts and data types. The accompanying R package, Evalue, provides the necessary tools to implement this analysis. The package is accessible at https://github.com/epiforecasts/Evalue. FL enhances security and privacy by ensuring no personal information is exposed. This framework utilizes smart contracts to securely aggregate models and ensures the integrity of training data. A detailed comparison of FL variants is provided to highlight their specific advantages and disadvantages. The study aims to offer comprehensive insights into IoV and establish a robust foundation for future research. By leveraging FL, the framework secures the training process and safeguards the data against external threats. Furthermore, blockchain technology enhances the security of the framework by providing an immutable and transparent ledger for the aggregation of machine learning models. Ultimately, this approach facilitates the secure training of machine learning models in IoV vehicles. This paper introduces a substantial millikelvin cooling platform at Fermilab, designed to support the large-scale development of quantum computing applications based on superconducting topological qubits. The system features a 200-liter dilution refrigerator achieving an evaporator temperature of approximately 5 mK. Its cooling architecture incorporates an extensive set of thermalization stages, including an integrated liquid helium dewar, a room-temperature vacuum chamber, a 77 K stage, a room-temperature-cryopump, a 4 K cryocooler, and a 10 K plate. To facilitate scientific applications, the refrigerator offers multiple options for thermal and electrical connections at the evaporator, alongside a variety of internal and external cryogenic instrumentation. The design prioritizes modularity, flexibility, and user accessibility, ensuring that cooling resources are available to users without requiring any modifications. Furthermore, the system is engineered to accommodate future upgrades and expansions. This paper details the architecture and components of the refrigeration system, alongside an overview of the planned cold-circuit instrumentation. The refrigerator is anticipated to be delivered in early 2022. Cryptocurrency, a decentralized digital asset, has seen a surge in the 2020s, prompting many software developers to adopt related technologies. This shift has led to a proliferation of the Python programming language and its cryptocurrency libraries. However, their rapid expansion has also spawned numerous misapplications. This study examines real-world Python cryptocurrency projects from GitHub to identify common misconceptions and errors. By analyzing these cases, we uncover the root causes of the issues and their consequences. Leveraging our findings, we propose general guidelines to assist developers in avoiding similar pitfalls. We aim for this research to raise awareness among practitioners regarding these problems and offer them practical support in utilizing Python's cryptocurrency libraries more effectively. This study introduces NuSPAN, a novel algorithm designed for seismic reflectivity recovery, which we demonstrate is a proximal mean (PM) method within the class of proximal gradient-type algorithms. NuSPAN is applied to inverse problems involving linear models with nonuniform $l_0$-norm sparsity constraints on reflectivity. We establish the convergence of NuSPAN to the minimum of the objective function and provide recommendations regarding parameter selection. A key advantage of NuSPAN is its capacity to produce sparse solutions, yielding fewer spurious events and cleaner results. The method's efficacy is validated through a synthetic example comparing it against the LASSO algorithm and a proximal thresholding algorithm termed SPoC. Furthermore, a field seismic data example is examined to demonstrate NuSPAN's effectiveness in practical applications. Finally, the algorithm is benchmarked against the Orthogonal Matching Pursuit (OMP) method, which is widely used in seismic deconvolution. These comparisons underscore NuSPAN's potential for seismic data processing. The study concludes by suggesting future research directions regarding performance improvements and extensions to address missing data. The code used in this work is accessible at: https://github.com/ehsan-ghafourian/NuSPAN. Additionally, supplementary materials, including code and Jupyter notebooks for the synthetic examples, are available at: https://github.com/ehsan-ghafourian/NuSPAN/tree/master/Supplementary_Materials. These resources also feature a Jupyter notebook detailing the field seismic data example. This article presents two main results regarding infinite-dimensional spaces of analytic functions on the unit disk that include the Bloch space and the space BMOA of analytic functions of bounded mean oscillation. Initially, we examine semigroups of analytic composition operators and establish a sufficient condition for a semigroup to map the space BMO into itself continuously and strongly continuously. Furthermore, we derive an equivalent condition specifically for Fock semigroups of composition operators, which involve exponential maps as their composing functions. Secondly, we investigate the integral operators T_ϕ defined by T_ϕ(f)(z) = e^(-ϕ(z))f(z) within BMO. We demonstrate that T_ϕ is bounded on BMO if and only if the function ϕ belongs to the disk algebra, and that T_ϕ is compact on BMO if and only if ϕ vanishes at the boundary of the unit disk. Additionally, we prove that T_ϕ is normal on BMO if and only if the function ϕ is constant. Finally, we establish that T_ϕ is self-adjoint on BMO if and only if the real part of the integral of e^(-ϕ(z)) over the unit circle is zero. These findings generalize several existing results found in the literature. Notably, when analyzing semigroups of analytic composition operators, we show that the infinitesimal generator is a weighted Bergman-type integral operator, whereas the infinitesimal generator associated with a semigroup of composition operators is a weighted Bloch-type space. In the context of Fock semigroups of composition operators, the infinitesimal generator is identified as a weighted Fock-Bloch-type space. The final section of the paper is dedicated to examples and counterexamples. Specifically, we provide a criterion for the analyticity of T_ϕ on the Dirichlet space, the space B, and the weighted Dirichlet space B_1/2. Additionally, we illustrate that T_ϕ is compact on the space BMO when the function ϕ is in the disk algebra and its modulus is less than or equal to 1. Finally, we demonstrate that T_ϕ is normal on the space BMO if and only if the function ϕ is constant, and that T_ϕ is self-adjoint on the space BMO if and only if the function ϕ is real-valued. These results extend and complement various theorems found in the literature. Keywords: Semigroup of analytic composition

We introduce a numerical framework for amalgamating probability distributions of Hermitian operators. By analyzing the probability distributions of the real parts of Hermitian operators within the Heisenberg spin chain, we demonstrate the presence of a universal finite-length correction term. This correction is determined by the overlap between the two distributions being combined and can be incorporated into Bayesian operator amalgamation. Additionally, we apply this method to a proposed conformal field theory describing the critical behavior of the Haagerup model, yielding constraints on its central charge. These results are derived from the spectral properties of the transfer matrix for the Haagerup lattice model. Our findings indicate that the operator amalgamation technique is highly effective for extracting universal properties from finite-size numerical data. The source code is publicly accessible at https://github.com/akimura0108/wfoverlap. Furthermore, the numerical data supporting this study is available at https://github.com/akimura0108/wfoverlap/tree/main/Ch1/data. Part-of-speech (POS) tagging serves as a fundamental NLP task that assigns categorical labels to words, enabling downstream applications like information retrieval, question answering, and document understanding. Although contemporary neural frameworks have achieved state-of-the-art results, they remain dependent on high-quality training data. The absence of such annotated resources for historical texts restricts the application of advanced NLP techniques to this domain. To address this limitation, we introduce a novel forecasting-based approach that generates POS tag predictions for historical collections without relying on labeled datasets. This technique involves training a neural framework on a temporal sequence of POS tags derived from corpora of varying sizes and periods. The study focuses on two primary collections: the Google Ngram corpus and a specialized subset known as the British Newspaper Archive (BNA) corpus, which covers a 300-year span. Experimental results indicate that this forecasting approach significantly enhances labeling accuracy for historical texts compared to standard POS tagging methods. Furthermore, we observe that the proposed system effectively handles challenges related to diachronic drift and authorial style. We anticipate that this forecasting-based framework will substantially improve text analysis and significantly benefit human paleographers in their interpretation of historical documents. The code for our model is accessible at https://github.com/abhishekkumar12345/POS-Tagging-with-Set-Valued-Forecasting. Additionally, we have released a newly annotated BNA corpus to support future research. We hope this resource will enable researchers to replicate our experiments and explore additional inquiries. The BNA corpus and its sample annotations can be found at https://github.com/abhishekkumar12345/pos-tagging-paleography. We apply concepts from renormalization group analysis to investigate the long-time behavior of non-linear partial differential equations. Our primary focus is on a specific class of parabolic equations characterized by non-smooth, homogeneous drift terms and super-linear diffusion. We establish the necessity of imposing a smallness constraint on the drift coefficient to guarantee stability. Furthermore, we demonstrate that when the drift's homogeneity degree falls within a particular interval, the diffusive property becomes essential for achieving stability. Finally, we analyze the asymptotic dynamics of these equations within the invariant manifold associated with the linearized operator, which is constructed based on the drift's homogeneity. These analytical findings are supported by numerical simulations. Additionally, we extend our results to the stochastic setting by introducing a novel stochastic integrability criterion. We derive key properties for the associated transition functionals and the associated Dirichlet forms, and we explore applications involving Kolmogorov-Skorokhod operators. Within this framework, we examine asymptotic behavior by constructing an invariant manifold for equations featuring drifts that may grow linearly. In this extended scenario, the asymptotic behavior is analyzed using tools from the theory of one-parameter semigroups. Finally, we present applications where drift functions are defined as functions of bounded variation on ${\mathbb R}^d$. In this context, we derive asymptotic results specifically for gradient systems. These applications also feature drift functions that depend on gradient variables, resulting in drift coefficients that are distributions. In such cases, we develop a methodology to construct invariant manifolds by utilizing the Riesz transform. This approach allows us to derive asymptotic results that hold in probability. As an application, we analyze the asymptotic behavior of solutions to the Navier-Stokes equations. We begin by establishing the existence of a unique solution for the associated non-linear parabolic equation, and subsequently, we determine the asymptotic behavior of its solutions. This is achieved by utilizing invariant manifolds derived from the parabolic equation, which are parametrized by finite-dimensional Sobolev spaces of velocity fields. We also address applications concerning the Navier-Stokes equations formulated in vorticity variables. In this context, the asymptotic behavior of the solution to the associated parabolic equation is derived using invariant manifolds parametrized by finite-dimensional Sobolev spaces of vorticity fields. Finally, we consider applications concerning the Euler equations, where the asymptotic behavior of their solutions is derived by employing invariant manifolds parametrized by finite-dimensional Sobolev spaces of the associated velocity fields. The successful delivery of smart city initiatives relies heavily on stakeholder expectations, leading to frequent conflicts between anticipated outcomes and real-world experiences. This study introduces a smart assistant designed to mitigate such disputes by converting user inputs regarding smart city services into precise formal specifications. Specifically, we developed a specialized language to model user expectations, featuring a formal grammar, a decision tree, and decision node labeling. These components enable the automatic translation of informal expectations into the target language, thereby facilitating early detection of requirements conflicts. Furthermore, the proposed transformation mechanism supports bidirectional translation. To demonstrate its efficacy, we applied this approach to analyze stakeholder expectations within the Smart City of Tbilisi project. Our results indicate that the formalization process assists stakeholders in defining smart city services at an early stage, allowing for the identification of requirement conflicts before significant resources are committed. Additionally, this process aids decision-makers in comprehending the scope of services expected by both citizens and enterprises. To our knowledge, this represents the first application of formal specification techniques to the domain of stakeholder expectation analysis in smart cities. The corresponding code is publicly accessible at https://github.com/sofya-kapralova/expectations-transformations. This work was supported by the University of Stavanger under grant number 49073/F20. Conventional two-dimensional quantum error correction codes, such as the surface code, demand a large number of physical qubits to realize computational states, a requirement that presents a significant bottleneck for near-term quantum processors. To address this challenge, we introduce a quantum algorithm called the Concealed Inverse Protocol (CIP), which enhances the reliability of quantum computations without increasing the physical qubit count. This algorithm relies on the non-local property of quantum entanglement, allowing operations to be concealed within an entangled state. By integrating CIP with existing hardware, the physical qubit number remains unchanged while the quantity of useful quantum states expands. Furthermore, the application of CIP does not require modifications to quantum error correction codes. Experimental results from a 64-qubit superconducting quantum processor demonstrate that CIP effectively improves the reliability of quantum operations and gate-based computations. Consequently, this algorithm offers a viable solution for large-scale quantum computing, paving the way for the practical implementation of large-scale quantum error correction codes. Our findings suggest that CIP can be readily applied to near-term quantum computing tasks, including quantum simulations and machine learning. Additionally, the implementation of CIP does not necessitate additional classical computational resources. These outcomes highlight the potential of CIP to advance large-scale quantum computing. This construct is termed a $\mathbb{D}$-cocartesian morphism (or simply a cocartesian morphism when $D$ is identity). The paper establishes a decomposition theorem for regular categories without pullbacks, analogous to the factorization theorem for categories with pullbacks, but substituting factorization along pullback-stable monomorphisms with factorization along $\mathbb{D}$-cocartesian morphisms. Additionally, the paper introduces and examines pre-order and equivalence connections, which serve as the counterparts to Cartesian connections found in categories equipped with pullbacks. A dedicated section details the interrelationships among these concepts and their various characterizations. To facilitate this, the paper defines $\mathbb{D}$-equivalence relations, $\mathbb{D}$-congruences, and $\mathbb{D}$-partitions, providing a factorization theorem for $\mathbb{D}$-congruences and an isomorphism theorem regarding cocartesian morphisms. Furthermore, it presents a modified version of the fundamental theorem of geometry, followed by an analysis of how cocartesian morphisms, connections, and equivalence relations interact. The text concludes with an exploration of $\mathbb{D}$-preorder and equivalence structures, along with an axiomatic characterization of $\mathbb{D}$-cocartesian morphisms. Finally, the paper presents a version of the synthetic differential geometry adapted to $\mathbb{D}$-cocartesian categories and establishes a correspondence between classical toposes and $\mathbb{D}$-cocartesian toposes. Marine engineering and science necessitate precise estimates of extreme ocean conditions to ensure the safety and stability of offshore infrastructure and coastal areas against events like storms and tsunamis. A critical requirement for these fields is a robust statistical tool to forecast simultaneous, extreme observations across multiple spatial locations. This study introduces a new method for predicting multivariate spatial conditional peaks in extreme environments, utilizing a novel multivariate spatial Peaks Over Threshold (POT) model. The process involves two key steps: first, a multivariate Cox-Roberts Copula accurately captures the dependence structure among extreme events; second, a Bayesian Kriging technique interpolates the remaining marginal uncertainty at unobserved locations. The method's performance is evaluated using observed significant wave data from the UK Continental Shelf. Furthermore, to demonstrate its utility in marine engineering, extreme sea states across the North Sea are predicted using buoy observations from the European Marine Observation and Research Network. The results show that the proposed method outperforms a recent alternative and effectively balances accuracy and computational efficiency. Consequently, this approach offers a valuable tool for generating extreme environment forecasts and assessing the potential risks to marine structures and coastal zones. Supplementary materials, including code and additional results, are available at https://doi.org/10.1016/j.eswa.2021.114244.sdc. Keywords: Extreme environments; Offshore structures; Copula; Copula Kriging; Copula-based spatial POC; Copula-based POC Kriging.

Natural language serves as a vital complement to visual representations for interpreting vision-language models. However, current text representations often lack descriptive richness, limiting their utility in model understanding. To address this, we introduce VT-CLIP, a framework that enhances existing text representations by generating visual-directed descriptions based on input images. These new descriptions capture fine-grained details and dependencies, thereby enriching the overall textual representation. VT-CLIP employs a dual mechanism: a language model generates visual-directed text guided by both image and plaintext inputs, while a contrastive alignment module ensures the synergy between original text and visual-directed descriptions through a cross-modal contrastive loss. Extensive experiments indicate that VT-CLIP significantly boosts performance across various image recognition tasks, particularly when paired with smaller text encoders. Additionally, the visual-directed descriptions produced exhibit high quality and are effective for image captioning. The code and configurations are accessible at https://github.com/ruixiangwang/VT-CLIP. The paper can be found at https://arxiv.org/abs/2104.01980.

Controlling noisy quantum systems remains a significant challenge. This study introduces a unified theoretical framework to analyze the impact of noise on the evolution of arbitrary matrix systems acting on qubits, revealing an intrinsic limitation in open quantum dynamics. Specifically, we demonstrate that noise from a single qubit system can degrade the fidelity of any other qubit system upon measurement. Furthermore, we develop a universal algorithm for implementing any matrix system on noisy qubit systems, which can be executed on any universal noisy matrix system. This approach extends the capabilities of existing operator switching protocols used for universal quantum gate sets, offering valuable insights for quantum error correction. Additionally, we propose an efficient strategy for universal quantum system simulation by decomposing the problem into independent matrix evolution and operator switching components. These findings suggest that universal noisy matrix systems can be implemented across diverse physical platforms, potentially opening new avenues for quantum error correction research. Finally, this work offers a comprehensive method for designing and implementing quantum error correction schemes, enabling the creation of various quantum computational architectures. We anticipate that these results will serve as a valuable resource for advancing quantum error correction. The code for this research is accessible at https://github.com/zhongqiangwang1988/Operator-Switching. Supplementary materials are available at https://www.mdpi.com/2073-8931/10/1/10. This article was submitted to Quantum Information and Active Matter, an open access publication service of MDPI. Consequently, we establish that the Sm-descent of these Segments constitutes a representable sheaf in dg-differential graded modules over the Sm-prestific of smooth $S$-preschemes. As a corollary, we demonstrate that the relative Voevodsky cycle category over $S$ possesses an $\mathrm{Ext}$-structure derived from the Segments. Quantitative analysis in radiology and histopathology depends on digital annotations and measurements. However, the data from digital imaging and analysis in these fields lacks a standardized format, complicating storage, transfer, and interoperability. To address this, we created Highdicom, a Python library that enables the encoding and decoding of image annotations and measurements using the Health Level Seven International (HL7) Information Modeling Meta Foundation (IMM) dictionary. This dictionary serves as the foundation for the DICOM Part 10 Secondary Capture Module and is also utilized in the Pathology Part 10 and Part 20 DICOM domains. Highdicom simplifies the development of applications that generate, process, and analyze quantitative data in these imaging contexts. It offers a straightforward API for creating annotation objects, supports serialization to various formats, and provides utilities for validating and comparing annotations. Additionally, we demonstrate how Highdicom facilitates the creation of robust and portable annotation objects for the open-source machine learning framework PyRadiomics. By integrating Highdicom into your quantitative imaging workflow, you can ensure that your annotations and measurements are compatible with established standards in these domains. The library is freely available on PyPI and can be installed via pip. For further details, visit our website or explore our examples. Our team is actively engaged in further development and welcomes your feedback. For inquiries, please contact us at info@highdicom.org. For contributions, see https://github.com/highdicom/highdicom.

This paper introduces a new surface term for the Einstein-Hilbert action that explicitly features the induced metric. We also present the corresponding Noether charge and derive the first law of thermodynamics for stationary black holes. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the Virasoro algebra can be constructed using this new surface term. Finally, by utilizing the surface expression and variation formula of the Noether charge, we calculate the surface term for the variation of the nonlocal part of the entropy and reformulate the surface term for the total variation of nonlocal entropy. Leveraging these results, we re-examine the first law of thermodynamics for stationary black holes with diffeomorphism gauge transformations. Additionally, we re-derive the Bekenstein-Hawking law and the Cardy formula. Finally, we examine a specific class of stationary black holes characterized by gauge transformations with a nontrivial dependence on the induced metric. For this class, we compute the surface terms associated with both the energy-momentum and Virasoro algebra generators. As an illustration, we apply our method to the Kasner and BTZ black holes. In the latter case, we also examine the effect of nonlocal entropy on the surface term for the first law of thermodynamics. Deep learning has emerged as a vital instrument for addressing complex challenges within the life sciences. Nevertheless, most deep learning algorithms necessitate extensive training datasets labeled by human experts, a requirement that is often impractical for numerous applications in DNA analysis. To overcome this limitation, we introduce a technique for unsupervised embedding of DNA sequences. This approach enables unsupervised pretraining of sequence embeddings using a next nucleotide prediction model, followed by the training of a Shallow Restricted Boltzmann Machine (SRBM) on a short DNA sequence dataset. We demonstrate that our proposed method surpasses existing techniques for unsupervised learning of DNA sequence embeddings. Furthermore, we validate the method's efficacy by applying it to two specific DNA analysis tasks. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/GenomicsML/DNAEmbedding. The synthesis of transition metal oxide ultrathin films has been a focal point of intense research. This study examines the metal-insulator transition in V$_2$O$_3$ films grown on Al$_2$O$_3$(1102) substrates. V$_2$O$_3$ thin films were created via magnetron sputtering, utilizing an oxygen plasma to manage surface stoichiometry. By adjusting the oxygen partial pressure during deposition, we controlled the metal-insulator behavior of these films. Furthermore, we analyzed the influence of post-growth annealing on the film's electronic properties. Our findings indicate that the surface composition of V$_2O$_3$ can be tuned during synthesis, and that oxygen incorporation at the surface is critical in driving the metal-insulator transition. These results offer valuable insights for optimizing the synthesis of transition metal oxides with tailored properties. Furthermore, our observations align with recent theoretical predictions regarding the electronic properties of ultrathin V$_2$O$_3$ films. This paper investigates the extension of conjugation operations on mechanical systems to the Lie-Poisson framework. We demonstrate that when the generating 1-form of a conjugation is Ad-invariant, it induces a Clebsch conjugation on the Lie-Poisson space, thereby transporting the original system to a linearized version. Furthermore, we establish an additional sufficient condition under which the linearized system remains equivalent. These findings generalize earlier work by J. C. Kuiper and A. Weinstein, extending their results from 3-dimensional space to $n$-dimensional settings. Finally, we apply these generalized results to the conjugation of mechanical systems on SO(3). Specifically, we show that a Lagrangian describing a conjugation with an Ad-invariant generating form corresponds to the kinetic energy of a linear system where the Lagrange multiplier associated with the constraint acts as the angular velocity. We also explore how the Euler top can be derived as the conjugate of such a kinematical linearization. In the final section, we apply the general theory of Clebsch conjugation to construct linearizations for various conjugate pairs by selecting an appropriate Lie algebra representation. We demonstrate that for any conjugation pair, a specific representation exists such that a linearization is achieved via the Clebsch method using the Ad-invariant form. Consequently, we provide explicit examples of linearizations for mechanical systems on SO(3) derived through Clebsch conjugation. Notably, the Euler top emerges as the conjugate of a conjugation where the generating form is the kinetic energy of a free particle. Additionally, we examine a linearization arising from the conical pendulum, which is the conjugate of a system where the generating form is the kinetic energy of a particle moving on a sphere with a specific constraint. In this case, the linearization is obtained using a representation where the Lagrange multiplier for the constraint functions as angular velocity. We also analyze the effects of the magnetic linearization on SO(3), which results in a linearization of a conjugate system where the Lagrange multiplier for the constraint is represented by angular velocity. Finally, we explore a linearization derived from a conjugation where the generating form is the magnetic potential of a magnetic monopole. In this scenario, the linearization is achieved using a representation where the Lie algebra element associated with the linearization is identified with the magnetic field. We introduce a thorough investigation of 2018 sub-prime-field exoplanets detected by the Korean Microlensing Exoplanet NET (KMTNet), representing the most extensive sample of its kind examined to date. Our analysis identifies 11 planets with well-determined planetary anomalies, characterized by significant deviations between planet-to-lens mass ratios ($q$) and lens mass estimates derived from parallax and orbital fitting. Among these anomalies, 10 involve planets with masses below 10 $M_{\rm Jup}$, which are predominantly young ($t_0 < 1$ Gyr) and located at relatively large projected separations ($0.5-2.0$ au). We demonstrate that the $q$ anomalies of these 10 young, widely separated low-mass planets can be explained by dynamical mass migration, a process driven by tidal interactions between planets and their companions. Furthermore, we show that the lens mass estimates from parallax and orbital fits are consistent with stellar masses, whereas they are generally inconsistent with brown dwarf masses. We also demonstrate that the previously identified massive planetary system KMT-2018-BYC-001 likely consists of a brown dwarf and a planet. Additionally, we confirm that the binary lens KMT-2018-BYD-001 contains a planet, and we report the discovery of a new planetary system, KMT-2018-BYD-002. Finally, we discuss the implications of our findings for understanding the formation and evolution of planetary systems. Building upon the previous article by the same authors, we present an innovative computational framework designed to maintain the stability of entropy solutions within a practical and robust numerical scheme. This approach is specifically tailored for entropy-conserving or entropy-dissipative methods, including finite volume, entropy-stable spectral element, and high-order finite element discretizations. We present numerical results across diverse test cases to demonstrate the efficacy of our method. Specifically, we analyze solutions to various entropy inequalities and utilize these to track material entropy evolution in experimental data, applying this methodology to shock-capture simulations of interstellar medium flows and shock-capture simulations of high-speed compressible turbulence. Furthermore, for entropy-dissipative schemes where our approach is not directly applicable, we derive an upper bound on entropy production to ensure the entropy stability of the entire simulation. This technique is demonstrated in entropy and entropy-dissipation preserving finite volume discretizations, as well as entropy-stable spectral element discretizations. We emphasize that our computational method is broadly applicable to any high-order finite element or spectral element discretization that adheres to entropy stability or conservation principles. Additionally, we extend this methodology to entropy-quasi-stable discretizations, where entropy is preserved up to a bounded, controllable error. This capability enables simulations of turbulent flows with a material entropy that remains nearly constant, thereby validating the hypothesis that compressible turbulence evolves according to an entropy-conserving mechanism. Finally, we demonstrate the application of entropy stability to nonlinear degenerate hyperbolic systems, such as the PDE models governing traffic flow and granular material flow. In these contexts, entropy stability is essential for preserving non-negative solutions and enforcing non-negative entropy. Our methodology is also applicable to entropy-dissipative methods in these scenarios, where entropy is preserved up to a bounded, controllable error, resulting in simulations that yield non-negative entropy. Furthermore, we show the utility of entropy stability in these nonlinear degenerate systems, underscoring the importance of these principles in modeling complex physical phenomena. Overall, our methodology serves as a valuable tool for a wide array of applications, ranging from computational fluid dynamics and turbulence modeling to the study of traffic flow and granular material flow. By leveraging entropy conservation and stability, we can derive physically accurate solutions from experimental data, thereby enhancing the predictive capabilities of computational models in these fields. Ultimately, entropy conservation and stability act as constraints on the solution space, ensuring that numerical solutions remain consistent with the underlying physical principles of the system being modeled. This study evaluates the performance of 21 machine learning algorithms using 11 feature engineering techniques on a machine-readable Not-Paid-As-Due (NPD) dataset. The dataset was created by scraping 1.5 million records from the Chinese government's National Credit Information Sharing Platform (NCISP) website. The analysis reveals that interactions between machine learning models and feature engineering methods significantly influence the accuracy of default classification, with specific combinations proving highly effective. Furthermore, tree-based models, specifically XGBoost and LightGBM, demonstrated superior predictive accuracy compared to other algorithms. Additionally, feature significance analysis within the NCISP context aligns with existing literature on credit risk assessment. These findings offer valuable insights for financial institutions managing NPD accounts and for data scientists developing automated default classification systems. Ultimately, the research aims to assist financial institutions in mitigating losses from NPD accounts and to enable automated identification of high-risk borrowers. This work represents a pioneering exploration of machine learning algorithms and feature engineering applied to a large-scale NCISP dataset for NPD classification. The accompanying online repository provides access to this dataset, the analysis code, and a step-by-step tutorial. Given that NCISP data is increasingly utilized in academic research, the repository also serves as a practical guide for researchers entering this field. The source code and data can be accessed at: https://github.com/ChenYi2019/NPL-ML-Assessment-and-Feature-Significance-Analysis. Additional details regarding the analysis and dataset are available at: https://github.com/ChenYi2019/NPL-ML-Assessment-and-Feature-Significance-Analysis/tree/master/website. Researchers interested in replicating this analysis are encouraged to consult the tutorial available at: https://github.com/ChenYi2019/NPL-ML-Assessment-and-Feature-Significance-Analysis/tree/master/tutorial. The detailed methodology is outlined in the paper: "Assessment of Machine Learning Algorithms and Feature Significance Analysis on NPL Dataset," published in the 2021 15th International Conference on Computational Intelligence and Security (CIS), IEEE Xplore, pp. 1018–1024, doi: 10.1109/CIC51151.50581.

This work presents an extended abstract of a recent paper that defines Dyck symmetric functions within the basis of Schur functions using non-negative integer-valued coefficients, thereby generalizing Gessel's theorem as the unique case where these coefficients equal 1. This outcome stems from an extended Lagrange inversion formula that incorporates Schur functions and utilizes the inverse of the shift of the generating function for Dyck paths, which is also known as the inverse Catalan series. The methodology for determining the coefficients relies on concepts from q-rook theory. The study presents two distinct proofs: the first connects q-rook theory with generalized Lagrange inversion, while the second, authored by the second and third authors independently, employs symbolic methods. Both approaches yield Gessel's theorem when applied to Schur functions. Additionally, the first proof can be adapted to utilize Schur functions instead of monomials within the Lagrange inversion framework. The paper concludes with a strong conjecture proposing that the coefficients are unimodal and provides empirical evidence supporting this claim. Finally, the endnotes address Gessel's second theorem, which involves the expansion of Dyck paths into Schur functions with alternating signs. This section also briefly outlines the connection between our approach and that of Chen and Liang. For further details, see arXiv:2102.01001. The content in this endnote was contributed by the first author and draws on his 2019 thesis.

This paper introduces a convolutional architecture designed to address orientation invariance and under-sampling issues within traditional convolutional neural networks (CNNs). The proposed solution involves utilizing multiple copies of a network with distinct orientations, where the convolutional layers are tuned to sample in specific directions. We have developed an architecture comprising three such networks with fixed orientations at 0, 120, and 240 degrees, connected via a median pooling layer. We demonstrate that this approach achieves superior sampling in direction-agnostic directions while maintaining high accuracy in orientation-specific ones. Additionally, the architecture exhibits increased robustness to color variations in input images. Extensive experiments conducted on the CIFAR10 and FashionMNIST datasets confirm these findings. The source code will be made available upon request. Keywords: Convolutional Neural Networks, Orientation Invariance, Robustness to Color Variation.

A graph $G$ is defined as $F$-free if it does not contain any $F$-subgraph, where $F$ represents a simple graph. In this work, we demonstrate that for any integer $r \geq 2$, there exists an integer $t_0$ such that for all $t \geq t_0$, the vertices of the graph $G[(1-1/r)n]$ can be partitioned into $t$ independent sets in $C_{K_1+K_{1/2}}$-free $n$-vertex graphs $G$, provided that $r$ divides $n$. Furthermore, the bound $t_0$ is determined as $256\Delta^4$, with $\Delta$ denoting the maximum degree of $F$. The term $C_{K_1+K_{1/2}}$ refers to the graph formed by a clique $K_1$ augmented with an independent set of size $1/2$. Our findings represent the first application of the stability method to the study of independent sets. Additionally, our result confirms the conjecture proposed by M. Kierstead and A. R\"odl regarding $K_{1+K_{1/2}}$-free graphs. Specifically, we show that the conjecture holds for $n$-vertex graphs when considering a subset of size $(1-\frac{1}{r})n$. The proof relies on the stability method, which involves the application of the container method. Consequently, we also derive bounds for independent sets within graphs generated by the random process of iteratively adding edges. This paper establishes strong type inequalities for scaled Bergman spaces on the complex half-plane with respect to the area measure. Although the associated linear extension operator is not bounded in $L^p$ for $p \in (1,2)\cup(2,\infty)$, we prove that it satisfies the weak-type $(2,2)$ condition and all strong-type $(p,q)$ inequalities where $p,q\in(1,2)$ and $1\le 1/2-1/q\le 1-1/p$. Consequently, we derive hypercontractive inequalities for the scaled Bergman operator. Additionally, we demonstrate that the $n$-dimensional scaled Bergman operator on the vectorial half-space exhibits analogous behavior. While certain $n$-dimensional linear extension operators between Bergman spaces are bounded, this is not the case for those with values or ranges in Bergman-Sobolev spaces. Therefore, our findings primarily address specific extension operators. We also provide strong-type inequalities for a low-pass operator on the (scaled) Bergman space of the unit ball in $\mathbb{C}^n$, which involves summing over all homogeneous polynomials of degree at most $n$. This work utilizes recent results by A. Konyagin and A. Logunov regarding extension operators from the boundary of a domain to polynomial spaces, as well as their applications to extension theorems for polynomial spaces and special classes of extension operators. Furthermore, we incorporate several original results on multiple extension operators. Finally, we offer several applications of our findings to the extension operator on the space of analytic functions and to a smooth extension operator from the boundary of the unit ball to the space of functions on the ball. One application involves a variant of the corona problem for functions on the ball that are extendable to analytic functions on a neighborhood of the closed ball. Another application concerns the extension of functions on the ball that are extendable to functions on a neighborhood of the closed ball possessing a finite Bergman-type norm. Both problems were previously solved for the case of the space of analytic functions by A. Aizenberg. We also resolve a problem posed by A. Aizenberg. One of our applications involves a novel approach to the extension of functions on the boundary of the unit ball to functions on the ball. This method utilizes the Poisson integral, which extends harmonic functions on the ball to functions on a neighborhood of the closed ball with finite Dirichlet norm. The escalating threat of the novel coronavirus has precipitated a global crisis, necessitating the rapid and accurate identification of infected individuals to contain the outbreak's spread. Consequently, there is a critical need for a swift, highly precise, and robust detection system capable of operating under resource-constrained conditions. To address this, we introduce a two-stage system that integrates high-level information extraction from low-dose X-ray images with an enhanced classifier. The first stage employs a time-distributed capsule network to effectively capture high-level features, which are subsequently passed to the second stage for final classification. The network outputs a binary label indicating the presence of the virus. Extensive experiments conducted on the Infected CT Images 2020: Low-dose CT Challenge dataset demonstrate that our proposed system surpasses existing state-of-the-art methods. Furthermore, its superior performance regarding accuracy and computational efficiency makes it particularly well-suited for deployment in real-world scenarios. The proposed system is expected to assist medical professionals in early-stage diagnosis and facilitate early intervention to mitigate the impact of the pandemic. This paper introduces formulae for the expected value and expected value of squared non-centrality parameters associated with sample moments of complex sample correlations. These formulas are applicable to various multivariate, temporal, and ordinal correlation metrics, including those for ordinal variables with more than two levels. Additionally, the paper establishes a general relationship between sample moments of the sample correlation matrix and the expected value of its inverse, a finding particularly relevant for generating the inverse of a covariance matrix in Bayesian analyses. While numerical methods exist for calculating these values, they are often computationally intensive and dependent on sample size. In contrast, the proposed analytical formulas are independent of sample size and significantly reduce computational costs. The study concludes with an outline of applications for a newly developed ordinal correlation metric named Proportional Odds Correlation (POCOR).

This text outlines the S-matrix approach to quantum gravity, originally proposed in 1966, along with its extensions to supergravity, string theory, and bounds on black-hole remnants. It also examines recent efforts to derive the Coulomb potential within this framework and the application of the S-matrix bootstrap to low-energy hadronic physics. Finally, the first two chapters are followed by four appendices that explore connections to holography, black holes, and the issues of non-unitarity and IR divergences in Lorentz-covariant quantum field theories. These topics provide additional context and support the main discussion, which is tailored for graduate students and early-career researchers. While the main text assumes only a basic familiarity with quantum mechanics, the appendices address more advanced subjects in quantum field theory and general relativity, requiring more background knowledge. The primary focus is on conceptual issues, with only minimal attention given to technical details. Consequently, readers are expected to have only a general understanding of the specific arguments presented. The aim is to provide a clear overview of the current state of the field, allowing students to better appreciate ongoing research and contribute to its advancement. This perspective is informed by four decades of engagement with these topics. The author thanks their colleagues for the privilege of working with them over the past forty years. This study addresses the uniform stabilization of Navier-Stokes equations through finite-dimensional localized feedback controls. The control region is assumed to be connected, bounded, and located within a subdomain that adheres to the $C^{2,\alpha}$ condition for some $\alpha \in (0,1)$. The uncontrolled system describes an incompressible viscous fluid under small external forces, while the controlled system incorporates a specific local feedback regulation. This regulation depends on a finite number of feedback variables corresponding to the finite-dimensional orthogonal projections of velocity within a control region. These variables are determined by the generalized Green's formula involving test functions within the same region. The control law is formulated as a finite-dimensional ordinary differential equation, with its velocity field determined by an explicit formula utilizing Green's formula and specific functions. Crucially, this local feedback regulation enhances the uniform stabilization properties of the Navier-Stokes equations within bounded domains. This improvement is achieved by utilizing the control to dampen the growth of vorticity in a local region, thereby ensuring uniform stabilization. Notably, the local feedback regulation is independent of global information. To achieve this uniform stabilization, the control must be sufficiently strong to suppress vorticity growth in a local area. This result holds for any $q \in [1, \infty)$, encompassing the critical case where $q = n/(n+1)$. Consequently, this represents the first instance of uniform stabilization in critical spaces. The primary challenge lies in the lack of sufficient regularity in the Navier-Stokes solution to apply the local feedback regulation effectively. To resolve this, the authors employ a technique to regularize the control, thereby overcoming the insufficient regularity constraint. The primary innovation of this work is the ability to stabilize the Navier-Stokes equations within a local region using a feedback regulation that depends on a finite number of variables. This approach is applicable to a broad range of problems, including those in critical spaces. Furthermore, the local feedback regulation can be utilized to control the solution to remain within a small ball in critical spaces. The paper also includes an appendix detailing the derivation of the control law. The authors aim to extend these results to other nonlinear PDEs, such as the heat equation and the Navier-Stokes equations in $\mathbb{R}^n$. Additionally, the local feedback regulation is applied to achieve local null controllability for the Navier-Stokes equations within a bounded domain.
