Recent studies have explored using natural language to explain algorithmic black-box recommendations, with LIME-RS being a prominent method in this field. However, these prior works have largely overlooked the stability of such explanations. This paper aims to assess the compliance and stability of LIME-RS by introducing a stability metric for LIME-based algorithmic explanations. We demonstrate that LIME-RS is inherently unstable when applied to algorithmic black-boxes, particularly in how it addresses user compliance. Our analysis reveals that the instability of algorithmic black-box explanations stems from the stochastic nature of the LIME approach and the inherent complexity of the underlying machine learning models. Furthermore, we identify the specific components of LIME-RS responsible for this instability and propose an instability-reduced variant. We provide an analytical proof of this reduced version's stability and support our findings with numerical experiments. Ultimately, we conclude that the instability of LIME-RS is not intrinsic to the concept of compliance explanations for algorithmic black-boxes but is instead attributable to LIME-RS itself. Additionally, we offer practical guidance for future research aiming to enhance compliance explanations for algorithmic black-boxes. Finally, we outline several potential avenues for future work in this domain. To support the community, the code for this paper is available at: https://github.com/SebastianSchaefer1992/compliance-stability-lime-rs. The paper can be accessed at: https://arxiv.org/abs/2201.07017. Our findings are expected to assist future research on compliance explanations for algorithmic black-boxes. In semiconductor quantum wells, near surfaces can alter the electronic band structure, often leading to the self-fixation of quantum confined states due to near-surface defects. This phenomenon is particularly pronounced in indium arsenide (InAs) quantum wells because of their high indium content. We demonstrate that this fixation can be mitigated by employing indium-rich gradient buffers, which enable adatom relaxation and reduce near-surface damage. Through photoemission spectroscopy, we compare InAs quantum wells fabricated with gradient buffers against those made without them. Our findings indicate that gradient buffers facilitate adatom relaxation, shift the Fermi level, and reduce near-surface damage. Furthermore, we confirm that these wells maintain a constant capacitance, indicating that the gradient buffer does not induce additional capacitance. These results highlight the critical role of gradient buffers in managing near-surface effects in InAs quantum wells. Finally, we discuss the implications of these findings for developing high-performance indium arsenide-based quantum devices. Deep neural networks (DNNs) are vulnerable to adversarial attacks, where subtly altered inputs trigger incorrect outputs. Although various defenses exist, they often suffer from limited generality. Regional Queries (RQ) represent a recent, novel defense strategy that enhances DNN robustness against adversarial examples by incorporating an auxiliary mechanism. This approach enables models to focus on regions unlikely to contain adversarial perturbations, thereby improving resilience. However, the effectiveness of RQ is not guaranteed across all attack scenarios. We demonstrate that RQ fails to boost robustness when attackers have access to the regional mask, as seen in black-box gradient attacks. Furthermore, we identify specific conditions under which RQ is most potent, revealing that it excels in scenarios where models previously struggled, such as attacks originating from noisy or corrupted images. Additionally, we show that RQ can be adapted for data poisoning attacks and that it scales efficiently to large-scale datasets. Finally, we analyze the trade-off between robustness and accuracy, proving that RQ allows for improved accuracy on clean data without sacrificing robustness. Our comprehensive evaluation offers new insights into defense design and highlights avenues for future research. Code is available at https://github.com/ashwinb/RegionalQueries-Code. This paper introduces a novel and straightforward algorithm for calculating the exact cost of optimal transport between two $n \times 2$ or $2 \n\times n$ "collinear" transport plans, achieving linear time complexity, $O(\max\{m,n\})$. This result stems from a new class of "triangular" plans, for which we derive a precise, tight characterization of the exact optimal transport cost and marginals that surpasses current $O((m+n)\log\log\max\{m,n\})$ approximate bounds. This advancement enables the first linear-time exact computation for general $O(m+n)$ "pyramidal" plans, advancing toward the ultimate goal of linear-time exact optimal transport for $O(mn)$ plans, $O(mn)\log\log\max\{m,n\}$ approximate algorithms, or $O((m+n)\log\log\max\{m,n\})$ exact approximate algorithms. The primary innovation is a "shifted" Sinkhorn iteration, which offers a new perspective on the algorithm's behavior and facilitates the creation of a new "zoom in" procedure. This approach allows for the construction of a precise "stopping criterion" that guarantees exact solutions in linear time. Additionally, this work presents the first linear-time precise computation for any $O(mn)$ "annular" plan, defined as the optimal transport problem between two $[a,b]\subset\mathbb{R}^d$ point clouds. This represents a significant step toward the broader objective of linear-time exact algorithms for arbitrary $[a,b]\subset\mathbb{R}^d$ point clouds. Finally, the developed techniques yield the first linear-time exact algorithm for the $k$-center clustering problem with outliers. Empirical evaluations demonstrate that the proposed algorithm is up to 100 times faster than the fastest existing optimal transport algorithm. Furthermore, applications include linear-time clustering of images and video, as well as linear-time and precise phylogenetic tree reconstruction. The code is accessible at https://github.com/mbertin-hubert/RapidSinkhorn. The AU Microscopii (AU Mic) system serves as a critical benchmark for studying the evolution of planetary systems around active M-dwarfs. This study investigates the temporal variability of AU Mic's far-ultraviolet (FUV) emission by analyzing archival data from the International Ultraviolet Explorer (IUE), the Galaxy Evolution Explorer (GALEX), and the Hubble Space Telescope (HST). Our observations reveal that the star's accretion-driven FUV emission remains stable during quiescent phases, while coronal emission shows significant variability. The FUV light curve exhibits a strong correlation with H$\alpha$ emission, indicating that accretion events drive most FUV variability. Furthermore, FUV flux increases by approximately 1.5 to 2 times during flares compared to the previous 10 days, a finding consistent with prior observations of flaring M-dwarfs. We demonstrate that the FUV emission from AU Mic's accretion streams is sufficient to destroy the atmospheres of both AU Mic b and c. Additionally, we find that FUV photoevaporation can account for the observed low mass and radius of AU Mic b. Finally, we estimate the cumulative FUV flux received by the system throughout its history, revealing that the young system has been exposed to a FUV flux roughly 100 times higher than that received by the Solar System. These findings underscore the necessity of accounting for high FUV fluxes when studying the evolution of planetary systems around active M-dwarfs. This framework is applicable to any resistive substance, though the drag coefficient model specifically represents a resistive environment. We introduce the SkyMapper Quasar Database, a collection of 1,000 quasar candidates identified through the Ultra-bright High-redshift Quasars from SkyMapper (UHQS) survey. These objects exhibit $r$-band magnitudes of $r \leq 14.5$ and $i$-band colors of $r-i \leq 1.0$, with redshifts determined via spectroscopy. The dataset comprises 790 new quasar discoveries, including 600 previously unspectroscoped objects, alongside 210 quasars and 90 galaxies already known to the community. The UHQS survey covered approximately 1,000 square degrees, reaching a depth of $r \leq 19.5$ and a color depth of $r-i \leq 1.0$. Analysis of the database's luminosity function (LF) reveals that at $z \geq 3$, it follows a power law with a slope of $-2.5 \pm 0.1$, a trend consistent with $z \leq 2$ but steeper than LF models derived from deep surveys. Furthermore, the radiant end of the LF at $z \geq 3$ is characterized by a slope of $-1.5 \pm 0.1$, indicating a decline in number density toward the highest luminosities. This slope is flatter than that observed at $z \leq 2$ and suggests a maximum absolute magnitude of $M_{1450} = -29.5$. The distribution of $M_{1450}$ for $z \geq 3$ is notably broader than at $z \leq 2$, implying that the most luminous quasars at $z \geq 3$ are intrinsically more variable. These findings highlight the existence of an extreme quasar population at $z \geq 3$ that is both more luminous and more variable than their lower-redshift counterparts. The UHQS database offers a unique opportunity to study this population, which is largely inaccessible to current deep surveys. We conclude that the UHQS Quasar Database is essential for understanding the evolution of the most extreme quasars. The data are accessible via http://skydatabases.astronomy.org.au/skydatabases/UHQS. We introduce a method for directly observing charge tunneling between a quantum dot and a superconductor using capacitance measurements. By integrating a high-impedance gate near the tunneling site with standard low-impedance gates connected to readout resonators, we modulate the charge dot state and directly link these changes to the capacitance of the high-impedance gate. This approach enables the direct detection of charge transfer without requiring time-resolved measurements. Furthermore, gate sensitivity can be enhanced by utilizing gate-capacitance matrices to pinpoint optimal locations for detecting charge tunneling. This technique is broadly applicable to investigate charge dynamics in various systems, including quantum dots, quantum wires, quantum Hall edge states, and Majorana modes. Furthermore, we demonstrate the direct observation of quasiparticle charge tunneling into and out of a superconductor, which is mediated by Majorana modes and involves a charge transfer of $2e$. This finding confirms that these charge tunneling events between the quantum dot and superconductor are predominantly driven by Majorana modes. This conclusion is supported by the observation of tunneling between two superconductors, which does not involve the quantum dot and is not mediated by Majorana modes, resulting in a charge transfer of $-4e$. These findings provide direct evidence regarding the nature of charge tunneling between a superconductor and a quantum dot. Additionally, the presented methods are widely applicable for investigating the charge-tunneling mechanisms of Majorana modes. This is illustrated by employing gate detection to measure the interaction between a spin-polarized Andreev bound state and a charge-excited Andreev bound state, which involves a charge transfer of $-4e$. This result is consistent with the expectation that the coupling between these two states is mediated by Majorana modes. Thus, gate detection serves as a valuable tool for investigating the nature of charge tunneling mediated by Majorana modes. Finally, our findings suggest that gate detection can aid in the detection of Majorana modes. This is demonstrated by the successful detection of Andreev bound states using gate detection, which shows gate-dependent parity transitions between the ground and charge-excited states. These findings indicate that gate detection can contribute to the detection of Majorana modes. Overall, this work establishes a foundation for the further development of gate detection as a versatile tool for investigating charge dynamics in quantum systems. This research focuses on the conservation laws framework, specifically addressing entropy solutions to balance laws. It introduces two novel contraction properties—entropic contraction and generalized entropic contraction—designed to facilitate uniqueness proofs and establish $L^1$-contraction. The study demonstrates superposition formulas for these laws and presents examples of systems where neither of the new contraction types nor the classical ones are fulfilled. Furthermore, examples are provided where entropy dissipation alone is insufficient to guarantee solution uniqueness. Finally, the paper offers a uniqueness theorem for the generalized entropic case, alongside a contrasting scenario where this theorem does not apply. Additionally, the work confirms the $L^1$-contraction property within the framework of generalized entropic contraction. To achieve this, a new concept of solution is proposed, termed the "generalized entropy solution." The paper concludes by illustrating systems for which this new solution concept aligns with the standard entropy solution definition. These general findings are supported by various examples, including gas dynamics models and heat transfer equations. Gas dynamics applications extend to isothermal flow, pressureless flow, and Euler equations in both one and three dimensions. Moreover, specific instances involving heat transfer equations are examined. In the context of Euler equations, the study addresses a longstanding open problem regarding the uniqueness of entropy solutions. These results rely on the concept of "relaxed entropy solutions," which represent a generalization of entropy solutions originally proposed by the first author. Relaxing the strict entropy solution definition enables the demonstration of the $L^1$-contraction property for entropy solutions. This confirmation serves as the primary contribution toward resolving the uniqueness problem for entropy solutions in gas dynamics. To ensure the validity of these results, the paper also introduces the concept of "generalized entropy solutions," thereby advancing the solution hierarchy beyond "entropy solutions." This work marks a significant step toward addressing the uniqueness challenge for entropy solutions in gas dynamics. Additionally, it marks the first instance of an entropy solution being proven to possess the $L^1$-contraction property. The paper also explores the relationship between entropy and generalized entropy solutions, alongside the broader implications of these solutions within the systems of preservation laws framework. These concepts are further supported by various gas dynamics examples, such as pressureless flow, isothermal flow, and Euler equations across one, two, and three dimensions. Furthermore, the study addresses uniqueness issues regarding entropy solutions in pressureless fluid dynamics and heat transfer. Creating a 360° "Eternal View" from a single input image is a valuable tool for real-world applications like creating 3D virtual real estate listings. While recent methods attempt to generate these views, they often produce unrealistic results, such as duplicate objects or incorrect colors, because they lack constraints to ensure the output matches the input. To address this, we present DiffDreamer, a reliable Single-view Eternal View Producer (SEVEP) that utilizes conditional diffusion models. By leveraging the high generative capabilities of these models, DiffDreamer creates high-quality Eternal Views (EVs) that maintain the textures and colors of the original images. Specifically, DiffDreamer employs a high-resolution conditional diffusion model to enhance generation quality and a self-supervised training strategy to improve the realism of the background. Additionally, the method uses a specialized transformer-based prior model to enforce consistency between the input and output images. Extensive experiments demonstrate that DiffDreamer outperforms state-of-the-art EV generators in both realism and similarity to the source image. Furthermore, user studies confirm that the generated results are highly appealing to the general public. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/ChenYi-CH/DiffDreamer. This paper introduces a framework that integrates prediction, performance improvement, and regulation into a single, purely data-driven approach for networked processes. Specifically for networked systems of biological or technological processes, we utilize a non-parametric, unsupervised machine learning technique to generate a network of state-predictors. These state-predictors are derived from historical data and states of neighboring processes without requiring a process model, thereby capturing the network's intrinsic dynamics. Consequently, state-predictors with superior performance can be identified and extracted. We demonstrate that the prediction accuracy of these state-predictors directly correlates with the communication topology of networked processes. Leveraging this relationship, we propose a performance enhancement method that optimizes the network's communication topology to minimize prediction errors. Furthermore, we develop a state-regulator that optimizes the process state to achieve desired performance, showing that its performance aligns with that of the state-predictors. Finally, we apply networked processes modeling, prediction, performance enhancement, and regulation to the networked SIS epidemic model using real-world data from the COVID-19 pandemic in the United States. Our findings indicate that networked processes with high prediction performance are associated with high infection rates, suggesting they are more likely to occur in regions with high population density. Additionally, we show that the proposed performance enhancement approach outperforms existing methods in both achieving low infection rates and minimizing control energy. To our knowledge, this represents the first application of network process modeling, prediction, and performance enhancement to the COVID-19 epidemic model. Numerical simulations confirm the proposed framework's effectiveness. [The source code is available at: https://github.com/AmirHosseinR/Network-Process-Prediction-and-Regulation]. Experimental and numerical investigations examine the breakup of a liquid film coating a fiber within a shear flow. The initial state involves a uniform liquid layer on a stationary, elastic fiber that can expand radially in response to slip-induced stress from the surrounding fluid. As the surrounding fluid slows, relative slip between the liquid and the fiber generates an axial slip velocity at their interface. This slip slip triggers a reconfiguration of the liquid's cross-sectional shape, initiating Rayleigh-Plateau instability in the presence of axial slip. We analyze the growth rate and characteristic wavelength of this slip-augmented instability as functions of slip velocity and other relevant parameters. Furthermore, we evaluate how slip-augmentation impacts the breakup process and the resulting drop spacing, demonstrating that it can be amplified by up to an order of magnitude due to the fiber's radial compliance. These findings are corroborated by high-speed imaging and time-lapse microscopy images documenting the complete breakup process, which align with our theoretical predictions. Our numerical simulations utilize an axisymmetric formulation of the Navier-Stokes equations with surface and slip-induced stress jump boundary conditions. Finally, we discuss the broader implications of these findings for both fundamental understanding and potential applications. Additionally, it may influence the formation of secondary droplets or liquid rings during the retraction of liquid droplets from solid substrates. **Context:** Ultrasound imaging is increasingly utilized in clinical practice to assess pediatric scoliosis. However, interpreting these images requires specialized training, creating a significant barrier to widespread adoption. Robotic ultrasound systems offer a solution by ensuring consistent probe positioning and pressure, as well as precise movement along the spine. **Objective:** The present study aims to evaluate the dependability of robotic ultrasound imaging for scoliosis when compared to manual techniques. **Material and Methods:** Scoliosis cases were recruited from the Department of Orthopedics at the University Medical Center Göttingen. Ultrasound scans from 20 patients (ages 10–17) were performed using both robotic and manual systems. The robotic system employed an optical navigation system to guide the probe along the spine's longitudinal axis. **Results:** Both methods successfully identified the entire spine in 90% of patients. Discrepancies existed in 10% of cases: seven patients showed higher segment coverage with the robotic system, while three had greater coverage with manual imaging. **Conclusion:** Ultrasound imaging of scoliosis using a robotic system demonstrates high dependability. Future research will investigate the clinical relevance of the observed differences in segment coverage between the two methods. **Discussion:** The consistent and reproducible nature of robotic ultrasound suggests it could facilitate new diagnostic and monitoring approaches for scoliosis. With the increasing popularity of social media, online hate speech has become more pervasive, posing significant threats to individuals and groups. Although general methods for detecting hate speech exist, they often suffer from low accuracy due to the absence of specific target information. To overcome this limitation, this paper introduces a novel approach for identifying hate speech directed at specific attributes. The method involves training a model to extract key characteristics from input text, which are then utilized to construct a classifier for detecting attributed hate speech. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed model outperforms existing state-of-the-art approaches in accurately recognizing targeted hate speech. Furthermore, the effectiveness of the model has been validated through an ablation study. Finally, the study analyzes the detected attributed hate speech to offer fresh insights into the root causes of online hatred. This paper outlines the design and experimental assessment of a new control strategy designed to achieve flat motion profiles in a robot joint. The strategy merges classical control methods with an optimization process that maximizes the flatness index, defined as the ratio between actual and maximum acceleration. The resulting controller relies solely on position and velocity data from the motor. Flatness-based control was evaluated against a traditional Position Hold (PH) method, which utilizes position, velocity, and current feedback. While the primary sensor (encoder) for the flatness-based approach failed during testing, the method still outperformed the PH technique. This outcome demonstrates the potential of the developed approach to surpass traditional Position Hold strategies, even when relying on lower-grade sensors compared to more complex control schemes. Furthermore, the study confirms the robustness of flatness-based control against the model parameter uncertainties typical of robot joints. The paper also addresses challenges in tuning the optimal trajectory duration and damping factor. Experimental results indicate that increasing the damping factor enhances the stability of the transient response. Finally, the paper presents an optimization framework for selecting the most suitable control parameters. The proposed flatness-based control was tested on an industrial robot joint, with results compared against other strategies reported in the literature. The paper includes an analysis of the advantages and disadvantages of flatness-based control relative to other approaches. The tested joint features a direct drive motor, a harmonic drive, and a harmonic reducer. To broaden the scope of the experiments, secondary sensors (resolvers) originally mounted on the output link were removed. The loss of these secondary sensors significantly increased tracking errors and reduced the robot's overall performance. The paper concludes that the primary benefit of flatness-based control is its ability to deliver high-performance results even after the de-coupling of secondary sensors. **Background:** Life course epidemiology seeks to clarify how early-life factors influence the timing of when adverse health outcomes occur. **Aim:** We propose Multiple State Evaluation (MSTE), a novel strategy for analyzing time-to-event data from populations experiencing multiple health transitions. **Methods:** MSTE is a model-based approach that extends traditional state-transition models. It is applicable to datasets containing multiple observations per subject across varying time points, enabling the estimation of transition rates between all possible states. **Results:** Using a simulated dataset, we demonstrated that MSTE can accurately recover known transition rates even when data are incomplete or missing. **Application:** We applied MSTE to a 30-year life course health trajectory of 1,000 myocardial infarction patients, tracking state changes over 100 time points from age 30 to 120. The analysis revealed that while inflammation and obesity increased transition rates to adverse states during early life, these associations diminished after age 50. Conversely, the protective effects of exercise against adverse states were most pronounced during midlife. **Conclusion:** MSTE offers a robust statistical framework for elucidating how early-life factors impact the timing of time-to-event outcomes throughout the life course. We introduce a quadrature technique for evaluating the molecular response to an external stimulus, specifically addressing the $n$-electron molecular response equation featuring Coulomb interactions, which is solved on a multi-site basis. The approach is applied at the Hartree-Fock level using the PySCF software and in-house developed response and perturbation routines. To facilitate efficient computation, the Coulomb two-electron integrals are represented via a Coulomb expansion, which transforms the integral-differential response equation into a system of algebraic equations solvable through standard linear algebra methods. Numerical tests are conducted on the water ($H_2O$) and methanol ($CH_3OH$) molecules. The presented results include first hyperpolarizabilities, single-frequency second hyperpolarizabilities, and frequency-dependent second hyperpolarizabilities. Additionally, we report frequency-dependent second hyperpolarizabilities for methanol at various levels of theory, utilizing single and double $\zeta$ basis sets. These findings demonstrate that the quadrature method is both efficient and straightforward to implement. Furthermore, the study confirms that second hyperpolarizables for $H_2O$ and $CH_3OH$ are accurately described using a single double-$\zeta$ basis set. Finally, we observe that frequency-dependent second hyperpolarizables for methanol are significantly influenced by electron-electron Coulomb interactions. This is evidenced by the substantial differences between results from PySCF's Hartree-Fock implementation and our Coulomb-based quadrature method. Consequently, this serves as a proof-of-principle for a computational framework capable of addressing many-body response properties on multi-electron systems. Such a framework is essential for investigating the impact of Coulomb interactions on frequency-dependent nonlinear optical properties in many-electron systems. This work establishes a foundation for future investigations into the effects of Coulomb interactions on frequency-dependent nonlinear optical properties within many-electron systems. Hothouse Earth scenarios, where elevated greenhouse gas concentrations drive global temperatures 3–5°C above preindustrial levels, are examined to assess their impact on the hydrologic cycle. Although a warmer climate is anticipated to intensify precipitation, the temporal and spatial scales of these events remain uncertain. By applying a theoretical framework to the coupling between the land and ocean components of a water balance model, we demonstrate that episodic downpours are likely to occur in these hot-house settings. This novel mechanism stems from a delayed response in the ocean component, which amplifies the initial moisture gain following a brief warm period. Consequently, the land surface experiences a prolonged increase in the Clausius-Clapeyron rate of evaporation. This delayed feedback creates a positive feedback loop, resulting in a significant surge in precipitation. Furthermore, we show that this mechanism is more pronounced in low-latitude regions, indicating a greater likelihood of downpours in the equatorial band. These episodic downpours are projected to increase by 100% to 200% in a 3°C world and exceed 300% in a 5°C world. While the model does not account for the atmosphere's radiative balance, we argue that this process remains viable in the real world, as the atmosphere is expected to reach a new radiative equilibrium through changes in clouds and other factors. The heightened frequency of downpours in hothouse environments could have profound implications for both human and natural systems. For instance, the risk of catastrophic flooding could rise dramatically, and the transport of nutrients and pollutants via runoff from rivers could be substantially amplified. Finally, we demonstrate that the model can be extended to include a simple representation of vegetation, which further reinforces the Clausius-Clapeyron feedback. Overall, the increased frequency of downpours in modeled hothouse environments represents a fundamental shift in the climate system, with potential consequences for society and ecosystems. This study underscores the need to integrate episodic downpours into climate models to accurately predict the impacts of further global warming. This paper introduces the twistor lifts of the recent elevated-spin formulation of (self-dual) Yang-Mills theory. By incorporating fields with non-zero twistor weight alongside physical fields, we construct the corresponding master action and outline the process for obtaining theory-specific equations through descent. As an application, we present an increased-twistor-field extension of self-dual Yang-Mills that yields the previously described single-field model upon descent. In this framework, the twistor extension of the holomorphic Chern-Simons theory on the twistor space $PT$ governs all interactions. We also discuss how to adapt "no-twistor" interactions for the pure elevated-spin Yang-Mills theory via descent, noting that this results in a non-deforming extension involving fields with non-zero twistor weight. Furthermore, we demonstrate that a specific linearization of the increased-twistor extension of $\int_{PT} \omega \wedge \omega \wedge \omega$ leads to an elevated-spin extension of the self-dual Yang-Mills theory through covariantization. Finally, we offer some preliminary observations regarding the eponymous "no-twistor" extension of the Chern-Simons form on $PT$. Deep learning has emerged as a highly effective tool for automatic image categorization. However, the necessity of large-scale, high-quality datasets and the substantial computational resources demanded by these models often restrict their application, particularly in fields like medicine. This paper introduces a robust image categorization framework designed to enhance the robustness of medical image classification models against label noise. The proposed approach integrates two primary strategies: first, it employs the Bayesian Generalized Expectation Maximization (BGEM) algorithm to mitigate label noise within the training dataset; second, it utilizes a regularization mechanism based on a Gaussian Process to enhance robustness during the training and testing phases. The study first investigates the characteristics of noisy medical datasets and the impact of label noise on deep learning models. Subsequently, the label-noise alleviation mechanism is detailed, demonstrating its ability to refine training data by removing erroneous labels. Finally, the model is trained using this mechanism to validate its efficacy. Experimental results indicate that the proposed framework outperforms existing state-of-the-art image categorization methods. Furthermore, the computational efficiency of the mechanism is analyzed, confirming its suitability for practical deployment in medical imaging. Timed definitions offer an enhanced variant of standard hol_defint, allowing proof terms to remain valid only up to specific computational durations. This paper explores the theoretical foundations of timed definitions and demonstrates their implementation within the HOL4 theorem prover. We examine several application scenarios, including extended computation and circuit analysis, and contrast our hol4_timed_defint tool with the prior hol_time_defint solution from holmes. Furthermore, we validate the correctness and soundness of our approach by providing proof terms for key lemmas and theorems. Our proposed methodology successfully increases discursion depth, enabling the system to automatically discharge complex lemmas that were previously unprovable. Additionally, we illustrate that timed definitions effectively manage problems involving extensive hardware computation. However, the application section acknowledges certain limitations of the current implementation, which we have also discussed. Given these constraints, our implementation serves as a foundational framework that can be readily adapted for other methodologies. Finally, we emphasize that the correctness proofs for timed definitions, which rely on inductive reasoning, can also be executed within HOL itself. Timed definitions function as meta-proofs, thereby providing a mechanism to prove their own correctness. Our implementation reflects this approach, as we have explicitly demonstrated. Our contribution to the community includes the hol4_timed_defint tool, which is available on GitHub. We believe this tool will significantly advance research utilizing timed definitions. Furthermore, we have showcased a case study on program verification, which also leverages hol4_timed_defint, available on our project website. We hope this case study will inspire additional applications within the broader community. Overall, we demonstrate that hol4_timed_defint is more flexible and powerful than hol_time_defint, and we look forward to its adoption by various research groups. We extend our gratitude to the reviewers for their insightful comments and suggestions.

This study introduces a framework for enhancing the boundary turbulence indicator, $u_{bu}$, which quantifies the thickness of the turbulent boundary layer in high-Reynolds-number wall-bounded flows. This indicator is part of a coherent framework used to forecast shear stress, mixing, and wall pressure statistics across various flow types, including canonical, separated, and rotating scenarios. The model's prediction of $u_{bu}$ is significantly improved by calibrating its three empirical constants using data from ten distinct twodimensional separated flows. This required developing a machine learning-based data processing method to accurately estimate $u_{bu}$ from high-fidelity numerical simulations. The resulting improvements enable more precise predictions of $u_{bu}$ in complex three-dimensional flows, such as the rotating disk and the oscillating airfoil wake trailing behind the NACA0012 airfoil. Furthermore, the elevated levels of $u_{bu}$ observed in the optimized model for the oscillating airfoil correlate with increased turbulence production, thereby supporting more accurate forecasts of other turbulence metrics in the same flow. These findings underscore the value of the optimized model for generating instantaneous turbulent flow data, which can subsequently inform the prediction of unsteady flow-induced loads. Additionally, the study demonstrates that machine learning offers a viable approach for creating coarser, more efficient, and highly accurate turbulence models. These advances are critical for advancing the next generation of high-fidelity computational fluid dynamics tools, which will facilitate more accurate and cost-effective design and analysis of unsteady, rotating, and transonic flows. We investigate self-dual vortex/quantum Hall solitons within a generalized non-linear sigma model (NLSM) that incorporates both standard Born-Infeld and logarithmic Skyrme terms. This specific combination enables the model to remain asymptotically flat while maintaining self-duality. By solving the model equations for a single vortex, we derive the energy as a function of flux. We demonstrate that the logarithmic Skyrme term is essential for achieving full asymptotic flatness and can regulate self-dual soliton energies to a finite value. Furthermore, we establish that the model supports self-dual multi-vortex solitons, where we analyze the asymptotic behavior of individual vortices and the total energy. We also detail the procedure for constructing approximate solutions with finite energy. Finally, we outline an extension of the framework to a "quantum" Skyrme field, showing that it supports AS-maps and self-dual solitons. In this context, we derive the energy and explicitly construct self-dual multi-vortex solitons. Additionally, we generalize the model to include maps with non-trivial degree, which support AS-maps and finite energy configurations. We provide an analysis of the energy spectrum for maps with degree $n$, highlighting a family of AS-maps where vortices reside on the real axis. These findings suggest that similar solitons may exist in other effective theories, such as various non-linear sigma models featuring AS-maps with real parameters. Consequently, these results may offer valuable insights for both condensed matter and high-energy physics applications. Notably, our findings regarding logarithmic Skyrme fields and their ability to ensure asymptotic flatness are directly relevant to the recent advancement of asymptotically flat axion crystals. We also address the issue of asymptotic behavior in maps with non-trivial degree, demonstrating that our approach extends to these maps as well. Finally, we show that our findings are applicable to a broad class of NLSMs that admit AS-maps and finite energy maps with non-trivial degree. This broader category encompasses various effective field theories in both condensed matter and high-energy physics. We introduce a Hofstadler-Weyl semimetal, representing the first Hofstadler model to exhibit Weyl semimetal characteristics under external fields that break time-reversal symmetry. This phase emerges when the Hofstadler mesh aligns with the spacing of lattice sites projected onto the plane perpendicular to the magnetic field. The lattice potential, characterized by a sufficiently large flux per unit cell, partitions the electronic spectrum into bands separated by large gaps. Consequently, the low-energy effective theory is determined by the specific set of gaps adjacent to the Fermi level, which in turn defines the positions of the Weyl points. Furthermore, we demonstrate that certain configurations of these Weyl points can be manipulated by adjusting the external fields, offering significant potential for experimental control. Finally, we calculate the anomalous Hall conductivity for various distributions of the Weyl points, revealing that the lattice-induced gaps generate extremely large values for this quantity. This suggests that Hofstadler-Weyl semimetals could display exceptionally strong anomalous Hall effects, even at relatively high magnetic fields. Additionally, we show that the Hofstadler model satisfies the criteria for a lattice version of the Chern-Simns term, which may further contribute to the magnitude of the anomalous Hall conductivity. Overall, Hofstadler semimetals appear to hold great promise for investigating the physics of Weyl semimetals at strong flux levels. This is particularly relevant given the recent experimental progress in realizing Hofstadler moiré lattices. We anticipate that the Hofstadler model will become a valuable tool for exploring the fundamental physics of Weyl semimetals. Specifically, the tunability of Weyl point positions within this model offers new degrees of freedom for investigating the topological characteristics of Weyl semimetals. Finally, we outline the necessary experimental conditions for observing Hofstadler-Weyl semimetals. Notably, we propose that certain types of Weyl semimetals, such as Mn$_3$Sn, may already fall into this category. This is because the model allows for the prediction of Weyl point positions based on the spectrum of a single electron within the unit cell. This approach could prove useful in guiding experimental efforts to discover materials with specific target features. We have created and experimentally validated a hybrid dielectric-plasmonic nanoantenna capable of achieving effective and unidirectional light emission. This system comprises a silicon nanopillar integrated with a gold nanosphere, positioned on a gold film situated above a silicon waveguide. By carefully selecting the sizes of the nanoparticles and adjusting the excitation conditions, we successfully coupled the localized surface plasmon modes of the gold nanosphere with the guided modes of the silicon waveguide. This hybridization of resonances results in the creation of unidirectional, luminous, and highly efficient light sources. These nanoantennas can function as emitters when excited by localized light or as sensors when excited by waveguide modes. This proposed nanoantenna system offers a novel, simple, and effective approach for developing unidirectional and highly efficient integrated optical components, such as nanoemitters, sensors, and sensors that operate within the guided optical system. Furthermore, the unidirectional emission from these nanoantennas could facilitate the development of new, simpler, and more efficient integrated laser sources. The interaction of electromagnetic waves with granular materials has been a subject of significant research interest, driven by both fundamental scientific inquiry and practical applications. This study focuses on the phenomenon of "dipole decoupling" within such materials, which results in the counterintuitive appearance of total light absorption. The proposed theory posits that incident photons are completely absorbed by individual dipoles, causing their oscillations to remain uncoupled to the external optical field. Although this concept is not entirely novel, the current work provides a fundamental understanding of the underlying physics and validates the mechanism through experimental measurements. Furthermore, the study compares these experimental results with finite-difference time-domain simulations and analytical models, confirming the Anomalous Shielding Theory. This study investigates the electronic properties of silicene supported on hexagonal boron nitride (hBN) using first-principles calculations. Specifically, we examine how Mn adatoms modify the Dirac cone within the Dirac energy gap. Our findings indicate that adatoms situated above the Si surface break sublattice symmetry, opening a bandgap in the Dirac cone. The size of this gap correlates directly with the adatom's vertical distance from the Si sheet; notably, Mn atoms positioned 3.0 Å above the sheet open a gap of approximately 0.1 eV. Furthermore, the adatoms induce an on-site potential on the Si atoms, generating an electronic dipole moment. Additionally, the spin-polarized adatoms produce an exchange potential that splits the valence and conduction bands near the Dirac cone. Finally, the presence of magnetic moments from the adatoms results in magnetic ordering among the adatoms. These results demonstrate that the electronic characteristics of spin-polarized silicene on hBN can be tuned by the position and type of adatoms. Such materials hold significant promise for spintronic and spin-wave device applications. Sgr A East, a radio source situated approximately 8 kpc from the Galactic center, is hypothesized to be the remnant of a supernova explosion involving a massive star. The spatial distribution of its emission is characterized by a central region roughly 10 pc in diameter, exhibiting radial symmetry, alongside an elongated structure spanning about 100 pc along an east-west axis. This paper aims to clarify the origin of this source by investigating the location of the supernova explosion. We propose a model in which a high-velocity outflow from the explosion site propagates through a low-density medium, subsequently filling a higher-density region to generate the central emission. The elongated structure is formed by this high-velocity outflow expanding into an even lower-density medium. By applying a self-similar expansion model to the observed radio source, we determine that the explosion occurred roughly 10 pc from the center. This finding is consistent with the presence of a high-mass star cluster in that area. Furthermore, we examine the initial conditions of the explosion site, including the density of the surrounding medium and the velocity of the outflow. Finally, we discuss the viability of this model for Sgr A East and compare it with other radio sources generated by stellar explosions. These findings offer valuable insights into the physical conditions of the progenitor star and the surrounding environment. Additionally, this study underscores the necessity of high-resolution observations to investigate the origin of Sgr A East. The scarcity of training data remains a significant hurdle in text classification. Artificial oversampling methods offer a solution by generating additional samples from the limited original data. This study evaluates various oversampling techniques across multiple categories, examining their performance under different curation strategies. The research investigates how the degree of overlap among synthesized samples influences classification accuracy and explores the impact of varying original sample sizes on model performance. Ultimately, this work aims to elucidate the effects of diverse synthesizer configurations to guide future applications in large-scale text classification. The experiments were conducted using three distinct text synthesizers on three different datasets. To address the challenge of multi-category classification, the study employs a standard one-versus-all strategy. The original datasets utilized are the English Wikipedia category pages (for the three 10-category experiments) and the SemEval-2013 Task 15 (original 6-category dataset). Synthesized samples were generated using three distinct methods: WordNet-based synthesizers, SynSense, and Sense2Syn, all of which leverage lexical knowledge bases. To manage computational demands, a sampling strategy was implemented to limit processing to a maximum of 5,000 samples per category. Furthermore, to mitigate the "cold-start" problem, a warm-start strategy was adopted, utilizing models trained on smaller datasets as initialization for larger datasets. Finally, a standard one-versus-all classifier was trained on samples from each category. Given the substantial computational requirements, a grid search was conducted to identify optimal hyperparameters for the synthesized datasets. Finally, results were aggregated by calculating mean accuracy across all categories rather than averaging individual category accuracies. The outcomes indicate that: (1) leveraging lexical knowledge base (LKB) resources is highly effective for multi-category classification; (2) WordNet-based LKB methods generally outperform SynSense and Sense2Syn LKB approaches; (3) sampling strategies significantly affect performance, particularly when dealing with limited original data; (4) increasing the volume of original data enhances the efficacy of LKB-based oversampling; and (5) the degree of overlap in synthesized samples is a critical factor influencing multi-category classification accuracy. These findings suggest that LKB-enhanced oversampling is a viable approach for multi-category classification tasks. However, the study also notes that the current sampling strategy may not be optimal for datasets with an extremely high number of categories, such as the 100-category YouTube Lakh dataset. The COVID-19 pandemic has sparked intense interest in how regional news organizations have responded. This research examines the correlation between news coverage, regional audience volume, and COVID metrics (cases, fatalities, and vaccinations) across the 500 largest U.S. regional outlets, covering the period from April 2020 to April 2021. Coverage was quantified by analyzing daily press releases from the organizations' blogs, while audience data was sourced from the Pressforward Audience Insight platform. The study found no significant correlation between news coverage and the pandemic's progression (cases, fatalities, or vaccinations). However, coverage was positively correlated with audience size. Although the study's cross-sectional design prevents definitive conclusions regarding the causes of coverage volume or variations in audience size, it offers valuable insights for news organizations aiming to enhance coverage or boost audience engagement. Furthermore, the findings indicate that these organizations can effectively leverage existing tools to measure coverage volume and audience size for evaluating coverage quality and effectiveness. The Rapid Multipole Technique (RMT) is an efficient approach for preserving angular momentum during the integration of the Poisson equation in spectral methods. It offers the computational economy of standard spectral evolution equations, which differ from finite-difference methods only by higher-order derivative terms. This paper extends the RMT to vector fields and imposes stricter constraints on the basis functions to ensure unambiguous results. Furthermore, the method is applied to the integration of the 2.5-order general relativistic Poisson equation, with angular momentum conservation tested across low angular momentum modes up to $\ell=16$. The study confirms that the integration process inherently preserves angular momentum without requiring additional constraints. Finally, an example is provided of a neutron star perturbed by a quadrupolar mode under the slow rotation approximation. In this scenario, the gravitational potential's angular momentum is conserved to machine precision, deviating by no more than $10^{-16}$. This demonstrates that the quadrupole radiation formula accurately describes the energy and angular momentum loss of a neutron star under the weak and slow rotation approximations. Additionally, the analysis quantifies the error in the quadrupole radiation formula, which is found to be approximately 1% when the angular velocity $\omega$ is 0.1. These findings suggest that future studies of neutron star spin-down could benefit from including gravitational wave emission. Finally, the method is applicable to the slow rotation approximation of the Einstein-Klein-Gordon system, enabling the study of scalar field energy and angular momentum loss for a rotating neutron star within the test field approximation. In this context, the derived radiation formula aligns with the corresponding electromagnetic radiation formula. The code implementing this method is available at https://github.com/zhenghao1992/rapid_multipole_technique. Future work will focus on extending the RMT to higher orders. (Abridged)

Furthermore, we propose a novel method for measuring these functions using a specific set of polarization asymmetries. Our findings indicate that, when employing transverse polarized beams for both electrons and protons, the proton spin is faithfully transmitted through the interaction. We introduce a method for creating an expert system composed of multiple "parametric specialists," where each specialist possesses domain-specific knowledge defined by a multivariate regression function. These regression parameters are determined by analyzing data within the specialist's multivariate input space. The system is designed to manage the learning process and execute inference tasks across a broad input domain, even when a specialist receives an input it cannot learn to handle. To achieve this, we propose a technique that enables specialists to collaborate and interactively refine their knowledge. This approach also facilitates the assignment of new data points to the appropriate specialist. We validate our method using a teapot extraction task derived from point clouds. This demonstration highlights a key shortcoming of the specialist architecture: despite each specialist accurately learning its specific input space, they fail to extract the object. Our data enhancement solution rectifies this by providing each specialist with a more comprehensive understanding of the overall input space. Furthermore, we show that this data selection mechanism allows the system to generalize to teapots that were unseen during training. This study examines the simultaneous production of two Higgs bosons in conjunction with a vector boson at the Large Hadron Collider. The analysis focuses on a 37.4 fb$^{-1}$ proton-proton collision dataset collected by the ATLAS detector at $\sqrt{s}=$ 13 TeV. Utilizing an extended likelihood method, upper limits at 95% confidence level are established for Higgs pair production cross-sections across various final states: HZZ4l, HHZ2b2t, Htt4l, and Htt2l2nu. These bounds are derived under two scenarios: Standard Model (SM) Higgs boson pair production and Higgs production mediated by a dimension-6 effective operator. For each specific HZZ or Htt channel, the most stringent cross-section limits are reported. Furthermore, the study investigates Higgs pair production via gluon-gluon fusion followed by Z boson emission, denoted as gg->HHZ, and sets its corresponding upper limits. In every analyzed channel, the established limits for the effective operator cross-sections are found to be several orders of magnitude below the anticipated SM values. Consequently, the results indicate that the ATLAS experiment has successfully set the tightest constraints to date on Higgs pair production through effective operator interactions at the LHC. Additionally, the research explores Higgs pair production involving jet activity, specifically Hjj2l2nu and Hjj4l channels, setting upper limits for the effective operator cross-sections. For the Hjj2l2nu channel, the derived limit is approximately 1.5 times more restrictive than the previous best limit obtained by the CMS collaboration. Finally, utilizing these upper limits, the study determines the 95% confidence level constraints on the effective operator coefficient for each analysis channel. The resulting constraints on the effective operator coupling constant are also presented. Overall, this work demonstrates that ATLAS has achieved the most restrictive limits on Higgs pair production via effective operator contributions in all analyzed channels. This outcome is attributed to the detector's superior jet energy resolution and jet identification capabilities. The findings are expected to contribute to future investigations into Higgs boson self-coupling. Furthermore, the established upper limits on effective operator contributions will serve as a foundation for future research into Higgs pair production mechanisms at the LHC. The 2019 Nobel Prize in Physics was awarded for the development of two key technologies: the laser and the maser. The maser, an acronym for Microwave Amplification by Stimulated Emission of Radiation, was initially realized in 1954 in a gas discharge tube at Bell Labs. This device utilized a radio-frequency field to excite hydrogen molecules to their vibrational energy levels, creating a population inversion that enabled stimulated emission at millimeter wavelengths. Although this original maser operated at room temperature, it demanded a constant supply of molecular hydrogen. Consequently, subsequent versions cooled the system to approximately 1 K to reduce thermal vibration and prevent a reversal of the population inversion. In this study, we introduce a novel maser concept termed the "digital alkaline spin maser." This device leverages the naturally occurring nuclear spin of alkaline earth metal atoms within a room-temperature solid-state matrix, eliminating the need for gas flow or cryogenic cooling. By employing an all-digital approach, we achieve two primary benefits: (i) the ability to manipulate the spin system using arbitrary waveforms, and (ii) the application of a static field to maintain atomic species in a hyperfine state with a specific spin projection, thereby facilitating maser operation. We demonstrate that this system can sustain a maser action for several hours, driven by the long coherence times of the nuclear spin system. This digital alkaline spin maser holds significant potential for applications in quantum sensing, metrology, and communication. Furthermore, it could facilitate the operation of masers across the entire electromagnetic spectrum, thereby enhancing the capabilities of quantum radar and imaging technologies. Additionally, the system's compatibility with all-digital integrated circuits and the Internet of Things (IoT) paves the way for the widespread deployment of masers as a practical alternative to lasers and CMOS transistors. This paper investigates variations of Hodge structure over complex Siegel domains, with a specific focus on the moduli space of K3 surfaces. By applying the theory of Mumford domains, we develop a theory of generic Picard numbers for K3 surfaces. As an application, we utilize this framework to examine a conjecture by Poonen and Rubinstein regarding the frequency with which K3 surfaces attain their maximal Picard number. Furthermore, we derive an application to the transverse Kuznetsov conjecture, demonstrating that it holds true at least within the context of K3 surfaces parameterized by a non-compact Calabi-Yau moduli space. Additionally, we establish an application to the Shafer conjecture concerning the non-existence of K3 surfaces with large Picard numbers as a function of their Kodaira dimension. Our approach is particularly relevant to the work of L. Chen, who has recently constructed a family of K3 surfaces over an affine space. In this scenario, Chen's family resides within a Siegel domain, and Chen has already computed its Mumford dimension. We show that the Kuznetsov conjecture is satisfied for a subfamily of points whose size is determined by the Mumford dimension of Chen's family. Finally, we outline several open questions and areas for future research. Specifically, one line of inquiry involves the theory of generic algebraic cycles over complex analytic spaces, which extends the concepts of algebraic cycles and algebraic cycles with values in a local coefficient bundle. Another direction concerns the theory of generic Mumford domains, as many standard tools in complex geometry may fail over non-compact domains. In this context, we explore the relationship between Mumford domains and Mumford-Tate domains. Furthermore, the theory of generic Picard numbers could serve as a foundation for formulating a modern version of the Shafarevich-Mumford conjecture. This conjecture would assert that, given a Calabi-Yau moduli space $\mathcal{M}$ of K3 surfaces with $b_2(\mathcal{M})=20$ and a positive integer $k$, there exists a proper algebraic subset $Z \subset \mathcal{M}$ such that no K3 surface in $\mathcal{M} \setminus Z$ possesses a Picard number exceeding $k$. This study revisits the concept of neutral dark energy, in which neutralino dark matter gradually decays into dark energy. In this framework, neutralino decay functions as a mechanism that transforms matter into dark energy, effectively countering matter radiation. We demonstrate that the gamma radiation spectrum emitted during this decay process is highly detectable in future experiments. Specifically, the decay of Majorana fermions with electric dipole moments generates a distinctive gamma radiation signature, while decay into Majorana fermion pairs with antiparticles also produces a unique signal. Consequently, the gamma ray background offers a critical probe for understanding dark energy origins and the nature of neutralino dark matter. Our findings indicate that the gamma ray spectrum can be observed by the upcoming AMEGO mission, and to a lesser extent, by the current INTEGRAL satellite. Furthermore, we establish stringent new limits on the lifetime of neutralino dark matter, ranging from $10^{20}$ to $10^{28}$ years. Although the lower limit is comparable to previous constraints, the upper limit is significantly improved. These results are derived from the fact that the gamma radiation spectrum from neutralino decay lacks a cutoff and is easily distinguishable from other gamma-ray sources. Our analysis shows that for a neutralino mass of approximately $100\ GeV$, the gamma ray spectrum is well within the sensitivity range of AMEGO, whereas for a mass of about $1000\ TeV$, the spectrum falls within INTEGRAL's sensitivity. We conclude that future investigations into neutralino dark matter decay into dark energy should prioritize observations of the gamma radiation spectrum. This approach will enable the direct detection of neutralino decay and provide a deeper understanding of dark energy. Additionally, we note that the gamma ray spectrum from neutralino decay is not suppressed by the matter density parameter $\Omega_m$, making it a favorable channel for studying neutralino dark matter. Our findings suggest that the gamma ray spectrum is a promising avenue for future research on neutralino dark matter. Finally, we emphasize that the upper limit on the neutralino lifetime is significantly improved, and this finding should be considered in future studies of neutralino dark matter. Our conclusions highlight the potential of gamma-ray observations to advance our understanding of neutralino dark matter and dark energy. In 2018, Fournier, Kriesell, and Li introduced the concept of thick graphs, a class where the maximum genus is known to be solvable in polynomial time. This paper presents an algorithm with polynomial complexity to determine the genus of thick graphs. Additionally, we propose a conjecture suggesting this algorithm is optimal. Furthermore, our approach resolves a conjecture proposed by Fournier, Kriesell, and Li, demonstrating that their original method is not efficient. Finally, we illustrate an application of our findings in solving the Steiner genus problem for complete graphs containing one or two Steiner points. To achieve this, we generalize the definition of thick graphs and define the class of post-thick graphs, proving that this new class also admits a polynomial-time complexity algorithm for calculating the genus. We conclude by conjecturing that this method is optimal for post-thick graphs. To support this conjecture, we present an algorithm capable of decomposing the edge set of such graphs into exactly $g$ Eulerian subgraphs for any given genus $g$. The correctness of this algorithm relies on an extension of the existence theorem regarding the maximum genus of thick graphs. Consequently, we propose a conjecture asserting that the algorithm is polynomial in complexity for post-thick graphs. Our work thus establishes that the post-thick genus problem is in NP, and we conjecture it is in P. To substantiate this conjecture, we present an algorithm that estimates the maximum genus of post-thick graphs; we conjecture this algorithm is optimal, thereby proving that the post-thick maximum genus problem is NP-complete. Throughout this paper, we also address several related problems, many of which we conjecture are polynomial-time solvable. To support these claims, we provide algorithms for each case and assert their optimality. The foundational step for all these algorithms is a method we propose for estimating the genus of thick and post-thick graphs, which we conjecture to be optimal. This paper is structured into two sections. The first section outlines our approach to estimating the genus of thick graphs, while the second section details our methodology for post-thick graphs. Our primary contribution lies in this estimated genus approach, which we believe is optimal. This work was partially funded by the National Natural Science Foundation of China (Grant No. 11771018). This paper introduces and analyzes the Randomized Newton Method (RNM) for large-scale stochastic convex optimization. In this approach, a stepsize of one is applied to a step-direction derived from a subsampled Newton vector potential. We establish convergence rates for both primal and dual objectives under conditions of strong convexity and smoothness, as well as for primal constraints and dual feasibility set sizes, within the framework of bounded nonnegative matrix factorization (NMF). Additionally, we present a distributed variant, the Distributed Randomized Newton Method (DRNM), where workers compute subsampled Newton vectors independently and a coordinator aggregates them into a subsampled Newton matrix before solving a potential. For large-scale stochastic bounded NMF, we demonstrate that the DrNM iteration achieves linear convergence in both primal and dual variables. Furthermore, we extend the RNM analysis to a broader class of problems, offering convergence rates for weakly convex and smooth objectives, weakly convex smooth constraints, and weakly convex smooth nonnegative matrix factorization. Finally, numerical experiments confirm that the DrNM iteration outperforms two existing distributed algorithms. These findings indicate that RNM iterations are highly effective for large-scale stochastic convex optimization, while DrNM offers a practical solution for distributed environments. High-resolution gas time projection chambers featuring recoil detection are highly effective for measuring dark matter, neutron decay, and fundamental neutron properties. We introduce measurables optimized to enhance the measurement resolution of these systems. As a proof of concept, we apply these measurables to analyze proton and neutron recoils from a neutron source in the 1–30 keV range using simulated data for a 7 cm FE-44 diamond detector. The simulation results indicate that our measurables improve energy resolution from 2.1% to 1.5% for protons and from 1.8% to 1.2% for neutrons. This improvement stems from the ability to correct for non-uniform electric fields within the detector. Furthermore, we demonstrate that protons and neutrons can be distinguished with 99.9% efficiency in the 1–30 keV range, achieving a relative misidentification rate below 0.01%. This misidentification rate remains constant across the recoil energy spectrum and is independent of the specific measurables employed. Finally, we outline how to integrate these measurables into the analysis framework of existing recoil detectors. Our findings suggest that these methods can be readily applied to other gas TPCs that detect ionization and scintillation from recoil particles in narrow energy windows. This includes detectors currently in use, such as XENON10 and SNOLAB's NEUTRINO-EDM, as well as upcoming experiments like nEDM, JUNO, and PICO. Additionally, these techniques are applicable to future neutrinoless double beta decay experiments that utilize recoil detection for background suppression, including CUORE, NEXT, and KATRIN's beta decay endpoint search. Ultimately, these measurables offer a straightforward means of achieving the highest possible resolution in gas TPCs with recoil detection. This is particularly advantageous for next-generation neutron dark matter searches and fundamental neutron properties experiments, where such advancements could be decisive. We introduce a stochastic field theory where field evolution is modeled as a geodesic on a Riemannian manifold, with the metric defined by the two-point correlation function of a Gaussian random process. This correlation function serves as both the manifold's metric and the theory's interaction term. We demonstrate that the geodesic equation, utilizing this specific metric, aligns exactly with the theory's equation of motion, thereby confirming that our framework describes geodesic motion within a Gaussian stochastic field manifold. Furthermore, we establish that this theory represents the continuum limit of quantum Heisenberg spin chains, where the manifold's geometry arises from the large-spin approximation. We also examine the emergent symmetries of the theory and their connection to its emergent Hilbert space. Finally, we analyze the theory's phase structure by deriving its Euclidean action and calculating the geodesic distance in phase space using the associated metric. This distance quantifies the information gain resulting from a single site measurement. We conclude by discussing the potential applications of this model in quantum field theory and quantum information science. Additional details can be found in our supplementary material. A comparative analysis of "timeless" versus "time-lapsed" exposures in astrophotography reveals that for deep-sky objects, time-lapsed techniques can yield superior results even with significantly reduced total integration times. This approach is particularly advantageous for highly detailed and dynamic objects where the image is not saturation-limited. The study also examines "banding" in time-lapsed images and proposes a novel filtering technique to enhance results. This method involves creating multiple versions of the object using varying numbers of exposures, followed by a specific "best of" merging process. The paper illustrates this with the Lagoon Nebula (M20) and the Veil Nebula (N8), demonstrating that this strategy can produce interestingly detailed and dynamic images. The associated Python scripts are provided in an online repository. The methodology is easily extensible to create a wide variety of detailed and dynamic deep-sky objects. The creation of quark-gluon plasma (QGP) in heavy-ion collisions is indicated by the enhanced production of light optical hadrons, which act as sensitive probes of the QGP's initial conditions. This study examines the influence of neutron-rich environments on light hadron production by analyzing Au+Au and Ne+Au collisions at $\sqrt{s_{\textrm{NN}}}=200$ GeV using data from the PHENIX detector at the Relativistic Heavy Ion Collider (RHIC). We observe a significant rise in $\pi^0$ and $\eta$ yields at intermediate transverse momentum ($p_{\textrm{T}}$) in Au+Au collisions, alongside a notable increase in $\pi^0$ yields at low $p_{\textrm{T}}$ compared to expectations derived from superposition of $p$+Pb data. Similar findings regarding light hadron production are reported for Ne+Au collisions. Furthermore, we find that the $\pi^0$ nuclear modification factor ($R_{\textrm{AA}}$) in Au+Au collisions exhibits a marked dependence on charged particle density, with a stronger suppression observed at higher densities. These results suggest that "optical hadrons" can serve as an effective tool for investigating QGP properties under varying initial conditions. Our findings align with theoretical predictions regarding hadron production from QGP generated via hydrodynamic evolution. Additionally, the data support an alternative scenario involving direct fragmentation from a quark-gluon string. These results underscore the critical role of strangeness in shaping hadron production within the QGP. Overall, our findings demonstrate the utility of light optical hadrons as probes for exploring the phase diagram of QCD matter. This study introduces a new approach to estimating the linear Koefman operator for systems exhibiting chaotic dynamics. The algorithm integrates sparse grid methods with the neural adaptive spectral approximation technique. Utilizing the periodic nature of trajectories in such systems, a spectral adaptive sparse grid algorithm is developed to achieve a highly accurate, sparse matrix representation of the linear Koefman operator. This enables a low-rank approximation of the system's dynamics alongside efficient prediction of unobserved states. Numerical experiments on various systems with chaotic and periodic behaviors demonstrate that the method accurately captures both the chaotic and periodic behaviors of these nonlinear systems. Furthermore, the results indicate that the proposed algorithm outperforms existing methods regarding both accuracy and computational efficiency. Finally, the study applies these findings to model the dynamics of a 2D fluid flow. The accompanying source code is accessible at https://github.com/ChenchenWang1993/SSGK. Additionally, the method is employed to predict the chaotic dynamics of a 3D fluid flow. Due to the high-dimensional nature of the data, a high-rank approximation is necessary, which is addressed by incorporating the proper orthogonal decomposition method. This leads to the development of a sparse grid-driven adaptive subspace spectral Koefman technique, which is also shown to be both accurate and efficient. The corresponding source code can be found at https://github.com/ChenchenWang1993/SSGKPOD. Future research will explore extending this approach to other turbulent flows. A novel complex scaling approach, termed the Outside Complicated Scaling (OCS) method, has been developed. This technique employs a piecewise complex scaling function applied solely to the tail region of radial coordinates, utilizing asymptotic analytic wave functions as a basis. Notably, OCS achieves high accuracy even with minimal scaling depth or a narrow scaled region, thereby preserving computational efficiency while maintaining robustness. The method's efficacy in calculating ionization rates for atoms and molecules within strong direct current fields is demonstrated through ionization rate ratio computations for helium and neon atoms, as well as for water and ethylene molecules. Furthermore, OCS successfully yields resonant states for atoms and molecules under these strong field conditions, effectively overcoming the challenges associated with the numerous virtual states that typically hinder the computation of resonance parameters. Furthermore, the application of OCS to systems incorporating short-range electron-electron correlations is shown to be feasible by achieving reasonable accuracy in resonance energy computations for helium and water. The Sinkhorn algorithm is a prominent iterative technique for addressing the Schrödinger problem, which involves characterizing the evolution of an interacting particle system through two marginal densities. Typically, this method generates an optimal solution; however, scenarios exist where no solution to the Schrödinger problem exists2,3. In such cases, we demonstrate that the Sinkhorn algorithm converges to a solution of the asymptotic power minimization problem, provided one of the marginal densities exhibits subgaussian concentration of measure. This convergence result relies on establishing tight bounds for the Sinkhorn distance relative to the asymptotic Sinkhorn distance. Notably, the proof employs techniques from rough path theory, specifically majorizing controls, to manage rough interactions between densities. The primary examples illustrating the existence of solution nonexistence include cases with compactly supported densities and those exhibiting superdiffusive behavior. This work builds upon a 2021 preprint of identical content3. These methodologies are anticipated to find applications in various fields, including image processing, machine learning, and genetics. For instance, they could facilitate the reconstruction of phylogenetic trees from single-cell sequencing data, where strong interactions between transition and cost matrices arise due to significant genetic divergence between species. Furthermore, this research may inspire novel algorithms capable of addressing solution nonexistence within the Schrödinger framework. This study examines the production of top quark pairs in proton-proton collisions at a center-of-mass energy of 5.02 TeV using the ATLAS detector at the Large Hadron Collider. The analysis utilizes a dataset with an integrated luminosity of 35 fb$^{-1}$, collected during the LHC Run 2 period. The observed cross-section of 38.9 $\pm$ 0.3 (stat) $\pm$ 0.6 (syst) pb aligns with Standard Model predictions and is consistent with the cross-section measured at 13 TeV. Additionally, the $t\bar{t}$ production cross-sections for events with and without additional jets are reported as 37.9 $\pm$ 0.3 (stat) $\pm$ 0.6 (syst) pb and 38.1 $\pm$ 0.3 (stat) $\pm$ 0.6 (syst) pb, respectively. The latter measurement shows agreement with next-to-next-to-leading order QCD predictions. The combined cross-section result is derived from a maximum likelihood fit applied to the complete set of observed event categories.
